news.title: Firouzja Leads Before Final Round As Arjun, Gukesh Beaten
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Alireza Firouzja goes into the final round of the 2026 Quantbox Chennai Grand Masters with a half-point lead after making a draw against GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov while his co-leader GM Arjun Erigaisi lost to GM Nihal
body: GM Alireza Firouzja goes into the final round of the 2026 Quantbox Chennai Grand Masters with a half-point lead after making a draw against GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov while his co-leader GM Arjun Erigaisi lost to GM Nihal Sarin. The other big story of the penultimate round was World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju dropping to within three points of 2700 after losing a winning position for a second day in a row, this time against GM Pranesh M. In the remaining game, GM Dmitry Andreikin sacrificed a bishop against GM Hans Niemann but soon settled for a draw.
Round seven starts one hour earlier on Wednesday, July 22, at 4:30 a.m. ET/10:30 CEST/2 p.m. IST.
Round six witnessed two decisive games, both in the all-Indian clashes.
Firouzja's fourth draw in a row has given him a half-point lead, though Arjun can overtake him if he wins their final-round game. Abdusattorov is also lurking half a point behind the leader.
Once again, Gukesh seemed set to win his first game on home soil since claiming the world championship title, but just as against Arjun, disaster struck.

Pranesh won an online qualifier on Chess.com to play the 2025 Challengers and performed so well that he could even lose the last round and still win the title and qualify for this year's Masters. The 19-year-old lost in round one, but since then had made four draws in a row. His first reaction to beating the world champion? "It feels kind of a relief—after six rounds I’m getting the first win!"
"I just got bored of too many draws," he said on the live stream, while adding his inspiration: "I had breakfast with Adhiban!" That encouraged him to meet Gukesh's Caro-Kann with the rare 6.h4!?.
There was an unexpected shoutout for WFM Anna Cramling's Cow Opening, with Pranesh commenting: "I just wanted to play the Cow Opening! This is objectively the best way to play the Cow Opening."
He did indeed put knights on b3 and g3, as is characteristic of that opening, but a pro tip is perhaps not to try the Cow if you ever encounter a world chess champion at the board.
Pranesh admitted he couldn't find a move when Gukesh went on the offensive, and 21...Nxb4!! was a blow he'd overlooked.
If you capture with the queen, 22...Bxc5! is crushing, while capturing with the bishop leaves the knight on f4 en prise.

Pranesh struggled on with 22.Kb2, admitted he'd decided "it's gone!" but had one hope: "The clock is the only thing I can aim for, so I’m just playing fast!" In normal circumstances that wouldn't be enough against the Gukesh who stormed to the top of the chess world, hitting a 2794 rating in October 2024 before going on to win the world championship title.

At the moment we're facing a very different Gukesh, however, and, for a second day in a row, he slipped far behind on the clock, blundered away his advantage, and then failed to find the moves to save a still defensible position. By the end Pranesh had an overwhelming advantage.
That's our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao analyzes in detail below.
Pranesh's first win meant he's back to 50 percent in his first supertournament, and has gone a long way to fulfilling his pre-tournament goal: "Play well and prove that I'm one of them!"
—Pranesh M on his goal going into the 2026 Chennai Grand Masters

For Gukesh, meanwhile, the post-world-championship slump continues. He's now fallen over 90 points from his high, and almost 75 points behind his world championship challenger GM Javokhir Sindarov. He's down to 31st place and 2702.9 on the live rating list.
Something almost unimaginable a year or two ago is now a real possibility—Gukesh will be out of the 2700 club if he loses to Niemann in the final round in Chennai.
GM Nihal Sarin, at world number-25, is now 16 points higher rated than Gukesh after taking down the Indian number-one.

If Arjun had won this game he would have gone into the final round as the sole leader, but it seems he never does anything in the Chennai Grand Masters the easy way. For most of the game Arjun was on top, and then when he lost his edge it seemed the players were just liquidating into an obviously drawn position. Nihal had a bishop against a knight, however, and when Arjun swapped off the rooks, with both players down to a minute on their clock, he was suddenly lost.

That meant that Firouzja only needed a fourth draw in a row to take the sole lead, and that's what he got against his key rival Abdusattorov. In fact, it was Firouzja, playing the French, who got some chances, after yet another shaky game with the white pieces for Abdusattorov in Chennai.
In the end, however, the advantage fizzled out into an extra pawn that wasn't felt in a rook endgame.

That kept Firouzja half a point ahead of Abdusattorov, but if the Uzbek star can win in the final round he has excellent chances of a playoff. To do that, however, he'll need to beat a player who's made six draws so far—Andreikin.
Andreikin got to be the aggressor against Niemann in round six, executing a strong bishop sac on h3. From there, however, the game quickly ended peacefully.

That draw left Niemann frustrated and winless with one loss in Chennai, though if he draws against Gukesh in the final round he avoids last place. Of course, he may be tempted to play for a win and the bragging rights of sending the world champion below 2700.

The battle that really matters, however, is at the top. Firouzja is guaranteed the title if he beats Arjun, while a draw may also be enough and will at worst lead to a tiebreak with Abdusattorov. If Arjun wins then Abdusattorov must win to force a playoff or the Indian takes the title at his fourth attempt.

The fourth edition of the Quantbox Chennai Grand Masters is taking place July 16-22, 2026, in Chennai, India. The event is an eight-player round-robin, with 90 minutes for all moves, plus a 30-second increment from move 1. The top prize is ₹25,00,000, which is around $26,000.

news.title: Firouzja Wins 2026 Chennai Grand Masters, Andreikin Snatches 2nd
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Alireza Firouzja has taken clear first place in the 2026 Quantbox Chennai Grand Masters after making a draw with GM Arjun Erigaisi in the final round. GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov could have forced a playoff with a win, b
body: GM Alireza Firouzja has taken clear first place in the 2026 Quantbox Chennai Grand Masters after making a draw with GM Arjun Erigaisi in the final round. GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov could have forced a playoff with a win, but instead he overpressed and lost to GM Dmitry Andreikin, who edged second place on tiebreaks. World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju preserved his 2700 status by sacrificing a bishop to make a quick draw against GM Hans Niemann, but both players overlooked that Niemann could have played on. GM Nihal Sarin vs. GM Pranesh M was the day's other draw, with both players finishing on 50 percent.
Andreikin scored his first win of the 2026 Chennai Grand Masters in the final round.

Firouzja finished half a point clear of Andreikin and Arjun, with Andreikin having the better tiebreaks. Gukesh finished a point adrift in last place, but avoided the worse fate of dropping out of the 2700 club—he ended on 2703.1.

There were two big storylines on the final day of the Chennai Grand Masters. Of course the main one was who would win the title, but we got an answer to the other one first—would Gukesh stay in the 2700 club?

It's only four years since Gukesh barged his way into the 2700 club, while a year later, at 17, he beat GM Magnus Carlsen's record as the youngest player to cross 2750. In the run-up to the 2024 world championship match, Gukesh reached 2794, and when he won the title it seemed as though the only question was whether he'd go on to cross 2800 or become world number-one. It's stunning, therefore, that we're where we are now.

Gukesh is still only 20, so that fluctuations are no surprise, but the slump since defeating GM Ding Liren has been shocking. Going into the final round in Chennai, Gukesh had lost three games and won none in his home supertournament, and was one loss away from falling out of the 2700 club. By way of comparison, Carlsen crossed 2800 at the age of 18 and has never fallen below that mark in the intervening 17 years.

In the end, Gukesh made a quick draw in the final round and limited the rating loss to 13.9 points, so that although he ended in last place he at least stayed in the 2700 club, on 2703.1 on the live rating list.

In some ways it was a performance that didn't reflect Gukesh's play—he'd been completely winning against Arjun and Pranesh and, if he'd pushed his h-pawn one square instead of two, might have survived a tricky endgame against Firouzja—but, on the other hand, the final round could also have ended in disaster!
On move 12 of a known position seen in over 100 high-level games, Gukesh thought for six minutes and went for a novelty—sacrificing his bishop on h6.
The computer screams blunder and indicates capturing the knight, but, after thinking for nine minutes, Niemann took the bishop immediately and the game hurtled toward a 19-move draw.

Niemann had in fact seen the computer's top line, but he commented: "I saw everything, but I don’t think I believed that I could have received such a ridiculous gift! It’s very rare you are just winning out of the opening with Black against the world champion, so perhaps I should have been more optimistic, but it was just a very weird game."
I saw everything, but I don't think I believed that I could have received such a ridiculous gift!

Black wouldn't be completely winning in the best line, but Gukesh would have been under immense pressure with his 2700 club status on the line. Niemann claimed being the one to demote the world champion wasn't a motivation for him: "I really don’t care. My job is to win chess games and it doesn’t matter who I play—I’m indifferent."

Niemann avoided last place but ended winless, with some missed chances to look back on. For Gukesh, it's another event to forget in a hurry, and poses some questions for India's Olympiad captain. Gukesh was the absolute star in Budapest in 2024, scoring 9/10 for a 3056-performance individual gold on board one, but where will he play in Samarkand in September? Could he even be left out?
When Niemann was asked why Ding and Gukesh had struggled so much after winning the title, he responded, "They were never the best players in the world, so it’s not a major shock."
They were never the best players in the world, so it's not a major shock.
—Niemann on Ding and Gukesh struggling after winning the world championship
Don't be surprised, however, if Gukesh storms back in the near future to get back to where we assumed he belongs.
Meanwhile, after that early action, the battle for first place continued elsewhere, with all the remaining games stretching to full length.

Firouzja ultimately eased to victory on his debut in the Chennai Grand Masters, and put it down to his fast start: "I think after I won the first two games I had a comfortable lead and didn’t take as much risk."

The French star entered the final round knowing a draw would at least guarantee him a playoff for the title, while Arjun needed to win on demand with the black pieces. Arjun went for the Sicilian Defense, but Firouzja opted for the solid Alapin with 2.c3, and while Arjun did a good job of prolonging the game he never came close to winning a very drawish endgame.

That left Abdusattorov as the only player still able to catch Firouzja and force a playoff, but the Uzbek star's hopes of claiming the title were smashed against the rock of Andreikin, who had drawn his previous six games. Abdusattorov had Black and never got real chances for the win he needed, while after 27...Nf6? 28.Nc5! he was losing.
Abdusattorov would get one more chance to escape, but in the end Andreikin went on to score a deserved win and take second place in a rare supertournament appearance.
That's our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao analyzes below.
It was a tough finish for Abdusattorov, who dropped from fifth to eighth on the live ratings with that loss, and, more significantly, missed out on any FIDE Circuit points.

Firouzja's win, meanwhile, earned 24.915 Circuit points and should take him up to seventh place in that race for a 2028 FIDE Candidates spot. Arjun moves up to sixth, despite the disappointment of only tying for second place again in Chennai.

Abdusattorov finished level on 50 percent with Nihal and Pranesh, who played out a largely uneventful draw. Both could be satisfied with suffering only a single loss in Chennai, since they also picked up big wins. Nihal took down Arjun, while Pranesh has the bragging rights of beating the world champion.
That's all for this year's Chennai Grand Masters—we hope you enjoyed the show!

The fourth edition of the Quantbox Chennai Grand Masters took place July 16-22, 2026, in Chennai, India. The event was an eight-player round-robin, with 90 minutes for all moves, plus a 30-second increment from move 1. The top prize was ₹25,00,000, which is around $26,000.

news.title: Giri Signs With Basilisk Esports
news.author: nathanielgreen
news.excerpt: GM Anish Giri, the longtime top-10 chess player and instructional author, has signed with Basilisk Gaming (stylized BASILISK), the esports organization announced in a press release and on social media Thursday. Giri will
body: GM Anish Giri, the longtime top-10 chess player and instructional author, has signed with Basilisk Gaming (stylized BASILISK), the esports organization announced in a press release and on social media Thursday. Giri will begin representing Basilisk in competitions shortly, at the Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz starting on July 31.

Giri noted after signing on that, "Often my preparation resembles scientific work, and that connection between science, chess, and esports is what makes Basilisk a perfect fit. I am excited to be joining a team that brings these worlds together." Christopher Bothur, CEO and co-founder of Basilisk, added, "Anish brings a rare combination of competitive drive and an orientation towards continuous learning. We are thrilled to have him join Basilisk."
Anish brings a rare combination of competitive drive and an orientation towards continuous learning. We are thrilled to have him join Basilisk.

Giri joins GM Vincent Keymer at Basilisk, giving "Science's Esports Team" two top-10 chess players on its roster. Basilisk was founded in 2020 by Bothur and Hans Kassier and has partnered not only with top esports athletes in strategy-focused games such as chess, Starcraft, and Evo, but also scientific endeavors such as The Planetary Society and Caltech. Keymer signed on in 2025, and now Giri joins him as a key part of the equation at Basilisk.

Giri has been one of the world's very best chess players for over a decade, becoming a grandmaster in 2010 at just 14 years old, then first reaching a top-10 world ranking in October of 2014. He has won several major events, most notably Tata Steel Chess in 2023. In addition, he has one of the game's most notable social media presences, and has also been a longtime contributor to Chessable, with its scientific approach to teaching patterns.

Chess players have been signing with esports teams for years, but there was an explosion of activity before chess made its debut at the Esports World Cup in 2025. Giri, who joined Team Secret in April of that year, now has a new home in the esports ecosystem.

Other notable grandmasters who were signed by esports organizations in recent months include GMs Liem Le, Wei Yi, Alexey Sarana, Javokhir Sindarov, Denis Lazavik, Hans Niemann, Sina Movahed, Pranesh M, and IM Faustino Oro.

news.title: Dvorkovich Suspends FIDE Presidency After EU Sanctions; Anand Named Interim President
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: The President of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), Arkady Dvorkovich, has decided to suspend his authority as the head of the chess governing body after being sanctioned by the European Union. Five-time world ch
body: The President of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), Arkady Dvorkovich, has decided to suspend his authority as the head of the chess governing body after being sanctioned by the European Union. Five-time world champion GM Viswanathan Anand is taking over as interim president.
[Editor's note: This story was updated with Dvorkovich's statement and the official confirmation of the sanctions.]
He shared his decision in a statement on FIDE's website on Thursday. He described the sanctions as "unlawful and unfair" and said he would challenge them through all available legal means.

"However, given that until a formal court decision is rendered and/or such decision is cancelled or amended, these sanctions could hinder the stable functioning of FIDE, I have decided to voluntarily suspend the exercise of my powers and duties as FIDE President with immediate effect," Dvorkovich added.

The decision appears to bring Dvorkovich's eight-year tenure as the head of FIDE to an end, although it's not a formal resignation. The 54-year-old Russian remains FIDE president in name, but has handed over the rights, duties, and authority attached to the office for as long as the sanctions remain in place under EU and Swiss law.
"In accordance with the FIDE Charter, the duties of the President will be assumed by the FIDE Deputy President, the 15th World Champion, Viswanathan Anand," Dvorkovich said.

Today, the EU decision to include my name in the 21st sanctions list was published. I want to state unequivocally that I consider this decision unlawful and unfair, and this decision will be immediately challenged by all possible means. I am confident that justice will prevail.

However, given that until a formal court decision is rendered and/or such decision is cancelled or amended, these sanctions could hinder the stable functioning of FIDE, I have decided to voluntarily suspend the exercise of my powers and duties as FIDE President with immediate effect and for as long as I remain subject to sanctions under the EU and Swiss laws and regulations. In accordance with the FIDE Charter, the duties of the President will be assumed by the FIDE Deputy President, the 15th World Champion, Viswanathan Anand.

I would like to emphasize that I believe in the FIDE Council and I am confident that the FIDE Council and administration will overcome all challenges and do the utmost to safeguard the continuous work of FIDE, its events and social programs.
Taking into account the statement above, the FIDE Council has decided the following:

The FIDE Council accepts and ratifies the decision of Mr. Arkady Dvorkovich to suspend the exercise of his rights, duties and prerogatives as President of the FIDE. Accordingly, Mr. Dvorkovich will not exercise the responsibilities, duties, rights and prerogatives provided by the FIDE Charter, particularly article 18 of the FIDE Charter, and other regulations as long as the measures provided by the “Ordonnance instituant des mesures en lien avec la situation en Ukraine” and the EU Regulations No 269/2014, are in force. Specifically, Mr. Dvorkovich shall not act in the capacity of “détenteur de contrôle” (“owner, holder or controller”) of FIDE or its assets.

In accordance with article 19.2 of the FIDE Charter, Mr. Anand Viswanathan, Deputy President of FIDE, shall act as Interim President as long as Mr. Dvorkovich is subject to the restrictive measures provided by the Swiss and EU laws and regulations in force.

Dvorkovich's statement came hours after Ukraine's Minister of Youth and Sports Matvii Bidnyi revealed on Facebook that Dvorkovich had been included in the 21st sanctions package against Russia, alongside Mikhail Degtyarev, Russia's Sports Minister and President of the Russian Olympic Committee.

"Arkady Dvorkovich promotes the interests of the Kremlin while holding the position of president of the International Chess Federation," Bidnyi wrote. "Both of them consistently use their positions to spread the narratives of the aggressor state and legitimize Russia in world sports."

"The inclusion of them in the EU sanctions list confirms that Kremlin officials and their lobbyists have no place in the civilized sports community. Sports cannot exist separately from international law during a war," he added.
The FIDE president has previously said publicly he would resign if sanctioned.

The EU's 21st sanctions package targets Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. EU member states reached an agreement on the package after weeks of negotiations, with a written procedure to complete its formal adoption.

The EU’s official sanctions entry accuses Dvorkovich of using his position as FIDE president to support Russian policies undermining Ukraine’s territorial integrity. It also cites his previous senior roles in the Russian government and notes that the Kremlin had welcomed his 2022 reelection as FIDE president as a “victory” for Moscow. The EU says Dvorkovich had publicly supported the annexation of Crimea and referred to occupied Ukrainian cities as Russia’s “new territories.”

The entry also cites his membership of the Russian Chess Federation’s Board of Trustees, which includes several other EU-sanctioned Russian officials. The EU says the Russian federation had organized tournaments in the occupied regions of Crimea, Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson, and describes Dvorkovich as playing a key role on the board.
It concludes that Dvorkovich was supporting “actions or policies which undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine.”

The 54-year-old, who served as Deputy Prime Minister in Russia from 2012 to 2018, has led FIDE since 2018, when he defeated Georgios Makropoulos 103-78 in the presidential election. He was reelected in 2022, defeating the Baryshpolets-Nielsen ticket with 157 votes against 16. His campaign at the time included a pledge to limit FIDE presidents to two terms, and FIDE declared after his reelection that his second term would be his last. However, delegates voted in 2023 to abolish the restriction, clearing the way for him to seek a third term in 2026.

Dvorkovich had previously avoided EU sanctions after Viktor Orban’s Hungary vetoed proposals to blacklist him. But Orban lost power in April to the more pro-Western Peter Magyar, whose new government did not block Dvorkovich’s inclusion this time.

Once the legal acts come into force, Dvorkovich will be subject to an asset freeze and a ban on entering or transiting through the EU's 27 member states. EU citizens as well as companies will be prohibited from making funds or economic resources available to him, directly or indirectly.

The restrictions apply to Dvorkovich personally, rather than to FIDE, and do not automatically remove him from office or sanction the chess governing body. However, the practical consequences would be significant given that the Russian citizen will no longer be able to attend tournaments or other official FIDE activities in most of Europe. Dvorkovich could also face sanctions-compliance checks from EU-based federations, organizers, sponsors, and banks.

FIDE has previously rejected the allegations used to justify the proposed sanctions on Dvorkovich. In a response to EU Observer in February, FIDE disputed claims that Dvorkovich had supported Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, or been responsible for organizing chess activities in the Ukrainian territories by Russia. It also said FIDE had neither rated nor recognized tournaments held in the occupied Ukrainian territories during Dvorkovich's presidency.

Jan Henric Buettner, who is challenging Dvorkovich for the FIDE presidency, said in a statement to Chess.com that he has personal respect for the incumbent. He also argued that the sanctions reinforced the need for FIDE to demonstrate its independence.

Throughout our interactions, I have always found him to be courteous, knowledgeable, and deeply committed to chess. Whatever our differences as candidates in this election, I do not take any satisfaction in personal difficulties faced by anyone.
Whatever our differences as candidates in this election, I do not take any satisfaction in personal difficulties faced by anyone.—Jan Henric Buettner
The German businessman said the developments highlighted the challenges facing an international federation operating amid increasing geopolitical tensions.
Recent events once again underline how important it is for our federation to be seen as independent, politically neutral, and focused exclusively on serving the global chess community.
Buettner insisted that his campaign was not directed against Dvorkovich personally.

My campaign has never been about personalities. It has always been about strengthening FIDE's governance, increasing transparency, empowering our 203 member federations, and ensuring that chess remains a bridge between people rather than a reflection of geopolitical divisions.
IM Malcolm Pein, who is running for Deputy President on Buettner's ticket, also highlighted his personal regard for Dvorkovich, despite being a major critic of FIDE's leadership.
"I am not celebrating this on a personal level at all," Pein told Chess.com.
I am not celebrating this on a personal level at all.—Malcolm Pein

"I have always had an enormous personal regard for Arkady as a chess lover first and foremost and a highly competent leader and administrator. We have always enjoyed an excellent personal relationship, and I hope this will continue," he added.

However, Pein described the sanctions as inevitable and as a significant victory for Ukraine. "It was notable that the EU allowed the Ukrainians to make the announcement," he said. "It's another blow to Russia and, in its own small way, I hope will contribute to ending the war as Russia sees its sphere of influence diminishing."

Pein also linked the decision directly to the presidential campaign. "If mine and Jan Buettner's campaign in FIDE is successful and there is a president without Russian links or business interests, FIDE has a bright future," he said.

Two days before the sanctions were announced, Dvorkovich told the state-controlled Russian news agency Tass that he was preparing to formally enter the presidential race and was awaiting confirmation from several federations willing to nominate him.

"The process has taken this long solely because of the risks associated with the 21st sanctions package," he said on Tuesday. "We had information that my name was included in some proposals. Therefore, we decided that while there was still a possibility, we should wait to avoid a false start."
The process has taken this long solely because of the risks associated with the 21st sanctions package.—Arkady Dvorkovich

Wadim Rosenstein, the other candidate in the FIDE presidential election, did not immediately respond to Chess.com’s request for comment. The election takes place in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, at the end of September, and sanctions on Dvorkovich, as well as the consequences for FIDE, are now likely to become a central issue in the campaign.

Curiously, this is not the first time FIDE has faced a similar crisis. In 2015, then President Kirsan Ilyumzhinov stepped down after he was sanctioned by the U.S. Department of Justice for "providing support to the government of Syria."

The controversial Russian, who recently announced a surprising run in the 2026 FIDE Election, was then replaced by Deputy President Georgios Makropoulos. Anand, the current Deputy President of FIDE, will now take over the position as the head of the organization in the months leading up to the election.

Dvorkovich now joins GM Sergey Karjakin and GM Anatoly Karpov in being sanctioned by the European Union. Karjakin, who challenged GM Magnus Carlsen for the World Championship title in 2016, was added to the EU's sanctions list in February last year, after becoming a member of Russia's Federation Council representing illegally annexed Crimea. The 36-year-old has also actively supported the war, and paid several visits to Russia's armed forces. Former World Champion Karpov was targeted as a member of Russia's State Duma for voting in favor of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Dvorkovich recently appeared with Karpov during an event in Moscow.

The nomination deadline in the election is July 26, which means that Dvorkovich's ticket would have to decide whether Timur Turlov, his candidate for Deputy President, should replace him as the presidential candidate.

Tarjei J. Svensen

news.title: Timur Turlov Bids To Become FIDE President, Vishy Anand As Deputy
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: Moscow-born Kazakh billionaire Timur Turlov has put himself forward as a candidate to become FIDE president, with GM Viswanathan Anand as his deputy. Turlov was planning to run for deputy president under Arkady Dvorkovic
body: Moscow-born Kazakh billionaire Timur Turlov has put himself forward as a candidate to become FIDE president, with GM Viswanathan Anand as his deputy. Turlov was planning to run for deputy president under Arkady Dvorkovich, but the European Union's sanctions on the current FIDE president have made that ticket impossible. Turlov joins Wadim Rosenstein, Jan Henric Buettner, and former FIDE President Kirsan Ilyumzhinov in announcing bids to run the international chess federation.

Since Dvorkovich was sanctioned yesterday by the EU for "supporting actions or policies which undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine, or stability or security in Ukraine," events have moved fast. Dvorkovich announced he had "decided to voluntarily suspend the exercise of [his] powers and duties as FIDE President with immediate effect" and passed his role to his deputy.
Anand accepted, saying his focus will be on "ensuring continuity and serving the global chess family."

Anand had been expected to step back from FIDE duties after the next election, but instead he's once more a candidate to become FIDE deputy president, this time under Turlov, who announced his candidacy on Facebook. Turlov says of FIDE, "a federation with a century of history stands at a crossroads," and states recent progress, "must be intensified, given fresh energy, and carried forward."

Turlov has been based in Kazakhstan since 2011, and renounced his Russian and St. Kitts and Nevis citizenships to become a citizen of Kazakhstan in 2022 after the outbreak of the full-scale war in Ukraine. In 2023, he became the president of the Kazakhstan Chess Federation, while he also heads the newly established International School Chess Federation (ISCF).

Turlov's NASDAQ-listed Freedom Holding company has been the major sponsor for numerous events, including the 2024 World Rapid & Blitz Championships that were held on Wall Street in New York. He says he's invested more than $75 million into chess, while his company has also acquired the German company ChessBase.

Turlov ends his announcement of his "open and uniting" vision for FIDE by referring to Anand as, "a great champion, a legend of world chess, and FIDE Deputy President since 2022," adding, "It is a true honor for me to share with him a common vision for the future of chess worldwide."

The FIDE presidential election will take place during the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan this September, with four candidates currently likely to stand. Turlov is joined by Rosenstein and Buettner, as well as Ilyumzhinov, who served as FIDE president from 1995 to 2018. The latter has gained the support of the Russian Chess Federation, although the federation itself is currently suspended.
Russian Chess Federation President Andrey Filatov told Russian state-run news agency TASS, "one is out [Dvorkovich], and the other is in," of the potential Russian candidates.

Colin McGourty

news.title: Fedoseev Adopts The Field In 3 0 Thursday
news.author: coachjkane
news.excerpt: In chess slang, adoption means beating an opponent 10 games in a row. It's an impressive accomplishment against any strong player, but GM Vladimir Fedoseev managed it against a whole field of opponents in 3 0 Thursday on
body: In chess slang, adoption means beating an opponent 10 games in a row. It's an impressive accomplishment against any strong player, but GM Vladimir Fedoseev managed it against a whole field of opponents in 3 0 Thursday on July 23. He won his first 10 games in the third tournament before succumbing under time pressure against GM Jeffrey Xiong in the final round. It didn't matter for the standings, as Fedoseev still won the tournament by a 1.5-point margin. Earlier in the day, GM Oleksandr Bortnyk won with a similar dominant performance, marred by a final-round defeat. The only winner to run all the way through the finish line was GM Christopher Yoo in the second tournament. He could have afforded a loss as well, as his 10 points put him 1.5 points ahead of GM Pranav Anand in second place.
The final score didn't show it, but Bortnyk dominated throughout the first event of the day. He won his first seven games, including this dominant performance against GM Ihor Samunenkov

Bortnyk scored another two draws and a win in rounds eight through 10, leaving him with nine points and tournament victory with a round to spare. GM Pranav V flagged Bortnyk in a long opposite colored bishop endgame in the final round, which allowed GMs Hikaru Nakamura and Rudik Makarian to tie for first place, but Bortnyk's superior tiebreaks assured him of the title.
Nakamura recovered from two early losses to win his final six games. He also played perhaps the most impressive combination of the day, an amazing queen sacrifice against WIM Margarita Potapova.
Potapova bounced back to nearly take the title for the top woman in the event, but WIM Zarina Nurgaliyeva won their final-round game to take that prize with 6.5 points.
In the second tournament, Yoo won in the first five rounds. That fifth game proved critical, as his opponent finished the tournament in second place.
Yoo drew his sixth and seventh round games before starting another winning streak. One of his best games came in the tenth round against Fedoseev.

Yoo won the final round as well to finish with an impressive 10/11 score. Pranav Anand took second with 8.5 points, ahead of GMs Sina Movahed and Pranav V on tiebreaks. Potapova took the women's prize with seven points, highlighted by victories over Bortnyk and GM Benjamin Bok.
Perhaps Fedoseev used his defeat against Yoo as motivation in the next tournament, where he played arguably the most impressive 3 0 Thursday in history, winning his first 10 games.
In the seventh round he confidently defeated GM Alexander Grischuk from the black side of a Caro-Kann Defense.

Fedoseev continued with victories against past 3 0 Thursday winners GM Jose Martinez and IM Yoseph Theolifus Taher in rounds eight and nine. In the 10th round, he won a miniature against IM Reza Mahdavi, another previous winner of the tournament.

With a 2.5 point lead on the field, Fedoseev continued to play sharp chess in the final round. However, Xiong out-calculated him to prevent Fedoseev from reaching the first-ever perfect score in a 3 0 Thursday event. That win gave Xiong second place with 8.5 points. Grischuk took third with eight points and IM Le Thao Nguyen Pham captured the women's prize with six points.

3 0 Thursday is a set of three weekly Swiss tournaments for verified titled players featuring their favorite time control. Each of the three tournaments is an 11-round Swiss with a 3+0 time control. The combined prize fund is $3,000 every week.
NM Jeremy Kane is the Instructional Content Manager for Chess.com, and the author of several courses in the Starting Out series, Queen’s Gambit Accepted, Trompowsky, and Tarrasch.

news.title: Alice Lee Eliminates Women's World Champion With 6-Point Margin
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: IM Alice Lee upset Women's World Champion and reigning WSCC Champion GM Ju Wenjun on Friday in the 2026 Women's Speed Chess Championship Quarterfinals. Lee dominated all three portions and won the match with a shockingly
body: IM Alice Lee upset Women's World Champion and reigning WSCC Champion GM Ju Wenjun on Friday in the 2026 Women's Speed Chess Championship Quarterfinals. Lee dominated all three portions and won the match with a shockingly one-sided 9.5-3.5 score.
The last quarterfinal, GM Hou Yifan vs. GM Anna Muzychuk, takes place on Monday, July 27, at 8:00 a.m. ET / 14:00 CEST / 5:30 p.m. IST.
Until this week, Ju had never lost a single match in the WSCC. She won the previous two editions, but this year her reign has come to an end. Lee earns $4,326.92 and Ju $673.08 by win percentage.

The commentators' uncontroversial prediction was that Lee was the favorite in the bullet segment, but needed to stay afloat in the slower time controls to keep the match close. In fact, the American IM shockingly dominated all three segments.

Lee, the supposed underdog, started the match full throttle, winning three games in a row. Even in the fourth and last game, she won a pawn, but with limited time was not able to solve the problem of her trapped knight.

In game one, Lee played with a rook against two minor pieces, and when she captured on f4, Ju had to realize (with two seconds) that the only way to draw was to take on a7 and hold a fortress with bishop vs. rook. Instead, we saw Lee win a king and pawn endgame.

The next game, Ju had just fought her way back from a worse endgame but lost on time. Repeatedly, it was Lee who was up on time and superior in time scrambles. It happened again in game three: Ju outplayed her opponent on the board, but in the time scramble completely lost control.

Ju took the last game, taking advantage of a trapped knight on b6. Though the position was level, it was far easier for Black to play, and Lee went down after sacrificing her knight for activity. It was better to sit and wait, but in a blitz game that's a very difficult policy to follow.
Ju started the segment with a second win in a row, but Lee won three out of the next four games, with one draw.
It looked like the Chinese grandmaster would make a comeback when she strung together a second win in a row. Lee grabbed a pawn, but her queen was trapped on the next move.

The rest was all Lee. She won a game, then pulled a draw from a worse or losing position, and then won two more. The last game was the biggest fight, as Ju sacrificed the exchange for an advantage, but in the mutual time scramble Lee found a counter that reversed the trend—and won again to take a four-point lead.

When Lee won the first game of the bullet portion and took a five-point lead, it was clear that Ju needed to be on the better side of a miracle to turn the match around. She won a game and lost two more, but the match was virtually beyond recovery.
The final sequence in game one was a picture of domination for Lee, who made it so that the women's world champion could hardly move.
Ju won a rook endgame, but it was hardly any consolation. Lee won the remaining two games, including another rook endgame in the last game.

It would be an understatement to say that the match result was a surprise. In the post-match interview, Lee remembered losing horribly to Ju in the WSCC two years ago, and added, "I was not expecting too much from this match." The match against GM Alexandra Kosteniuk was much more two-sided, whereas in this one, "I was just trying to keep the lead up and once it got to three or four I felt pretty confident in my chances."

"Maybe her internet was not very good," Lee said, adding that she hadn't prepared too much. Though, at the 2026 U.S. Junior Championship, she played a lot of blitz, she said. Waking up 30 minutes before this match, she played some bullet warmup games, though she also said they didn't go too well! She went 1/5 in her warmup.

In the Semifinals, Lee will take on FM Anastasia Avramidou, who had just upset GM Kateryna Lagno in the Quarterfinals. Lee said, "I think she's very good and I'm not sure how I'll approach the match, but I think it will be quite difficult." That match will take place on July 27, at 10:30 a.m. ET / 16:30 CEST / 8:00 p.m. IST.

The format changes slightly as we enter the Semifinals and Final. Rather than lasting an hour and a half, the match clocks for the remaining matches will be longer, totaling two and a half hours each. Lee said she's excited for more games and thinks it gives more chances for comebacks.
You can watch the broadcast on Twitch and YouTube. The games can also be checked out on our dedicated events page.
The live broadcast was hosted by IMs Jovanka Houska and Anna Rudolf

The 2026 Women's Speed Chess Championship, which takes place from July 6-31, is a Chess.com event where some of the strongest female chess players in the world battle for a $75,000 prize fund. The main event sees 16 players compete in a single-elimination bracket in matches played at 5+1, 3+1, and 1+1 time controls.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Aronian Wins Biel Masters 2026
news.author: vsaravanan
news.excerpt: GM Levon Aronian emerged as the winner of the Biel Masters—Grandmasters Triathlon event of the Biel Chess Festival, Switzerland, pocketing the top prize of CHF 10,000 (roughly €10,750 or $12,250). The 59th edition of the
body: GM Levon Aronian emerged as the winner of the Biel Masters—Grandmasters Triathlon event of the Biel Chess Festival, Switzerland, pocketing the top prize of CHF 10,000 (roughly €10,750 or $12,250). The 59th edition of the festival had a total of 14 events spread over 15 days, the crown of them being the triathlon with three different qualification stages in classical, rapid, and blitz formats followed by the final phase.

There was another Generation Challenge—Invitational Triathlon with the same format, won by 16-year-old IM Vaclav Finek of the Czech Republic. 14-year-old IM Christian Gloeckler of Germany was the surprise winner of the Masters Open.

The Masters began with a change in field at the last moment, as Uzbek GM Nodirbek Yakubboev could not reach Switzerland in time due to visa issues and was replaced by Azerbaijani GM Aydin Suleymanli just three days before the event.
The multi-stage Masters Triathlon event had a complex path of formats in the following order:
The final standings were decided by the total number of points scored across all the above formats.
After the initial Chess960 event decided the draw numbers and the pairings, the rapids got underway, and Aronian emerged as the dominant winner.
Aronian's four victories and a draw were an impressive performance that underlined his domination of the event. He had his winner's luck in his game against GM Martinez Alcantara.

Aronian's best effort was in the fourth round when he defeated GM Le Quang Liem with black pieces in a topsy-turvy game, which exemplifies the famous adage attached to his style, "Aronian and the art of slow-motion swindling." Even in a rapid game, Aronian played his brand of imaginative chess in a wild position and steadily posed problems for his opponent.
Thus, when the classical games began, Aronian had a three-point lead over the rest of the field.
The segment proved to be a disappointing affair, as 11 of the 15 games ended in draws, though all of them were hard-fought.

The last-minute entrant to the tournament, Suleymanli, continued to show his resolute play by winning one game and drawing the rest to finish second, just as he did in the Rapid section. He inflicted the tournament winner's only loss in the final game of the segment, exploiting the former's tactical error in the middlegame.
The winner of the segment, Liem showed his class in a long, grinding win in the endgame against GM Matthias Bluebaum, an endgame specialist himself.
Thus, when the segment ended, the top four standings were: Aronian 16.5, Suleymanli 16, Liem 15, and Erdogmus 13.

Blitz was a typical, well, blitz event with the regular dose of uneven games. But it was evident that Aronian staged the most turnarounds, while 15-year-old GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus played the expected amount of exciting games.
Thus, at the end of the blitz segment, the combined standings were: Aronian 25, Suleymanli 21, and Liem and Erdogmus 19.5. This enabled them to qualify for the finals.

The final proved to be a lackluster affair, with all the games ending in draws, and thus all the players added 4.5 points apiece to their final scores and finished identically in the overall standings.

Finek produced dominating performances in Rapid and Classical, while 17-year-old Chinese GM Tong Xiao won the Blitz segment. The Final event was once again an all-drawn affair, producing the following final standings.
Finek has a logical style of play, which helped him play evenly throughout the tournament. His win against GM Rameshbabu Vaishali in the Classical segment is an example of his style.
The 10-round Swiss event was limited to players above Elo 1900 and had a total of 94 participants from 29 countries.

Gloeckler comes across as a talent to watch out for, winning the tournament with a round to spare with eight points from the first nine rounds. His ability to play tactical positions was evident in the win against GM Peter Acs in the sixth round, as were his wins against IMs Savitha Shri and Qingfeng Cao in the crucial seventh and eighth rounds.
You can rewatch the broadcast on our YouTube live page, and the games can be reviewed on the 2026 Biel Grandmasters Triathlon page.
The live broadcast was hosted by GM Arturs Neiksans and Angelika Valkova.

The Biel Masters Triathlon was the main event of the 2026 Biel Chess Festival, taking place in Biel/Bienne, Switzerland, during July 14-24. The six players competed in Chess960 (the tiebreaker), blitz (3+2 games), rapid (15+5 games), and classical chess (120 minutes for the first 40 moves, followed by 30 more minutes for the rest of the game and a 30-second increment per move after move 40).

news.title: 20-Point Comeback Seals Stunning Tiebreak Victory For Le
news.author: jackrodgers
news.excerpt: Against all odds, Vietnamese GM Tuan Minh Le produced one of the most unexpected comebacks in Bullet Brawl after closing a 20-point gap in 16 minutes and edging out GM Hikaru Nakamura on tiebreaks on Saturday. In the fin
body: Against all odds, Vietnamese GM Tuan Minh Le produced one of the most unexpected comebacks in Bullet Brawl after closing a 20-point gap in 16 minutes and edging out GM Hikaru Nakamura on tiebreaks on Saturday. In the final 16 minutes, Le added 27 points to his score and finished on 159, joining Nakamura who accrued just seven points in the same timeframe.

Le earned the $400 first prize for the first time since 2024, Nakamura will receive $250 for second, while GMs Oleksandr Bortnyk and Arjun Erigaisi's third- and fourth-place prizes, respectively, were also decided by tiebreaks. FM Anastasia Avramidou took the $100 best women's prize once again.
The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, August 1, at 12 p.m. ET/6:00 p.m. CET.

For much of Saturday's Bullet Brawl, it appeared Nakamura was cruising toward his 63rd career title and 14th of the year. After posting an eight-game winning streak to kick off the arena, Nakamura shadowed the fast-starting GM Sam Sevian and eventually passed him just before the halfway point.

Pinpoint precision and tactical awareness, as exemplified in a game with Dutch FM Gachatur Kazarjan, helped Nakamura win some of his early games in fewer than 20 moves and amass 91 points in the first hour.

Meanwhile, Le was producing sacrifice-riddled art against many of his opponents and keeping himself in contention. Against WIM Vesal Hamedi Nia, he kept his eyes on the prize with devastating back-to-back brilliant moves, 21...Qg3!! and 22...Rxf3!!.
Soon after, Le uncorked one of the most picturesque moves of the day, a penetrative sacrifice that led to decisive material loss for Italian FM Danilo Brozzi.
Yet by the time the final 16 minutes arrived, it was Nakamura who held a commanding 20-point lead over the field, and Le seemed destined for a silver medal finish.

Despite this, Nakamura had a premonition of sorts 10 minutes earlier that teased the notion of a comeback when he stated on Kick: "I'm going to make this way too interesting. I'm playing bad game after bad game."

In his last nine games, Nakamura scored a lackluster 2/9 (partly attributable to him playing 3200+ rated GMs in all of these games) and opened the door for what would become one of the most unlikely comebacks in Bullet Brawl history.

A simultaneous seven-game streak for Le allowed him to catch Nakamura and when the arena clock expired, coincidentally aborting a game between the pair at the 12-move mark, they had the exact same score, making Le's last-minute miniatures all the more important in retrospect.

Tiebreak-wise, Le was declared the winner thanks to having the longest winning streak (nine vs. eight), and this win made him only the second person to finish ahead of Nakamura in an edition of Bullet Brawl in 2026.
How to review games? The games from this week's Bullet Brawl can be found here.

Bullet Brawl is an exciting arena featuring Chess.com's top bullet specialists. It takes place weekly on Saturdays. The format is a two-hour arena with a 1+0 time control; the prize fund is $1,000. Like Titled Tuesday and Arena Kings, Bullet Brawl often features top GMs, including Hikaru Nakamura, Andrew Tang, Tuan Minh Le, and many more!

news.title: Akopian Wins U.S. Senior Championship
news.author: vsaravanan
news.excerpt: GM Vladimir Akopian defeated top-seeded GM Alexander Onischuk in a blitz tiebreak playoff to win the 2026 U.S. Senior Championship held at the Saint Louis Chess Club, which concluded on Saturday, July 25. Akopian was awa
body: GM Vladimir Akopian defeated top-seeded GM Alexander Onischuk in a blitz tiebreak playoff to win the 2026 U.S. Senior Championship held at the Saint Louis Chess Club, which concluded on Saturday, July 25. Akopian was awarded $26,000 for his efforts, which included the winner's bonus of $5,000.

WGM Anjelina Belakovskaia was the runaway winner of the U.S. Women's Senior Championship by a full-point margin at seven points from eight games. She received the first prize of $17,750, which included a winner's bonus of $2,750. This was the first time that the championship has been held concurrently with the other senior and junior championships.

GM Andy Woodward retained his title at the U.S. Junior Chess Championship, overtaking the 2023 U.S. Junior Champion GM Abhimanyu Mishra in the final two rounds to win by a full-point margin. Woodward received $23,000 for his efforts, which included a winner's bonus of $3,000.

FM Zoey Tang retained her U.S. Girls Junior Chess Championship title with a thumping two-point margin, scoring 7.5 from nine games, remaining undefeated throughout the tournament. She received $15,000 for her efforts, which included a winner's bonus of $2,500.

For the first time ever, the U.S. Championships for seniors, senior women, juniors, and junior girls were held together at the Saint Louis Chess Club, with a combined prize pool of $285,000. The main beneficiary of this was the senior women's championship, whose total prize fund got enhanced to $60,000 from the previous year's $8,400.

Onischuk seemed to start the tournament as a huge rating favorite thanks to his incredible Elo of 2618. Though undefeated throughout the main event, he had a relatively slow start, unable to score fluent victories till the final stretch, with his only noteworthy win being against GM Joel Benjamin in the sixth round.

Champion of the 2024 edition, Akopian impressed with his steady play throughout the tournament, having taken the early lead with three wins from as many games at the start. His most noteworthy win was in the fifth round against GM Alexander Goldin, his other co-2500+ Elo rated player.
Though he lost in the fourth round to GM Alexander Shabalov, Akopian scored successive wins in the next two rounds to gain the lead with five points from six games.

Meanwhile, the defending champion GM Alexander Fishbein had a decent run throughout, scoring three wins in the first seven games with no losses. Thus, at the end of the seventh round, the leaderboard read:

In the two dramatic final rounds, while Akopian scored just two draws, Onischuk scored wins against GM Stuart Rachels in the penultimate round and a crucial win against Fishbein in the final round. Fishbein scored just half a point from the final two rounds.
So at the end of the round-robin stage, Akopian and Onischuk had tied for the top spot with a score of 6.5 points each from nine games, thus ensuring a quickplay playoff.
After the first tiebreak match with a rapid time control of 15+10 ended in a victory each for both players, the second tiebreak match with a blitz control of 3+2 ended in a 2-0 win for Akopian.
The first blitz game had its especially dramatic moments, with Akopian being alert to capitalize on Onischuk's errors.

The final blitz game was an even more thrilling see-saw encounter, which again ended in a win for Akopian, enabling him to capture the tournament title. By the way, don't miss the final twist in the tale!
The tournament was reduced by one participant when WCM Diana Lanni withdrew after playing the first round due to a medical event.

Top-seeded Belakovskaia, the winner of the 2023 edition with an Elo of 2168, won the event comfortably with six wins and two draws, finishing a point ahead of twice defending champion WFM Natalia Tsodikova. Belakovskaia was almost never in danger of losing a game except for her second-round draw against WIM Beatriz Marinello. Her steady win against Catherine Dodson in the fifth round is an example of how easily she won the tournament.
Being on the receiving end of the 'winner's luck,' Belakovskaia scored a topsy-turvy win in the eighth round against WIM Alexey Root.

Defending Champion Woodward was the only undefeated player of the event, and his score of four wins and five draws was surprisingly enough to win the event outright. Rated at an identical 2638 Elo, it was Mishra who called the early shots, capturing the lead on 4/5 with a miniature win against GM Nico Chasin.

Mishra kept up the lead right until the seventh round, all the way pursued by Woodward half a point behind. Woodward scored a hard-fought endgame win against GM Brewington Hardaway in the penultimate round to finally catch up with Mishra on 5.5/8.

It was a test of nerves for the joint leaders in the final round, where Woodward came out on top. He managed to keep his cool from a slightly inferior position and went on to win the game, whereas Mishra squandered a winning advantage and even ended up losing to IM Bach Ngo.

Just as in the women's senior category, this too was a one-horse race, with Tang winning the tournament with a two-point margin to retain her title for the third year in a row. Though by no means flawless, she showed good resourcefulness in many of her games to grab her chances whenever presented with the opportunity.

You can rewatch the broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club's YouTube channel. Below is the embed of the U.S. Seniors playoffs. The games can also be played through on our dedicated 2026 U.S. Junior & Senior Championships events page.
The live broadcast was hosted by GM Yasser Seirawan, GM Cristian Chirila, IM Irine Sukandar, and WGM Katerina Nemcova.

The U.S. Junior and Senior Championships took place in St. Louis, Missouri, on July 12-25. Each group was a 10-player round-robin. The time control was 90 minutes for the first 40 moves, followed by 30 more minutes for the rest of the game, with a 30-second increment per move. Draw offers were not allowed.

news.title: Alice Lee Storms Into Women's Speed Chess Final 19.5-4.5
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: A run of 11 wins in 12 games saw 16-year-old IM Alice Lee overwhelm FM Anastasia Avramidou to reach the Final of the 2026 Women's Speed Chess Championship. She'll face the winner of GM Bibisara Assaubayeva vs. GM Hou Yif
body: A run of 11 wins in 12 games saw 16-year-old IM Alice Lee overwhelm FM Anastasia Avramidou to reach the Final of the 2026 Women's Speed Chess Championship. She'll face the winner of GM Bibisara Assaubayeva vs. GM Hou Yifan, after the women's number-one entered the 1+1 section trailing GM Anna Muzychuk 5.5-3.5 but then powered to victory with a 5-0 clean sweep in bullet chess.

The Semifinals and Final of the Women's Speed Chess Championship add an extra hour to the match clock—75 minutes instead of 45 minutes of 5+1 chess, 50 minutes not 30 of 3+1, and 25 minutes not 15 minutes of 1+1. Lee said, "At some point toward the end I felt like I was running a marathon," while for her Greek opponent it was torture.

Both players had reached the Semifinals by similar paths, narrowly winning in the first round before scoring upset wins by a shocking six-point margin in the Quarterfinals—Lee took down Women's World Champion Ju Wenjun 9.5-3.5, while Avramidou beat speed chess legend GM Kateryna Lagno 10.5-4.5.

The first game of the match especially suggested a battle ahead. Lee would later describe it with, "I felt like I had a very good position out of the opening and eventually she found some very nice resources to make my position quite difficult." The teenager was close to winning and had a healthy lead on the clock, but she went astray and came under a powerful attack.
Little did we know at the time, but it would take Avramidou another 14 games before she got her second win.
The second game established a pattern of the match, as Avramidou got down to three seconds at the end while Lee had over a minute, and a blunder followed in a drawable position.

I thought in general this match went quite smoothly. I felt like I was managing my time pretty well and eventually later she would get very low on time, and even if the position was OK, it was very hard to play for her, so I think that was probably what basically did her in the match—time management.

The third game was a thriller, with Avramidou having fought her way back to a drawn position only to put her king in the way of her pawn on the h-file, while if it went to any square on the f-file she could have held the draw.

Lee had taken the lead, and from there it was one-way traffic as she won the remaining four 5+1 games to take a commanding 6-1 lead. She commented, "It seemed like I was getting good positions every game and she was never quite able to come back after that."
A new session is always a chance to change the momentum of a match, but Avramidou began the 3+1 section in disastrous fashion—11.Bf4?? walked into 11...Bxf2+!, winning the white queen.
Lee won the next game as well to make it eight wins in a row, though there was a fleeting chance for Avramidou to turn the tables.
Avramidou did manage to draw the next game, but the bleeding didn't stop for long, as she lost the next three games before finishing the 3+1 with a draw.
At 14-3 it was just about physically possible for Avramidou still to win the match, and she did start the bullet with a win.
The next game summed up the match, however, with Avramidou briefly having the chance to score a second win in a row before getting checkmated a few moves later.
Lee went on to win another five games, also making three draws, and talked about struggling to maintain her motivation:

In the bullet portion I was mainly just making sure that the games were long. I don’t know if I was playing my best, and I think she did play well, but it’s simply the margins—I have so much room for error I don’t feel the same pressure to win every single game.

A missed win in the final game meant Lee didn't quite reach 20 points, but she'd sailed into the Final, also picking up $7,250 ($4,000 for the match win + $3,250 by win percentage), while Avramidou earned $750.

Sixteen-year-old Lee will be the youngest ever Women's Speed Chess Championship finalist. Her opponent will either be Assaubayeva, or Hou, who overcame Muzychuk in the day's other action—the last quarterfinal.
For most of this match, the battle was incredibly tight, with the momentum swinging from one side to the other.
Hou demonstrated her tactical alertness in the first game by picking up a pawn with 14.Nxf6+! (allowing the c6-bishop to capture on f3)...
When Hou won the next game as well she looked to be in control, but surprisingly she ended the five-minute section by offering a trade of rooks... into a lost pawn endgame.

Misplaying endgames is not something we associate with the women's number-one, but Hou did it again in the first three-minute game, managing to lose a pawn endgame she started with an extra pawn and a winning position.
Muzychuk then took the lead with a third win in a row, before Hou pushed too hard in a slightly better endgame to lose the last game of the session and enter the bullet trailing by two points.

It seemed the first bullet game might go the way of the three-minute games, with Muzychuk pushing in a close-to-equal endgame. This time, however, it's Hou who emerged victorious. Then she leveled the scores in a brutal miniature. 11...Qd7? ran into 12.Nxe5!.

Hou took the lead in the chaotic next game, then made it a two-point lead by winning on time after spoiling a winning position. The final clash summed up the one-minute section for Muzychuk, as she was winning, then spoiled the advantage, then stumbled into mate-in-two.
She resigned rather than delaying the checkmate for one move with 46.Bc4 Bxc4#.

Muzychuk earned $982.14, while Hou claimed $4,017.86 ($2,500 for the match win + $1,517.86 by win percentage). More importantly, Hou, a two-time Women's Speed Chess winner and two-time runner-up, is through to the Semifinals, where she's going to face Assaubayeva. The winner will then take on Lee in the Final.
You can watch the broadcast on Twitch and YouTube. The games can also be checked out on our dedicated events page.
The live broadcast was hosted by IMs Jovanka Houska and Anna Rudolf.

The 2026 Women's Speed Chess Championship, which takes place from July 6-31, is a Chess.com event where some of the strongest female chess players in the world battle for a $75,000 prize fund. The main event sees 16 players compete in a single-elimination bracket in matches played at 5+1, 3+1, and 1+1 time controls.

Colin McGourty

news.title: U.S. Takes 5-3 Lead Vs. Uzbekistan In Miami Rapid Chess
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: The U.S. leads 5-3 against Uzbekistan after day one of the WR Chess Rapid & Blitz Miami 2026. GM Levon Aronian was the MVP, putting up the highest individual score on his team, 2.5/3. GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov's 3/4, the
body: The U.S. leads 5-3 against Uzbekistan after day one of the WR Chess Rapid & Blitz Miami 2026. GM Levon Aronian was the MVP, putting up the highest individual score on his team, 2.5/3. GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov's 3/4, the highest on team Uzbekistan, was not enough to tie the score.
There's one more day of this event, with eight rounds of blitz coming up. That's on Tuesday, July 28, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST.

This new tournament, organized by FIDE presidential candidate Wadim Rosenstein, invites five top players from the U.S. and another five from Uzbekistan and pits them in a two-day Scheveningen match. The first day features rapid chess, with a 15+10 time control, and the second day is all blitz, with 3+2.

Each round features four boards (a different player sits out per round), and a team victory per round is worth two points—regardless of whether you win 4-0 or 2.5-1.5 in individual matchups. In the blitz portion, on Tuesday, each match win is also worth two points.

The United States led from start to finish on day one. Round two was especially critical as Uzbekistan was one draw away from winning the round, which in hindsight, we know would have been enough to tie the score.
Round one was a convincing victory by the U.S. GM Wesley So scored the only win, against GM Mukhiddin Madaminov, with three draws in the other games.

So came armed with a novel pawn sacrifice in the Berlin Defense, and for the missing pawn he had the bishop pair and Marshall-like compensation. White eventually returned the extra pawn, and Black was better with the two bishops. So felt his conversion was shaky, but the computer indicates he never let go of the win.

Perhaps understanding that So was already winning on the board next to him, thus claiming the match, GM Leinier Dominguez let go of a win against GM Shamsiddin Vokhidov and steered the game into an opposite-color bishop draw. GM Fabiano Caruana vs. GM Javokhir Sindarov and GM Hikaru Nakamura vs. GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov were solid draws.

So proved instrumental to the team in round two as well, winning his game against Vokhidov to tie the match score. At first, the U.S. was in trouble when Nakamura lost a quick game in 22 moves against Sindarov, who credited the win to opening preparation. He knew he had a great position when he played 16.Bf7!, but not that it was flat-out winning. He played every best move with an overall accuracy of 99.7. Yikes!
Sindarov told Chess.com's FM Mike Klein, "That game for me was very easy because I have a very good opening preparation... I think he knows everything, but he forgets this line."

As Nakamura explained, it was a "slight mishap, but Wesley saved us." With draws on the other two boards (though Caruana was a piece up against Abdusattorov at one point), it was up to So to win what was objectively a fortress position, and after the mistake 61...g6??, with Black overlooking the response, the American was able to do just that.

Abdusattorov, who has for the first time brought his brother to a chess tournament, told WIM Fiona Steil-Antoni that the second round was the decisive one in the match. "I think after the second round it was a bit tough," he said.

The U.S. picked up another two-point win in round three, scoring 2.5-1.5. Nakamura nicely outplayed Vokhidov in a queen-and-bishop endgame, while Aronian won with his signature creativity against Sindarov. The paradoxical 13...Nxh5!, grabbing a pawn on the edge of the board and leaving his own e-pawn hanging, was not on GM Yasser Seirawan or WGM Anastasiya Karlovich's radar, but Aronian played it calmly.

Abdusattorov, in that same round, converted the exchange-up endgame by realizing that his king belonged on the queenside. The monarch marched right over, hid behind the black pawns, and his rooks took care of the rest. Still, it was Uzbekistan's only win of the round.

In round four, there was one draw between Madaminov and Caruana; elsewhere, the teams traded blows with an American win by Aronian against GM Nodirbek Yakubboev and an Uzbek win by Sindarov against Dominguez. The deciding game of the match was So vs. Abdusattorov, a dynamic game with opposite-sides castling. The Uzbek ultimately won with the rook against two minor pieces, with queens still on the board.

Abdusattorov was still optimistic about his team's chances. He said, positively, "In general we played very well. We have good chances to win all the matches too." He looks forward to the blitz, though he thinks the Americans are favorites. "We have to be confident in our level and then maybe we have the same chances," he said.
While Abdusattorov is "very excited and ready to play," Sindarov said he looks forward to playing cards with Aronian this evening!
You can watch the official broadcast on YouTube or see Hikaru Nakamura's stream on Kick. The games can also be checked out on our dedicated events page.
The live broadcast was hosted by GM Yasser Seirawan and WGM Anastasiya Karlovich.

U.S.A. vs. Uzbekistan: WR Chess Rapid & Blitz Miami 2026 takes place on July 27 and 28 in Miami. Some of the strongest players in the U.S. meet Uzbekistan's brightest stars in Miami for a two-day rapid and blitz showdown. The format is a Scheveningen match across four boards, with a rapid stage followed by a blitz stage. The time control is 15+10 for rapid and 3+2 for blitz.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Geneva To Host Gukesh-Sindarov 2026 FIDE World Championship Match
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: Geneva, Switzerland will host the 2026 FIDE World Championship between Indian World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju and his Uzbek challenger GM Javokhir Sindarov, with the 14-game match running November 24 to December 12. FIDE
body: Geneva, Switzerland will host the 2026 FIDE World Championship between Indian World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju and his Uzbek challenger GM Javokhir Sindarov, with the 14-game match running November 24 to December 12. FIDE Interim President GM Viswanathan Anand said strong bids were received from India, the United States, and Cyprus, but that the decision was taken to hold the event "on neutral soil."

The International Chess Federation is itself based in Switzerland, and in today's announcement Anand describes Geneva, on the shores of Lac Leman, as "a city with a historic tradition of bringing nations and cultures together."

This will be the first world championship match in Switzerland since GM Vladimir Kramnik beat GM Peter Leko in Brissago in 2004, in a match that was also the last time the champion automatically held the crown in case the match was tied after the classical games.

Andre Voegtlin, the President of the Swiss Chess Federation, called it "a truly special day for Swiss chess," and referred to the earlier match as he vowed to boost the popularity of chess in the country:

Twenty-two years after Brissago, an event of global chess significance is returning to Switzerland. For us, this is far more than wonderful news – it’s a defining moment for chess in our country, one that fills us with both joy and motivation.
No details have yet been announced of the prize fund, regulations, sponsorship, or exact venue.

The choice of a neutral location has been the default in recent years in chess, with only Anand in Chennai in 2013 and GM Veselin Topalov in Sofia in 2010 playing on home soil in the last 22 years. Both lost, with playing at home often considered to bring extra pressure without any of the benefits of cheering crowds in other sports.

Sindarov, who qualified for the world championship match by scoring a crushing victory in the 2026 FIDE Candidates Tournament, commented at the time: "For me, if it will be in December, probably I'll choose some hot country, like Cyprus, because I don’t want to play a world championship match in cold weather."
I don't want to play a world championship match in cold weather.

Sindarov may need to wrap up warm in Geneva in November and December, but it's curious that Cyprus did in fact bid for the event, while Uzbekistan, as far as we know, didn't. They may have respected the wishes of their player, or feel that organizing a world championship in the same year as they host the 2026 FIDE Chess Olympiad is a step too far.

Gukesh plays the match as the reigning world champion after defeating GM Ding Liren 7.5-6.5 in another neutral venue, Singapore, in 2024. The Indian star has had a rough time since, and currently finds himself live-rated 74 points below Sindarov for what's set to be the youngest world championship match in history. Both players will be 20, with Sindarov turning 21 during the match.
Can Sindarov claim the crown, or will Gukesh hit back to prolong his reign? We'll find out in around four months' time!

Colin McGourty

news.title: 7-Game Win Streak Carries Firouzja Through Titled Tuesday
news.author: nathanielgreen
news.excerpt: GM Alireza Firouzja returned to Titled Tuesday on July 28 and won the event outright with a score of 9.5/11, including ripping off seven straight wins from rounds four through 10. The win was Firouzja's first of 2026 aft
body: GM Alireza Firouzja returned to Titled Tuesday on July 28 and won the event outright with a score of 9.5/11, including ripping off seven straight wins from rounds four through 10. The win was Firouzja's first of 2026 after he posted four victories in 2025, and he finished ahead of a group of six players on nine points, topped by GM Arjun Erigaisi, who finished second on tiebreaks.

Firouzja's only loss in the tournament came in round three against Lithuanian IM Gleb Pidluznij, but Firouzja otherwise scored every point until making a quick draw in the very last round. Still, he was not one of the 18 players to reach the first break on a perfect score. By the end of round six, just three of those 18 were still left on 100 percent: GMs Jeffery Xiong, Liem Le, and Ihor Samunenkov.

For much of the seventh round, Le appeared on his way to a brilliant victory against Xiong. Against long odds, however, Xiong kept Le's e-pawn from promoting, before turning things around and wrapping up with a smothered mate—but not the one you typically see in puzzles.
Samunenkov, meanwhile, was held to a draw by GM Benjamin Bok. As a result, Xiong had the sole lead on seven points, and Samunenkov was the only one on 6.5, followed by 15 players on six points.

In the key seventh-round matchup, a lot of material remained on the board as Samunenkov and Xiong's clocks each approached one minute left. Samunenkov was up by an exchange for a pawn, and he soon won the pawn back while going 10 seconds up on the clock. Samunenkov finished the job to take the lead entering the second break, and next week's winner can now double their prize with a perfect score, as the bounty for that achievement reaches $2,500.

Samunenkov couldn't retain the lead coming out of the break (and indeed had scored his final point of the tournament). The tempting 42.Bg5 set up a discovery threat on GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda's king, but failed for a few-moves-deep reason that Duda demonstrated on the board.

At the same time, Firouzja was continuing to roar back from his third-round setback. He needed just 30 moves to topple GM Alexey Sarana for his sixth straight win and set up a 10th-round clash with Duda. Arjun also tied Duda on 8/9 and got White vs. GM Pranav Venkatesh in round 10.

Firouzja vs. Duda was very even for a long time, but both players had less than 10 seconds left when Firouzja caught Duda premoving 71.Ke5??, which effectively gave Firouzja the sole lead with just one round left in the tournament.

Pranav defeated Arjun in the other top game that round, then took Black against Firouzja in the final round. A trade-heavy, 31-move draw by repetition followed, which locked up the tournament for Firouzja. Pranav ended up finishing third, jumped in line by Arjun, who steadily ground down GM Pranesh M's position in just 34 moves to take second place.
*Bounty grows by $250 per week without a perfect score, and resets once a perfect score has been achieved.
These winners are announced by Thursday each week. If you would like to nominate a game or a move (including your own) in this or future weeks, click here!
Titled Tuesday is Chess.com's weekly tournament for titled players. It begins at 11:00 a.m. Eastern Time/17:00 Central European/20:30 Indian Standard Time.

Nathaniel Green
