news.title: USA Beats Uzbekistan 14-10 In WR Chess Miami Rapid & Blitz
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: Team USA won the match against Uzbekistan in the inaugural WR Chess Rapid & Blitz Miami 2026. They clinched the match 13-9 with a round to spare. They played the final round anyway, and tied, so the final score was 14-10
body: Team USA won the match against Uzbekistan in the inaugural WR Chess Rapid & Blitz Miami 2026. They clinched the match 13-9 with a round to spare. They played the final round anyway, and tied, so the final score was 14-10.

Team USA consisted of GMs Fabiano Caruana, Levon Aronian, Wesley So, Hikaru Nakamura, and Leinier Dominguez, while Team Uzbekistan brought GMs Javokhir Sindarov, Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Nodirbek Yakubboev, Shamsiddin Vokhidov, and Mukhiddin Madaminov (all ordered by how well they performed individually across the two days).

The atmosphere in the tournament was friendly, with players from opposing teams spending time together on Monday evening. Even so, the teams largely consisted of Olympiad team members, and it's tempting to speculate about what the match shows for the upcoming Olympiad in September—in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, mind you. The entire Uzbek national team played in this event, while on the American side, the younger GMs Hans Niemann and Awonder Liang will step in for Nakamura and Dominguez.

It was a close match, with the U.S. taking a 5-3 two-point lead in the rapid portion on day one. In blitz alone, on day two, the U.S. scored 9-7, thus beating the younger team in both speed chess formats.

Somebody has to lose, and Uzbekistan took the experience well. Abdusattorov told WIM Fiona Steil-Antoni, "One thing I like about team competitions is that there are no more boring draws. Everyone is going to fight and for sure there will be some interesting games." He spoke highly of his team and said they've played together since early childhood. "What separates us from the rest of the teams is friendship and very good team spirit," said Abdusattorov.
What separates us from the rest of the teams is friendship and very good team spirit.

The U.S. was proud of their win. Nakamura reflected, "I think all of us had our moments of greatness and stupidity, but ultimately when it mattered, we came through." Aronian jumped in: "I was not aware that my teammates were crushing [in the match-winning round seven], so that was a pleasant surprise!" Aronian also concluded that he'd been a good boy.

So joined the interview as well and commented especially about the next world championship challenger, Sindarov. "Uzbekistan is no joke. They're still improving each year... Sindarov, his talent is limitless, his potential is limitless, also Nodirbek—the first Nodirbek!"
Sindarov, his talent is limitless, his potential is limitless.

Finally, Dominguez pinpointed the turning point, saying he was, "very happy with the way the team came through in the last three rounds, which were the most important." Nakamura said, and Aronian agreed, "We're a little stronger on boards three and four, and that's really the only thing that separated us."
Nakamura also said, "My form was not good, but it was good enough when it mattered." Feel free to listen to more of Nakamura's thoughts in a 48-minute, in-depth recap.

As you can see in the round-by-round score tally, the U.S. won four of the rounds while Uzbekistan won three. Several times, the round outcomes were decided by a single blunder. Though Uzbekistan tied the match after round five, the U.S. finished strong in rounds six and seven.

Uzbekistan started the day by evening the score at once (they were down from the rapid portion on Monday). Abdusattorov won the only decisive game in round one, against Nakamura. "Every sacrifice Hikaru made was accepted," observed GM Yasser Seirawan about this impressive game, where no trick worked for the American super-GM.
With this win, Uzbekistan won two match points and evened the score 5-5. Curiously, Abdusattorov matched Sindarov's miniature against Nakamura in rapid chess the day before: both lasted 22 moves.

In rounds two and three, the U.S. struck back and regained the two-point lead. In round two, the one decisive game was again the encounter of Nakamura vs. Abdusattorov (with colors reversed), but this time ending in favor of the American. Abdusattorov was the one pressing, and could have still gotten a slightly better endgame, but 37...Rxe4?? was a move Seirawan had just pointed out as unplayable. Had this one game gone the other way, Uzbekistan was that close to gaining the lead.

Uzbekistan's Yakubboev told Steil-Antoni that his role on the team was to hold draws, and the match strategy was to maximize on the wins of Abdusattorov and Sindarov. But asked about the U.S. match strategy, Nakamura said, "I wouldn't know. I drove home like a normal person last night." Nakamura, indeed, resides in Florida, but he didn't think playing a home match is necessarily beneficial. "I think it's better when you're in a foreign place that you don't know and you don't have any distractions."

The U.S. won again in round three, though it was a big fight. Sindarov took down Nakamura in their first game, and he was so pleased with his move 32...Nd3! that he struggled to suppress his laughter during the game.
Nakamura played on a few more moves, but the position on move 33 was unsightly—that is to say, hopeless.

But Caruana and So won to bring two points to the team, more than making up for that loss. Caruana overtook Abdusattorov in a Sicilian Najdorf, while So's quiet play in the opening (a Berlin) belied the potential danger in the endgame. It's well known that knights are unpredictable in blitz.

"It feels very shaky, especially in the first round today," said So after his win. "We're the favorites, but they're up and coming... they're very motivated, so it's tough." Caruana agreed, assessing the Americans as slight favorites, but Aronian thought it was the other way around: that they were favorites in rapid but not blitz.

Uzbekistan then won the next two rounds, four and five, in a row to even the score. In both rounds, they scored a resounding 3-1 against the U.S., and a comeback looked realistic again. In round four, the two scorers for Uzbekistan were Abdusattorov (against Caruana) and Yakubboev (against Aronian). White was winning, but lost control, and the glorious 36...Nf1! was the opening salvo of a terrible counterattack to come.

In round five, all games were decisive. Aronian's one win against Madaminov (a torturous massage in the endgame) was not enough to impact the match score, which was now 9-9. Abdusattorov beat Dominguez, Yakubboev beat Caruana, and Sindarov outwitted So with the out-of-nowhere 32.Qb4!, a game-ending move.

Rounds six and seven went to the U.S., who clinched the match with a round to spare. The most exciting game of round six was Caruana vs. Yakubboev. As Caruana explained, "I was completely losing, it's just in the time scramble some crazy things happened." He added, "I didn't even know the match situation, I was just trying not to lose on the spot."
Had Yakubboev won this game, it would have been Uzbekistan in the lead. But Caruana survived a mate-in-four, then went on to not only draw but win the game.

Round seven was just domination as Team USA won 3.5-0.5. Caruana drew Vokhidov, but Aronian beat Sindarov and So took down Abdusattorov. Nakamura squeezed out an endgame win against Madaminov and called it "probably the best game that I've played" in the event.

The match was effectively over, but the teams played out the last games. With a 2-2 draw in the round, the match ended 14-10. Congratulations to both teams for putting on a great show and best wishes in the Olympiad!
You can rewatch the official broadcast on YouTube or see Hikaru Nakamura's stream on Kick. The games can also be checked out on our dedicated events page.
The live broadcast was hosted by GM Yasser Seirawan and WGM Anastasiya Karlovich.

U.S.A. vs. Uzbekistan: WR Chess Rapid & Blitz Miami 2026 took place on July 27 and 28 in Miami. Some of the strongest players in the U.S. met Uzbekistan's brightest stars in Miami for a two-day rapid and blitz showdown. The format was a Scheveningen match across four boards, with a rapid stage followed by a blitz stage. The time control was 15+10 for rapid and 3+2 for blitz.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Bodhana Adds More Records With 1st IM Norm, 2600+ GM Win
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: Eleven-year-old FM Bodhana Sivanandan added two more age records with a stunning performance at the Dole Open in France last week, becoming the youngest girl ever to score an international master norm and the youngest gi
body: Eleven-year-old FM Bodhana Sivanandan added two more age records with a stunning performance at the Dole Open in France last week, becoming the youngest girl ever to score an international master norm and the youngest girl known to defeat a 2600-rated player in classical chess.

The nine-round Masters tournament, held from July 18-26, featured 46 grandmasters competing among the nearly 300 players, fighting for the €30,000 prize fund. Armenian GM Robert Hovhannisyan claimed the title and the €8,000 first prize after defeating fellow Armenian GM Haik Martirosyan 2-0 in a playoff after both had finished with 7.5/9.
GM Leon Luke Mendonca finished third and led a six-player group on 7/9. That group also included GMs Bharath Subramaniyam, Gergely Kantor, Amin Tabatabaei, Raunak Sadhwani, and Aksel Bu Kvaloy.

However, the main story of this piece is yet another one of Bodhana's record-breaking performances. Bodhana finished the nine-round Masters tournament with 5/9 and a 2463 rating performance after facing four grandmasters and two international masters.
Her second WGM norm had already been secured with one round remaining. In the final round, she held IM Samrug Narayanan to a draw in a long endgame to score an IM norm as well.

It was a remarkable return to the tournament where she, almost on the day one year ago, had become the youngest to ever score a WGM norm. This time the English prodigy went one step further and made history before the norm was even secured.

Bodhana began the tournament with a bang, as she scored the biggest win of her career, defeating 2628-rated GM Marc'Andria Maurizzi. The 19-year-old is no ordinary 2600-level opponent, having won the 2023 World Junior Championship and last year also becoming the French Champion. The teenager also had one of 2025's best tournament performances when he won the Djerba Open with a spectacular 2900 performance, scoring 7.5/9.

Maurizzi held the advantage in much of the game, but the position changed dramatically after 27...Qb6?, when he was forced to give up his queen. She had no problems converting the material advantage, and he resigned on move 39.

At 11 years, four months, and 11 days, Bodhana becomes the youngest girl known to have defeated a grandmaster rated over 2600. FIDE does not track these age-related statistics, but the record was likely held by GM Hou Yifan, who defeated GM Nikita Vitiugov two weeks before her 13th birthday. As a side note, Hou followed up the next day by also defeating 2629-rated GM Emil Sutovsky.

It's worth noting that just five players in history have ever defeated a 2600+ opponent at a younger age than Bodhana, according to Chess.com's research. GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov holds that record, while FM Ashwath Kaushik has the record as the youngest to defeat any grandmaster.

The historic opening-round win was only the start of Bodhana's remarkable performance. Later in the tournament, she held GMs Maxim Rodshtein and Paul Velten to draws, and then defeated FM Thomas Morais. Her last-round draw secured the norm.

Her IM norm makes her the youngest girl to achieve an IM norm, a record that was previously held by GM Judit Polgar, who earned her first IM norm at the New York Open in 1988. Bodhana, at 11 years, four months, and 19 days, has lowered that record by almost four months.

Bodhana's achievement adds to an extraordinary list of records since she first emerged as an international chess sensation. At eight, she became England's first World Youth Champion in 25 years as she swept the girls' under-eight world titles in classical, rapid, and blitz with a perfect combined score of 33/33.

At nine, she became the youngest player to score a WIM norm and then the youngest to represent England at a Chess Olympiad. After becoming the youngest player to score a WGM norm, she earned her third WIM norm at the 2025 British Championship at 10 years, five months, and three days, breaking GM Zhansaya Abdumalik's previous record for the youngest WIM by approximately a year. She completed the title by defeating GM Peter Wells in the final round, which also made her the youngest girl ever to defeat a grandmaster in a classical game.
Earlier this year, shortly after turning 11, she also crossed 2300 to earn the FM title, making her higher rated than Polgar was at the same age.

Sivanandan now has two WGM norms and one IM norm. She needs one more WGM norm to complete that title, already having achieved the required 2300 rating, while the IM title requires two additional norms and a rating of 2400.

Another standout performance came from Norwegian GM Aksel Bu Kvaloy. The 17-year-old began as the 54th seed, but finished eighth on 7/9 and a 2685 performance. His biggest victory came in round five, when he won over top seed GM Ian Nepomniachtchi.

The 2735-rated two-time Candidates winner struggled in the tournament, and was also held by 2439-rated GM Yair Parkhov in round two and 2498-rated IM Patryk Cieslak in round four. The loss to Kvaloy left him with only 3/5.

Nepomniachtchi followed up with three straight wins, but then lost again in the final round against GM Gergely Kantor. In the end, he finished 25th with 6/9, dropping 16 rating points to 2719, his lowest rating in 10 years.

Another 11-year-old prodigy also left Aix-en-Provence with a major achievement. FM Advik Amit Agrawal scored 5.5/9 and a 2456 performance, which secured him his third IM norm. He still lacks 25 rating points to secure the IM title, but it's only a matter of time before he crosses the threshold.

Agrawal earned his first norm at the Baku Open in May, where he scored 5.5/9, produced a 2486 performance, and reportedly crossed the 2400 rating barrier. His second followed at the Pune International GM Round Robin earlier in July, where he scored 5/9 against a field containing three grandmasters and several international masters.

Tarjei J. Svensen

news.title: Global Chess League Contenders Returns On August 7 As Pathway To World Stage
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: The Tech Mahindra Global Chess League (GCL) is returning for its fourth season with GM Magnus Carlsen headlining the field in Bengaluru, India. With a stellar lineup of the strongest players in the game teaming up in exh
body: The Tech Mahindra Global Chess League (GCL) is returning for its fourth season with GM Magnus Carlsen headlining the field in Bengaluru, India. With a stellar lineup of the strongest players in the game teaming up in exhilarating matchups, the fourth season is set to be one of the most exciting yet.

Amateurs and professionals once more have the chance to enter the world stage through the GCL Contenders, a series of online open qualifiers. The GCL Contenders runs from August 7 to August 22, with qualifiers held at different times to accommodate players across multiple time zones. Register to play in the GCL Contenders now for an opportunity to join Carlsen and other stars in the main event:

Last year, GM Jose Martinez, IM Mai Narva, and IM Faustino Oro prevailed in the Finals of the GCL Contenders, rising above more than 20,000 other participants to earn their spot in the GCL. This year, players will again battle for three spots in the main event, with one man, one woman, and one junior qualifying.

Whether you are a titled player aiming for the next stage of your career, or an amateur ready to test yourself in a global arena, the GCL Contenders is your chance to compete for a place alongside the game's biggest names. Register now and start your road to the GCL!

This year's GCL Contenders features three sections: men, women, and juniors, matching the GCL's team composition. The event features a $12,000 prize fund, with Chess.com Diamond Memberships also going to the winner of each arena. The top player from each section qualifies for GCL's main event in Bengaluru, India.

The GCL Contenders begins with the GCL Opens, a series of three-hour arenas with a 5+0 time control, open to all non-titled players. Each section will have six arenas, with the top two players from each advancing.

The next stage is the GCL Contender Titled Swiss, where titled players join those who advanced from the previous phase to compete in a seven-round Swiss with a 10+0 time control. The top player from each Swiss becomes a GCL Ambassador and wins a trip to Bengaluru to attend the GCL. The top six from each Swiss earn cash prizes and become eligible to play in the GCL Players Swiss.

In the GCL Players Swiss, all sections are combined into a single event, with all Ambassadors and GCL players eligible to join. Players compete in a five-round Swiss with a 10+0 time control for cash prizes.
Check out the table below for the full GCL Contenders schedule:

The GCL is the world's first major official franchise-style chess league. Teams compete in a series of rapid games, where wins with Black award more points than with White, inviting players to take risks and injecting drama into the competition. The event attracts the game's biggest legends every year, with players such as Carlsen, GMs Hikaru Nakamura, Fabiano Caruana, Viswanathan Anand, Hou Yifan, and Ju Wenjun among previous participants.

Fans who are not competing in the GCL Contenders still have a lot to look forward to when the GCL returns for its fourth season. Follow the main event's official broadcast to watch Carlsen and a world-class lineup of stars battle for their teams in the world's biggest chess league.
Who do you look forward to seeing at this year's Tech Mahindra Global Chess League? Let us know in the comments below!

news.title: Teamwork And Chaos Return For Chess.com Bughouse Championship Starting August 3
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: Who says chess needs to be an individual game? Call up your buddy and get ready for the madness of the Chess.com Bughouse Chess Championship! The event features a $5,000 prize fund and will take place from August 3 to Au
body: Who says chess needs to be an individual game? Call up your buddy and get ready for the madness of the Chess.com Bughouse Chess Championship! The event features a $5,000 prize fund and will take place from August 3 to August 7.
Bughouse is one of the most popular chess variants in the world. In fact, it's hard to go to any chess gathering without spotting a few people playing Bughouse.

In this variant, two players team up to play on separate boards, with one playing White and the other playing Black. Whenever a player captures their opponent's pieces, those pieces join their partner's piece bank. That player can then place that piece on their board, making it a part of their army. If any player on a team wins their game, the team wins the match.

With this mechanic, Bughouse becomes a beautiful, chaotic mess of crazy attacks and wild king hunts! Taking the initiative becomes more important than ever, inviting players to sacrifice material to aid their partner's attack.
Here's a video of GM Hikaru Nakamura reacting to Bughouse games and explaining how this variant works:

The action starts with eight qualifiers, each a two-hour arena with a 3+0 time control, taking place from August 3 to August 6. Every member of the community can participate by checking the qualifier schedule and clicking the Join button. Players can join as a team or come solo and be automatically paired by our system—but please note that only teams can qualify for the Final.

We may require players to join a video call for fair play checks, where players must set up two cameras from different angles in the room. Failing to comply will result in a team's removal from the event.

The winning team from each arena then qualifies to play in the Final, taking place on August 7. The Final consists of a double-elimination knockout bracket, with a match clock for every match and a 2+0 time control. Teams earn points for wins or draws, and the team with the most points when time runs out wins.

Last year, Bughouse specialists NMs Janak Awatramani and Isaac Chiu won the title after an undefeated run. To claim the title, the two national masters had to overcome a field that included the 2024 Bughouse champions and star players GMs Awonder Liang and Jeffery Xiong. Will any of the previous champions take the title for a second time, or will a new team rise to the top?
Are you excited to play in the Chess.com Bughouse Championship? Join the qualifiers between August 3 and 6!

While the Qualifiers are open to all players, only players who team up with the same partner throughout the entire arena can qualify for the Final. Individuals without a fixed playing partner can join the arenas and will be randomly assigned new partners throughout the event. However, they won't be eligible to qualify for the Final. To partner with a single teammate and be eligible for qualification, please follow the instructions in our help article after joining the arena.

news.title: Alexandra Botez To Host Chess Arena Event With Star Creators On July 31
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: WFM Alexandra Botez's venture into the game development world continues with a new chapter. Last year, the Canadian creator announced her involvement with Chess Arena, a fast-paced chess-themed battle royale game. Now, s
body: WFM Alexandra Botez's venture into the game development world continues with a new chapter. Last year, the Canadian creator announced her involvement with Chess Arena, a fast-paced chess-themed battle royale game. Now, she's hosting the Chess Arena Creator Brawl, an event for superstar creators from the chess world and beyond, with a $2,500 prize fund.

The event takes place on July 31, starting at 10:30 a.m. PT / 1:30 p.m. ET / 19:30 CEST. Alexandra and Andrea Botez, WGM Dina Belenkaya, and WGM Nemo Zhou are among the prominent chess personalities competing. They'll be joined by streamers from other communities, including Gorgc, Artosis, T90official, and past PogChamps competitors MrLlama and Sardoche. Fans can watch the event's live broadcast on BotezLive.

The game, which has now officially launched for the general public at chessarena.gg, is free to play and offers its battle pass for free until September 28, 2026. Click the button below to go to Chess Arena's official website and download the game:

Alexandra describes Chess Arena as a combination of chess and Fortnite. In its main mode, the game pits 40 players against each other on a massive board, from which only one player can survive. Unlike regular chess, there are no turns—all players move in real time, using special abilities and summoning chess pieces to outmaneuver their opponents. Battles can range from one-on-ones to multiple players all trying to survive, eliminate others, and collect experience points simultaneously.

The game has attracted the attention of players and content creators alike during its playtest and beta stages. Chess creators like Nemo and WFM Anna Cramling have publicly praised Chess Arena, with the game also ranking in the top 20 for most-watched categories on Twitch during its beta.

Since its inception, Chess Arena has evolved to include several game modes, skins, pets, characters, and more. Players can also create their own game modes and enjoy different events and cosmetics for each of the game's seasons.
Have you played Chess Arena yet? Let us know in the comments below!

news.title: Russian Attack Destroys Historic Kherson Chess School And Its 5,000-Book Library
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: A Russian artillery attack destroyed the 121-year-old building that housed Kherson’s Children’s and Youth Sports School for Chess and Checkers, consuming what the regional chess federation says housed a library of more t
body: A Russian artillery attack destroyed the 121-year-old building that housed Kherson’s Children’s and Youth Sports School for Chess and Checkers, consuming what the regional chess federation says housed a library of more than 5,000 chess books.

According to local authorities, the historic building caught fire during a massive bombardment of residential areas in Kherson, Ukraine, early on Saturday, July 25. The resulting fire gutted the school, leaving little more than its charred exterior walls. The destruction of the chess center was reported by local outlet Hryvna, while Italian news agency ANSA confirmed that the historic former Italian consular building had also been hit and set on fire.

The attack on the chess school came during a wider artillery bombardment of residential areas in Kherson. A 47-year-old man was killed and seven other civilians were injured, two of them seriously, according to Kherson Regional Police.

Vitaly Bogdanov, President of the Kherson Oblast Chess Federation, told Chess.com that he was informed of the destruction in a call from the city’s Military Administration and immediately went to inspect the site.

"It was a black night for Kherson sports and our history," he said. "What I saw with my own eyes cannot be described in words—the scale of the disaster is total. All that remains of the historic building where generations of talented children were raised are charred walls."
All that remains of the historic building where generations of talented children were raised are charred walls.—Vitaly Bogdanov

Bogdanov also took the photographs of the destroyed school that were published by Ukrainian media. He has headed the regional federation since 2005. The historic school has been the center of Kherson’s chess community throughout his tenure.
"This school was my second home, the work of my life, a space for the development of intellect and children’s dreams," he said.
The strike didn't just destroy the building itself, but teaching materials, historical documents, and an extensive chess library that consisted of 5,000 books are all gone, Bogdanov said.

"It was an invaluable intellectual collection that had been built up over generations by coaches and trainers. The enemy did not just burn walls—they tried to destroy our knowledge and our chess heritage."

Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Bogdanov said Kherson hosted around 100 chess tournaments each year. It also hosted national championships, while the school halls were used for events with hundreds of children and adults. "These are, without a doubt, completely different times," Bogdanov said.

Russian forces occupied Kherson during the first months of the full-scale invasion. Ukraine recaptured the city in November 2022, but Russian troops remain positioned across the Dnipro River and continue to subject the city to artillery fire and drone attacks.

"Since the war began, many students and coaches have moved abroad or to other regions of Ukraine," Bogdanov said. "Due to this, combined with the daily shelling, tournaments are becoming fewer and further between, and they are held strictly underground in safe locations."
Due to this, combined with the daily shelling, tournaments are becoming fewer and further between, and they are held strictly underground in safe locations.—Vitaly Bogdanov
Some chess activities have continued online, while children in the city have gathered to play underground, he said.
Kherson’s chess school developed several top Ukrainian players, who went on to compete successfully at international level. Among them is GM Natalia Zhukova, two-time European Women's Champion.
She shared Bogdanov's pictures on Facebook with the text: "This is my chess house in Kherson, where I grew up 💔 And someone is talking about equal conditions for athletes."

Other prominent players raised by the Kherson chess system include GMs Yuri Solodovnichenko and Egor Bogdanov, as well as IM Inna Gaponenko, who played on the Ukrainian team that won team gold at the 2006 Women's Chess Olympiad.

In May 2021, the club was visited by GM Viktorija Cmilyte-Nielsen, the 2011 European Women's Champion, who served as the speaker of Lithuania's parliament. She played a 10-board simul against students inside the building.

Asked for his fondest memory of the club, Bogdanov recalled not a particular tournament or victory, but the children who once filled its halls. "My fondest memory will always be the shining eyes of the children during our massive celebrations, when the Sports School halls were packed to capacity with hundreds of young players," he said.

"The unique, creative atmosphere remains unforgettable: the sun-drenched rooms, the majestic sculpted portraits of world champions on the walls, and the ringing silence right before the start of each round."
Several notable personalities in the chess world have condemned the attack. Among them are the 13th world champion GM Garry Kasparov, who shared Nielsen's post on X/Twitter.
Jan Henric Buettner, one of three candidates in Septembers FIDE election, condemned the destruction in a statement that was also shared with Chess.com.

"No chess player, no child, and no civilian should have to fear for their safety simply because they gathered around a chessboard. Attacks that harm civilians and destroy places dedicated to learning, culture, and community deserve our unequivocal condemnation.”

Buettner said his thoughts were with those who had lost a place that meant so much to Kherson’s chess community. "I hope that the club can one day be rebuilt and once again become a place where people meet in peace," he said.
"Chess teaches us that even the fiercest contests are governed by rules and respect. War reminds us of the terrible consequences when those principles are abandoned."
Chess teaches us that even the fiercest contests are governed by rules and respect. War reminds us of the terrible consequences when those principles are abandoned.—Vitaly Bogdanov

The historic building was not the only distinctive feature of the chess school. Behind it was a large courtyard with a fountain and an old oak tree that had stood through generations of Kherson’s history. Although the building was gutted, Bogdanov said the tree miraculously survived.
"It has seen so much in its long life, including the Russian occupation," he said.
Last month, the Chess Federation of Russia (CFR) was suspended from the International Chess Federation after it refused to cease organizing chess events in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.

During the more than eight months in which Russia controlled Kherson in 2022, occupation authorities attempted to establish their own regional chess organization and advertised classes for children, Bogdanov said.
"They almost immediately registered a fake Kherson federation and ran television advertisements inviting children to join the classes. But Ukraine drove them out."
The historic building that was once home to thousands of children and adults is gone, but Bogdanov remains convinced that Kherson’s chess community will return.
For the future, Bogdanov is convinced that chess in Kherson will rise again and that they will rebuild the chess center.

news.title: Firouzja Back In Top 10, Erdogmus Overtakes Gukesh On August FIDE Rating List
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Alireza Firouzja is back in the top 10 on the August 2026 FIDE rating list after his victory in the Quantbox Chennai Grand Masters, while GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov's last-round loss to GM Dmitry Andreikin saw him drop
body: GM Alireza Firouzja is back in the top 10 on the August 2026 FIDE rating list after his victory in the Quantbox Chennai Grand Masters, while GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov's last-round loss to GM Dmitry Andreikin saw him drop two places to eighth. For a second month in a row, World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju suffered, this time dropping 14 points to 2703 after three losses in the same tournament—he also slipped below 15-year-old GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus on the Junior FIDE rating list. On the Women's list, IM Polina Shuvalova climbed into the top 10 (+24 points) after scoring her second GM norm.
GM Magnus Carlsen extended his 15 years unbroken as world number-one, with the top five remaining unchanged on the August FIDE rating list.

news.title: Maghsoodloo Rallies To Win 3 0 Thursday On Tiebreaks
news.author: jackrodgers
news.excerpt: GM Pranav Venkatesh added another feather in his cap in the first 3 0 Thursday tournament of the week, finishing with an undefeated 9.5/11 and outscoring no fewer than eight super-GMs. Wins over GMs Aravindh Chithambaram
body: GM Pranav Venkatesh added another feather in his cap in the first 3 0 Thursday tournament of the week, finishing with an undefeated 9.5/11 and outscoring no fewer than eight super-GMs. Wins over GMs Aravindh Chithambaram, Sergei Zhigalko, Hans Niemann, and Sina Movahed cemented his spot at the top, while the tournament's other undefeated players, GMs Dmitry Andreikin and Matthias Bluebaum, had to settle for third and fourth.
In the second and third tournaments, GMs Parham Maghsoodloo and Jeffery Xiong claimed the top spot, with the former requiring tiebreaks to best GM Sergey Drygalov.

Despite coming from a country overflowing with prodigious talent, Pranav has emerged as one of India's brightest stars in recent years. Currently, he sits 45th in the world with a FIDE rating of 2670 after a string of elite performances, and it's fair to predict that he might join the 2700 club in the future.

In the first tournament, Pranav started with 7/8, rising to equal first alongside Niemann, who participated alongside numerous other super-GMs including Hikaru Nakamura, Andreikin, Bluebaum, Xiong, Liem Le, Aravindh, and Bogdan-Daniel Deac.
As early as round two, Pranav showed that he meant business when he left his knight en prise for three moves in a row against Brazilian GM Alexandr Fier.

Pranav and Niemann clashed in round nine and given that they both possess a penchant for aggressive chess, it was no surprise that the result was decisive. Pranav gained the upper hand early but missed a chance to consolidate his lead. Later, Niemann gave Pranav another opportunity to take control with 21...Be5? and this time, Pranav capitalized.

Pranav closed out the tournament with a draw with Deac, before turning the tables on Movahed in a time scramble. With nine wins and two losses to his name, Niemann had to settle for second place, while the top-performing women's player was IM Karina Ambartsumova.
Maghsoodloo's road to victory in the second tournament was anything but smooth. In round six, a loss to Drygalov saw him slump to 4/6, which would have had many pundits counting him out.

Like a phoenix from the ashes, though, the Iranian clawed his way back to the top with an inspiring 5/5 at the tail-end of the Swiss. Maghsoodloo bowled over previous winners and GMs Denis Lazavik and Oleksandr Bortnyk on the way.

With everything to play for in the final round, Maghsoodloo found himself on the brink of defeat against Uzbekistan's IM Mukhammadzokhid Suyarov, however, he was saved by Suyarov's nerve-induced blunder, 51.Rd8?.

With this victory, Maghsoodloo moved to 9/11 and into equal first alongside Drygalov. Given the latter defeated the former, it would be reasonable to assume that tiebreaks would favor Drygalov, however, a round-one loss for the 27-year-old all but sealed him the silver medal. Taking home bronze on tiebreaks was Suyarov, and WFM Anastasiia Hnatyshyn was the best women's player.

It is extremely rare to see a player dominate a tournament in such a fashion that they can afford to lose the last two rounds and still guarantee at least equal first. Yet, that is the exact situation Xiong was in on Thursday.

Xiong kicked off the third tournament with three wins before drawing with Maghsoodloo and IM Renato Terry. Then, Xiong went on a four-game tear, dispatching NM Shelev Oberoi, as well as GMs Aravindh, Alexey Sarana, and Vladimir Fedoseev.
Off the back of his comprehensive victory a week ago, Fedoseev came in with plenty of momentum, but was stunned by Xiong's queen sacrifice in response to his deadly-looking 28...Rc3.
Earlier, Aravindh faced another of Xiong's dramatic sacrifices which exposed his king and prompted his resignation four moves later.

In the penultimate round, GM Steven Zierk toppled Xiong in just 26 moves, though the leader would still only need a draw with White to secure clear first. When an opposite-colored bishop endgame arose in Xiong-Le, Xiong's victory crystallized.
Aravindh and Terry finished second and third respectively, while the women's world number-nine GM Tan Zhongyi finished 23rd and took the top women's prize.

news.title: Nakamura Wins 50 Games, Claims 63rd Bullet Brawl Title
news.author: jackrodgers
news.excerpt: GM Hikaru Nakamura reclaimed the Bullet Brawl throne with relative ease on Saturday one week after missing out on the $400 first prize due to inferior tiebreaks. With 50 wins, eight draws, and only 11 losses to his name,
body: GM Hikaru Nakamura reclaimed the Bullet Brawl throne with relative ease on Saturday one week after missing out on the $400 first prize due to inferior tiebreaks. With 50 wins, eight draws, and only 11 losses to his name, Nakamura convincingly won the two-hour arena with a score of 176, 21 points clear of the previous winner, GM Tuan Minh Le.
Rounding out the top four and winning $150 and $100 respectively were GMs Haowen Xue and Pranesh M, while FM Anastasia Avramidou completed her best women's prize hat trick.
The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, August 8, at 12 p.m. ET/6:00 p.m. CET.

From the moment Saturday's Bullet Brawl commenced, it became clear that Nakamura was on a mission to secure his 63rd title without allowing any of his competitors a similar window of opportunity to the one he gave to Le a week ago. Following a draw with Xue in his first game, Nakamura defeated 12 titled players in a row and catapulted himself into the lead.

During this streak, Nakamura racked up three brilliant moves and remarkably, all three used similar tactics to take advantage of his opponent's weak back ranks. Against Turkish CM Mert Can Sevig, Nakamura saved the game after his opponent entrenched a passed pawn on a2. See if you can solve the three one-move puzzles below.
In the very next game, Nakamura found another shrewd sacrifice against WIM Irina Mikhaylova.
Finally, Nakamura dispatched Pranesh, one of the top seeds in the event, off the back of a mass liquidation tactic that forced the game into a winning king and pawn ending.

Nakamura eventually came unstuck in another clash with Sevig, but his devastating run in the first quarter had already amplified his status as the favorite. In spite of this, Le loomed once again, having posted a nine-game streak of his own to keep himself in contention.

When the pair came face to face for the first time, it was Nakamura who came out of the Catalan Opening: Closed, Traditional Variation up by a pawn due to navigating the central tension better. The American then made consolidation look easy and Le eventually resigned on move 35.

Although last week's hero would go on to score 6/12 against Nakamura, this wasn't enough to curb his streak-hungry rival. Other contenders, such as GMs Xue, Pranesh, Oleksandr Bortnyk, and IMs Yoseph Taher, Sergey Sklokin, Renato Terry, and Reza Mahdavi, also prevented Le from building streaks and hawking down the leader.
In the second half, relentless ruthlessness helped Nakamura extend his lead to 21 points. FM Ivan Vihor was one victim who felt the fury of a galvanized Nakamura.

Despite having the arena wrapped up with five minutes to go, Nakamura remained critical of his own play. Against Terry, Nakamura stated the following on Twitch: "That does nothing, what am I doing?" before mounting a stunning comeback and winning the game.

With this victory, Nakamura is one victory away from having as many wins as there are squares on a chess board. It is nigh impossible to imagine his feats in the Bullet Brawl arena being surpassed in the near or distant future.
How to review games? The games from this week's Bullet Brawl can be found here.

Bullet Brawl is an exciting arena featuring Chess.com's top bullet specialists. It takes place weekly on Saturdays. The format is a two-hour arena with a 1+0 time control; the prize fund is $1,000. Like Titled Tuesday and Arena Kings, Bullet Brawl often features top GMs, including Hikaru Nakamura, Andrew Tang, Tuan Minh Le, and many more!

news.title: Hou Yifan Wins, Sets Date With Alice Lee In Final
news.author: vsaravanan
news.excerpt: GM Hou Yifan prevailed over GM Bibisara Assaubayeva with a final score of 12-10 in the second semifinal of the 2026 Women's Speed Chess Championship. The match climaxed in the 1+1 bullet phase, where Hou staved off her o
body: GM Hou Yifan prevailed over GM Bibisara Assaubayeva with a final score of 12-10 in the second semifinal of the 2026 Women's Speed Chess Championship. The match climaxed in the 1+1 bullet phase, where Hou staved off her opponent's expected resurgence after triumphing in both the 5+1 and 3+1 blitz segments.
The stage is now set for the proverbial legend-versus-prodigy summit clash, where the four-time Women's World Champion will face the 16-year-old IM Alice Lee, who is exactly half her age.

A factor of this semifinal is the time difference between the two players. The match started with Assaubayeva in Saint Louis at 8 p.m. CDT on August 1, playing Hou in Beijing at 9 a.m. CST (China Standard Time) on August 2—two extreme time zones. This prompted commentator IM Jovanka Houska to exclaim, "One player is playing from the future, the other one from the past!"
One player is playing from the future, the other one from the past!

Hou prevailed in both the 5+1 and 3+1 blitz segments with scores of 4.5-3.5 and 4.5-2.5, thus gaining a three-point lead going into the crucial bullet segment. It was essentially decided in bullet, where Assaubayeva has shone in the previous matches with her quick-wittedness.

Hou started briskly with two wins, and she impressed with good control throughout. Employing the Chekhover Variation in the first game and the Rossolimo in the third, she showed her readiness in facing her opponent's Sicilian Defense, prompting commentator GM Arturs Neiksans to exclaim, "The Chinese grandmaster seems to be really well-prepared!"

Though the final part of the game wasn't flawless, Hou looked to be deserving of this win. The second game was even more impressive, as she exploited hidden tactical possibilities when the white queen was trapped.
By the time the first short break arrived after four games (in the style of the 2026 World Cup?), Hou was leading the match 3-1 and showed good form.
The fifth game was the first turning point, as Hou went on a pawn-munching spree in the early middlegame, prompting Houska to quip, "She is not going to go hungry tonight!"

It is always an interesting scenario when one of the sides goes on a pawn-grabbing spree, even if the compensation is not very clear for the player who sacrifices them. But when such escapades happen in quick time controls, they sure help the side with the initiative.
Assaubayeva equalized the match score at 3.5-3.5 after a win in the seventh game thanks to blunders from Hou with less than a second remaining on the clock.

Pressure began to show on both players, as the eighth was error-prone, and Assaubayeva slipped in the final seconds of the game. Thus, at the end of the 5+1 blitz segment, the scoreboard read an extra point for Hou.

Hou looked to be warming up for the games as we saw her stretching before the segment started. She also seemed to have come with a clear game plan: in general, she started playing much faster than in the earlier segment. And, leaving her preference for off-beat variations of the Sicilian Defense with White, she switched to facing the mainlines of the Najdorf Variation. She was also helped by a puzzling piece sacrifice from Assaubayeva in the second game, which never yielded any compensation and thus gave an extra-point lead for Hou.

When Hou won the fifth game of the segment, she had taken a four-point lead, which seemed to pull the match steadily in her favor. Assaubayeva pulled one back with an impressive grinding win in the sixth game.
But Hou struck back in the next game, exploiting a tactical slip by Assaubayeva.
This enabled Hou to win the segment 4.5-2.5 and move into Bullet with a three-point lead.

The final 25 minutes of excitement began with expectations of an Assaubayeva comeback. The bullet segment was anticipated with much interest, as Assaubayeva has clearly demonstrated in the past that this is her forte. It only remained to be seen if she could perform her bullet magic against such a formidable opponent as Hou.
After winning the first game of Bullet fluently, Assaubayeva really showed her quick-thinking brilliance by uncorking a shocker in the second game.
Unfortunately for Assaubayeva, she couldn't win the game. But when she won the fourth game, she had reduced her opponent's lead to just one point at 10-9.

The 20th game of the match, the fifth of the bullet segment, was the most crucial. Hou showed her grit and fighting spirit in this game, holding her nerve and playing remarkably with just a second remaining on her clock.

The final two games of the segment were drawn, thus enabling Hou to limit the damage in Bullet to a solitary point and win the match overall with a two-point margin. This enables Hou to meet Lee in the Final, with the schedule to be announced later.
You can watch the broadcast on Twitch and YouTube. The games can also be checked out on our dedicated events page.

The 2026 Women's Speed Chess Championship, which takes place from July 6-Aug 7, is a Chess.com event where some of the strongest female chess players in the world battle for a $75,000 prize fund. In the main event, 16 players compete in a single-elimination bracket in matches played at 5+1, 3+1, and 1+1 time controls.

news.title: Praggnanandhaa Takes Sole Lead On Day 1
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu had the best start on day one of the 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz, taking the sole lead with five out of a possible six points. He's trailed by two players a point behind, GMs Javokhir Sind
body: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu had the best start on day one of the 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz, taking the sole lead with five out of a possible six points. He's trailed by two players a point behind, GMs Javokhir Sindarov and Wesley So.
The first day featured three rapid games, and there are nine in total. Rounds four through six are on Monday, August 3, starting at 1:10 p.m. ET / 19:10 CEST / 10:40 p.m. IST.

Praggnanandhaa was the only player to win two games and make one draw. His closest rivals made two draws and scored just one win. There were five decisive games in total, and GM Levon Aronian was the only other player to both win and lose on day one.

The 2026 Grand Chess Tour, which started in May, concludes in August with its last three events. First is the Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz on August 2-6, followed shortly by the 2026 Sinquefield Cup on August 10-20 (which runs this year alongside the 2026 Cairns Cup), and finally the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals on August 22-27.

The first event of the month is the last rapid and blitz event on the tour, and as in previous years, there are two segments. The first three days are devoted to rapid chess, where a win earns two points, while the last two days feature blitz. The two formats count together as one cohesive tournament.

Returning players from last year are GMs Fabiano Caruana (2023 winner), So, and Aronian (the returning champion). GMs Anish Giri and Leinier Dominguez are veterans of the Saint Louis Chess Club and Grand Chess Tour events, but did not play last year, while Praggnanandhaa played just once before in 2024. The rest of the 10-player field features debutants: World Championship Challenger Sindarov (his first time playing in St. Louis), GM Vincent Keymer, GM Awonder Liang (a wildcard), and GM Jorden van Foreest.

Two-time winner GM Alireza Firouzja, who had accrued 18 Grand Chess Tour points after three events, has dropped out of the Grand Chess Tour and will instead participate in the 2026 Esports World Cup, which conflicts with the Sinquefield Cup. He's been taken out of the Grand Chess Tour and will be replaced in the Sinquefield Cup by GM Sam Sevian.
By the end of the Sinquefield Cup, the top-four full-tour players will advance to the Grand Chess Tour Finals. You can see the standings below.

Winning the tournament comes with $50,000, but even the player in last place walks away with a not-insignificant $7,000 consolation prize. The total prize fund enjoys a $25,000 increase compared to last year.

With all that out of the way, we can jump right into the chess. Praggnanandhaa's +2 score is a good result, and it's already a notable improvement over his debut in 2024, where he finished in last place. In the rapid portion that year, he scored 4/9 (with no draws). He said of this year, "I think the last two games were good. The first game, I could have put more pressure, but I can't complain too much, after scoring +2 in a day."

Praggnanandhaa's only draw was in round one, though this came as a massive surprise to Sindarov. Assuming Praggnanandhaa was on +3, and learning otherwise only in his interview, Sindarov exclaimed, "I thought he won that game! Then I still have a chance!" The draw was as clean as it gets, ending with bare kings after 99 accuracy for 49 moves.
Aronian took an early lead (with So) after round one. He won his first game against Van Foreest, who made an interesting exchange sacrifice but fell apart later with less material.

After the game against Praggnanandhaa, however, Aronian was back on 50%. The Armenian-American played the thematic pawn break 13...c5?, but it was mistimed. White grabbed the pawn and Black never quite found a way to win it back.
Following up on that in round three, Praggnanandhaa played the Game of the Day against last year's runner-up, Caruana. From the black side of a French Defense, Praggnanandhaa said:

It felt like an unpleasant position for me because I was not having space, but still I felt if I can get my pieces to some decent squares, I should have some counter. And once I got this knight takes d4 maybe I am even taking over.

His sister, GM Vaishali Rameshbabu, told him after the game that 43...Rxf3 was an easier win, but he still converted a winning advantage without much trouble—eventually reaching the rare imbalance of four pawns for a piece. GM Rafael Leitao goes over the full game below.

The other two players to score wins were So and Sindarov, with the American starting with the black pieces in both rounds one and two before getting the white pieces in round three. So pointed out that the field this year is "much stronger" than in 2025.

In both of his games with Black, So played the Berlin Defense. He had been pressing in the endgame against Liang with the bishop pair, but in the mutual time scramble, the younger grandmaster let go of his e-pawn and didn't get enough counterplay in return.

Sindarov, on the other hand, started with two draws before scoring a win in round three, against Van Foreest (a second loss for the Dutchman). The Uzbek GM said, "In general I'm happy I finished +1 because the second game [against Keymer] was tricky. At some moment I'm just losing, but in time trouble I managed to survive the position."

In round one, he had winning chances against Giri, but they slipped in the heavy-piece endgame, and in round two he was at one point worse against Keymer, but never losing. In round three, Sindarov finally won an opposite-color bishop endgame, with rooks on the board. 40...h5? was a move designed to slow down the white pawn expansion, but the pawn became a target surprisingly quickly.
Sindarov is cautiously optimistic: "In Warsaw I also finished +1 on the first day and on the second day I lost three in a row, so I will try to manage not to lose three in a row tomorrow!"
On day two, the leader Praggnanandhaa will have the white pieces twice. In his first game, he takes on Sindarov.
You can watch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz events page.
The broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan and Maurice Ashley, as well as IM Nazi Paikidze.

The 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz is the fourth leg and final rapid and blitz event of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players compete in a rapid (25+10) single round-robin followed by a blitz (5+2) double round-robin for their share of a $200,000 prize fund and to finish at the top of the tour standings.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: The Chess Odyssey Bots Are Here For August!
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: Every month, a new group of bots appear on Chess.com. This August, set sail on an epic chess adventure inspired by the legends of ancient Greece! Navigate dangerous seas filled with monsters, magic, and heroes from Greek
body: Every month, a new group of bots appear on Chess.com. This August, set sail on an epic chess adventure inspired by the legends of ancient Greece! Navigate dangerous seas filled with monsters, magic, and heroes from Greek mythology. Enter the Cyclops’ cave, follow the Siren’s song, survive Circe’s spells, brave Poseidon’s waves, and test your strategy against the legendary Odysseus.
🏆 These mythical bots come with a new challenge! Play them to unlock a special board, pieces, and flair!
The Cyclops may call you a puny human, but he’s a gentle giant…most of the time. Try not to make him mad, or you might end up as his next snack.
The Siren’s song is impossible to ignore, but her chess traps are even harder to escape. Lose yourself in her melody, and you may lose the game too.
Lord of the Sea, Poseidon commands the board with confidence and expects his opponents to admire his greatness. Try not to get swept away by his powerful attacks.
Circe is ready for a battle of wits with some magic. Just remember: losing a chess game is much better than being turned into a pig.
Odysseus is a legendary hero known for his clever thinking and impossible escapes. Outsmarting him will take a plan worthy of a legend.
What are the odds of you getting turned into a pig? Let us know in the comments below!

news.title: Praggnanandhaa Leads, Sindarov Trails By 2 Points
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu continues to lead the 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz at the end of day two. After six rounds, he has earned nine points out of a possible 12 and is two points ahead of GM Javokhir Sindarov, h
body: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu continues to lead the 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz at the end of day two. After six rounds, he has earned nine points out of a possible 12 and is two points ahead of GM Javokhir Sindarov, his closest rival. One point further back are GMs Vincent Keymer, Wesley So, and Anish Giri.
Day three, featuring the final three rapid games, is Tuesday, August 4, starting at 1:10 p.m. ET / 19:10 CEST / 10:40 p.m. IST.

Although there was plenty of fighting chess, somehow most of the games ended in draws. There were two decisive games out of 15, but plenty of flubs and saves along the way. Praggnanandhaa remains at the top of the scoreboard.

It's striking for a rapid tournament, but rounds four and six ended in all draws on five boards. Only round five featured two decisive games, but it wasn't for a lack of gambles and mistakes throughout the day.

Three games could have been decisive in round four, but not one was. Praggnanandhaa won a piece in the opening against Sindarov, but the world championship challenger stirred enough complications to survive; GM Leinier Dominguez had a tremendous position against Giri, but ultimately drew with a queen against rook and two minor pieces; and finally, GM Awonder Liang was winning against GM Jorden van Foreest, was then losing, and finally made a draw, smiling as the players shook hands as well as their heads.

A win for Praggnanandhaa over Sindarov would have extended his lead, but it was not meant to be. By move 13 in a King's Indian Defense, Praggnanandhaa trapped his opponent's bishop and looked sure to snag two more points. But Sindarov, as he's proven before (and would prove again), showed his resourcefulness to save what looked like a hopeless position.

In round five, Praggnanandhaa made up for that miss by winning with the black pieces against Liang, maintaining his lead in the tournament. With the kingside expansion of 14.g4 and 18.f4?, it looked like White (Liang) was the aggressor, but after 18...f6!, the tables turned. As Praggnanandhaa showed in the game, White's king was weaker, and he found a cheeky queen sacrifice on the last move of the game.

There were two massive turnarounds in that same round five. So, who was trailing the leader by one point, had been better or winning against Van Foreest for most of the game until he fell apart at the end of the game.

Sindarov, on the other hand, was winning right out of the opening against GM Levon Aronian. Somehow, the former world number-two survived with his king in the center into an exchange-down endgame—still losing. And after that, Aronian even got a winning position, with the knight versus rook, but agreed to a draw by repeating moves. Immediately after shaking hands, Sindarov showed his opponent the winning 66...Qd6!.
It's without a doubt the best save of the tournament, and GM Rafael Leitao goes over the Game of the Day below.

In round six, Sindarov showed his tenacity in defending a worse position against GM Fabiano Caruana, who has lost one game, made five draws, and is yet to win one. Full credit goes to the Uzbek superstar, however, as he found the exchange sacrifice 30...Rxc7!, a move Caruana saw, and then 35...Bf4!?, a move he did not see. The analysis below shows all the lines Caruana showed in his interview, checked against the engines.

Caruana explained that their previous game must have affected his encounter with Sindarov. Caruana survived a worse position against Dominguez, and Sindarov fumbled a winning position against Aronian. He called his play "not great overall" and summarized the two days so far:

Yesterday [I played] this complicated game against Pragg, which he played really well, and I made some poor decisions at a few moments. Today I should have probably struck in one of my white games, but I could have also lost the game against Leinier more likely than won it.
His goal is to finish the rapid on 50% and bank his hopes on the blitz.

The other key game in round six was Praggnanandhaa vs. So, where the Indian GM managed to give his opponent split pawns and achieve a stable advantage. But So managed to escape in the heavy-piece endgame, where Praggnanandhaa tried for 117 moves to win with the extra pawn but no real chances.
The last three rounds of rapid take place on Tuesday, and Praggnanandhaa will have the black pieces against Giri in the day's first game, which is round seven.

news.title: Carlsen Takes Titled Tuesday In Esports World Cup Warmup
news.author: nathanielgreen
news.excerpt: A week ahead of the start of the Esports World Cup main event, in which he will attempt to defend last year's title, GM Magnus Carlsen won Titled Tuesday on August 4. Carlsen scored 9.5 points and held a slightly better
body: A week ahead of the start of the Esports World Cup main event, in which he will attempt to defend last year's title, GM Magnus Carlsen won Titled Tuesday on August 4. Carlsen scored 9.5 points and held a slightly better tiebreak over GM Arjun Erigaisi. GM Hikaru Nakamura finished third on nine points after making draws with both Arjun in round 10 and Carlsen in round 11.

After six rounds, Carlsen, Arjun, and Nakamura were all on 100 percent, joined there by GMs Benjamin Bok, Jan-Krzysztof Duda, and Nodirbek Yakubboev. Only Carlsen and Arjun remained perfect after the seventh round, with Nakamura and Duda drawing each other. Carlsen was in big trouble out of the opening against Bok, but turned things around in the middlegame and won in 32 moves.
Carlsen got White against Arjun in the next round's battle of undefeated players, but Arjun was never worse and won with surprisingly little trouble.

Arjun was rewarded in the eighth round by again getting the second move, this time against a surging GM Hans Niemann, who was tied with GM Anton Demchenko on 6.5/7 before the round. Arjun found his light-squared bishop out of play on the queenside as he sacrificed the exchange on the kingside in a doomed attempt to thwart Niemann's attack.
(With a perfect score once again unattainable, the bounty for getting there moves to $2,750 next week, making it more valuable than the $2,500 first-place prize itself.)

Niemann wound up in sole first as Nakamura defeated Demchenko. GMs Alexey Sarana, Liem Le, David Paravyan, and Aravindh Chithambaram joined Carlsen, Nakamura, and Arjun on 7/8 entering the second break. Exiting the break, musical chairs continued at the top of the standings, Nakamura taking Black and defeating Niemann. The game got dicey for both players in the middle portion, but Nakamura was able to turn a worse endgame at first into victory by the end.
White won on the next three boards, including Carlsen on time over Paravyan, leading to a four-way tie for first with two rounds to go between Nakamura, Carlsen, Arjun, and Sarana.

Nakamura won a pawn in a minor piece ending against Arjun, but took a draw in what the computer, as Nakamura would find out soon on stream, saw as a winning position. Carlsen, meanwhile, converted strong knights on d4 and f4 into a pawn-up rook ending, eventually giving him the sole tournament lead with one round remaining.

Carlsen and Nakamura played the last round, but a quiet draw was in the cards, with Carlsen able to use the first-move advantage to create a tensionless position and secure a share of first place. Arjun, facing GM Aleksandar Indjic, was able to work his way back into a tie for the top position, but his tiebreak fell just short of victory, 77.5-77, and he settled for second place.
*Bounty grows by $250 per week without a perfect score, and resets once a perfect score has been achieved.

news.title: 5 Years After Emailing Keanu Reeves, Mitchell-Avila Beats Him At Chess
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: Bianca Mitchell-Avila was 16 when she cold-emailed Hollywood star Keanu Reeves asking him to support her chess documentary, and perhaps face her in a final battle against "John Wick." Five years later, she got her game.
body: Bianca Mitchell-Avila was 16 when she cold-emailed Hollywood star Keanu Reeves asking him to support her chess documentary, and perhaps face her in a final battle against "John Wick." Five years later, she got her game.
On Thursday, Mitchell-Avila defeated the Hollywood star in both of their on-stage games as Madwoman’s Game had its West Coast premiere at the Chicano Hollywood Film Festival in Pomona, California.

The documentary follows Mitchell-Avila, a young filmmaker and chess player from New Mexico, as she travels through the U.S., Mexico, and France to meet women whose lives have been shaped by the game. Using chess as a metaphor, the film explores identity, mentorship, family, sacrifice, and the difficult decisions involved in finding one’s place in the world.

Directed by Emmy- and Peabody Award-winning filmmaker Zach Zamboni, Madwoman’s Game grew from a planned short film about Mitchell-Avila’s childhood chess club into a six-year coming-of-age story. The documentary features IM Rusudan Goletiani, Rochelle Ballantyne, and WIM Sabrina Chevannes. The focus of the documentary, however, extends beyond ratings, titles, and tournament achievements.

In April, Variety revealed how Keanu Reeves joined the project as an executive producer in 2021, after Mitchell-Avila, then a 16-year-old with no Hollywood connections, contacted his representatives. He went on to mentor her throughout the five-year production.

At Thursday's premiere, the two met for the first time in person. The Matrix star, who revealed he had not played over the board for a year, seemed to enjoy himself on stage, entertaining the packed audience with theatrical despair as the games turned against him.
"I am a terrible chess player," he announced, before joking to Mitchell-Avila: "You’re just so terrible!" and "I hate chess!" he added. "I just hate chess! Did I say that? I just hate chess!"

The lighthearted matches preceded a panel with Mitchell-Avila, Reeves, Director Zach Zamboni, and Executive Producer Carla Berkowitz, followed by the premiere screening at The Union on Garey. The film had its world premiere at the Miami Film Festival in April.
Mitchell-Avila learned chess from her father when she was around five and played competitively for approximately five years through Learner’s Chess Academy in New Mexico.
The title Madwoman’s Game came from her grandmother, who encouraged her to continue playing in an environment where relatively few people around her were involved in chess.

"My grandma used to love that I played chess," Mitchell-Avila told Chess.com’s FM Mike Klein. "There was a part of her that was like, 'Women have got to play this game. The queen is the most powerful piece on the board.'"
"I think it was always just kind of teaching me that I have a place in this game."

Mitchell-Avila gradually stopped playing after entering middle school, when she felt increasingly pushed out by boys in the chess community. As with millions of others, Netflix’s hit series The Queen’s Gambit renewed her interest in the game.
"I was like, 'Wait, I forgot how much I love this game.' I used to play it all the time,” she said.
I was like, 'Wait, I forgot how much I love this game.' I used to play it all the time.—Bianca Mitchell-Avila

By then, filmmaking had already emerged as her career path and, having worked in the industry since she was 13 by making short films, she attended a media arts school and created a production company.

When productions shut down during the pandemic, her father suggested making something of their own. The initial plan was to make a short documentary about Learner’s Chess Academy, but Mitchell-Avila kept returning to one childhood memory.
Her club had taken seven players—five boys and two girls—to a tournament where only five could represent the team. Mitchell-Avila said the two girls were removed and had to play for other schools.
"I was like, 'I can’t be the only girl experiencing this,’” she said.

The concept expanded further when, as a 15-year-old, she was featured in a New York Times story about The Queen’s Gambit's effect on girls’ interest in chess. Some of the comments beneath the story dismissed their enthusiasm as a passing fad. Others bragged they could defeat the girls blindfolded.
"We were just young girls," Mitchell-Avila said. "We weren’t even adult women, and they’re saying these things. Why is that?"

The reactions helped convince her that the film should focus on the experiences of women in chess, although Mitchell-Avila did not want to frame the documentary as a battle between men and women. "I don’t want to do this documentary where it’s bashing people or making it like one side is better than the other," she said.
"I wanted to create something that was empowering, something that young girls could watch and see themselves in these women and be like, ‘Yes, I can do this too. Anything is possible.’"

I wanted to create something that was empowering, something that young girls could watch and see themselves in these women and be like, 'Yes, I can do this too. Anything is possible.'—Bianca Mitchell-Avila

Mitchell-Avila wanted to highlight relatable women who had experienced challenges and used chess to navigate or improve their lives. One of them is Rochelle Ballantyne, who appeared in the acclaimed 2012 documentary Brooklyn Castle.

Years later, Mitchell-Avila found herself playing Ballantyne in Washington Square Park in New York and interviewing her for a documentary of her own. "I saw Rochelle on the screen when I was maybe five or six years old and was like, ‘I want to be her. She’s so inspiring,’" she said.
"Then getting to interview her as an adult and seeing how much she’s grown—and how chess has helped her get to where she has gotten—it was crazy."

Mentorship also became one of the documentary’s central themes. Mitchell-Avila said she had struggled as a younger girl to find role models who looked like her and were pursuing the careers she imagined for herself.

Many of the women she interviewed ultimately became friends and mentors. "These chess players, it wasn’t just a one-time interview or meeting them one time and then never talking to them again," Mitchell-Avila told Chess.com in an interview on the red carpet.
"These people became very much like family. I still talk to a lot of these women today, and I ask them about my life."
Chess provided an immediate shared language, even when Mitchell-Avila had only just met the person sitting across from her.
“We’re both chess players. We connect on that level, and I think chess really just brought us together,” she said.
“I can trust you with telling these stories and these hard things that I’ve experienced because I feel like I already know you.”

The communities she visited had noticeably different characters. At Blitz Society in Paris, Mitchell-Avila found a quiet, close-knit atmosphere in which everyone appeared absorbed in their games. Washington Square Park in New York was filled with banter and energy.
Mitchell-Avila's biggest leap came when she imagined the documentary ending with a final chess game against Keanu Reeves.
"Having this epic chess battle against John Wick would be kind of crazy," she told Klein a couple of weeks before her dream came true.

She asked her father whether contacting one of Hollywood’s biggest stars was too unrealistic. He encouraged her to try, and the pair rewrote the email several times while searching for a way to reach Reeves’ representatives.
"One worked, and I remember it was such an insane moment, realizing it was all kind of happening," she said.
I remember it was such an insane moment, realizing it was all kind of happening.—Bianca Mitchell-Avila on getting Keanu Reeves on board
"The worst that could happen is I get a no. That was something my dad always taught me: always ask. The worst you’re going to get is no. If you don’t ask, you already got a no."
On the red carpet, Reeves was asked what persuaded him to work with a teenage filmmaker he had never met. “The power of this young person’s words,” he said, recalling her message.

"The power of this young person's words. 'Hello Mr. Reeves, I am interested in doing this. I have this idea. I play chess. Do you play chess? I want to explore my own questions about who I am, and how I am, the lessons I have learned through this game,'" the Hollywood star said.
"I could relate to that. So I guess that was kind of the... chess was the hook."
Mitchell-Avila quickly offered a less philosophical explanation. "I just wanted to play chess with you!” she responded.
I just wanted to play chess with you!—Bianca Mitchell-Avila to Keanu Reeves
Reeves joined the project in 2021. Although he does not appear in the finished documentary, his role became more significant than planned, Mitchell-Avila said.

"When I talk to him, I can tell that he’s actually hearing me and hearing my thoughts," she said. During periods when she questioned whether the project was taking too long or whether she should focus on something else, Reeves encouraged her to continue.

"He would always be there and be like, 'Trust the process. Trust your team. It’s going to happen. Your vision is going to come through,'” she said. "It was really nice to hear as a young person coming into this industry."
Speaking to Klein before her games against Reeves, she said she expected Reeves to be a strong opponent.
"I know he reads a lot of chess books, and I’m kind of scared," she said. "I know he definitely is a pretty good chess player."
Her advice to other young people considering a similarly unlikely project remains the same as when she decided to email one of Hollywood’s biggest stars.
"You get one life, one chance. It’s yours to take," she told Klein.
"You’ve just got to take that chance and go in. If that’s chess, if that’s something else—whatever you are passionate about, you might as well live your life doing something you’re passionate about."

Tarjei J. Svensen
