news.title: Bill Goichberg (1942-2026)
news.author: coachjkane
news.excerpt: FM Bill Goichberg, the most prolific tournament organizer in the history of American chess, has passed at the age of 83. He leaves behind a lifetime of dedication to American chess in numerous roles, including as a compe
body: FM Bill Goichberg, the most prolific tournament organizer in the history of American chess, has passed at the age of 83. He leaves behind a lifetime of dedication to American chess in numerous roles, including as a competitor, tournament director, groundbreaking organizer, and U.S. Chess Federation President.
The New York State Chess Association, an organization previously headed by Goichberg, announced his passing on Monday.

"Bill's legacy in chess in New York and the United States is unparalleled," the organization wrote in a Facebook post. "He leaves a legacy of greatness that is reflected in our New York State Scholastics, one of the largest tournaments in the country, that he created, and the continued success of the New York State Chess Championship, which is the longest-running chess tournament in the United States."
Bill's legacy in chess in New York and the United States is unparalleled.

Goichberg was born on November 11, 1942, the son of Sol Goichberg and Fannie Goichberg. Bill was a highly successful player, growing up in New York at a time when it was the heart of American chess. Many people who played in his events may not have known that he was a great competitor in his younger years.
His USCF rating peaked at 2530 on the July 1978 rating list and he secured the FM title with a FIDE rating over 2300. Despite that success, he never focused hard on earning the IM and GM titles.

Goichberg claimed that he wouldn't have earned higher titles, but he certainly could have progressed farther had he focused more on his own competitive career. His longtime friend David Hater told Chess.com that Bill was modest about his own level.
"I believe he was close to IM strength. He missed an IM norm in Gausdal 1978 by half a point. I think if he continued as a player, he would have made it. There's no doubt in my mind," he said.

The New York chess scene in the middle of the century was an exciting place. Hater tells the story of Goichberg playing an intense game against GM Arthur Bisguier. Right before the game was adjourned, Bisguier offered a draw. Goichberg was suspicious that a leading GM would offer a draw, so he spent most of his remaining time trying to find a win. He eventually accepted the offer against his prestigious opponent.

After the game, Bisguier told him that the position was even, but he wanted to end the game before he would have to debate the position with GM Bobby Fischer, who would have been responsible for adjudicating the result of the game!
Goichberg played many strong attacking games in his career. This wild game against IM David Strauss is one of his better-known performances.

GM Andy Soltis told Chess.com that after the final round of the 1962 New York City Junior Championship, Goichberg asked GM William Lombardy if it was hard running a tournament. "Very hard," Lombardy claimed.

In Soltis' words, Goichberg didn’t believe him, fortunately. Soltis also stressed Goichberg's playing strength, telling Chess.com that "in fact, his career score against me was something like three wins, one draw, and a single loss, in our final game."

While his playing career has been largely forgotten, Goichberg's contributions as an organizer will leave their mark on the American and global chess scenes for generations. Goichberg founded the New York City Chess Association in 1964. He began running popular events in the city, and in 1968 he expanded the organization throughout the country, changing its name to the Continental Chess Association (CCA).

The CCA went on to run thousands of the biggest tournaments in the United States over the coming decades. Its flagship tournament, the World Open has been held annually since 1973. The 1986 edition of the event had 1506 players, which for many years remained the world record for an open tournament.

The World Open, along with other major annual CCA events, like the Chicago Open, North American Open, and U.S. Open, offered unique opportunities for both amateurs and professionals to earn USCF and FIDE ratings, and compete with opponents from around the world. Many players earned norms required for the IM and GM titles at these events.

Goichberg never publicized it, but he actively supported numerous up-and-coming players by providing free entry fees to those in need. Several strong GMs today were sponsored by Bill on their way up. Hater said, "Bill never took credit for it, but this is the part of Bill that people never saw."

Goichberg and the CCA founded most of the major scholastic events in the U.S. Between 1969 and 1991, he founded the National High School Championship, the National Junior High Championship, the National Elementary School Championship, and the combined National Scholastic K-12 Grade Championship. After founding each of these tournaments, and ensuring their success, he donated them to the United States Chess Federation (USCF), which has continued to run and grow these tournaments ever since.

Besides their popularity, Goichberg's tournaments were notable for several innovations. In 1973, he banned smoking at the board in his events, which eventually led to it becoming standard practice throughout the world. In contrast to the large tournaments that he became famous for, Goichberg was the first person to run quad tournaments in the US in 1969. These four-player round-robin events have become popular, particularly among scholastic tournaments. Remember, USCF-rated scholastic events were another of his innovations.
The CCA announced on its website that it will continue to run events on schedule, in accordance with Goichberg's wishes.

As Bill’s health declined in recent years, he entrusted authority to the trustees of Continental Chess Incorporated. The trustees have overseen the business for several years and will continue to do so. Continental Chess will continue to operate without interruption, in accordance with Bill’s wishes and as an enduring part of his legacy.
Throughout his entire career, Goichberg held various positions with the USCF.
In 2018, he was also inducted into the U.S Chess Hall of Fame.
In the hours after his passing, many players who have played in Goichberg's tournaments posted memories and tributes.

IM Danny Rensch, CCO of Chess.com, shared that, "I grew up competing in Goichberg events. Bill provided an incredible service to all "up and comers," and the CCA established a number of staple, American events that I hope will carry his legacy forward for many years to come."

IM Jay Bonin, who may have played more of Goichberg's events through the years than anyone else, told Chess.com: "In December 1972, I played in my first chess tournament, the Greater New York High School Novice. It was run by Bill Goichberg. I tied for first. In 1977, I played in a Futurity run by Bill Goichberg and got my first FIDE rating. In 1980, he opened the Chess Center of New York, running tournaments every day and beginning my legacy. He ran a lot of great tournaments, the World Open, Foxwoods, Liberty Bell Open, National Congress… One of my IM norms was in an international at the CCNY in 1983. He was pretty much there throughout my whole chess career and now he’s gone. RIP, Bill."

On his blog, FM Dennis Monokroussos describes Goichberg as follows: "He’s almost certainly the most important U.S. chess organizer of at least the last 50 years, and you’ll probably need binoculars to spot whoever the number two organizer might happen to be."
Other notable chess personalities also shared their memories.

GM Dmitry Gurevich wrote: "I met Bill at the Chess Center of New York 46 years ago and played in hundreds of the events he organized. It was a wonderful time and it’s hard to believe I’ll never see him again… Bill, thank you for everything you’ve done for chess! RIP"
GM Maxim Dlugy said: "Oh my, RIP, Bill. You have raised generations of chess players that would never have played chess without you."
Goichberg's legacy in the chess world will endure through the tournaments that he founded and the opportunities he's offered to generations of chess players. He will be missed.
NM Jeremy Kane is the Instructional Content Manager for Chess.com, and the author of several courses in the Starting Out series, Queen’s Gambit Accepted, Trompowsky, and Tarrasch.

news.title: Praggnanandhaa Leads 3rd Day, Trailed by Sindarov, Wesley So
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: For a third consecutive day, GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu finds himself at the top of the standings in the 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz. He finished the rapid portion with 12 points on Tuesday and stayed in the lead ev
body: For a third consecutive day, GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu finds himself at the top of the standings in the 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz. He finished the rapid portion with 12 points on Tuesday and stayed in the lead even after losing to GM Jorden van Foreest in the last round. He's closely followed by GM Javokhir Sindarov, one point behind, and GM Wesley So, another point further back, as we head into two days of blitz.
Day four, featuring the first nine rounds of blitz, is Wednesday, August 5, starting at 1:10 p.m. ET / 19:10 CEST / 10:40 p.m. IST.

The standings look similar to what they have been for the last two days, with Praggnanandhaa at the top and Sindarov and So close behind. In the next two days of blitz, each win will now just count for one point, as opposed to two in the rapid.

Praggnanandhaa has been a picture of stability in the first three days of the Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz. Across the nine rounds, he won four games, drew four, and only lost the very last one. For the first time in his career, Praggnanandhaa has broken into the world top-10 in rapid chess on the live rating list.

Round seven, which was the first of the day, saw two decisive games, but they were won by players who find themselves at the bottom of the standings, GMs Fabiano Caruana and Vincent Keymer. For both of them, it was a first win; Caruana got back to 50% and Keymer, who previously made six draws, was suddenly two points behind the leader.

Caruana defeated GM Awonder Liang by targeting the weak pawn on e5. With the doubled f-pawns fixed in place, unable to defend the e-pawn, it was effectively isolated, and Caruana's maneuver of ...Rd4-Rd5 was a nice find to win material.
Keymer, on the other hand, scored his victory against Van Foreest. It was also an endgame, but this one was decided by a one-move blunder.

For both Caruana and Keymer, it would be their only win in the rapid portion—and they'd both go on to lose in round eight. Though the other three games in round seven were drawn, interested readers should definitely check out the brilliant fight between So and GM Levon Aronian.
In round eight, there were three decisive results. Praggnanandhaa defeated Keymer, So took down Caruana, and Sindarov landed another blow on Liang.

It wasn't hard to choose the Game of the Day: So's win against the U.S. number-one. He explained that after 12.Qb3, he was caught in Caruana's preparation, and that by this point, "I realized I either lose slowly or I go all out." GM Rafael Leitao takes us through the adventures seen in this game below.

Meanwhile, Praggnanandhaa scored a critical win at just the right moment to maintain his lead. This round was a close call for the leader; he was an exchange up, but the position spun out of control as both players pushed connected passed pawns. Keymer found the impossible-looking 59...Ne1! to keep his chances alive, and if he had found 60...Nd3!!, he could have saved this game (or more). Despite the chances we may find in analysis, the game ended when the German number-one let go of his bishop with check.

In the same round, Sindarov's win against Liang was a masterclass in playing against isolated pawns. After 24...g6?, Black ended up with four isolated pawns. Even after he sacrificed the h6-pawn, the others stayed weak.

Sindarov regretted not converting what should have been an easy win against Aronian in round five, but shared, "You need to forget this after the game finishes, but it's not easy." He is still in a good tournament position and has every chance to catch Praggnanandhaa in the blitz portion.

Referring to his seventh-ninth place finish in the Super Rapid & Blitz Poland 2026 earlier this year, he said, "I think the U.S. is better than Warsaw, but tomorrow is a tough day. We'll see, hopefully I'll try to get more points."

Round nine featured just one decisive game, though one of the draws—GM Anish Giri vs. Caruana—was a big miss for the American, who was winning but could not see it through. Giri and GM Leinier Dominguez are the two players to make nine draws in nine games.

Van Foreest scored the only win against the tournament leader, and he revealed that his mind-bending 18.a3!! was all preparation. "This is some prep I've had for ages. I didn't expect to get it over the board or anything," he said.

Van Foreest, who played spoiler against both So and Praggnanandhaa in the rapid portion, still finds himself three points above last place. He reflected, "Especially in these rapid and blitz tournaments, if things go bad, they can really go bad."

The blitz portion is a double round-robin, with 18 games in total. The first nine start tomorrow, and the leader Praggnanandhaa faces Keymer in round one on Wednesday. Sindarov, on the other hand, plays Aronian, the player who had escaped and nearly swindled him in round five.
You can watch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz events page.
The broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan and Maurice Ashley, as well as IM Nazi Paikidze.

The 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz is the fourth leg and final rapid and blitz event of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players compete in a rapid (25+10) single round-robin followed by a blitz (5+2) double round-robin for their share of a $200,000 prize fund and to finish at the top of the tour standings.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Praggnanandhaa Leads After Surviving Losing Pawn Endgame Vs. Sindarov
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: The 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz has only had one leader for four days, and he has been GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu. The Indian grandmaster put up the highest score in nine rounds of blitz, scoring 6/9, and is ahead o
body: The 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz has only had one leader for four days, and he has been GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu. The Indian grandmaster put up the highest score in nine rounds of blitz, scoring 6/9, and is ahead of GM Javokhir Sindarov by 1.5 points. The gap could have potentially been one point closer, but in their direct encounter Sindarov allowed a draw in a king and pawn endgame where he had the extra pawn.

The tournament concludes with the final nine rounds of blitz on Thursday, August 6, starting at 1:10 p.m. ET / 19:10 CEST / 10:40 p.m. IST. All players will face each other again but with the opposite colors.
The tournament looks like a two-horse race between Praggnanandhaa and Sindarov, though in nine more rounds of blitz, anything is still possible.

Praggnanandhaa did more than just maintain his lead; he put up the highest score in the blitz section alone. GM Levon Aronian is right there with Sindarov, scoring just a half-point less, but his 50% score in the rapid leaves him 3.5 points behind the leader.
At the start of the day, Praggnanandhaa led Sindarov by one point and GM Wesley So by two, and the race was essentially between these three players.

In round one, Praggnanandhaa defeated GM Vincent Keymer, but So kept pace by defeating GM Jorden van Foreest, while Sindarov made a draw with Aronian. In GM Maurice Ashley's words, the game So vs. Van Foreest was an "unmitigated disaster." So sacrificed one pawn, and then another, to deliver that disaster on the h-file.

Keymer, on the other hand, defended exceptionally well against Praggnanandhaa while playing on the increment for a long time, but eventually cracked when he allowed a passed pawn. Blunders in time pressure would continue to haunt Keymer throughout the day as he scored just 2.5/9, the same as GM Leinier Dominguez.

Round two slowed down the leader's closest rivals as GM Fabiano Caruana beat So and Van Foreest defeated Sindarov. Caruana won with an outside passed pawn, while Van Foreest found an unstoppable king march to the g3-square as Sindarov's pieces could do nothing but sit back and watch.

Nearly all the games in round three ended in draws except that, in an equal knight endgame, Dominguez lost on time against So. Even still, So and Sindarov lagged two points behind Praggnanandhaa by this point.

Though he was further back in the standings, Aronian played the brilliancy of the day in round four against GM Anish Giri. The game ended with checkmate on the board on move 30, and it featured a piece sacrifice, followed by an imaginative exchange sacrifice, a true "throw the kitchen sink" kind of game. GM Rafael Leitao analyzes the Game of the Day below.
Sindarov scored a hat trick in rounds four through six to stay in contention with Praggnanandhaa, while So drew Praggnanandhaa, lost against Aronian, and finally beat Keymer in the same rounds.

Sindarov's three wins came against Caruana (who blundered a piece), GM Awonder Liang (with a kingside attack), and finally against Dominguez, although Sindarov did miss an unusual mate-in-one in the conversion stage. He won anyway, with the three extra pawns.

So was thwarted by Aronian in round five when he blundered a piece to the nasty, although not difficult, 34...Rxc5!. If White captures the rook, he loses his queen. It was a second win in a row for Aronian, though he'd lose to Van Foreest in round seven.

So's win in round six, against Keymer, seemingly came out of nowhere as after 47.Nc2?? Qa2, White had the move but simply no good way to defend the b3-pawn. This would be So's last win as he'd draw the next three games.
All the while, between rounds four and six, Praggnanandhaa drew So, beat Van Foreest (with four pawns for a knight!), and drew Caruana.

Round seven brought an end to Sindarov's winning streak, though he was fortunate to even Giri. Sindarov sacrificed a pawn out of the opening, missed a one-ply response, then sacrificed an exchange out of desperation. Giri had a +3 advantage in the following position, but Sindarov weaseled his way out and, with resourceful defense, made a draw.

In the position below, 16.gxf3 wins for White, but Sindarov said in his interview he knew Giri would not play the most critical line. As predicted, Giri instead went for 16.Bxb6, was still up a pawn, but had very little time to convert it later.
Meanwhile, Praggnanandhaa continued his winning ways against Dominguez, who blundered a pawn, and Aronian took down Caruana, who blundered his queen.

In the final two rounds, the round-eight direct encounter between Sindarov and Praggnanandhaa was the most important. When the players traded queens on move 22, the predominant feeling was that it should be a draw. Then, Praggnanandhaa overlooked a tactic and blundered a pawn—Sindarov was winning. Finally, in the pawn endgame, Sindarov made a shocking mistake and let go of the full point. It was right in his hands.

Explaining his decision to play 43.Kf4?, Sindarov said, "I saw I'm winning [with] any move." As any chess-playing mortal knows, any move wins except the one you end up playing in such cases. "I was just playing moves," said Praggnanandhaa, who was in too much time pressure to evaluate whether the position was losing or drawn.

Had Sindarov won this game, he would have been a half-point behind the leader, with confidence and momentum. Even still, Sindarov thought he was playing "very well." He summed up his strategy for the final day: "Don't lose."

In the final round, all three players at the top of the standings—Praggnanandhaa, Sindarov, So—drew, leaving the Indian grandmaster still in the lead after four days. Praggnanandhaa reflected on the day, "My quality could be better, but +3 is still a good score." As for his strategy on day five: "Basically not to do anything stupid."
You can watch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz events page.
The broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan and Maurice Ashley, as well as IM Nazi Paikidze.

The 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz is the fourth leg and final rapid and blitz event of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players compete in a rapid (25+10) single round-robin followed by a blitz (5+2) double round-robin for their share of a $200,000 prize fund and to finish at the top of the tour standings.

news.title: USA Top Seed Without Nakamura As India Prepares Olympiad Double-Gold Defense
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: The USA is again missing GM Hikaru Nakamura for the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad, but with GMs Fabiano Caruana, Wesley So, and Hans Niemann, it remains the top-ranked team in the Open section. Defending champion India, host
body: The USA is again missing GM Hikaru Nakamura for the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad, but with GMs Fabiano Caruana, Wesley So, and Hans Niemann, it remains the top-ranked team in the Open section. Defending champion India, host nation Uzbekistan, and 2018 winner China follow close behind in what looks like a four-horse race. India is also the favorite in the Women's section, while China's omission of their stars is the biggest surprise.

The biennial Chess Olympiad, which takes place this year in Samarkand, Uzbekistan on September 16-27, is one of the biggest and most celebrated tournaments on the chess calendar. The lineups for 2026 have just been released and show 208 teams registered for the Open section, an increase of 13 compared to 2024. In the Women's section, there are 192 teams, making a total of 400 teams—20 more than in Budapest.
Among the 1971 players competing in the two tournaments, 233 are GMs, and 214 are IMs. The board order is not yet finalized and could still change until the very start of the event.
After going through the team lists, we have collected nine talking points.

news.title: Neuro Is Back Again For Another Year Of Focus And Chess

body: Chess.com and Neuro are extending their partnership for another year. Neuro will continue to help advance Chess.com's mission to grow chess by supporting events like the Speed Chess Championship and the Champions Chess Tour.

Neuro became Chess.com's official energy and memory partner last year. Since then, Neuro has become a familiar presence throughout Chess.com's biggest events and has supported some of the game's top creators, like WFM Anna Cramling and IM Levy Rozman.
As part of the renewed partnership, Neuro has launched a new watermelon flavor and invited Chess.com's CCO, IM Danny Rensch, to try it out:
Neuro is also offering an exclusive 20% discount on all orders for Chess.com members. Use code CHESS20 at checkout to fuel your next blitz session with Neuro's focus and energy gums.

"Neuro has been an outstanding partner to Chess.com over the past year," said Danny. "They've supported some of our biggest events, worked with creators across the chess community, and consistently embraced what makes our game special. We're delighted to extend this partnership and see what we can continue to accomplish together."

"Since we first partnered with Chess.com, we've seen just how well Neurogum fits into the chess community's world of long games and sharp focus," said Matthew Tilley, Neuro's VP of Partnerships. "Renewing this partnership means we get to keep building on that momentum together—and we've got some exciting things planned for the year ahead."

Neuro is a gum and mint brand founded in 2015 by Kent Yoshimura and Ryan Chen. Their products are designed as chewable alternatives to coffee and energy drinks, helping people stay focused throughout the day. Today, Neuro is one of the largest brands in the nootropic edibles space.
Have you tried Neuro's new watermelon-flavored gum yet? Go to their website to enjoy your 20% off and try it out now!

news.title: Praggnanandhaa Wins 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz With Round To Spare
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu won his maiden title and $50,000 in the 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz on Thursday. Though GM Javokhir Sindarov came within a half-point of catching him, Praggnanandhaa never let go of the le
body: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu won his maiden title and $50,000 in the 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz on Thursday. Though GM Javokhir Sindarov came within a half-point of catching him, Praggnanandhaa never let go of the lead in all five days of the event. He won with a round to spare when he held a pawn-down endgame against Sindarov in the penultimate round.
We don't have to wait long for the next event in the Grand Chess Tour. The 2026 Sinquefield Cup, the last event before the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals, starts on Monday, August 10.
Praggnanandhaa ended the tournament with a 1.5-point advantage over Sindarov, his closest trailer.
The Indian grandmaster takes home $50,000 and 13 GCT points for finishing in sole first, without a playoff. It would have been 12 if he hadn't won outright.

The top four players at the end of the Sinquefield Cup will advance to the Grand Chess Tour Finals, which comes with a minimum prize of $50,000 just for qualifying—and the chance to win the $200,000 first prize. Despite finishing second-to-last in this event, GM Vincent Keymer is still the weakest link, just ahead of Sindarov.

In the final nine rounds of blitz, Praggnanandhaa lost one game, drew five, and won three. He shared that one of his goals was to win both the rapid and blitz individually, and he did just that, putting up the highest score in each segment.

He also said, "When you see the score... everything looks smooth, but it wasn't the case. It was crazy. I mean, kudos to Javokhir, he kept the fight to the end." Indeed, Praggnanandhaa's lead was never secure until the penultimate round of the tournament, as Sindarov kept up the chase.

But before we get to their direct encounter in round 17 of blitz, let's start from the beginning. Praggnanandhaa's start was shaky; he made a solid draw with GM Vincent Keymer but then self-destructed against GM Awonder Liang in round 11. On the previous day, he said that his goal was "not to do anything stupid," but at the end of the tournament he said, "I managed to do it against Awonder... I managed to not take the draw and then I lost the game, which is exactly what I wanted to avoid."

In the following position, Black has a perpetual check anytime he wants it, but when Praggnanandhaa played 45...Qh2 it was clear he was going a little overboard. Black had no checkmate, and after 47...Qg1?, no perpetual check either.

Meanwhile, Sindarov made a draw with GM Levon Aronian in round 10 and then beat GM Jorden van Foreest in round 11, just in the nick of time. Just as Praggnanandhaa gifted his opponent a win, Van Foreest gifted Sindarov a piece.

Going into round 12, Sindarov was just a half-point behind the leader. A point and a half behind Sindarov was GM Wesley So, who won after GM Fabiano Caruana blundered a piece. So's last move in the game was a nice one; if the knight is taken, White recaptures on c6 with the rook and regains the piece on c5. It was Caruana's second loss in a row.

Sindarov, as close as ever to Praggnanandhaa, won a second game in a row, against Keymer in round 12, but Praggnanandhaa kept the lead by also winning, against GM Anish Giri. It was a positional squeeze in the Reti Opening, with an instructive breakthrough on the queenside. GM Rafael Leitao analyzes the Game of the Day below.

At the same time, Aronian won his last two games, against Keymer and Liang, to match So on 17 points in third-fourth place. With an extended streak, he might have joined the race, but Aronian went on to score just one more win in the remaining rounds, losing three and drawing two.
In round 13, Caruana lent Praggnanandhaa a helping hand and knocked Sindarov back down. He made it look easy with the passed a-pawn.

Meanwhile, So had a great opportunity in his direct encounter with Praggnanandhaa, but perhaps alarmed by having just 12 seconds, went for a threefold repetition. In the comfort of our screens, we can see 42.Re8 trades into a fairly risk-free queen endgame, and in fact the computers say it is borderline winning. As far as stopping Praggnanandhaa, this was So's last chance.

Having been cut some slack, Praggnanandhaa continued to speed ahead in round 14 with a win over Van Foreest after the Dutchman blundered a pawn to a tactic. After 29...f5?? 30.Bxf5!, White just grabbed the pawn, seeing that he'd win the queen if his bishop were captured. It was after this game that Sindarov, in hindsight, said he knew Praggnanandhaa would win the tournament.

Praggnanandhaa led Sindarov by 1.5 points as they made draws in round 15 with, respectively, Caruana and GM Leinier Dominguez. Meanwhile, So won two games in a row by this point, against Aronian and Keymer. But they would be his last two wins in the tournament, and So would go on to finish third behind Sindarov.

In round 16, the chase continued as both Praggnanandhaa and Sindarov won their games. Praggnanandhaa won on time against Dominguez in an equal knight endgame, while Sindarov outplayed Giri in a pure opposite-color bishop endgame. This set the stage for the all-important round 17, where Praggnanandhaa faced Sindarov with the white pieces.
A draw was enough for him to clinch the tournament, and Pragg held a pawn-down rook and knight endgame. In the end, he showcased how to defend with the distant opposition.
That was essentially the end of the tournament, though the final round still occurred. Praggnanandhaa held a draw against Aronian and Sindarov made a Berlin draw against So.

Sindarov wasn't upset with the outcome and said of his one loss against Caruana: "I learned from this game a lot, so I mean that game, I think my mistake was to exchange queens on b6 and I didn't understand the pawn structure is so bad for Black. But, in general, I'm fine. I tried my best chances, but Pragg played really well." He concluded: "Sometimes, playing really well is not enough. You need to be lucky."
Sometimes, playing really well is not enough. You need to be lucky.
Up next is the Sinquefield Cup, which features nine rounds of classical chess. It will run alongside the 2026 Cairns Cup, the strongest invitational tournament for women in the United States.
You can watch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz events page.
The broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan and Maurice Ashley, as well as IM Nazi Paikidze.

The 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz was the fourth leg and final rapid and blitz event of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players competed in a rapid (25+10) single round-robin followed by a blitz (5+2) double round-robin for their share of a $200,000 prize fund and to finish at the top of the tour standings.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Artemiev, Maghsoodloo, Wei, Bortnyk, Grischuk Grab Last Spots In Esports World Cup
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GMs Vladislav Artemiev, Parham Maghsoodloo, Wei Yi, Oleksandr Bortnyk, and Alexander Grischuk have snatched the five spots available in the $1.5 million 2026 Esports World Cup after competing in the three-day Last Chance
body: GMs Vladislav Artemiev, Parham Maghsoodloo, Wei Yi, Oleksandr Bortnyk, and Alexander Grischuk have snatched the five spots available in the $1.5 million 2026 Esports World Cup after competing in the three-day Last Chance Qualifier in Paris. They're all guaranteed at least $20,000 in prize money, but still need to finish in the top-two of Tuesday's eight-player Play-In to join the likes of defending champion GM Magnus Carlsen, GM Hikaru Nakamura, and GM Alireza Firouzja in the final 16.
The main event of the Esports World Cup starts on Tuesday, August 11 at 6 a.m. ET / 12:00 CEST / 3:30 p.m. IST.

The Esports World Cup is back, this time in Paris, and it's only grown from the event that first hosted chess players in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in 2025. The total prizes available have increased to $75 million, with over 2,000 players in action across 24 esports titles over seven weeks, from July 2 to August 23. In chess, there's $250,000 on offer for first place, while the winning esports team will take home $7 million.

A scheduling clash with the Grand Chess Tour has deprived us of the likes of GMs Fabiano Caruana, Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Levon Aronian, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, Wesley So, and Anish Giri, but the 14 players qualified for Wednesday's Group Stage—all already guaranteed $40,000—represent formidable chess talent.
The remaining two players will be decided in an eight-player Play-In on Tuesday.

As you can see, the Play-In features three players who qualified from DreamHack Atlanta—GMs Aravindh Chithambaram, Liem Le, and Andrey Esipenko—with five players from the Last Chance Qualifier. It was originally going to be four, but GM Alexey Sarana qualified directly to the Group Stage and so didn't need to take up his DreamHack spot in the Play-In.
That brings us to the Last Chance Qualifier, an opening event in Paris providing a last route into the Esports World Cup.

The Last Chance Qualifier was open to anyone, with 86 players ultimately competing in four seven-round Swiss groups before a 16-player knockout. It attracted strong grandmasters, but also players just wanting to savor the atmosphere. For instance, IM Malcolm Pein took a break from chess politics.

In the end, however, the groups, each with four qualifying spots, largely saw the expected players go through. Each had a clear winner: Wei (6/7 in Group A), GM Daniil Dubov (6.5/7 in Group B), GM Andrew Tang (6/7 in Group C), and Grischuk (6/7 in Group D). Strong players missed out, including GMs Laurent Fressinet, Eduardo Iturrizaga, Loek van Wely, Rinat Jumabayev, Saleh Salem, and Aleksandar Indjic, but in just one group were tiebreakers needed to separate the top four from the rest of the pack.

GM Velimir Ivic was the unlucky player to miss out on 5/7, after GM Peter Leko came through in a game of high drama. Both he and his opponent, two-time African Chess Champion GM Bilel Bellahcene, needed to win on demand, but that seemed impossible for Leko when he blundered the exchange.
From there, however, sheer willpower took over—that, and the black position being surprisingly tricky to play with little time and no increment.

The players who finished at the top of their group, however, had the privilege of starting the 16-player knockout in the Winners Bracket, while those in third and fourth started in the Losers Bracket, with just one "life" and having to win four matches in a row to reach the Esports World Cup. None of those eight players managed, with Leko knocked out 1.5-0.5 in the first clash of the day against French GM Jules Moussard. Let's take a look at how the five qualifiers made it.
For players starting in the Winners Bracket, the goal was simple—win two matches and you were in the main event. That was achieved by Artemiev and Maghsoodloo.

All the matches in both brackets were played using the same system—best-of-two 10+0 games, or best-of-four whenever the winner would qualify for the Esports World Cup. If tied, a single bidding armageddon game would be played, and we got to see that in Artemiev's first victory against Grischuk. After two incredibly tight games, Artemiev had to win on demand with the white pieces and he did, though only after 46.e5? almost let things slip away.
Artemiev took a spot in the Esports World Cup 2.5-1.5 after winning game two against Bortnyk on time, then losing game three, before clinching the match in game four.
Bortnyk didn't hide his disappointment, but the day wasn't over as he dropped down into the Losers Bracket.
Maghsoodloo was the other player to need just two matches. First up was Tang, who not for nothing is often considered the fastest player in online chess.
This time, however, he blundered when under pressure in the first game...
...then hit back, then blundered again at the end of the armageddon decider.

Maghsoodloo then faced the formidable Wei, but managed to win 3-1 after grinding out a win in a drawn position in game two and then taking advantage of Wei's desperate Modern Defense in the final game.

Wei began the day by beating GM Yaroslav Zherebukh 1.5-0.5, before losing to Maghsoodloo. That parachuted him down into the Losers Bracket, but meant he still had to win just a single match to qualify. He did, overcoming Grischuk 2.5-1.5 in a match that was far less smooth than it looked on the surface. Grischuk missed a huge chance in the first game.
Grischuk's horror was visible as he played through that game afterward.

It would go from bad to worse for the Russian, as in the next game he was lost in 12 moves, but the match very nearly went to armageddon—Grischuk was winning the final game on demand, but failed to convert.
The other player to hit back immediately and qualify after losing in the Winners Bracket was Bortnyk.

Bortnyk narrowly missed out on qualifying for the Esports World Cup via DreamHack Atlanta, but started the knockout in Paris with a tough challenge—against group top-scorer Dubov. That challenge looked even tougher when Dubov won the first game, but Bortnyk hit back in the second, squeezing out a win from a drawn rook-and-pawn endgame. That momentum carried on into an armageddon win, but then Artemiev won their qualification battle.
Bortnyk shrugged that off, however, and qualified with a 3-1 win over Tang. The first win was the narrowest—at least on the clock. Bortnyk delivered checkmate with just 0.6 of a second to spare.
Tang bounced back immediately and then had chances in both the following games, but Bortnyk grabbed two more wins to seal qualification.
There was still one last chance for Tang in an extra match for fifth place, but instead it was three-time World Blitz Champion Grischuk who made it through.

The final match featured two players who suffered match defeat twice over the course of the day. Grischuk lost to Artemiev, but then knocked out both Moussard and Dubov 1.5-0.5, before running into Wei.

Grischuk got one final chance, however, in a match with Tang, and he got off to a perfect start with a crushing win with the white pieces. Tang looked on course to hit back in the second, but lost his way in a winning position.

That left Tang with the almost impossible task of winning the next two games on demand to force armageddon, but Grischuk never lost control in the third game and ultimately won again to clinch a 3-0 win.

Tang still took $8,000 for sixth place in the Last Chance Qualifier, but now the prizes on offer begin to grow rapidly. First, the task of Grischuk and his fellow last-chance winners is to finish in the top-two in Tuesday's Play-In and join Carlsen and co. in the 16-player Group Stage. If they do, they're guaranteed at least $40,000.
Don't miss next week's action, as Carlsen attempts to crush his rivals' keys and defend his Esports World Cup title!

The 2026 Esports World Cup in Paris, France, features chess for the second time, with a $1.5 million prize fund and $250,000 for first place, while chess players are also part of esports teams that share a $30 million prize fund. 16 players qualified via the Champions Chess Tour, DreamHack Atlanta, India Rising, or as defending champion (GM Magnus Carlsen), while another five qualified via the Last Chance Qualifier (August 4-6) in Paris. That event had a $50,000 prize fund, with four Swiss tournaments and a 16-player knockout. The main event (August 11-15) features a Play-In to cut the field to 16 players, then a Group Stage with two double-elimination groups to halve it again to eight. Those players then compete in the Playoffs, a single-elimination knockout for the title. The time control for all games is 10 minutes, with no increment.

Colin McGourty
          
  

    
            
  
      
      
    
                        
                
                            
      
      
      
    
      


              
          Colin McGourty led news at Chess24 from its launch until it merged with Chess.com a decade later. An amateur player, he got into chess writing when he set up the website Chess in Translation after previously studying Slavic languages and literature in St. Andrews, Odesa, Oxford, and Krakow.

In the second tournament of the day, GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda caught GM Alexey Sarana in the final round and passed him on tiebreaks to take first place. In the third event, IM Anthony Atanasov recovered from a first-round loss to win the tournament, finding powerful queen sacrifices in three different games!

news.title: 14-Year-Old Jumps 469 Rating Points To 2454 In One Month, Earns 1st IM Norm
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: WCM Modipalli Deekshitha soared from 1985 to a live rating of 2454 in four European tournaments, climbing to second in the world among girls under 20.
body: WCM Modipalli Deekshitha soared from 1985 to a live rating of 2454 in four European tournaments, climbing to second in the world among girls under 20.

Just over a month ago, the 14-year-old Indian from Hyderabad was rated below 2000. Now she has reached a live rating of 2454, earned her first international master norm, and became the second-highest-rated girl under 20 in the world and the fourth-highest-rated Indian woman, ahead of GM Harika Dronavalli.

Deekshitha earned an extraordinary 469 rating points during a four-tournament tour of Europe, beginning in France and then moving to Spain and Portugal. The last two tournaments alone—the Pontevedra Open and Leca Open—added 297 points to her rating.
"It feels amazing," she told ChessBase India. "I wasn't expecting this much, but I was expecting WGM norms, or at least WIM norms. So it's very surprising for me as well."
It feels amazing. It's very surprising for me as well.—Deekshitha Modipalli

It's a remarkable climb, but it didn't come entirely without warning. At the KCA International Chess Festival last year, just months after she turned 13, she defeated GM Manuel Petrosyan, rated more than 600 points above her. In the Indian Women's Team Chess Championship earlier this year, she defeated IM Padmini Rout, who represented India in the Chess Olympiad on multiple occasions.

During her European tour, the highlight came in Pontevedra, Spain, from July 24-30. Deekshitha was seeded 81st with a rating of 1985 among the 92 participants. She finished 13th with 5.5/9, with all nine opponents titled, including two GMs and five IMs. Deekshitha scored five draws and won three games, two of them against IMs.
The highlight was her win against 2402-rated IM Facundo Vazquez.
The result secured Deekshitha a 2465 performance, a rating gain of 184 points and her first IM norm, as well as a WGM and a WIM norm.

Deekshitha Modipalli, just 13 or 14, was rated under 2000 last month, but made an IM norm in Pontevedra! 🇮🇳🤯She matched Sarayu Velpula's ridiculous feat from 3 years ago (!), and like Sarayu then, she's also gaining over 400 Elo from mainly Pontevedra & the Leça Open!📷: CBI pic.twitter.com/DtvYmDXr5w

But her European tour hadn't reached its final destination. The Leca Chess Open in Portugal, some hours south, started on July 31, the day after the Pontevedra event ended. It didn't take long before she proved that her result in Spain had not been a one-off.
In the second round, she defeated 2373-rated FM Lennert Lenaerts.

Vazquez, one of her victims from Spain, got his revenge in Portugal, but Deekshitha responded with consecutive victories over IM Daniel Rivera Kuzawka and FM Samuel Jesus Pereira Goncalves. A draw against FM Miguel Sismeiro took her to 4.5/7, in contention for her second IM norm.
However, the 14-year-old lost her last two games, finishing with 4.5/9 and a 2302 rating performance, enough to secure her second WIM norm. She also added 122 points to her rating.

Before her rampage in Spain and Portugal, Deekshitha scored two great results in France. At the La Plagne Masters, she scored 5/9 finishing 45th with a 2322 performance. She then played the Les Menuires Masters, where she finished on 4.5/9, gaining 29 rating points.
Her coach, IM Krishna Teja at his Velocity Chess Academy in Hyderabad, tells Chess.com that one of Deekshitha's greatest strengths is her ability to recover when tournaments are going badly.
"Deekshitha is comparatively good at handling pressure," he said, pointing to a recurring pattern of strong comebacks in the second half of events.

That was evident throughout her European trip. According to Krishna, Deekshitha scored enough points for a WIM norm at La Plagne but missed out because she had not faced enough titled opponents. At Les Menuires, she struggled through the first six rounds before winning her final three games.

Pontevedra was where everything came together. Krishna noted Deekshitha was slightly worse in several games against 2400-rated opponents but managed to defend difficult positions. At other times, instead of defending, she created imbalances and managed to turn inferior positions into wins.
He was arguably even more impressed with her chess in Portugal.

"Her last tournament games were the best, except the last two games," he said, highlighting three or four attacking victories against higher-rated opponents. He also praised two games she eventually lost after continuing to fight rather than looking for an easy draw.
ChessBase India visited Krishna's successful chess academy in Hyderabad last year.

By the conclusion of the four tournaments, Deekshitha’s live rating had climbed from 1985 to an incredible 2454. The rating gain also transformed Deekshitha’s place on the world rankings. At 1985, she was around 30,000th among active players worldwide. With a 2454 rating, she is now among the top 1000 highest-rated players in the world—a leap of about 29,000 places in little more than a month.

Deekshitha’s journey in chess has been unusually fast. Her father said in an interview with ChessBase India that she began playing in early 2021, during the COVID-19 period, when she was nine. Less than a year later, Deekshitha won the 2023 National Schools Under-11 Girls Championship. Rated just 1226, she scored 7.5/9 and took the title on tiebreak.
Her progress continued in 2025 by dominating the Indian National Under-13 Girls Championship unbeaten with 9.5/11.
Curiously, there is a parallel between her breakthrough and the spectacular rise of another student of Krishna and his chess academy.

In 2023, Chess.com reported on how then 17-year-old WIM Sarayu Velpula, rated only 1845 at the time, played the same Pontevedra-Leca double. She scored one of the most sensational results ever by finishing second in Pontevedra with 6.5/9 and a 2575 rating performance, earning WIM, WGM, and IM norms.

Three years later, Deekshitha has followed the same route through Spain and Portugal. While her rise spread across four tournaments, the effect was similarly noteworthy as she is yet another example of a heavily underrated Indian teenager climbing hundreds of rating points in a matter of weeks.
The difference is that Deekshitha is only 14—and she has already crossed 2450. "I am completely focused on chess," Deekshitha said in the ChessBase India interview.
She explained that she does not attend regular classes and goes to school only to take her examinations. Her father said she had stopped attending school regularly in early 2023.
Deekshitha has also had to become independent at a young age. By 13, she was traveling alone to local tournaments because her parents were not always available to take her.
“My parents are not that available to drive me to every tournament,” she said. “For local tournaments, I have to go by myself.”
Her ambitions are equally clear. “My ultimate goal is to become a GM and world champion,” Deekshitha said, “but my current goal is to become a WIM or a WGM.”
Deekshita is now returning to India, and her next challenge will be maintaining the level once her official rating catches up.

news.title: 16-Year-Old Alice Lee  🏆 Wins Women's Speed Chess Championship
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: IM Alice Lee is the youngest ever winner of the Women's Speed Chess Championship after winning the final two bullet games to clinch an 11.5-9.5 victory over women's number-one GM Hou Yifan. The final clash couldn't have
body: IM Alice Lee is the youngest ever winner of the Women's Speed Chess Championship after winning the final two bullet games to clinch an 11.5-9.5 victory over women's number-one GM Hou Yifan. The final clash couldn't have been tighter, with neither player managing to open up a two-point lead until the very last moment, in a game that could easily have seen the match go to tiebreaks.
16-year-old Lee said it was "extremely great to win this tournament," after also knocking out former and reigning Women's World Champions Alexandra Kosteniuk and Ju Wenjun along the way.

Hou is a two-time Women's Speed Chess Championship winner, but for a second year in a row had to settle for the runner-up spot. Lee is the first U.S. winner as well as the youngest player to win the title yet.
The final was played with the longer format of 75 minutes of 5+1 blitz, followed by 50 minutes of 3+1, then 25 minutes of 1+1 bullet chess.

It couldn't have been closer, with both the 5+1 and 3+1 sections finishing dead level. The 1+1 could also have finished level and gone to tiebreaks, but Hou missed some chances in the final bullet game and Lee emerged victorious by an 11.5-9.5 scoreline.

Lee confessed that she hadn't felt too confident going into her quarterfinal match against Ju, but after sweeping aside the women's world champion her confidence grew. By the time she reached the final she explained: "Against Hou Yifan I had a bit more confidence, because I felt like I got very familiar with playing these time controls and my general strategy."

The first game already established some of the patterns of the match. Lee opened with the Petroff Defense (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6), commenting, "I settled on the Petroff because I thought it would be quite solid and I know the main lines quite well, so she would maybe have to go for some of the sidelines that she did." One of those later would be 1.e4 e5 2.Ne2!?, but at least initially the Petroff didn't bring success.
The other pattern of the match was incredible fighting spirit. The solid opening ultimately led to a chaotic position where Lee was briefly winning, but went on to lose.
In the next game Hou had chances to do something she ultimately never managed in the match—win a second game in a row—but she let them slip and then blundered in a time scramble with 80...Kf4??.
After 81.e6 Hou could no longer stop the pawn, because her own king prevents her bishop getting to d6. If the king had gone to any of the three other legal squares the position would be drawn.
Hou hit back in the next game with a powerful attack, before Lee leveled the scores once more with a nicely spotted trapping of the black queen.
After four wins for White, it was Lee who scored the first win with Black, and also took the lead for the first time.
She did it with a powerful kingside attack, which GM Rafael Leitao analyzes as the Game of the Day below.

Lee wasn't able to break away either, however, with Hou striking back immediately with a powerful attack of her own. It then seemed she'd end the five-minute section by regaining the lead, but Lee somehow escaped from a seemingly overwhelming attack.

Lee shared afterward that she felt she was on the defensive all match, but enjoyed it: "In difficult positions, it’s kind of easier to play than in better positions, because if you lose, you lose—but otherwise, if your opponent doesn’t find the win..."
In difficult positions, it's kind of easier to play than in better positions.
With the scores level, the players moved on to 50 minutes of 3+1.
The pattern of strike and counterstrike continued, with Lee starting with a nice win only for Hou to hit straight back, after landing the heavy blow 14.e5! in the opening.

Then, suddenly, we hit a run of four draws in a row. Only the first two were relatively quiet, however, with Hou completely winning in the next—she needed to play one more defensive move to clinch the win, but promoted her pawn instead.
Hou Yifan was on the brink of taking the lead, but she promotes a pawn at the wrong time and walks into a draw by perpetual check! https://t.co/rOgPSO7u94#SpeedChess pic.twitter.com/WznTOSKrKm

As so often in the match, however, the players mirrored each other. In the next game, after a break, Lee was the one with an overwhelming advantage, but she walked into an avoidable knight fork and lost her extra rook.
The more familiar decisive action then returned, as Hou took the lead with a fine win with the black pieces, only for Lee to hit back in the very next game and level the scores again.

Lee had won 5-0 in bullet in her semifinal and was perhaps considered the favorite, but she admitted she'd been on the back foot in the match even in this section. Hou was pressing in a 93-move draw in the first game, before taking the lead once more in the next. Lee correctly rejected a draw in the next game, however, and hit back again after out-pacing her illustrious opponent.
Hou had a chance to regain the lead at a crucial moment, with the match clock running down, but, in a time scramble, she repeated moves for a draw when 78.g4! is a simple win.

If Black captures with the h-pawn, the white h-pawn is unstoppable, while if she captures with the f-pawn, the f-pawn runs. If Black moves the king, all three moves by the g-pawn win. That miss would prove critical.

"I think the final two games were very shaky, definitely a lot of nerves there," said Lee. In the first, she gambled, allowing Hou a big advantage, then built up a huge attack, then let Hou almost escape, before finally clinching victory. The evaluation graph told the story.
There were only three minutes remaining on the match clock, and it turned out we'd only have one final game.
In the end, though, Lee picked up another win and claimed a richly deserved Women's Speed Chess Championship title.

As well as the title, she added another $11,607.14 to her winnings ($7,500 for the win + $4,107.14 by win percentage), while Hou earned $3,392.86 by win percentage. Lee has come a long way since her online debut...

...but the world-beater still has modest tastes. Asked how she would celebrate, she commented: "I’m not sure. I got a lot of money from this match, so definitely I’ll be buying myself some ice cream!"
I got a lot of money from this match, so definitely I'll be buying myself some ice cream!

So that's all for the 2026 Women's Speed Chess Championship! Lee's career is just beginning, and there are two chances to see her in action again soon. She's one of the 10 players in action in the Cairns Cup 2026 that starts Monday in St. Louis, and then she takes on the world's best again in next month's 2026 FIDE Women's Chess Olympiad, when she'll be representing the USA in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
You can rewatch the broadcast on Twitch and YouTube. The games can also be checked out on our dedicated events page.
The live broadcast was hosted by IM Jovanka Houska and GM Arturs Neiksans.

The 2026 Women's Speed Chess Championship, which took place from July 6-Aug 7, was a Chess.com event where some of the strongest female chess players in the world battled for a $75,000 prize fund. In the main event, 16 players competed in a single-elimination bracket in matches played at 5+1, 3+1, and 1+1 time controls.

news.title: 'Orangutan' Opening Stars Again For Xiong In Bullet Brawl
news.author: jackrodgers
news.excerpt: GM Jeffery Xiong is off the mark in 2026 after he won August's second Bullet Brawl off the back of an explosive 10/10 start. Playing more than 70 games in the two-hour arena, Xiong accrued a score of 159 and earned the $
body: GM Jeffery Xiong is off the mark in 2026 after he won August's second Bullet Brawl off the back of an explosive 10/10 start. Playing more than 70 games in the two-hour arena, Xiong accrued a score of 159 and earned the $400 first prize, leaving IM Yoseph Taher, GM Nihal Sarin, IM Sergey Sklokin, and IM Renato Terry to squabble over the $250, $150, and $100 second-fourth prizes.
For the fourth week in a row, Greek FM Anastasia Avramidou won the best women's prize, this time with a nine-point margin over Iranian WIM Melika Mohammadi.
The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, August 15, at 12 p.m. ET/6:00 p.m. CET.

The 25-year-old Xiong is always a delight to watch in the Bullet Brawl arena due to his adventurousness in the opening phase and tactical panache. On Saturday, in a field featuring GMs Nihal, Oleksandr Bortnyk, Alexey Sarana, Sergei Zhigalko, David Paravyan, and 180 other titled players, Xiong announced himself immediately with a 10-game winning streak.

Yet, it wasn't the length of the streak that caught the attention of his adversaries and spectators, but the fact he played 1.b4!? or 1...b5!? (1...a6!? was played against 1.e4 with transposition in mind) in all of these games.
The anti-theoretical openings, known as the Orangutan, Sokolsky, or Polish for White, and the Polish Defense for Black, are rarely played at master level; however, this was not Xiong's first rodeo.

In his first clash with a GM, Martyn Kravtsiv, Xiong highlighted the benefit of unorthodoxy. By move four, the game began spiraling into obscurity, and the players were forced to freestyle their way through the middlegame. By move 20, Kravtsiv was submitting his resignation.

Against Romanian CM Mihnea-George Coman in the next game, Xiong fought his way back from a worse, albeit complicated, position before spotting a bone-crunching, decisive sacrifice on move 31. See if you can spot the combination below.

After Xiong's streak was snapped by IM Reza Mahdavi, he went through a lean patch where he managed to score just 3/10, allowing a pack including Zhigalko, FM Havard Haug, Taher, and Terry to overtake him.
The lead changed hands several times at the top until the final quarter, which is when Xiong returned from the abyss, reclaimed his throne, and never let go.
A late comeback win over Bortnyk from a piece down exemplified the grit of the American en route to a 13-point victory.
With this being his third win, Xiong moves up to equal eighth on the all-time leaderboard and is the 11th player to win three Bullet Brawls.
How to review games? The games from this week's Bullet Brawl can be found here.

Bullet Brawl is an exciting arena featuring Chess.com's top bullet specialists. It takes place weekly on Saturdays. The format is a two-hour arena with a 1+0 time control; the prize fund is $1,000. Like Titled Tuesday and Arena Kings, Bullet Brawl often features top GMs, including Hikaru Nakamura, Andrew Tang, Tuan Minh Le, and many more!

news.title: National Masters Chiu & Awatramani Beat Super-GMs Xiong & Awonder For 2nd Title
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: NMs Isaac Chiu and Janak Awatramani are the first duo to win the Bughouse Championship twice. Their biggest rivals were 2024 champions GMs Jeffery Xiong and Awonder Liang. The super-grandmasters lost the first match, won
body: NMs Isaac Chiu and Janak Awatramani are the first duo to win the Bughouse Championship twice. Their biggest rivals were 2024 champions GMs Jeffery Xiong and Awonder Liang. The super-grandmasters lost the first match, won the second encounter, but finally lost in the Grand Final Reset. Chiu and Awatramani earn $1,500 for their title defense.
Next month, the Duck Chess Championship 2026 takes place September 2-4.

As with the other community championships, there were eight qualifier tournaments, on August 3-6, to determine which eight teams would fight for the title on Friday. Each qualifier was a two-hour arena with a 3+0 time control. The winning team of each qualifier advanced to the knockout.

The knockout featured an eight-team double-elimination bracket. Each match had a 20-minute countdown timer, with both sides striving to win as many games as possible in the allotted time. The time control for every game was two minutes per side with no increment.
The clear favorites were the two teams that had won the event before, and they proved again that they were the best two teams in the field: Chiu & Awatramani and Xiong & Liang.

The teams to advance after the first match were: Chiu & Awatramani (8-5 against Aronsson & Dubansky), FM Eilia Zomorrodian & Michael Shinder (8-6 against GM Guillermo Vazquez & FM Roee Aroesti), Xiong & Liang (8-1 against NM Jalen Wang & Grace Ferguson), and NM Vincent Baker & FM Daniel Yeager (7-4 against GM Lars Oskar Hauge & IM Mark Plotkin).

With a two-minute time control and pieces flying from one board to another, we were bound to see numerous checkmates. Seven minutes into the match, Bok called out a checkmate just before Dubansky landed it against Chiu, although the latter's team won the match. "That's surprising, even I saw that!" said Bok.

Less than a minute later, before Bok could even finish his sentence, Vazquez landed another checkmate on the board, this time on the g7-square. His team may have won the battle, but as in the other example, the opposing team won the match.

With six minutes on the match clock, we saw Dubansky's king go on an odyssey from the right side of the board to the left. Just as Cuenca announced, "It's crazy, he's surviving here!" that king got checkmated, a predictable end to this voyage.

The two teams to advance were, coincidentally and unsurprisingly, the two teams to win the event in its previous two editions. Chiu & Awatramani defeated Zomorrodian & Shinder with a dominant 13-2 score, while Xiong & Liang made a comeback to win with a close 6-4 margin.

Chiu & Awatramani vs. Zomorrodian & Shinder was a blowout, but the 2024 champions were nearly knocked out of the Winners Bracket in their second match. Xiong managed to land a checkmate with one second left in the following game...

... but it didn't change the fact that their opponents would start with a 4-2 lead. In a wild game where both sides were attacking, with Cuenca pointing out a possible smothered-mate idea for Xiong, it was Xiong who got mated in one move with a queen coming to e2.

With six minutes on the match clock, however, Xiong & Liang made their comeback by winning four games in a row, first evening the score and then surpassing their opponents. When they picked up their fifth point, it was an incredible case of both sides having a checkmate-in-one move, with both sides stalling on the clock. Baker & Yeager were the team that had to blink first—and lose.
After winning one more game, Xiong & Liang completed the comeback and advanced to the Final against the 2025 champions.
It was a close match, but the team of national masters overcame their super-GM opponents 10-8.
The NMs started with a 4-1 lead. The following game, where they scored their third win, lasted just over 30 seconds in total, with Bok narrating it as "typical Italian theory" (a joke).

Later, however, the grandmasters came back to tie the score 5-5. The game below was the second win in a row, and Liang managed to checkmate with two pawns on the board, just as his partner's king was in big trouble.

By the time the match clock reached zero, the teams were still tied 7-7. The first team to gain a two-point lead won the match. At first, Awatramani led his team to an 8-7 lead when he checkmated Liang with a knight on g2.
But Liang tied it back up at 8-8 by returning the favor, checkmating with a pawn on g3 (on the smaller board):
The NMs won the next two games, with Chiu flagging Xiong in the final game to win the match and advance to the Grand Final.
Xiong & Liang dropped down to the Losers Final and faced the team of Hauge & Plotkin, who had won two other matches to reach this stage. The grandmasters won 7-4.

At first, Xiong & Liang coasted to an early 2-0 lead, but their opponents tied the score with two back-to-back wins as well. In game three, Bok said, "I think Jeffery is getting crushed. The question is if Awonder can get it done," but the opposing team won on time.
In game five, Xiong outstalled Plotkin, in a position where they were mutually losing, to regain the lead 3-2.
They won again to go 4-2, and in the game that followed Liang delivered the following checkmate by fianchettoing his knight in his opponent's camp. The score was 5-2 with six minutes remaining.
Both teams won two more games apiece for a final score of 7-4, in favor of the grandmasters. Xiong delivered the following checkmate to end the match (on the small board).

In the first half of the match, the two teams went blow for blow, but the grandmasters broke away to win the second encounter between these two powerhouse teams. The match clock for the Grand Final was 30 minutes, rather than the 20 minutes in the other matches.
Neither team gained a two-point lead for a long time. The NMs won game one, but the grandmasters returned, and the same happened in games three and four and also in games five and six.
The national masters gained a 4-3 lead with a very quick win, the game lasting about 50 seconds.
But Xiong tied it up once more at 4-4 with the following retort. Bok said by this point, "Both teams definitely deserve to be in the Final."
"Wow, impressive stuff!" exclaimed Bok as Xiong checkmated Chiu in the middle of the board, gaining a 5-4 lead.

The GMs won again to achieve a two-point gap for the first time, but then the NMs struck back with two consecutive wins. In the second of those wins, Liang somehow walked his king right into a checkmate.

From there, the grandmasters took over for the rest of the match. In game 15, Xiong played one of the nicest checkmating attacks of the day, chasing the opponent's king up the board with a bishop and three knights (and one more bishop appearing out of thin air at the end).
By the time the grandmasters achieved a 12-8 score, it was mathematically over. But they won two more games after that to win the match 14-8.
There were 20 minutes on the match clock this time. While the GMs seemed to start stronger, the NMs took over in the second half, a reverse of what happened in their second encounter.

At first, Xiong & Liang started with two wins in a row, making it six consecutive wins if including the last match. But the NMs cut down that streak by winning one game, and then another when Chiu forked Xiong's queen.
And then the NMs won again to take a 3-2 lead. Bok said of game six, "I think the story of this game is that Jeffery is getting crushed," but the game ended in a hilarious draw (found by Liang).
The NMs won two more games to gain a three-point lead, 5.5-2.5. "I don't get anything!" said Cuenca as Liang struck back to bring the gap down to two points.
But the NMs won two more games to essentially secure the match with two minutes to spare. This was the decisive moment, as both Chiu and Awatramani were drumming up winning attacks.
Although the grandmasters won the last game, it was only enough for a final score of 7.5-4.5.
Congratulations to the returning champions! Tune in next month to watch Duck Chess as the variant!

The Chess.com Bughouse Championship returned in 2026 as part of the Chess.com Community Chess Championships. The qualifiers occurred August 3-6 and the main event took place on August 7. Eight qualifying teams progressed to an eight-team double-elimination knockout. Matches consisted of a 20-minute countdown clock format, with two minutes for each side for the entire game (no increment). Only the Grand Final had a 30-minute match clock. The prize fund was $5,000.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: 10-Year-Old Aarit Kapil Wins GM Tournament To Score 2nd IM Norm
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: Indian prodigy FM Aarit Kapil has taken another major step toward the international master title, scoring his second norm with a round to spare before going on to win a round-robin tournament in Serbia ahead of three GMs
body: Indian prodigy FM Aarit Kapil has taken another major step toward the international master title, scoring his second norm with a round to spare before going on to win a round-robin tournament in Serbia ahead of three GMs and three IMs.

Extraordinary results from increasingly young prodigies have become almost routine in modern chess, but Aarit added another distinction to his growing list of achievements: at just 10 years old, he not only scored a norm—he won a tournament ahead of several grandmasters and international masters.

It has been just four months since Chess.com reported on the 10-year-old securing his first IM norm, as one of the youngest ever to do so. Even before that breakthrough, he came close to defeating none other than GM Magnus Carlsen in Titled Tuesday, ultimately settling for a draw.

Now the New Delhi prodigy has done it again. At the Rudar XXXVA GM Round Robin in Serbia,  Aarit went unbeaten to score a 2527 performance. His three wins came against GM Momchil Nikolov (2421), GM Radoslav Dimitrov (2489), and IM Kirill Klukin (2400), while six draws completed a result that also saw him finish first in a field featuring three grandmasters and three international masters.

Aarit had already secured the norm with a round to spare. He raced to 3.5/4 after beating Klukin, Nikolov, and Dimitrov, then made four consecutive draws to reach the required mark after eight rounds. A final-round draw took him to 6/9 and sealed the tournament victory.
"I was very happy, as I was just playing my natural game. And God is very kind," Aarit told Chess.com. He also expressed gratitude for the support from his coaches, school, and sponsors.
I was very happy, as I was just playing my natural game. And God is very kind.—Aarit Kapil
Aarit's win against Klukin was impressive, as he outplayed his opponent from start to finish.

This was Aarit's fifth consecutive tournament in Serbia this summer. Ahead of scoring his second IM norm, he dropped 25 rating points when he scored 2.5/9 and finished last in another closed round-robin tournament that qualified for GM and IM norms.

At the Serbia Open Masters earlier in July, he scored 6/9 and finished 30th with a 2316 performance. For Aarit, his second IM norm was a huge turnaround and yet another reminder of how quickly his level can change—a quality his coach GM Srinath Narayanan highlighted when Chess.com spoke to him earlier this year.

"Players of his level of talent tend to improve at a rapid pace, almost like they are getting better every day," Srinath said after Aarit's first IM norm. "I won't be surprised to see him become a GM in the next two to three years."
Aarit became one of the youngest players ever to earn an IM norm at the Menorca Open in April, when he scored 5/9 with a 2453 performance.
As Unstoppable_Aarit he also became the youngest player to ever reach a 3000 blitz rating on Chess.com. He recently set a personal high by hitting 3100, also becoming the youngest to reach that mark.

The result leaves Aarit with two of the three norms required for the IM title. He will still need a third norm and to reach the 2400 rating requirement before the title can be awarded. So there's still a long way to go, but he's certainly edging closer to the target.

Just one day after finishing Rudar GM 35, Aarit began another nine-round closed tournament in Serbia in a field that includes three GMs and four IMs. The 10-year-old started well with draws against a GM and IM, but lost in round three. The event runs August 8-15 and has an average rating of 2404. He will get no time to rest, as he will also take part in the Abu Dhabi Chess Festival on August 15-23.

That gives the 10-year-old immediate opportunities to chase the third and final norm he needs. Aarit's father, Vijay Kapil, says his son does not get tired of playing. "Chess is his first love," Vijay told Chess.com. "And he enjoys playing. That's why he does not get tired of chess."
