news.title: Caruana Scores 1st Win In Sinquefield Cup; Tan, Divya, Lee Lead Cairns Cup
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Fabiano Caruana took sole lead of the 2026 Sinquefield Cup after round one on Monday after beating GM Jorden van Foreest with the white pieces. All other games ended in draws—that is, GM Javokhir Sindarov vs. GM Levon
body: GM Fabiano Caruana took sole lead of the 2026 Sinquefield Cup after round one on Monday after beating GM Jorden van Foreest with the white pieces. All other games ended in draws—that is, GM Javokhir Sindarov vs. GM Levon Aronian, GM Vincent Keymer vs. GM Wesley So, GM Sam Sevian vs. GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, and GM Anish Giri vs. GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave.

There were three decisive games in the 2026 Cairns Cup. 2024 champion GM Tan Zhongyi defeated the 2025 defending champion IM Carissa Yip, GM Divya Deshmukh laid the hammer on her compatriot GM Vaishali Rameshbabu, and IM Alice Lee successfully ground out a rook endgame against GM Alexandra Kosteniuk. There were two draws, GM Anna Muzychuk vs. GM Bibisara Assaubayeva and GM Humpy Koneru vs. IM Stavroula Tsolakidou.
Round two of both tournaments is on Tuesday, August 11, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST.
Caruana, the defending 2025 Grand Chess Tour champion, was the only player to win in round one.
The leaderboard is already split in the Cairns Cup. Tan, Divya, and Lee are the frontrunners.

The tournament is a 10-player round-robin with a time control of 90 minutes for 40 moves followed by 30 minutes for the rest of the game, plus a 30-second increment. The event features two wild cards, Aronian (who started as a full tour participant but withdrew), as well as Sevian, who replaces GM Alireza Firouzja. All of the other players had already been in St. Louis for the 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz the week before, except for Vachier-Lagrave. The top seed, Caruana, is the defending Grand Chess Tour champion, though So won the Sinquefield Cup last year.

On top of the $475,000 prize fund, the players also vie to reach the Grand Chess Tour Finals. Just qualifying comes with a minimum of $50,000, with the chance to win the $200,000 top prize. The Sinquefield Cup is the last event on the Grand Chess Tour,  and we will know our four finalists, at latest, on Thursday, August 20.
All but one of the games in round one were drawn, but there's still plenty to talk about. For starters, it was Praggnanandhaa's 21st birthday.

There was potential for a bloody fight with Sevian from the opening moves, in a Ruy Lopez Neo-Arkhangelsk Variation, but it fizzled into a 99-accuracy exchange-fest. The end of the game, with four knights on the board, was entertaining.

Keymer played an experimental opening against So and gained a tiny advantage, but it was never serious. Sindarov, on the other hand, got a tangible advantage against Aronian in an opposite-color bishop endgame with rooks on the board, but couldn't make the most of it. It's humbling to see the world championship challenger admit to not understanding the following endgame position. He was sure the two-pawns-up endgame was winning.

The first game to finish was Giri vs. Vachier-Lagrave. There was a sharp possibility for Giri to grab a pawn on the 12th move, but he decided not to jump into those complications with the French tactician.

Vachier-Lagrave has finished in the top-three of the Grand Chess Tour for the last eight years, but he's at risk of falling out this time. He needs to win the Sinquefield Cup to qualify for the Finals. He said, "I obviously think there is a shot, but I have to play well to be ready to take my chances," and he would have taken his chances in round one if he got any.

He also mentioned that if Caruana goes into "beast mode," as round one seems to suggest, there's only so much one can do. The world number-two had a lackluster performance in the 2026 Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz last week, but the Sinquefield Cup is a clean slate. He and Van Foreest sped down a topical line of the Italian Opening, but Caruana finally took a 38-minute think before playing the move 15.Qf1.
In the interview, Caruana said he remembered looking at this position five years ago with Aronian.
Later on, Van Foreest's case became alarming when he dropped down to one minute on move 28 (he'd only get an additional 30 minutes added after move 40).
Caruana converted the game with his signature accuracy and control. GM Rafael Leitao analyzes the Game of the Day.
It's a good start for Caruana, but there are still eight more rounds to play. In round two, he has Black against Giri.

The Cairns Cup has the same time control and format as the Sinquefield Cup, but with 10 of the top women in the world. World number-five Assaubayeva is the highest seed in this powerhouse lineup, but we should mention Lee is coming in fresh from her win against world number-one GM Hou Yifan in the Women's Speed Chess Championship, where she also defeated World Champions Kosteniuk and Ju Wenjun. Any player in this field is capable of winning the tournament.

The only tame draw in the round was Muzychuk vs. Assaubayeva, and even there the opening was a Taimanov Sicilian. When both players perform with 98 accuracy, what can you do? In the other draw, Humpy had a winning advantage against Tsolakidou but let it go.

Tan found a beautiful exchange sacrifice against Yip, but then sacrificed a pawn for the initiative—a mistake. Yip found several accurate moves to hold the balance, but in her final minute, on move 35, she made a one-move blunder and resigned after White's move.

In the all-Indian clash, it was Divya who outdid Vaishali this time. Divya equalized convincingly and saddled White with an isolated d-pawn. The defense already required White to sacrifice the pawn, just to make sure a knight did not land on the d4-square. 27.g4 was imperative, preventing the knight from reaching f5.
Finally, Lee won a very long rook endgame after a single mistake by Kosteniuk, who was down to her last 37 seconds.
In round two, the marquee matchup is clearly the co-leader clash of Divya vs. Lee. Tan, also sharing the lead, plays Humpy.
You can watch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Sinquefield Cup or 2026 Cairns Cup Events pages.
The Sinquefield Cup broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Maurice Ashley, Cristian Chirila, and Peter Svidler, while the Cairns Cup was covered by IMs Nazi Paikidze and Almira Skripchenko.

The 2026 Sinquefield Cup is the fifth and final leg of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players competed in a classical round-robin tournament with a $475,000 prize fund and counts for qualification into the Grand Chess Tour Finals. It runs alongside the 2026 Cairns Cup, which is also a 10-player round-robin featuring some of the strongest women in the world, with a prize fund of $250,000.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: 🏀 Wemby, GothamChess Headline Hoop Gambit Festival
news.author: coachjkane
news.excerpt: NBA star Victor Wembanyama, Wemby to his fans, loves chess almost as much as basketball. For the second straight year, Wembanyama organized a summer Hoop Gambit Festival, combining his two favorite activities. The festiv
body: NBA star Victor Wembanyama, Wemby to his fans, loves chess almost as much as basketball. For the second straight year, Wembanyama organized a summer Hoop Gambit Festival, combining his two favorite activities. The festival was held on the outskirts of Paris on August 8 and 9. Along with a basketball tournament, the event included two chess tournaments and several side events featuring streamers like IM Levy Rozman, better known as GothamChess, and IM Julien Song.

The celebration of chess and basketball featured two days of rapid chess tournaments. Wembanyama visited both tournaments and played practice games with some of the younger participants. The kids were up to the challenge, and defeated their much taller opponent in every game.

Wembanyama also tried his luck against the famous chess streamers, but they were at least as strong as the children. These games against Song and Rozman were played on center court in a front of an excited crowd. During Wembanyama's matchup with Rozman, Song provided commentary in French for the fans. He switched to English when Rozman "sacrificed the rook" against the basketball star.
Wembanyama observed many of the games in the rapid event. Would you be nervous playing in front of a celebrity? The competitors didn't seem too worried.
While the basketball star got a taste of chess, the chess players got to test their skills at basketball. Rozman was up for the challenge.

Hoop Gambit debuted last year and continues to grow. Wembanyama plays chess frequently, recently competing with Mohammadreza Firouzja, perhaps better known as Alireza Firouzja's brother. Rozman analyzed their games.
NM Jeremy Kane is the Instructional Content Manager for Chess.com, and the author of several courses in the Starting Out series, Queen’s Gambit Accepted, Trompowsky, and Tarrasch.

news.title: Esipenko, Wei Yi Join Carlsen & Co. In Esports World Cup Last 16
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GMs Wei Yi (Team Nemesis) and Andrey Esipenko (Virtus.pro) are through to tomorrow's 16-player Group Stage of the $1.5 million 2026 Esports World Cup, where they'll take on the likes of GMs Magnus Carlsen, Hikaru Nakamur
body: GMs Wei Yi (Team Nemesis) and Andrey Esipenko (Virtus.pro) are through to tomorrow's 16-player Group Stage of the $1.5 million 2026 Esports World Cup, where they'll take on the likes of GMs Magnus Carlsen, Hikaru Nakamura, and Alireza Firouzja. Wei needed just six games in the Play-In, beating Esipenko, then GM Oleksandr Bortnyk, and finally GM Vladislav Artemiev without losing a game.

Esipenko, meanwhile, bounced back from losing to Wei to win four matches in a row, against GMs Liem Le, Alexander Grischuk, Parham Maghsoodloo, and Artemiev. If he wins a fifth consecutive match it'll now be against reigning champion Carlsen.
The Group Stage of the Esports World Cup starts on Wednesday, August 12 at 6 a.m. ET / 12:00 CEST / 3:30 p.m. IST.

The Play-In was a double-elimination knockout to reduce eight players—five who qualified via the Last Chance Qualifier in Paris and three who qualified via DreamHack Atlanta—to two, who would advance to the Esports World Cup Group Stage. Each match was played over two 10+0 games, with an armageddon game to decide ties. Wei and Esipenko made it through, but by very different routes.

"Wei Yi is in cruise control & he's playing fantastic!" said IM Levy Rozman on the live stream, and it was hard to argue as the Chinese number-one navigated the fastest possible path into the Group Stage.

It began with a repeat of the 2025 FIDE World Cup Semifinals, where Wei beat Esipenko in a thrilling tiebreak. The outcome was the same again, with a quiet draw followed by a fine bishop sacrifice by Wei in the second game.
When Esipenko grabbed the bishop he was lost, and Wei went on to convert and consign his opponent to the Lower Bracket.
That's our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao has analyzed below.

Up next was Bortnyk, who had only been able to travel to Paris after crowdfunding via his stream. He made it through the Last Chance Qualifier, and then survived an extraordinary first game against Le. Bortnyk explained: "I’d seen the checkmate, so I’d already given up, but then he took the pawn on f5, and I saw that I could trade queens. And actually I’m up a pawn, which I’d missed. Maybe I can survive..."

In fact Bortnyk soon switched to trying to win on time, but Le in fact was the player to flag his opponent with a little over a second to spare. The game was drawn, however, due to insufficient material.

Bortnyk won the match with a crushing win against a likely demoralized Le, and said afterward: "I’m so happy to be here, and already so happy with my result, that I qualified. I don’t have a team, so no pressure, I’m just chilling, enjoying Paris, enjoying this beautiful event, organization, and all that."
I don't have a team, so no pressure, I'm just chilling, enjoying Paris!

Some of the warm glow was spoiled in the next match, however, as Wei scored a 2-0 win, starting with another game where he could have sacrificed a bishop on h6. He didn't, but he converted a win with some more sparkling tactics later on.
Bortnyk got some chances to hit back in the second game, but ultimately walked into the crunching 24...Rxd4!.
If you capture on d4 with the queen, 25...Bc5 is pinning and winning the queen. Bortnyk dropped down to the Lower Bracket, where he was knocked out by Maghsoodloo.

That left Wei needing to win one more match to qualify for the Group Stage, and that's just what he did, taking down Artemiev, who before that had found some of the moves of the day. Artemiev needed to win with White on demand in armageddon against Maghsoodloo, but was only slightly better when his opponent's 26...Nd5? allowed the sudden killer blow 27.Nf6+!.
Remarkably, Grischuk fell into the same trap of moving a knight to d5 to attack Artemiev's queen, with 19...Nd5? also met by a killer knight jump in response.

Artemiev's run came to an end against Wei, however, with the Chinese grandmaster surviving some pressure in the first game of their match before suddenly breaking through in the second. The finish was nice.
For Esipenko, meanwhile, it would all be much more difficult.

One of the trademarks of the Esports World Cup is that all players in the main event have a metal key, and if you're knocked out the player who eliminates you gets to crush your key. Wei didn't get to do that once, since all the players he beat got a second chance in the Lower Bracket, while Esipenko got to destroy no less than four keys as he fought his way back from losing the first match to Wei.

What did he change? "I don’t listen to anything—no music. In the first match against Wei Yi I was listening to some music, but after this I stopped and I’m just having fun with white noise in my ears."

It didn't work immediately, as Esipenko got off to the worst possible start in the Lower Bracket. After correctly sacrificing a piece against Le, he couldn't find a follow-up and was suddenly lost. He tried to rescue the situation by flagging, but ended up checkmated.

Esipenko needed to win on demand, but he did, surprisingly easily, and then he managed to do it again, this time with the white pieces in armageddon. Le was agonizingly close to the draw he needed, but as Esipenko pointed out, after 36.Qe8! it was no longer easy.

Up next was a player Esipenko described as "a legend of the game," Grischuk, who had got off to a wild start when GM Aravindh Chithambaram mouse-slipped away a queen in a drawn position in the first game. Then Grischuk lost on time in a game he only needed to draw.

Grischuk had no complaints about having no increment, however, calling 10+0 "a great time control." He only lamented his own mouse skills: "At the end, of course, any person with decent mouse skills would make a perpetual five times, any player like Bortnyk, GM Nihal Sarin, Andrew Tang, but I didn’t manage to."

Grischuk hit back to win in armageddon, however, before the loss to Artemiev we witnessed above. Then against Esipenko he survived a tricky position in the first game before managing to surprise his opponent in the opening in the second. Esipenko admitted he briefly thought he was lost, but instead he managed to take over and smoothly outplay the three-time world blitz champion.

Esipenko's third match win in a row came against a player who had an extraordinary story to tell—Maghsoodloo postponed appendicitis surgery so he could complete the Last Chance Qualifier and reach the Play-In.
Esipenko began their match with what was largely a very convincing win, though he almost allowed Maghsoodloo to escape at the end before ultimately delivering checkmate.

In the second game, however, Maghsoodloo managed to hit back after slowly applying pressure until, a pawn down and panicking, Esipenko left a full rook en prise. He said it wasn't so hard to recover from that blow, since his position had in any case been difficult.

Once again Esipenko was playing armageddon, and once again he managed to win on demand with the white pieces: "I got quite an unpleasant position in the opening, but he played, I think, too fast, and I got some chances, a little better position, and I converted it."

That left Esipenko, like Wei before him, facing Artemiev as the final boss. Everything was decided by the first game, which had a wild finish. Although Esipenko had an extra pawn, the position was drawn, but it was almost impossible for Artemiev to play with the five seconds he had on his clock. Esipenko missed mate-in-one the first time it appeared on the board, but not the second!

The advantage on the clock had been down to some opening preparation, with Esipenko telling GM Jan Gustafsson, "Yesterday I checked this line, but not for Vladislav but for some of my possible opponents, and I think it’s very hard for Black to play there. Vlad found everything, but lost six to seven minutes to find everything, and then it was quite hard for him to play with little time."
That meant Artemiev had to win on demand to force armageddon, but he found himself much worse and ultimately offered a draw.
Artemiev took $27,000 as the player to miss out on the next stage most narrowly, while both Wei and Esipenko are now guaranteed at least $40,000.
What's Esipenko's reward for winning four matches in a row? He starts the Group Stage with a match against the defending champion Carlsen!

Four players will qualify from that eight-player group, which also includes GMs Nakamura and Hans Niemann. Once again it's a double-elimination knockout (players have two lives), with all matches best-of-two.
Wei, meanwhile, starts against last year's runner-up, Firouzja.

The 2026 Esports World Cup in Paris, France, features chess for the second time, with a $1.5 million prize fund and $250,000 for first place, while chess players are also part of esports teams that share a $30 million prize fund. 16 players qualified via the Champions Chess Tour, DreamHack Atlanta, India Rising, or as defending champion (GM Magnus Carlsen), while another five qualified via the Last Chance Qualifier (August 4-6) in Paris. That event had a $50,000 prize fund, with four Swiss tournaments and a 16-player knockout. The main event (August 11-15) features a Play-In to cut the field to 16 players, then a Group Stage with two double-elimination groups to halve it again to eight. Those players then compete in the Playoffs, a single-elimination knockout for the title. The time control for all games is 10 minutes, with no increment.

Colin McGourty

An amateur player, he got into chess writing when he set up the website Chess in Translation after previously studying Slavic languages and literature in St. Andrews, Odesa, Oxford, and Krakow.

news.title: Titled Tuesday Vet Wins First Ever
news.author: nathanielgreen
news.excerpt: As the main chess event at the Esports World Cup began in Paris on August 11, Titled Tuesday continued apace. FM Artin Ashraf, who plays most weeks and has recorded multiple top-five finishes before, was the victor outri
body: As the main chess event at the Esports World Cup began in Paris on August 11, Titled Tuesday continued apace. FM Artin Ashraf, who plays most weeks and has recorded multiple top-five finishes before, was the victor outright on 10/11 points.

There were 17 players who made 4/4, despite early favorites GM Arjun Erigaisi (round three) and GM Alexey Sarana (round four) losing and GM Hans Niemann (round two) drawing. None broke back through into first place contention, making this a Tuesday featuring some different players than usual, including teenage Indian IMs Goutham Krishna (16 years old) and Borgaonkar Akshay (17). Ashraf, for his part, was one of the players on 4/4, but made a draw in round six; it would be his only non-win until the final round.

Goutham, along with GMs Maxim Matlakov and Nodirbek Yakubboev, was one of the few players to reach 6/6... but none of them made to 7/7. Yakubboev lost to GM Zhamsaran Tsydypov, while Matlakov and Goutham drew a dramatic endgame in which Matlakov had had all the chances. The perfect score bounty moves to an even three grand ($3,000) next week.

With those results, Tsydypov, Ashraf, and Akshay joined Matlakov and Goutham in first place on 6.5/7, and 12 players just trailed with six. In the eighth round, Goutham and Akshay had a direct confrontation, won by the one-year-older player. Matlakov got two different winning positions over Tsydypov and converted the second. Ashraf also pulled off the dub after finding a subtlety with 28...Rxa2!! that his opponent, IM Reza Mahdavi, missed, then winning a classic rook and pawn ending.

In the ninth round, Akshay quickly blundered a pawn and then an exchange against Ashraf, and their game was over in 20 moves. Matlakov kept up with Ashraf with a somewhat more subtle performance over IM Aleksandr Usov, in which Matlakov trapped a knight on h5 in just 10 moves and had roughly all day—six moves—to round it up.

With two rounds to go, the battlelines were clean. Matlakov and Ashraf had 8.5 each and faced off, GM Rudik Makarian and IM Renato Terry played each other on 8/9 each, and four more players had 7.5/9. Makarian defeated Terry, accurately winning a pawn on moves 35-37, and for some time it appeared that would earn him a share of first with a round left.

However, Matlakov blundered a drawn endgame late, keeping Ashraf in the sole lead. GM Nguyen Ngoc Truong Son and Akshay alson won their games to join Matlakov a point back of Ashraf and half a point behind Makarian.

Makarian had Black for his comeback effort, and couldn't muster up any real chances before the position repeated a third time on move 30, securing Ashraf the tournament victory. Matlakov and Nguyen caught up with Makarian, and second place went to Nguyen on tiebreaks, followed by Matlakov and Makarian in third and fourth. Nguyen's topped off his second place finish with a picturesque checkmate about 15 moves after Sarana's ill-advised check.
*Bounty grows by $250 per week without a perfect score, and resets once a perfect score has been achieved.
These winners are announced by Thursday each week. If you would like to nominate a game or a move (including your own) in this or future weeks, click here!
Titled Tuesday is Chess.com's weekly tournament for titled players. It begins at 11:00 a.m. Eastern Time/17:00 Central European/20:30 Indian Standard Time.

news.title: Shreyas Royal, Bodhana Sivanandan Make History As Youngest-Ever British Champions
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: GM Shreyas Royal became the youngest British Champion in history at 17, while 11-year-old FM Bodhana Sivanandan broke the age record for the British Women’s title. Fellow prodigy FM Supratit Banerjee, 12, also completed
body: GM Shreyas Royal became the youngest British Champion in history at 17, while 11-year-old FM Bodhana Sivanandan broke the age record for the British Women’s title. Fellow prodigy FM Supratit Banerjee, 12, also completed his third IM norm.

British chess's remarkable generation of young talents has produced two new national champions and two new age records. Royal, 17, won the 2026 British Chess Championships in Coventry on Sunday, scoring 7.5/9 to finish half a point ahead of GMs Luke McShane and Michael Adams.

Meanwhile, 11-year-old Sivanandan became the youngest British Women’s Champion in history after defeating WGM Trisha Kanyamarala in a rapid playoff. She had finished the main tournament on 5.5/9 with a 2398 rating performance. The highlight came in the fourth round when she defeated GM Ameet K Ghasi.

The historic achievements came from three of the brightest young talents British chess has produced in decades, all of Indian origin. Royal was born in Bangalore before moving to London with his family at the age of three, while London-born Sivanandan comes from an Indian family. Banerjee, who previously represented Scotland before switching to England, is also of Indian origin.
Royal was 17 years and 212 days old when he secured the title, beating the record Adams had held since winning his first British Championship in Plymouth in 1989. Royal lowered the mark by 65 days.
It was the latest age record for a player who had already become the youngest British grandmaster in history in 2024, earning the title at 15.

The teenager made the decisive move toward the title when he defeated top seed McShane in round seven, to move into the sole lead on 6/7. It was an impressive game by Royal, who outplayed one of England's leading players with the stunning 22.Rd4!!

Following a draw against nine-time British Champion Adams in the penultimate round, Royal was in a three-way tie on 6.5/8. He faced 2022 champion GM-elect Harry Grieve heading into their final round encounter.
There would be no need for a playoff. Royal defeated Grieve to reach 7.5/9, while McShane and Adams both finished on seven points.

The victory is a breakthrough for Royal, who was described by GM Chris Ward as "the best prospect the country has ever seen." He went through the nine rounds unbeaten to claim his first British title, and gained 19 rating points, taking his live rating to 2533.

Curiously, there was another historic moment at this year's championship, also involving Adams. The nine-time British champion, and former world number-four, lost his first classical game at the British Championships since round seven in 1988. That breaks an incredible unbeaten run of 87 games, over a total of 37 years, 361 days, according to the English Chess Federation.
The record fell to the 18-year-old Ukrainian IM Svyatoslav Bazakutsa, who currently resides in Liverpool.
If Royal’s record had stood since 1989, Bodhana had an even older benchmark to chase. The tie sent the championship to a two-game rapid playoff with Kanyamarala for the women’s title.

Her only defeat of the tournament came against Royal himself, while her biggest victory came with Black against Ghasi, her second win against a grandmaster in the British Championship after she defeated GM Peter Wells last year.

FM Tim Wall, Junior Development Director for the English Chess Federation, covered the tournament for the official site. He summed up the frequency with which Sivanandan has been rewriting the record books: "It feels almost superfluous to talk about Bodhana smashing records, as this was just the latest in what promises to be another in a long line of impressive achievements by the North London school student."
It feels almost superfluous to talk about Bodhana smashing records, as this was just the latest in what promises to be another in a long line of impressive achievements.—Tim Wall

After seven rounds, she also remained in contention for a second IM norm and WGM norm, less than two weeks after she scored her first norm at the Dole Open in France. Two draws in the final rounds ended those chances, but they did little to diminish another remarkable performance by the prodigy.

Her 5.5/9 score left her level with Kanyamarala for the women's title, sending the championship to a two-game rapid playoff. The first game was drawn, before Bodhana won the second to win the playoff 1.5-0.5. And what a finish it was. Can you find it?
"Unreal! Bodhana has won. She is unbelievable, a generational talent," commentator GM Daniel Gormally said in the closing moments.

That makes Bodhana the youngest British Women's Champion in history, breaking the record held by Akshaya Kalaiyalahan, who shared the title in 2013 shortly before her 12th birthday. Elaine Pritchard held the record as the youngest outright champion when she won it at 13 in 1939. Bodhana has now surpassed both.

The 11-year-old has now completed the triple crown, as she has previously won titles in rapid and blitz. At the age of seven in 2022, she shared the title as English Women's Blitz champion, breaking the age record by more than four years.

The title adds another entry to Sivanandan's increasingly long list of records. Last year, at 10, she became the youngest female player ever to defeat a grandmaster, the youngest player to earn the WIM title, and the youngest to score a WGM norm. And in France last month, at 11 years and four months, she became the youngest girl ever to score an IM norm, breaking a record previously held by GM Judit Polgar.
In France, she also defeated former world junior champion GM Marc'Andria Maurizzi, breaking GM Hou Yifan's record from 2007 as the youngest girl to defeat a 2600-rated player.
In an interview with Indian TV station NDTV, Sivanandan talked about her goal to "become a grandmaster as soon as possible".
The event also delivered a major milestone for another one of England's rising stars. 12-year-old Banerjee has been ranked among the world's highest-rated players in his age group since he was nine.

In Coventry, he secured his third IM norm when he scored 6/9, finished 14th, and delivered a 2503 rating performance. It was his best result ever; his victims included two IMs, and he held GM Ghasi to a draw.
His finish against 15-year-old IM Frederick Gordon was stunning.
Banerjee had gone into the final round on 6/8, just half a point behind the leaders and still in contention for an extraordinary finish, before losing to Adams.

It nevertheless completed an impressive sequence of three IM norms in little more than a year. The first one came at last year's British Championship, where he, as an 11-year-old, defeated GMs Simon Williams and Mark Hebden. His second norm came at an IM tournament in Sheffield, where he scored 6.5/9, finished joint first, and scored a 2454 performance.

"We are extremely proud of his progress and grateful to everyone who has supported and guided him throughout this journey — his coaches, mentors, clubs, tournament organisers, sponsors, friends and the wider chess community," his father Sudip Banerjee told Chess.com.

With all the norm requirements for the IM title completed, the rating requirement remains the last hurdle. At 2393, he is just seven points short of the required 2400 mark. He is targeting that mark at the Hotel Stockholm North Young Talents, which is currently underway in Sweden's capital and runs until August 17.
Royal is 17, Sivanandan 11, and Banerjee 12. The British Championship offered a glimpse of the future of British chess, and that future looks exceptionally bright.

Tarjei J. Svensen

news.title: Aronian Wins From Lost Position; Lee, Tan On 2/2
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: Round two of the 2026 Sinquefield Cup featured wins on four out of five boards, with the white pieces scoring every point. GM Levon Aronian came back from the dead to beat GM Vincent Keymer, GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave bea
body: Round two of the 2026 Sinquefield Cup featured wins on four out of five boards, with the white pieces scoring every point. GM Levon Aronian came back from the dead to beat GM Vincent Keymer, GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave beat GM Sam Sevian in a complicated ending, GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu outplayed World Championship Challenger Javokhir Sindarov, GM Wesley So left GM Jorden van Foreest with a second consecutive loss. The one draw was GM Anish Giri vs. GM Fabiano Caruana.

The 2026 Cairns Cup featured another three decisive games that left two players in the lead on a perfect 2/2, GM Tan Zhongyi and IM Alice Lee. Tan beat GM Humpy Koneru, while Lee defeated the third co-leader, GM Divya Deshmukh. IM Carissa Yip recovered from yesterday's loss and gave GM Alexandra Kosteniuk a 0/2 score. The two draws were GM Bibisara Assaubayeva vs. GM Vaishali Rameshbabu and IM Stavroula Tsolakidou vs. GM Anna Muzychuk.
Round three of both tournaments is on Wednesday, August 12, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST.
Caruana, who started the round as the sole leader, has been joined by four more players. Two rounds in, half the field is in the lead.
Remarkably, in the Cairns Cup, two players already lead by a full point.
There was just one draw, and in that game, too, Giri got a small advantage out of the opening. Caruana defended with 99 accuracy, however, and drew with an isolated d-pawn in the endgame.

Another game that looked like it was heading to a draw, after blows exchanged in the middlegame, was So vs. Van Foreest. As GM Yasser Seirawan put it on the broadcast: "Jorden is coming to grips with the horrible realization he's going to lose a rook and pawn endgame that was a draw." It's a second loss in a row for the Dutchman, who played both rounds with the black pieces but has generally been fine out of the opening.

The major turnaround of the day was Aronian vs. Keymer. In fact, it was Keymer who was winning for most of the heavy-piece endgame, which Aronian had to play with an open king. That Aronian would win was at some point unthinkable. But as he said after the game, "I think when you're growing up without electricity and water, and you live like that for four years, you're not afraid of anything anymore."

Praggnanandhaa lost twice against Sindarov in his most important tournament of the year, the Candidates. Since then, however, the Indian grandmaster has beaten the world championship challenger in the 2026 Super Chess Classic Romania and now the Sinquefield Cup. He said of this exciting, generational matchup: "We barely have draws... Javokhir is someone who pushes to the end and I enjoy going for it as well."

The game started as a Queen's Gambit Declined but we saw opposite-sides castling and, eventually, Praggnanandhaa squeezed out a win in a pawn-up endgame that was defensible for Sindarov. The torture lasted 95 moves.

Vachier-Lagrave played a surprise on the very first move. Rather than his lifelong 1.e4 opener, he opted for 1.c4 in this game. He explained in the interview, "e4 has quite too many direct lines" and that he wanted a fight.

The French super-GM, who was "happy to be showing very decent chess today and yesterday," said, "the position was really complicated from start to finish." It was, but the decisive moment came when Sevian, playing with a pawn for the exchange, overlooked the tactical blow 33.Ra8!. The Frenchman won the b-pawn and eventually the game, though defensive chances still existed with White's open king.
On Wednesday, just one pair of leaders faces off: the all-American Caruana vs. So. With half the field leading, all the games will have great significance.
The majority of games were decisive in the Cairns Cup as well with just two very solid, very accurate draws.

Tan picked up her second win against Humpy, a disappointing fate for the Indian grandmaster who was winning in yesterday's game but only managed to draw. In what started as a Colle System, Tan's 25.b4! was the star move of the game, ripping open the queenside. Just three moves later, Black gave up the exchange for not enough counterplay.
Lee, on the other hand, took out her co-leader by—just as she did in round one against Kosteniuk—outplaying her older opponent in a pawn-up rook endgame that could have been held.

Divya is on 50% after that loss, as is Yip after winning her game against Kosteniuk. The former world champion's Petroff was met with the energetic 9.h3 and 10.g4, and much later, her only defense was to trade queens and go into a two-pawns-down rook endgame. Missing that with 34.Qf6? only allowed Yip to show the superiority of her queen, centralized on e4.

In round three, Lee has the white pieces against Assaubayeva. Her co-leader, Tan, has the black pieces against Muzychuk. The leaders are set to play in round five—but who knows what will happen between now and then.
You can watch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Sinquefield Cup or 2026 Cairns Cup Events pages.
The Sinquefield Cup broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Maurice Ashley, Cristian Chirila, and Peter Svidler, while the Cairns Cup was covered by IMs Nazi Paikidze and Almira Skripchenko.

The 2026 Sinquefield Cup is the fifth and final leg of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players competed in a classical round-robin tournament with a $475,000 prize fund and counts for qualification into the Grand Chess Tour Finals. It runs alongside the 2026 Cairns Cup, which is also a 10-player round-robin featuring some of the strongest women in the world, with a prize fund of $250,000.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Kenyan Chess Star Hawi Kaloki Dies At 19 Ahead Of Olympiad Debut
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: The Kenyan chess community is mourning the loss of Hawi Kaloki, one of the country's leading chess players and a former national number one. He passed away at the age of 19, just weeks before he was due to make his Olymp
body: The Kenyan chess community is mourning the loss of Hawi Kaloki, one of the country's leading chess players and a former national number one. He passed away at the age of 19, just weeks before he was due to make his Olympiad debut.

The sad news was announced by Andrew Owili, President of the Chess Kenya Federation, in a post on social media on Monday, August 10. Kenyan media reported that Kaloki had died earlier that same day. The cause of death has not been made public.

"It is with profound sadness and a heavy heart that we announce the untimely passing of our champion, Hawi Kaloki," Owili said in a statement, adding: "His passing is an immense loss to his family, friends, teammates, and the entire Kenyan chess fraternity. We mourn not only a gifted chess player, but also a young life filled with promise and potential."
His passing is an immense loss to his family, friends, teammates, and the entire Kenyan chess fraternity.—Andrew Owili, Chess Kenya Federation

Kaloki, born in 2007, emerged as one of Kenya's brightest chess talents after climbing from a rating of 1559 to above 2000 as a 17-year-old in 2024. His rise continued, and in February 2026 he reached a career-high rating of 2173, which put him at the top of Kenya's rankings. His August rating of 2054 placed him fifth among the country's active players.

He played his last tournament in Botswana in June, finishing with 2.5/9 at the African Individual Championship. In round one, he faced Egypt's number-one player, GM Bassem Amin, losing to the eventual runner-up.

Kaloki was set to play the FIDE Chess Olympiad for Kenya in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, on September 16-27. That would have marked the Olympiad debut for the young player, who had already gained extensive international experience.

He had previously represented Kenya at youth and junior championships in several countries around the world, including the World Youth Chess Championships in Brazil in 2024 and Albania in 2025, as well as several editions of the African Youth Chess Championships, where he competed as a reigning national champion.

In Kenya, he won the National Junior Under-21 Championship in 2024 and followed that up by becoming the Kenya Under-18 Champion in 2025. He was also a two-time winner of the Victoria East Africa Chess Tournament, taking the title in both 2024 and 2025.

He played for the KCB Chess Team in the Kenya National Chess Premier League. KCB, a Kenyan bank, described Kaloki as “an exceptionally gifted young chess player whose talent, dedication and achievements brought great pride to KCB and the country at large.”
“Though his life has tragically come to an end, his remarkable achievements and the inspiration he offered to fellow players and the wider chess community will endure,” KCB said.

Chess Kenya Federation remembered him not only for his strength at the board, but for his character away from it. “Hawi was a beloved family member, friend, teammate, and an inspiration to many,” Owili of the chess federation said. “His passion for chess, exceptional talent, humility, and dedication to the game touched the lives of many within and beyond the chess community.”
His passion for chess, exceptional talent, humility, and dedication to the game touched the lives of many within and beyond the chess community.
His younger sister, WFM Zuri Kaloki, is herself one of Kenya’s leading players and was set to compete in Samarkand alongside her brother.
His death made headlines across Kenya and triggered an enormous response online. One Instagram post alone has generated close to 117,000 reactions and 3,200 comments.
Kaloki’s family has requested privacy as they mourn his death.
Chess.com extends its condolences to Kaloki’s family, friends, teammates, and the Kenyan and African chess communities.

Tarjei J. Svensen

news.title: Carlsen, Nakamura, Firouzja, Abdusattorov Reach Esports World Cup Playoffs
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: Defending Champion GM Magnus Carlsen said he was "in no shape to play chess," but he still beat GMs Andrey Esipenko and Hans Niemann 1.5-0.5 to reach Friday's Playoffs of the $1.5 million 2026 Esports World Cup. He's joi
body: Defending Champion GM Magnus Carlsen said he was "in no shape to play chess," but he still beat GMs Andrey Esipenko and Hans Niemann 1.5-0.5 to reach Friday's Playoffs of the $1.5 million 2026 Esports World Cup. He's joined by GMs Hikaru Nakamura, Alireza Firouzja, and Nodirbek Abdusattorov, who all won two matches to advance, while the remaining 12 players will battle it out via the Lower Brackets for the final four spots. Those include GM Ian Nepomniachtchi, who thumped the table three times after a painful armageddon defeat to Niemann.
Day two of the Group Stage of the Esports World Cup starts on Thursday, August 13 at 7 a.m. ET / 13:00 CEST / 4:30 p.m. IST.

The 16 players remaining in the Esports World Cup are split into two groups of eight, who compete in double-elimination knockouts. Each match is two 10+0 games followed, if needed, by armageddon, and the format is simple—win two matches and you're through to Friday's Playoffs, but lose two matches and you're out.
Let's look at how the four players qualified for the Playoffs, ensuring a top-eight finish and already earning at least $75,000.

To say Carlsen was feeling under the weather in his first appearance at the 2026 Esports World Cup would be an understatement. He commented after his first match: "It’s good to be back playing the tournament. Today is a bit difficult. I’m not in any shape to play chess, but I managed to survive the first match, so hopefully I can survive one more, and then we’ll see!"

For a player known for slow starts, the defending champion didn't have the easiest of pairings, since he faced Esipenko, who the day before had gone on a rampage four match wins in a row to qualify. Muscle memory came to the rescue, however, as Carlsen gained a small edge in the first game and never let go.
All he needed was a draw in the second to advance, but Esipenko got a great chance to force armageddon before losing his way in complications.

Carlsen's next opponent, for a spot in the Playoffs, was none other than Niemann, though it's not obvious that was Niemann's biggest grudge match of the day. First there was a clash with Nepomniachtchi, who took the lead by somehow weaving a mating net in a drawn queen endgame. The two-time world championship challenger smiled at the end.

When Nepomniachtchi reached what Niemann admitted was "such a dry endgame" he seemed to have wrapped up the match, but once again all it took was one false step for the draw to evaporate. Nepomniachtchi couldn't believe what had happened, while Niemann celebrated with a fist pump.

That set up an armageddon that Nepomniachtchi began with seven minutes, 20 seconds and the black pieces, needing only a draw. That seemed a distant possibility when he stumbled into a miserable position out of the opening, but the U.S. star failed to find a knockout blow, Nepomniachtchi came right back into the game, and at the very end he might have completely equalized with a fantastic tactic. In executing it, however, he first put his king on the wrong square (vulnerable to a check) and then seemingly mouse-slipped.
That's our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao has analyzed below.

GM Jan Gustafsson probed afterward with, "You and Ian played a match recently, there was some debate afterwards—you guys good? Is there some bad blood, what’s going on?" Niemann responded, "Well I guess you could call this the tiebreak!"

Up next was a match that could have even more bragging rights for Niemann, against Carlsen, but the defending champion explained, "I managed to get into fairly comfortable positions where I could play fairly quickly and rely mainly on intuition." Both players pointed out that defending a slightly worse endgame is very tough without an increment, and although Niemann held on a pawn down for a long time he finally slipped on move 81.

There were no real chances for Niemann to hit back in the second game, and Carlsen was through to the Playoffs, meaning he could take Thursday off. He commented, "It’s really, really important for me to get that day off—I feel like if I had to play tomorrow, it would be very, very tough."
For Niemann, meanwhile, the path to the Playoffs is very much open, as he only needs to win one match, against either GM Sina Movahed or GM Alexey Sarana.

Nakamura came through in the same group, but admitted he was "very lucky to save the draw" against Sarana in their first clash. He said he took it as "a wake-up call that I need to be more serious," though also saw it as deja-vu: "It was very similar to last year, because in the first match I played Javokhir Sindarov and in the first game I was completely lost, and then he got low on time and messed up."
In the second game, Nakamura eventually ground out a win in a queen endgame, wagging his finger at the end when Sarana put his king in the corner in an attempt to escape with stalemate.

Up next was GM Denis Lazavik, who had come through an extraordinary first match against Movahed. In the first game of that clash Lazavik had totally dominated, winning with no fireworks and without giving the slightest counterplay. 16-year-old Movahed struck back, however, celebrating before his opponent resigned the second game.

That was just the warmup to a remarkable armageddon game, where Movahed built up a crushing attack. Lazavik admitted: "It was brilliant for him, and obviously after 30.Rxg6!! I wanted to resign, but I decided to play this last move 30...Rh8 and probably for some reason he didn’t find the last move." There was actually a beautiful mate-in-three!
After coming through that clash, however, Lazavik faced Nakamura.
The drama didn't end, as Nakamura built up a winning advantage in the first game but ultimately only won in 124 moves after having to resort to what Gustafsson called "the dark arts."

Nakamura was indeed unhappy, commenting: "I completely outplayed him and was winning on the board, but then at some moment I tried to simplify and he had a little more time than I thought he did and, of course, at the end it should have been a draw, but time is part of the game, unfortunately."

Nakamura held relatively comfortably in the second game and was happy to win the match and reach the Playoffs, adding, "Denis, I think, was representing AG.AL, which is leading overall, so it’s very good to at least make it more difficult for him to obtain points for them." AG.AL leads the Esports World Cup standings, while Team Falcons, represented by both Nakamura and Firouzja, is second—this year Carlsen's Team Liquid is very far off the pace.

Firouzja was runner-up in 2025 and gave up his spot in the Grand Chess Tour to compete again this year in his home city of Paris, but he got off to a somewhat shaky start against GM Wei Yi, who had come through the previous day's Play-In unbeaten. In fact, the situation on the clock looked borderline hopeless in the first game, before Firouzja suddenly moved up a gear and outplayed his Chinese opponent.

He admitted to relaxing a little too much after that, and Wei managed to hit back to force armageddon. Firouzja's desire to get Black was visible as he bid under seven minutes, and it paid off—he made a draw from a position of strength to win the armageddon.

Then it was GM Arjun Erigaisi, who had overcome his countryman GM Nihal Sarin 2-0 in the first match. Firouzja noted, "I had very high-rated opponents, top 10 probably in rapid, so I’m very happy that I got out of today and looking forward to the playoffs." The pattern of the match was the same as before, with Firouzja winning the first game in a sudden tactical flurry.
Again Firouzja needed only a draw, and again he failed, as he was smoothly outplayed by Arjun.

The armageddon followed the script of the previous game, however. Firouzja bid six minutes 40 seconds, played against 10 minutes for Arjun, and effortlessly held a draw to clinch a spot in the Playoffs.

Abdusattorov was the only player to win all his games, and it was hard to argue when he commented, "It was a great performance by me, I think!" The tone was set when the Uzbek star spotted an early mistake by GM Pranesh M in the first game of the whole day—12...c5?
Pranesh got chances to hit back in the next game, but one tactical miscalculation was ruthlessly punished to close out the match.

In the second match Abdusattorov faced GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda, a player who had also cruised in the first round with a 2-0 win over GM Benjamin Bok. It was a repeat of the match-up at the same stage in 2025, when Duda mouse-slipped on move five and resigned a crucial armageddon game.

This time we got a full-blooded fight, with the first game turning on the question of whether a knight could escape from h6 alive. "I thought this knight should not be escaping," said Abdusattorov, but there were chances before Black finally went on to win.

Duda had to hit back on demand, but got nothing against Abdusattorov's Alapin Sicilian. In a desperate attempt to generate some chances he kept weakening his position, with Abdusattorov playing strictly for a draw until ultimately he was provoked into taking another win.

It's far from over for Duda, who only needs to win one match in the Lower Bracket to qualify, a situation that's shared by Arjun, Lazavik, and Niemann. The remaining players—Wei, Nihal, Bok, Pranesh, Esipenko, Nepomniachtchi, Movahed, and Sarana—all need to win two matches on Thursday to qualify. There's no margin of error for any of the above, since one loss will now see them leave the event, and have their Esports World Cup key crushed.

The 2026 Esports World Cup in Paris, France has a $1.5 million chess prize fund and $250,000 for first place, while esports teams also share a $30 million prize fund. 16 players qualified via the Champions Chess Tour, DreamHack Atlanta, India Rising, or as defending champion (Carlsen), while another five qualified via the Last Chance Qualifier (August 4-6) in Paris. The main event (August 11-15) features a Play-In to cut the field to 16 players, then a Group Stage with two double-elimination groups to halve it again to eight. Those players then compete in the Playoffs, a single-elimination knockout for the title. The time control for all games is 10 minutes, with no increment.

Colin McGourty
          
  

    
            
  
      
      
    
                        
                
                            
      
      
      
    
      


              
          Colin McGourty led news at Chess24 from its launch until it merged with Chess.com a decade later. An amateur player, he got into chess writing when he set up the website Chess in Translation after previously studying Slavic languages and literature in St. Andrews, Odesa, Oxford, and Krakow.

news.title: So Leads Sinquefield Cup; Divya Deals Kosteniuk 3rd Loss
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Wesley So broke out to the sole lead of the 2026 Sinquefield Cup with a win, with the black pieces, over GM Fabiano Caruana. There were two more decisive games: GM Vincent Keymer bounced back from yesterday's loss wit
body: GM Wesley So broke out to the sole lead of the 2026 Sinquefield Cup with a win, with the black pieces, over GM Fabiano Caruana. There were two more decisive games: GM Vincent Keymer bounced back from yesterday's loss with a win against GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and GM Sam Sevian pulled water from stone against GM Anish Giri in an opposite-color bishop endgame to win after 110 moves. GMs Maxime Vachier-Lagrave and Levon Aronian are a half-point behind So, after making draws with GMs Javokhir Sindarov and Jorden van Foreest.

Round three was the quietest so far at the 2026 Cairns Cup. GM Divya Deshmukh jumped to third place after a second win, against GM Alexandra Kosteniuk, a third loss for the latter. GM Tan Zhongyi and IM Alice Lee stay in the lead after making draws with GM Anna Muzychuk and GM Bibisara Assaubayeva. There were two more draws in GM Humpy Koneru vs. IM Carissa Yip and GM Vaishali Rameshbabu vs. IM Stavroula Tsolakidou.
Round four of both tournaments is on Thursday, August 13, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST.
So jumps to the sole lead, while Keymer is a point behind. Eight out of the 15 games in the first three rounds so far have been decisive.
Divya won the only decisive game to reach sole third, while Kosteniuk continues with zero points after three rounds.

So's victory against Caruana was the first game to end. It was an opening disaster for the world number-two, who had prepared something in the sharp Samisch Variation of the Nimzo-Indian Defense. What he had prepared wasn't clear, however, as he sank into a 30-minute think on move 14, with his pawn hanging on c4 and White needing to attack. Curiously, So said he studied the same line earlier this year, for White, in preparation for the U.S. Championship.

White's best continuation was the crude 14.Rf4, followed by Rh6 and dangling the coffeehouse threat of Bxh6 over Black's head. But Caruana instead played 14.e5, the bailout, transitioning into a pawn-down endgame. On this move, So said, "I'm not getting checkmated no more."

As his podcast co-host GM Cristian Chirila diagnosed, "The gods of chess simply punished Fabi in this one because he went against his nature. Rf4 was his nature, his fighting spirit... he tried to bailout, and it wasn't a clean bailout."

The second decisive result was Keymer vs. Praggnanandhaa, an opening disaster for the Indian grandmaster. Keymer lost a winning position against Aronian the previous day and said, "I guess it was about the most painful and unnecessary loss in a long time." Now he's back on 50 percent.
Something went wrong for Praggnanandhaa early on, and by move 11 in the Catalan Opening, GM Peter Svidler quipped, "There's risk-taking and then there's this."

Praggnanandhaa still put up a great fight and got back into the game—that is, until 37...Na3?, an instantly losing move. Keymer launched his queen onto the kingside and won with a unique checkmate, with two knights. GM Rafael Leitao goes over the Game of the Day below.

Meanwhile, Sindarov vs. Vachier-Lagrave and Van Foreest vs. Aronian ended in draws, but both games were sharp. Sindarov vs. Vachier-Lagrave was a Queen's Gambit Accepted; Black found a nice pawn sacrifice, and although White was better at some points, the advantage was never massive. Van Foreest was a pawn up with realistic chances to win, but Aronian escaped again—except with a draw this time, not a win.

Sevian vs. Giri reached an opposite-color bishop endgame that looked likely to be a draw, but the young American ground out a long win, with two pawns vs. one pawn on the same side of the board. Sevian missed a direct win on move 39, and it took him another 71 moves to get the deserved result.
Aronian has the white pieces against the leader on Thursday. An especially exciting clash of generations is Vachier-Lagrave vs. Keymer.

The majority of games were solid this round after the bloodshed over the two days prior. Divya scored the only win, and it was kind of a self-destruction by Kosteniuk in the opening. By move nine, Black was already better with 9...e6!. Kosteniuk's demons in the first rounds have multiplied as the former world champion sits on 0/3.

Muzychuk vs. Tan was a solid draw in the Alapin Sicilian (99.3 and 99.5 accuracy, respectively). We saw sharper fights in Lee vs. Assaubayeva, which even started in the King's Indian Defense, and Humpy vs. Yip, where both sides enjoyed advantages at different points of the game. But they ended in draws, leaving the rest of the scoreboard unchanged.

In round four, Tan has the white pieces against Vaishali, while Lee will defend with the black pieces against Tsolakidou. We will see if Kosteniuk can find her form on Thursday, but she's playing the highest seed, Assaubayeva.
You can watch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Sinquefield Cup or 2026 Cairns Cup Events pages.
The Sinquefield Cup broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Maurice Ashley, Cristian Chirila, and Peter Svidler, while the Cairns Cup was covered by IMs Nazi Paikidze and Almira Skripchenko.

The 2026 Sinquefield Cup is the fifth and final leg of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players competed in a classical round-robin tournament with a $475,000 prize fund and counts for qualification into the Grand Chess Tour Finals. It runs alongside the 2026 Cairns Cup, which is also a 10-player round-robin featuring some of the strongest women in the world, with a prize fund of $250,000.

news.title: Lazavik Ousts Nepomniachtchi, Joins Arjun, Nihal, Niemann In Quarterfinals
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: 19-year-old GM Denis Lazavik pulled off the day's biggest upset to defeat GM Ian Nepomniachtchi and book a 2026 Esports World Cup quarterfinal against GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov. He's joined by GM Nihal Sarin, who faces GM
body: 19-year-old GM Denis Lazavik pulled off the day's biggest upset to defeat GM Ian Nepomniachtchi and book a 2026 Esports World Cup quarterfinal against GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov. He's joined by GM Nihal Sarin, who faces GM Magnus Carlsen in a repeat of their 2025 quarterfinal, GM Arjun Erigaisi, who faces GM Hikaru Nakamura, and GM Hans Niemann, who will take on GM Alireza Firouzja.
The Esports World Cup Playoffs begin on Friday, August 14 at 7 a.m. ET / 13:00 CEST / 4:30 p.m. IST.

The Lower Bracket of each group was completed on Thursday, with four more players qualifying for the Playoffs. There was no longer a margin for error, as any match loss meant the player left the event and had their key crushed.
Let's take a look at the four players who qualified for the Playoffs.

Nihal had lost 2-0 to Arjun in his first match in Paris, so had to win two matches to qualify via the Lower Bracket. That's just what he did, beginning with a hard-fought victory over the formidable GM Wei Yi. It felt deserved, not least because Nihal had been a whole rook up in the first game, but let the win slip away.

The second game also saw Nihal pressing before it ended in a draw, while the armageddon was a tense battle, with Wei saying he thought he'd had the board-splitting 13...Bd4! on his computer while preparing.
The point is to interfere with the defense of the bishop on d5.

From there, however, Wei lost his way, got a rook trapped, and admitted he was lost—except that he had very decent chances of flagging his opponent to pick up the win. Wei never seemed to have his heart in it, however, and had even dropped lower on the clock when he decided to resign.
As he commented: "I think I didn’t have too much experience in bullet games, so maybe I should play more bullet after this!"

Wei was out, while Nihal advanced to face GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda, and once again the dilemma was posed: is it worth trying to flag Nihal? Duda had 14 seconds to Nihal's four, but decided to take a draw by repetition.

The Polish star explained: "I got a slightly better position but completely misplayed it, it was just a two-results game with better time and I managed actually to get a bit worse at some point. In the end, maybe I could have tried to flag him, but I don’t think I would have succeeded, to be honest, because it was pretty simple for him to play. He just goes after my e3-pawn, and everything was defended for him."

That miss proved costly when Nihal won the second game to clinch the match. Duda identified his main mistake as the "super-stupid" 27...Nc4?!, with the problem being that after 28.b3 he was planning to capture on e3, only to realize too late that Nihal could avoid the loss of three pawns.

Nihal's victory gave him a spot in the Playoffs and, as he would later find out, a rematch of the 2025 quarterfinal against Carlsen that he lost 2.5-0.5. Carlsen got to pick between Nihal and Arjun, and explained: "They’re both very, very good players but stylistically I think Arjun is very difficult for anybody and I thought out of two very, very good players this was the more sensible choice."
I think Arjun is very difficult for anybody and I thought out of two very, very good players this was the more sensible choice.
—Magnus Carlsen on picking Nihal Sarin instead of Arjun Erigaisi
Nihal admitted the defending champion wasn't his ideal opponent: "Not very happy, but I’ll just try to play my best and give as good a fight as I can and just see what happens!"
Arjun had won one match on the first day, so just needed to win one in the Lower Bracket and could wait as his potential opponents battled it out.

Those were GMs Pranesh M and Benjamin Bok, who competed in a real slugfest. The first game was remarkable, as Pranesh had a winning position and four minutes against his opponent's 20 seconds, so that it seemed he could win either on the board or the clock. Finding a clear win wasn't so easy, however, and Bok was even briefly winning in the wild finish that followed—but that was where he needed more seconds.

In the next game, however, Bok did manage to demonstrate great speed to hit back with a win. That meant armageddon, where Pranesh, playing with the black pieces, struck with some fine tactics and then forced the draw he needed to progress.

Up next was Arjun, who did Arjun things. In the first game, the Indian number-one entered an endgame a full pawn down, with the only question seeming to be whether he could survive. Instead he pounced on a mistake to gain counterplay, won a pawn, and then ground out a win in what should still have been a drawn endgame.
In the next clash Pranesh applied pressure and at times was winning amid the chaos, but Arjun remained icy cool, with a heartrate half his opponent's.
Eventually he prevailed and delivered checkmate again—it's understandable that Carlsen didn't want to face him. Instead, Arjun will take on Nakamura in Friday's Playoffs.
Niemann was another player who just needed to win one match, but it was an epic clash between arguably the most emotional players in the whole event.
16-year-old GM Sina Movahed's day started earlier, as he suddenly took over tactically against GM Alexey Sarana and delivered checkmate.
Sarana hit back, however, squeezing out a win in a queen endgame with a couple of seconds to spare—an outcome Movahed called "heartbreaking."

The youngster recovered for the armageddon, however, and noted that his opponent played into his preparation. Movahed was asked about the wild position he keeps getting and responded: "I would like to get more solid positions, but somehow I can’t. I would like to get decent, good positional chess, but I usually go for lines which require a lot of calculation, and somehow the game becomes really unclear."

There would be no quiet, positional chess in the next match either, with Niemann starting by squeezing out a win in a tricky endgame—Movahed could have held, but picked a line at the end that lost by a single tempo.

The second game was extraordinary, with Niemann mixing up his opening line but was still doing OK despite Movahed getting four pawns for a piece. Giving up a fifth pawn was uncalled for, however, and later just when he'd fought his way back into the game Niemann sacrificed a rook for nothing concrete, a decision he called "so stupid."

Armageddon beckoned, but one more slip and Movahed slammed the table mid-game as he realized he had to give up his queen. It was still anyone's game in the time scramble, but in the end Niemann managed to swap off everything for the draw he needed to clinch the match.
"He put up a great fight and it was a great match!" said Niemann, and it's clear Movahed is going to be a huge threat to the chess elite in the coming years.

Niemann, meanwhile, goes forward to the Quarterfinals, where he faces last year's runner-up, Firouzja. In fact, Niemann is just one of two players to qualify who didn't reach the same stage in 2025, when we saw the matchups Arjun vs. Nepomniachtchi, Abdusattorov vs. Firouzja, Carlsen vs. Nihal, and Nakamura vs. GM Levon Aronian (this year competing in St. Louis instead).
The other new player is 19-year-old Lazavik, who knocked out one of last year's quarterfinalists, two-time world championship challenger Nepomniachtchi.

Nepomniachtchi had perhaps the toughest task of the day, needing to beat two very tough opponents. First up was GM Andrey Esipenko, and the task got tougher when Esipenko took over with the black pieces. He later lamented: "I think in the first game I had a huge advantage in the endgame, I think it was just winning because I have two bishops, an extra pawn. I don’t know how I managed to lose it..."
It was a typical death by a thousand cuts, as Nepomniachtchi took over and ultimately weaved a mating net.
Nepomniachtchi gave Esipenko no real chances of a comeback in the second game, and advanced to play Lazavik.

Lazavik is already a monster of online chess, but when in the first game he failed to get anything with the white pieces it felt as though the momentum had swung to Nepomniachtchi. That impression increased when he correctly sacrificed a bishop in the second game.

The position was highly double-edged, however, with Lazavik responding in kind by picking up the pawn on b2. If Nepomniachtchi had played accurately he might have kept an advantage, but instead his position soon collapsed, with Lazavik finishing things off flawlessly. Nepomniachtchi was furious with himself.
That's our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao has analyzed below.
Lazavik was almost flawless on the chessboard, but hasn't quite mastered crushing keys yet.
He's already guaranteed $75,000, as are all the players in the Playoffs, and his next opponent will be Abdusattorov.

Abdusattorov was another player who got to choose, with Niemann the other option. He explained, "I played many games against Hans, so I thought that this time it would be interesting to play against Denis, because I mostly played against him online, so it would be interesting."
Lazavik had no complaints: "I think it’s nice, because I didn’t want to play against Alireza!"

The Quarterfinals follow the same format of 10+0 games, but now it's best-of-four instead of best-of-two, while the Semifinals will be best-of-six. We'll already know our two finalists by the end of Friday's session!

The 2026 Esports World Cup in Paris, France has a $1.5 million chess prize fund and $250,000 for first place, while esports teams also share a $30 million prize fund. 16 players qualified via the Champions Chess Tour, DreamHack Atlanta, India Rising, or as defending champion (Carlsen), while another five qualified via the Last Chance Qualifier (August 4-6) in Paris. The main event (August 11-15) features a Play-In to cut the field to 16 players, then a Group Stage with two double-elimination groups to halve it again to eight. Those players then compete in the Playoffs, a single-elimination knockout for the title. The time control for all games is 10 minutes, with no increment.

news.title: Praggnanandhaa Beats Van Foreest; Tan Leads By Full Point
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Wesley So continues to lead after round four of the 2026 Sinquefield Cup on Thursday. There was one decisive game, where GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu gave GM Jorden van Foreest his third loss. Praggnanandhaa is now ha
body: GM Wesley So continues to lead after round four of the 2026 Sinquefield Cup on Thursday. There was one decisive game, where GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu gave GM Jorden van Foreest his third loss. Praggnanandhaa is now half a point behind the leader, as are GMs  Maxime Vachier-Lagrave and Levon Aronian  (who drew GMs Vincent Keymer and So himself). We saw two other draws in GM Anish Giri vs. GM Javokhir Sindarov and GM Sam Sevian vs. GM Fabiano Caruana.

In the 2026 Cairns Cup round four, we saw three decisive games, and it could have been four. GM Tan Zhongyi leads by a full point after beating GM Vaishali Rameshbabu. There are four players behind her: GM Bibisara Assaubayeva (who gave GM Alexandra Kosteniuk her fourth loss), GM Divya Deshmukh (who saved a lost knight endgame vs. IM Carissa Yip), and IM Alice Lee, who lost to the fourth player in the tie, IM Stavroula Tsolakidou. The one draw was GM Humpy Koneru vs. GM Anna Muzychuk.
Round five of both tournaments is on Friday, August 14, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. It is followed by a rest day on Saturday.
Except for Praggnanandhaa rising higher, the standings are unchanged from round three. So leads the tournament by a mere half-point.
As if to make up for four draws in the previous round, we saw a majority of decisive games in the Cairns Cup. The Chinese grandmaster leads the event by a full point.

The results have simmered a little bit since the first three rounds, where eight out of 15 games were decisive. So far, we have had decisive games in every round; two times, the majority of games were decisive. You can see a graphic below that shows the win-rate in previous years at the Sinquefield Cup.

When Praggnanandhaa offered a sacrifice on move eight, and Van Foreest grabbed the pawn, it was clear that we were going to have a fight on our hands. Praggnanandhaa said he was surprised his opponent took the pawn, and had to take time to remember what exactly White is supposed to do. "This was like one of 10 things I looked at," he reminded the audience after the game.

Van Foreest captured twice on e4 and reached the following position. But after the most natural 10.Nc3, attacking the bishop, the Dutchman took 11 minutes to bring his bishop back to c6, a sign that perhaps he was thinking on his own.

The game blew up as, pretty soon, Black sacrificed his queen. On the plus side, Praggnanandhaa noted, "The good thing about this position is I can never be worse," after winning the queen. He went on to convert the material advantage, even though he saw many fortress opportunities for his opponent, and he eventually showcased how to win with queen vs. rook. Asked how much time he's spent studying such an endgame, Praggnanandhaa responded, "If I can't win this, I shouldn't be playing at this level!"

The rest of the games were drawn. The marquee matchup was Aronian vs. So, which was a true fight (in a Berlin Defense), but the sparks simmered to a threefold repetition by move 32. Showing the following fantasy variation he calculated, which did not happen in the game, Aronian joked, "Of course I saw Na4, but it seems so ridiculous, if you think about it. And my second, GM Aryan Tari, has been telling me, 'Don't do stupid things like you did before!' and I was just thinking of his face if I meet Nh5 with Na4, even if it's the best move!"
My second, Aryan Tari, has been telling me, 'Don't do stupid things like you did before!'

Aronian didn't "do stupid things" and, with no mistakes from either player, it was a draw. Vachier-Lagrave played 1.d4 against Keymer, got a brief advantage at some point, but it also ended by move 35.

Giri made the first draw of the day against Sindarov, and he observed that he once again defended a pawn-down opposite-color bishop endgame. But, unlike yesterday, he didn't lose this one. Speaking of the painful loss to Sevian in round three ("unimaginable," in Giri's words), he quipped, "If people would not be losing such positions, I would be out of work very quickly! I think, for the sake of chess, it's okay that White won that game."
If people would not be losing such positions, I would be out of work very quickly!

Sevian reached a position where he was up the exchange for a pawn, but the position never left the drawing margin for Caruana. It was the longest game of the day, but Caruana left no doubt that he'd hold the endgame.
Friday is the last round before a rest day. So will have the white pieces against round four's winner, Praggnanandhaa, in the marquee matchup.
Just as in round two of the Sinquefield Cup, we nearly saw four white wins in the Cairns Cup. Still, we saw three winners: Tan, Tsolakidou, and Assaubayeva.

The biggest miss was undoubtedly Yip's. A long fight in the Philidor Defense transitioned to a winning advantage for White in the knight endgame. She found the winning plan, sacrificing her knight for three passed pawns, but a single wrong move, 57.Kg4?, undid all that hard work. Divya drew the game without giving Yip any hope for a win from that point.

The only other draw, Humpy vs. Muzychuk, was a 99-accuracy affair by both sides. It featured the Samisch Variation of the Nimzo-Indian Defense—the same opening Caruana lost with White in round three—but both players just followed the top line, more or less. No chances.

Assaubayeva was the first to win, against the struggling Kosteniuk. She started with the Reti Opening, and she played a pawn sacrifice that looks like the Blumenfeld Gambit with reversed colors. Kosteniuk must have mixed something up in her preparation, however, and she played a losing move as early as move 10. Assaubayeva showed just how winning the white initiative was, with 12.c5! being the key move.

One of the two co-leaders, Tan, won another game, this time against Vaishali. White played a sort of Leningrad Dutch with reversed colors, with her 8.f4 being a move played several times by Caruana (twice last year against So). In the middlegame, Vaishali offered an exchange sacrifice, but one that could not be taken. Later on, however, she sacrificed another exchange, which had to be taken, but it didn't work at all. Vaishali resigned before making her 40th move, with Stockfish announcing a mate in nine moves.

Lee dropped out of the co-lead with the loss to Tsolakidou. The Greek international master's offbeat play in the London System paid off. And although she missed a brilliant (not-trivial) Greek Gift sacrifice on move 16—she surely considered it—the white attack was too hard for Lee to parry anyway. 20.Nf6+! was the beginning of the end for the American IM.
On Friday, Tan has the black pieces against her former co-leader, Lee.
You can watch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Sinquefield Cup or 2026 Cairns Cup Events pages.
The Sinquefield Cup broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Maurice Ashley, Cristian Chirila, and Peter Svidler, while the Cairns Cup was covered by IMs Nazi Paikidze and Almira Skripchenko.

The 2026 Sinquefield Cup is the fifth and final leg of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players competed in a classical round-robin tournament with a $475,000 prize fund and counts for qualification into the Grand Chess Tour Finals. It runs alongside the 2026 Cairns Cup, which is also a 10-player round-robin featuring some of the strongest women in the world, with a prize fund of $250,000.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: We're about to find out who'll win the second Esports World Cup Chess Finals. To celebrate another year of exciting chess on the esports world stage, we're offering all our basic members the chance to get 14 days of Diam
body: We're about to find out who'll win the second Esports World Cup Chess Finals. To celebrate another year of exciting chess on the esports world stage, we're offering all our basic members the chance to get 14 days of Diamond membership for free!

To earn your free membership, tune in to Chess.com's official Esports World Cup broadcast on Twitch starting August 15 at 7 a.m. ET / 13:00 CEST / 4:30 p.m. IST. Watch our broadcast for 30 minutes to collect your reward—but make sure you set up properly first.
To earn your reward, you must first connect your Chess.com and Twitch accounts. Here's how to do it:

1. On the Account tab of your Settings page, scroll down until you find the Connected Accounts option. From there, you'll see a button to connect your Twitch account. Click it and follow the instructions to link your accounts.
2. After connecting the accounts, you'll be eligible to receive 14 days of free Diamond membership. Watch 30 minutes of Chess.com's official Twitch broadcast of the Esports World Cup Chess Finals.

3. After watching the required stream time, go to your Twitch Drops & Rewards inventory page to claim your reward. You'll then receive an email with a unique link that will give you your free 14-day membership. You don't need to add any payment method to redeem your 14 days of free Diamond!
Members who already have a premium membership cannot redeem the reward themselves. However, they can forward the email with their unique link to any non-premium member.
