body: For the second week in a row, GM Pranesh M posted the best result of any player in 3 0 Thursday. He scored 9.5 points to win the second tournament of the day. GMs Alexey Sarana and Jeffery Xiong each scored nine points to win the first and third tournaments, respectively. IM Meri Arabidze took the first women's prize with seven points. WFM Veronika Shubenkova won her final four games against opponents above 2900 to reach eight points and take the women's prize in the second tournament. GM Oleksandr Bortnyk started the first tournament on a tremendous streak. He won his first seven games before running into Sarana in round eight.

news.title: Carlsen, Lazavik To Battle It Out In Esports World Cup Final
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Magnus Carlsen scored a 2.5-0.5 victory over GM Nihal Sarin and then won a 4-1 thriller against GM Alireza Firouzja to reach the Final of the 2026 Esports World Cup. Carlsen will face off against 19-year-old GM Denis
body: GM Magnus Carlsen scored a 2.5-0.5 victory over GM Nihal Sarin and then won a 4-1 thriller against GM Alireza Firouzja to reach the Final of the 2026 Esports World Cup. Carlsen will face off against 19-year-old GM Denis Lazavik, who pounced on mistakes and gave almost no chances to GMs Nodirbek Abdusattorov (3-2) and Hikaru Nakamura (3.5-1.5). Nakamura will face Firouzja in the Third-Place Match, with Team Falcons guaranteed all the points from that clash of teammates.
The final matches of the Esports World Cup start on Saturday, August 15, at 7 a.m. ET / 13:00 CEST / 4:30 p.m. IST.
An intense day's action left us with just two undefeated players.
Another intense seven-hour day of chess action in Paris saw all the best-of-four Quarterfinals and best-of-six Semifinals completed, so that just two matches remain. Let's start with the Semifinals.
There was a very familiar look to the four players who reached the Esports World Cup Semifinals, since they'd also faced off in the Speed Chess Championship earlier this year in London.
In fact, the semifinal pairings exactly matched those of the Final and Third-Place Match in London, with the same results.

Lazavik has a very particular style of play, with Carlsen describing it as follows: "He just doesn’t beat himself! He plays very, very solid positional chess and doesn’t really place his pieces on bad squares."

"I think he didn’t have any chance to win at any point," said Lazavik of his victory over Nakamura, and in fact it was the Belarusian who could have scored more heavily. Nakamura said he was "probably worse" in the first game, but he'd briefly been totally lost when he took on c6.
28...Ne2+ wins, since if the king moves to h1, the black queen gives check from h2 and White is suddenly busted.

The second game was, in Nakamura's words, "a dead draw from the opening," while the match hinged on the third game. "I made one bad move and I got punished for it," said the five-time U.S. champion, whose 26.Ne1? allowed Lazavik's light-squared bishop to invade the position. The conversion was flawless.

That left Nakamura in the difficult situation of needing to hit back, but he got nothing in the next game with Black and said it should probably have been "a boring draw." After a long think, however, he mixed things up and blundered a pawn with 27...Qf6?.

The simple 28.Qa8+! and 29.Qxd5 picked up the d-pawn, but this time there was nothing smooth about what followed. Lazavik allowed an easy way for Nakamura to strike back, but fortunately that was missed, since in the end we got to witness a "miracle" save with a sequence of checks and then a stalemate tactic with a desperado queen.

That's the kind of turnaround that could easily have been the start of a brilliant comeback, but Nakamura got nothing in the next game with White before collapsing in a still-holdable pawn-down rook endgame. He commented: "I spent five minutes on one move, and in this time control you can’t do that. Probably I could have made a draw later, but it is what it is."
Nakamura had no complaints, saying of Lazavik's win: "It’s very, very deserved! He played great, and we’ll see how he does tomorrow against Magnus."
That was a curious statement, given Nakamura's teammate Firouzja was yet to play his semifinal against Carlsen, but it would prove prophetic.

This was a repeat of both the 2025 Esports World Cup Final and the Speed Chess Championship Final earlier this year and it would, ultimately, have the same outcome. Carlsen commented after it was over: "I think this was by far my best performance so far in the tournament. I think it was a very, very good match. Last year I felt that I was playing better and pressing him on time as well. Today I pretty quickly realized that my best chance was to press him on time in a lot of these situations, and fortunately it managed to work out."
Today I pretty quickly realized that my best chance was to press him on time.
The first game was suggestive of the drama we'd witness, with Firouzja spotting some very sharp tactics.

19...Nf4! and 20...Nxg2! forced Carlsen to find a very narrow path to hold, but the three minutes Firouzja took to convince himself to go that route ultimately meant he was happy to take a draw when the dust had settled.

Objectively, Carlsen was then never better (or seriously worse) in the second game, much of which he spent a pawn down, but in terms of the clocks it was a nail-biter. Near the end he looked favorite to flag his opponent, but Firouzja showed his usual acceleration and precision to liquidate everything to bare kings—with 7.9 seconds to Carlsen's two minutes and 10 seconds. "Yes, I can take more time than the other players—at the end I can make many fast moves," Firouzja had said earlier in the day, but against Carlsen it was a dangerous game to play.

"The third game obviously was crucial," said Carlsen, with play initially going very smoothly for the world number-one, who seemed to be positionally outplaying his opponent. Complications arose, however, and the focus changed. Carlsen noted that Firouzja thought for too long, and felt that if he could "set up this construction that he cannot break," then the time difference would be a huge factor. 42.Qxc6? was a blunder, however, allowing 42...Qe3!, with the idea of ...Qf4+, ...Rb1, and attacking the white king.

Everything was balanced on a knife-edge: "I missed this idea he had of activating his pieces, and it was really kind of harrowing, where it felt as though I might lose quickly, but I also wanted to make sure he didn’t force a draw, because I didn’t know if I was going to get a better chance to win on time."
It felt as though I might lose quickly, but I also wanted to make sure he didn't force a draw, because I didn't know if I was going to get a better chance to win on time.
In the end, even Firouzja couldn't navigate the complications with so little time, and Carlsen picked up the win.

Carlsen led with three games to go, and would wrap up victory with another two wins, but it was anything but easy: "The last two games were absolute bloodbaths as well, but at that point at least I knew that I had some money in the bank, so I could afford to slip up once and still be OK, but I’m very happy with the way that I managed to fight in those last two games as well, because they were both really difficult. He just never goes down without a fight!"
Game four saw Carlsen as well as Firouzja getting into time trouble, and suddenly Firouzja took over on the board.

32.Rxd7! is even winning, though the full consequences of allowing 32...Ne2+ are hard to fathom. Instead 32.Qxe5? handed the initiative to Carlsen, and the world number-one kept the upper hand for almost all of the mayhem that followed.

That meant Carlsen now led by two points with just two games to go, so that Firouzja had to win both on demand to force armageddon. He actually did generate winning chances in the fifth game, but once again it was Carlsen who played faster and just well enough to clinch another win.
Carlsen was asked about some criticism he's received about his level of play recently and couldn't help but smile.

In the Final, a repeat of this year's Speed Chess Championship Semifinal, Carlsen and Lazavik will compete over two four-game sets, with a potential two-game decider if the scores are level at one set each. At stake is $250,000 for the winner, and $190,000 for the runner-up.

Carlsen said of his young opponent: "He’s really, really good! I think by this point anyone who underestimates him is in for a little bit of a surprise, so he’s earned his right to be here and it’s really no accident." Lazavik said, "I will be rooting for Alireza because I don’t want to play against Magnus!" but at the same time, he noted that in the Final is the best time to play the defending champion.
Both players will look to recharge after a very long day of chess.

Lazavik announced his form early on with an extremely convincing win over GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov. The Uzbek star had chosen his opponent the day before and may have regretted choosing such a brilliant technical player instead of the more unpredictable GM Hans Niemann. If anyone had chances in the four draws, it was Lazavik, but Abdusattorov's hope was that he won the bid to have Black in armageddon and need only a fifth draw.
It didn't happen, however, with Lazavik finding a way to win in what should have been a drawn pawn-up rook endgame.

Lazavik commented: "Such positions are very unpleasant, like with Sina [Movahed] I had something similar. It’s quite equal, but it’s not a draw, and finally you get low on time and it’s very hard to defend."
Lazavik even felt he would have won on time if they'd got down to bare rook vs. rook.

This clash also saw four draws followed by an armageddon win for White, but the first draw especially could easily have been more. In a strategically busted position—the black a-pawn is ready to run—Nakamura sacrificed a rook.
It was a brilliant but flawed concept, but to prove it GM Arjun Erigaisi had to find what could have been the move of the day. He didn't, and the game fizzled out into a quick draw.
The remaining three 10+0 games were tense draws. Then in armageddon Nakamura was surprised not to win after bidding 6 minutes 59 seconds. Arjun undercut him with 6:45.
Arjun only needed a draw, but he got his king stuck in the center, came under a heavy attack, and was unable to save the game.

This clash was effectively decided in one moment of the first game, when Niemann withdrew his bishop to a8, missing that Firouzja could fork the two black rooks from e6, since the black queen is pinned. A moment of terrible realization followed before Niemann simply resigned.

Niemann had a chance to hit straight back in game two, then narrowly escaped a match-ending defeat in game three, before the final game was a thriller. Black looked busted, but Firouzja found a way to hold things together—then escaped in 132 moves with 8.1 seconds to spare.
The final quarterfinal was a repeat of a quarterfinal in 2025.
The scoreline would also be exactly the same, with Carlsen getting off to a perfect start against Nihal.
That smooth combination of tactics and positional play is our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao analyzes below.

"The last two games were really messy, so I was really happy not to have to play a fourth!" said Carlsen, but he counterattacked in fine style to win the second, while the deciding game ended drawn with only brief moments of real danger for the defending champion.
...but will he manage to crush Lazavik's to defend his title? All will be decided on Saturday's final day of Esports World Cup chess action.

The 2026 Esports World Cup in Paris, France has a $1.5 million chess prize fund and $250,000 for first place, while esports teams also share a $30 million prize fund. 16 players qualified via the Champions Chess Tour, DreamHack Atlanta, India Rising, or as defending champion (Carlsen), while another five qualified via the Last Chance Qualifier (August 4-6) in Paris. The main event (August 11-15) features a Play-In to cut the field to 16 players, then a Group Stage with two double-elimination groups to halve it again to eight. Those players then compete in the Playoffs, a single-elimination knockout for the title. The time control for all games is 10 minutes, with no increment.

news.title: Caruana, Keymer Win As Vachier-Lagrave Misses; Tan Survives Vs. Lee
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Wesley So leads the 2026 Sinquefield Cup after round five on Friday, after making a quick draw with GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu. GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave had a winning position against GM Jorden van Foreest and coul
body: GM Wesley So leads the 2026 Sinquefield Cup after round five on Friday, after making a quick draw with GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu. GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave had a winning position against GM Jorden van Foreest and could have caught the leader, but the game ended in a draw. GM Fabiano Caruana entered the tie for second-fifth (all a half-point behind So) with a win against GM Levon Aronian, as did GM Vincent Keymer with a win against GM Anish Giri. GM Javokhir Sindarov's opening was neutralized by GM Sam Sevian, making another solid draw.

All five games in the 2026 Cairns Cup were draws. GM Tan Zhongyi was on the ropes against IM Alice Lee in round five, but the Chinese grandmaster escaped with her full-point lead over the field. Nobody scored a win in GM Vaishali Rameshbabu vs. GM Humpy Koneru, GM Alexandra Kosteniuk vs. IM Stavroula Tsolakidou, GM Anna Muzychuk vs. IM Carissa Yip, nor GM Divya Deshmukh vs. GM Bibisara Assaubayeva.
After a rest day, the tournament resumes with round six of both tournaments on Sunday, August 16, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST.
Caruana and Keymer climb up the ranks and are just a half-point behind the leader.
In the Cairns Cup, the standings are unchanged. Everybody gets a half-point.

Two draws came first, followed by (nearly) three decisive games. The tournament leader, So, made a virtually instant draw against Praggnanandhaa in a Four Knights Scotch. The main priority for So, he said, is to finish in the top four to qualify for the Grand Chess Tour Finals. Another draw gets him closer to that goal. He added, "If you're going to make a draw, it's better to make a draw in five minutes than six hours!"

The only other draw was Sindarov vs. Sevian, where the Uzbek grandmaster hoped to test his opponent's memory, and his opponent passed with flying colors. Sindarov explained, "Here Black has a lot of moves, and I thought if he doesn't remember, his position is a little hard to play." But he concluded, in the end, "I'm not happy with my game, probably not the best choice for the opening today."
I'm not happy with my game, probably not the best choice for the opening today.

Vachier-Lagrave outplayed Van Foreest from the black side of a Kan Sicilian, and when he reached a winning endgame, it looked like he would catch So in the lead, while dealing a fourth loss to the Dutchman. But, as the Frenchman explained, he was spoiled for choice in a pawn-up position. He said, "I had a flurry of options, and I think that is always what is difficult in chess. To choose from all very tempting lines.... I guess it happened to me yesterday as well with Vincent."

In hindsight, it's easy to say that 29...Bxc3 (which Vachier-Lagrave saw) would have led to a promising, clear-pawn-up rook endgame. Later, there was a more complicated line with 35...g5! that won quite cleanly. Finally, Vachier-Lagrave had already given up on winning when he played 41...Rxc3?, but even there 41...h4 could have won. "This is the very definition of snatching a draw from the jaws of victory," said GM Peter Svidler.
This is the very definition of snatching a draw from the jaws of victory.

"It's annoying," said Vachier-Lagrave after the game. "I mean, I feel I'm playing well, but the problem is playing well needs to bring points." As for his direct encounter with the tournament leader on Sunday, he said, "If I don't win against Wesley, it spells doom for my chances of outright first."
If I don't win against Wesley, it spells doom for my chances of outright first.

Moving on to the decisive games, Caruana vs. Aronian was a plain catastrophe. Aronian mixed up his opening lines in the Petroff Defense, and as a result he was borderline losing by move 21, having spent just over one minute of his starting time.
Almost as salt in the wound, Aronian even got a fighting chance with 23...Nd7! but missed it, and Caruana went on to win without giving any other chances.

It's a needed comeback for Caruana, who lost a tough game yesterday against the tournament leader. He said that game was "a cascade of bad decisions." On beating Aronian, however, he said, "Any win is great. It's not easy to get wins against this level of a player."

The second decisive game, and the last game to end, was Keymer vs. Giri. With the white pieces, the German number-one played the English Opening and a kind of Hedgehog Defense with colors reversed. Giri's 15...b5?! is perhaps a step in the wrong direction, but later, after allowing 24.h6!, followed by 25.d4!, Svidler confidently announced, "He is genuinely busted. It's not like it's slightly worse."
The conversion was extremely shaky at the end, with Vincent nervously playing on the increment in the endgame, but he got the job done. GM Rafael Leitao goes over the Game of the Day below.
After the rest day, the marquee matchup is certainly Vachier-Lagrave vs. So. The Frenchman sees it as a must-win game to get into the Grand Chess Tour Finals.

Going into round four on Thursday, Lee had co-led the tournament with Tan. But she lost to Tsolakidou and joined three other players a point behind the leader in the chasing pack. What a turnaround it would have been if Lee toppled Tan, immediately after her loss.

She came close, but in a winning queen and knight endgame, Lee had to find the calm, zugzwang-inducing 40.Kh2!. She could also have repeated moves once before finding it. But after 40.Ng8+ Kd7 41.a3?, Tan found the only move to survive, 41...Qa6!, and survive she did.

All the other games were drawn, though we can perhaps point to Muzychuk vs. Yip as a small missed opportunity. In a slightly better position, Yip accepted a draw by threefold repetition—a decision perhaps influenced by the painful memory of failing to beat Divya in a winning knight endgame the previous round.

There are no easy pairings in this tournament, and Yip next has the white pieces against top seed Assaubayeva. Tan, on the other hand, will have White against the struggling Kosteniuk, who has just stopped the bleeding by making her first draw after four losses.
You can watch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Sinquefield Cup or 2026 Cairns Cup Events pages.
The Sinquefield Cup broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Maurice Ashley, Cristian Chirila, and Peter Svidler, while the Cairns Cup was covered by IMs Nazi Paikidze and Almira Skripchenko.

The 2026 Sinquefield Cup is the fifth and final leg of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players competed in a classical round-robin tournament with a $475,000 prize fund and counts for qualification into the Grand Chess Tour Finals. It runs alongside the 2026 Cairns Cup, which is also a 10-player round-robin featuring some of the strongest women in the world, with a prize fund of $250,000.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Xiong Defends Bullet Brawl Title With 4-Point Margin
news.author: jackrodgers
news.excerpt: GM Jeffery Xiong mounted a successful title defense and won the $400 first prize in the Bullet Brawl arena on Saturday after winning a tight race to the finish line. Xiong posted a score of 162 points and eclipsed IM Ren
body: GM Jeffery Xiong mounted a successful title defense and won the $400 first prize in the Bullet Brawl arena on Saturday after winning a tight race to the finish line. Xiong posted a score of 162 points and eclipsed IM Renato Terry and GM Nihal Sarin by four and five points, respectively.

For their efforts, the second and third placegetters will receive $250 and $150, while GM Oleksandr Bortnyk earned $100 for his fourth-placed finish. Iranian WIM Melika Mohammadi finally unseated FM Anastasia Avramidou as the top-scoring women's player.
The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, August 22, at 12 p.m. ET/6:00 p.m. CEST.

Few players in the world can maintain the level and consistency required to win back-to-back Bullet Brawls, and on Saturday, Xiong proved that he is one of them. In a near carbon copy of his flying start from the previous edition, the American primarily used the Orangutan Opening and St. George Defense to score 16.5/17.
In his first game, Xiong stunned Turkish FM Yunus Emre Gunebakan with an exchange sacrifice, 22...Rxd2!!, and followed up with a second brilliancy two moves later.

Against Norwegian FM Nicolai Maxime Ostensen, Xiong had the opportunity to play a similar sacrifice on the f4-square. This time, however, his opponent survived the subsequent onslaught, only to discover he was too low on time to convert.
When the arena clock ticked past the first hour, Xiong was crossing the 100-point mark and had built a commanding 19-point lead.

Despite this, the path to victory wasn't as smooth as expected. Behind Xiong there loomed a dangerous pack of former victors, including GMs Nihal, Bortnyk, Jose Martinez, and IM Terry. Whenever Xiong stalled, they gained ground.

Nihal in particular proved to be a thorn in the leader's side. In one clash, the world number-25 dispatched Xiong in a mere 19 moves in the midst of a seven-game streak, where he bested the leader again as well as Bortnyk and Terry.

As if the arena were following a script, both Nihal and Terry, who have six titles between them, came within a point of Xiong in the final five minutes of the arena. Xiong caught a second wind and won two games in a row, keeping his nose in front.

A 17-move win over Romanian CM Matei-Valeriu Mogirzan was arguably the most important game for Xiong. Had his opponent played on after seeing he was losing a piece, the last seconds of the tournament could have played out differently.

With this being his fourth victory, Xiong scoots up the leaderboard and now has the same number of victories as GM Arjun Erigaisi and Martinez, though he still has a long way to go to join the "Big Five" of Bullet Brawl.
How to review games? The games from this week's Bullet Brawl can be found here.

Bullet Brawl is an exciting arena featuring Chess.com's top bullet specialists. It takes place weekly on Saturdays. The format is a two-hour arena with a 1+0 time control; the prize fund is $1,000. Like Titled Tuesday and Arena Kings, Bullet Brawl often features top GMs, including Hikaru Nakamura, Andrew Tang, Tuan Minh Le, and many more!

news.title: 🐐 Magnus Carlsen Retains Chess Esports World Cup Title In Paris
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Magnus Carlsen has retained his Esports World Cup title after a dominant victory over GM Denis Lazavik. Carlsen won both sets 3-1, with two wins in each, and ended his Paris run without losing a single game. Carlsen t
body: GM Magnus Carlsen has retained his Esports World Cup title after a dominant victory over GM Denis Lazavik. Carlsen won both sets 3-1, with two wins in each, and ended his Paris run without losing a single game. Carlsen takes $250,000, Lazavik $190,000, while GM Hikaru Nakamura clinched third place and $145,000. Nakamura took a two-game lead with two games to go after winning a fourth game disrupted by technical issues. GM Alireza Firouzja forfeited the next game to lose the match 4-1.
The Esports World Cup is over, with Carlsen clinching the final match by two sets to zero.

Carlsen was asked after the match was over, "Who or what can stop Magnus Carlsen?" and replied: "I don’t know. I think in this format it’s not easy at the moment. I think Alireza had a really good chance yesterday, but it’s not easy, especially now towards the end when the matches become a little bit longer, so it’s harder to rely on one or two game stuff."
The player tasked with stopping the inevitable was 19-year-old Lazavik.

"That's why I play chess, for such moments!" he said as he arrived on the stage, but any hopes of keeping things tight until Carlsen cracked under the pressure were ruined when, after defending accurately for 79 moves, a single blunder spelled disaster in the very first game.
That might look like a rare blunder by one of the most technically gifted players in chess, but Carlsen explained afterward that his match strategy relied on such situations:

I thought about it a lot. I was going through Denis’ games yesterday and talking to my coach as well, and I do feel that maybe especially Hikaru’s approach against him was not quite the right one. It’s funny, one of the things that I said was that he’s not great at defending rook endgames specifically, and that decided the first match, and I thought that I should keep it a lot tighter than Hikaru did, which I think I did. I’ve played Denis many times online as well where I’ve tried to play pretty riskily and been really, really punished for that, so I tried to not give him too many obvious positional advantages and take whatever chances I could find.
One of the things I said was that he's not great at defending rook endgames specifically, and that decided the first match.
The final was played over two sets, with just four games in each set, so that Lazavik had little time to hit back. The second game was sharp, but if anyone could have won it was Carlsen.

16...Bb7!, hitting the f3-bishop to stop the pin of the g4-knight, seems to give Black a big edge, while 16...Rxb2!? led to dynamic equality. That didn't mean the world number-one couldn't try his strategy of outplaying his young opponent in rook endgames, however. Carlsen, a minute up on the clock, looked ready to try and flag Lazavik, but the game was ended by an accidental repetition of moves on move 81.

The third game could potentially have seen Carlsen clinch the set with a game to spare, but instead was the quietest yet. It fizzled out into—you guessed it!—a rook endgame, but not one where anything was going to happen.

That left Lazavik with the unenviable task of having to beat Carlsen on demand to force armageddon. To his credit, the 19-year-old managed to complicate the game, but Carlsen sac'ed an exchange at the perfect time, took over in a game he only needed to draw, and then spotted a beautiful finish with 67...Bc3!.
68.Rxc3+ runs into 68...Kd4! and the rook can't stop the d-pawn from queening.

With one set over, Lazavik had a chance to reset, and he seemed to change his approach. Instead of aiming to go head-to-head with Carlsen in technical play, he came out all-guns-blazing with the Samisch Variation of the Nimzo-Indian. Up to a point it worked, as Carlsen looked visibly rattled for the first time in the match.
One inaccuracy was all it took for Carlsen to pounce with another exchange sacrifice, this time giving up a rook for a bishop on c1.

That blow removed the defender of the e3-square, so that the knight could jump in there next and fork the queen and rook—while if the white queen captured on c1, the other knight would fork on b3. Somehow the geometry of the chessboard simply works against you when facing an in-form Carlsen.

The second game of the set was quiet, which suited Carlsen fine, while the third was balanced, but also balanced on a knife-edge. Carlsen found himself seriously behind on the clock for the first time, but 27...Nxe4!, the fruit of deep thought, represented time invested well.
Soon, by a completely forced sequence for both sides, the game liquidated into a pawn-down endgame that Carlsen could hold with ease.

That left Lazavik with one do-or-die chance to win with the black pieces, force armageddon, and keep his tournament hopes alive. He played the Caro-Kann, but got hit by a beautiful queen sacrifice that would provide a fitting end to the tournament.

This is known, and a quick draw by perpetual check was possible. That would be no good for Lazavik, however, so we went into a vastly more interesting contest where he could still hope for something if Carlsen went astray. The world number-one didn't, however, and instead retained his title in brilliant style.
That's our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao has analyzed below.
Carlsen had retained his title and won another $250,000, plus 1,000 points for Team Liquid.

Carlsen hadn't lost a match in 2025, but this time he didn't lose a single game. He commented: "I’m thrilled to go undefeated, and generally that was a part of my strategy, for sure. I wasn’t trying to do anything out of the ordinary but kind of play pretty tight chess and take whatever chances I could find. Not losing a game speaks both to the success of that strategy and, of course, a little bit of randomness as well, but I’m very happy with that."
I wasn't trying to do anything out of the ordinary but kind of play pretty tight chess and take whatever chances I could find.
Carlsen also noted that every player he'd faced in the event was born after the year 2000. He tweeted, "It's nice to show that the old guard still knows how to move the pieces."
That makes it two Esports World Cups featuring chess, and two titles for Carlsen.

Meanwhile Lazavik had fallen just short in the final match, but only enhanced his reputation. He picked up the biggest payday of his career, $190,000, and that sum may increase if he gets to share in some of his esports team's winnings. Lazavik's 750 points for second place have helped cement his team AG.AL's lead in the race to win $7 million as the top team.
Behind AG.AL is Team Falcons, which had both players in the third-place match.

The third-place match is one no one wants to play, but the difference between third ($145,000) and fourth ($100,000) is a none-too-shabby $45,000. Nakamura took third in 2025, after beating GM Arjun Erigaisi, and he repeated the same feat in 2026, this time overcoming Firouzja, though with an unfortunate twist at the finish.

The match started with Firouzja winning brownie points for playing the French Defense in Paris, but it fizzled out into an uneventful draw. The second game, meanwhile, was vastly more interesting. Nakamura showed he'd come to play with the provocative 10...Nh6!?.

Firouzja thought for over a minute before capturing the knight and ruining Black's pawn structure, but the game remained very tense. The finale came when Nakamura spent over a minute, getting down to under a minute, before correctly grabbing a pawn. Nakamura saw his approach there as the difference from the day before:

I should have probably played that move in five or ten seconds. I used a little bit too much time, but I controlled my nerves in a way that I didn’t yesterday against Denis... in two of those games I got down to two minutes, 2.5 minutes, and I’m already freaking out and just completely losing my mind. In the game against Alireza I had two minutes, I used like 30-40 seconds, and I still was able to keep my nerve. That was probably the big difference, and I’m very happy with the way I played, especially the second game.
It helped that Firouzja, already in a difficult position, blundered a game-ending rook sacrifice—with none other than IM Levy Rozman commentating!

The third-place match was best-of-six, so that Firouzja had four games remaining to hit back. Things looked promising immediately in the next game, but the Frenchman was unable to convert strong pressure on the black side of a Sicilian.

Then came the fateful fourth game, which decided the match. Nakamura had begun to press with the black pieces, when suddenly the game had to be paused because of internet issues that saw multiple broadcasts collapse simultaneously. There would be more than one interruption, while on the board Firouzja's position suddenly collapsed in the space of a few moves until he was hit by a devastating blow.

That loss left Firouzja, who hadn't scored a win in 12 games since he defeated GM Hans Niemann in the first game of the Playoffs, needing to win two games in a row simply to force armageddon. That would be almost a mission impossible, but it was one he decided to skip. He didn't return to the stage and was given a forfeit loss for game five, so that Nakamura clinched the match 4-1.
Nakamura himself was frustrated by the interruptions and understood Firouzja's decision, though he later released a statement clarifying some of what he'd said in post-match interviews.

Overall, however, it had been another successful event for Nakamura, while Firouzja had been the one player to really have Carlsen on the ropes in a few games. Team Falcons is currently in second place in the overall standings, which would earn the team $5 million.
So that's all for the 2026 Esports World Cup—we hope you enjoyed the show!

The 2026 Esports World Cup in Paris, France had a $1.5 million chess prize fund and $250,000 for first place, while esports teams also share a $30 million prize fund. 16 players qualified via the Champions Chess Tour, DreamHack Atlanta, India Rising, or as defending champion (Carlsen), while another five qualified via the Last Chance Qualifier (August 4-6) in Paris. The main event (August 11-15) featured a Play-In to cut the field to 16 players, then a Group Stage with two double-elimination groups to halve it again to eight. Those players then competed in the Playoffs, a single-elimination knockout for the title. The time control for all games was 10 minutes, with no increment.

Colin McGourty

news.title: Giri Wins Dutch Battle; Lee Beats Humpy To Move To Clear 2nd
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Wesley So still leads GMs Fabiano Caruana, Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Vincent Keymer, and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu by half a point after round six of the 2026 Sinquefield Cup, with GM Anish Giri scoring the day's only w
body: GM Wesley So still leads GMs Fabiano Caruana, Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Vincent Keymer, and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu by half a point after round six of the 2026 Sinquefield Cup, with GM Anish Giri scoring the day's only win. He said he "went a little nuts there for a moment," but his opening gamble paid off against his Dutch colleague GM Jorden van Foreest, as a first win saw him catch GM Javokhir Sindarov in eighth place.

16-year-old IM Alice Lee is now in sole second place, half a point behind GM Tan Zhongyi, after scoring the only win of round six of the 2026 Cairns Cup. Lee surprised GM Koneru Humpy in the opening but was lost after grabbing a poisoned pawn. Humpy missed the chance in time trouble, however, and was soon put to the sword. Elsewhere, IM Carissa Yip came closest to a win, but one blunder allowed GM Bibisara Assaubayeva to escape a miserable position.
Round seven is on Monday, August 17, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST.
The changes in round six came at the bottom, with Giri moving up with a first win.
In the Cairns Cup, Lee has broken clear of what was a four-player pack in second place and is now only half a point behind Tan.

It was a day of the Berlin Defense in the Sinquefield Cup, with leader So playing the infamous endgame against second-placed Vachier-Lagrave, one of the few players who continues to enjoy the challenge of toppling that wall. The Frenchman soon gained a 45-minute lead on the clock and continued to press, but So is one of the hardest players in chess to beat in such a situation. The game fizzled out into a same-colored bishop endgame.

We also saw Keymer play the Berlin against GM Sam Sevian, who chose a different path with 5.Re1 and 6.a4, though the outcome was the same—although it turned into the longest game of the day, a decisive result never looked likely.

Perhaps the most anticipated clash was World Championship Challenger Sindarov taking on Caruana, with the world number-two gaining a powerful-looking outside passed pawn in a Ragozin. The question was whether the pawn could ever advance, and that was answered in the negative, with Sindarov carefully swapping off queens, before at the end Caruana liquidated to a draw.
There was much more life in the clash between Praggnanandhaa and GM Levon Aronian, with the Armenian-American recovering from an opening mishap and painful loss to Caruana before the rest day.

He told GM Maurice Ashley: "Generally I’ve been playing not great, so I kind of needed one day of rest just to recuperate, just to talk to my inner self and tell that everything will be fine, I just need to work, those are not your yard kids that you’re playing with, those are the best of the best, and you need to match the level of their energy."
Those are not your yard kids that you're playing with, those are the best of the best, and you need to match the level of their energy.

Aronian said his 8...b5 pawn sacrifice, a novelty, was an over-the-board inspiration, quipping, "Even if I prepare, I don’t remember my lines!" There were perhaps some chances for Praggnanandhaa if he'd later pushed his e-pawn to e5, but in the game things soon liquidated into a position neither player could hope to win.

Aronian is on 50 percent, a point behind the leader and half a point behind Praggnanandhaa and the other players in second place. It was suggested to him that he has a relatively easy run-in (games against Vachier-Lagrave, Giri, and Sevian) and is now playing for cash. He responded: "Since I cannot qualify [for the Finals], that’s basically what I’m playing for... and also for the beauty, and there’s always a chance to create beauty! I think my blitz game against Anish was one of the most beautiful blitz games I ever played, so I’ll try to do that in my next rounds."

The one win came in the clash of two struggling players, Dutch GMs Giri and Van Foreest, and it came for Giri despite his opening choices initially backfiring. 8.h4 is far from a new move, but Giri gave a long account of his decision-making at that point:

For inexplicable reasons—I had reasons but you better not even know them!—I decided to play the move 8.h4. I know you can play h4 always, it’s an interesting move, but it’s just the idea that you’re supposed to study theory in order to apply it in your games, but for some reason I reached a point that there’s too much theory for me, more theory than the games... so I start to go backwards instead of going forwards!

"I just went a little nuts there for a moment!" said Giri, who went on to play into a line where the inclusion of h4 and h6 favored Black—f3, to drive away a knight on e4, was temporarily impossible because the g3-pawn would hang.

As the game developed, however, Van Foreest, who had already lost three games in St. Louis, began to go astray, and Giri described what followed by referring to himself as the "grand maestro." For instance, he said of his bishop on b2 that seemed to have no prospects: "What does the maestro do? Through his mastery of chess he was able to transfer the bishop from b2, through the pawn on d4, to e5—boom!"
Later he added, "It's not about pawns, it's about domination!" That's what we got by the end of the game, with GM Rafael Leitao analyzing our Game of the Day below.

Giri's next challenge is Black against leader So, while Caruana vs. Praggnanandhaa, Keymer vs. Sindarov, and Aronian vs. Vachier-Lagrave will all be vital as the race to qualify for the Grand Chess Tour Finals comes down to the wire.

There was also just one decisive game in the Cairns Cup, but for most of the round at least two wins looked to be in the cards. Perhaps the quietest draw, in terms of evaluation, was GM Anna Muzychuk vs. GM Vaishali Rameshbabu, but it was remarkable for a couple of reasons. One was the time usage, with Vaishali ending with just 30 seconds less than she began, while Muzychuk got down to 14 minutes. The other was how the game finished—anything drew, but this did so spectacularly!

GM Divya Deshmukh won a pawn against IM Stavroula Tsolakidou but couldn't squeeze out more, while leader Tan seemed to have some chances before swapping off queens and making a solid draw against GM Alexandra Kosteniuk.
The one draw that looked sure to be a win was Yip's game against Assaubayeva.
The young American grandmaster took over early on and dominated, until 32.f6?, played in seconds despite a 15-minute lead on the clock, allowed Assaubayeva a game-saving tactic.
The only win came for the youngest player in the field, Lee, who moved into sole second place with a win which was logical, given how the game went, though also somewhat lucky.

Lee said she'd planned to be solid against a strong opponent, but Humpy played into her prep and, "I got a huge time advantage on the clock and I think my position was pretty decent also." Lee didn't stop to think until after move 19, when she was already almost 50 minutes up on the clock. Time would be crucial, as when Lee grabbed a poisoned pawn, saying, "I felt 28...Qh3 would have been more natural, but I also like taking pawns!" Humpy got down to under five minutes on her clock before replying.
The climax of the game came on move 30, when 30.Nxg7!! should win for White. Instead, Humpy played the natural move Lee was expecting, 30.Qg4?, and was instantly lost.

Lee has gained 15.8 points to climb to number 26 on the Women's Live Rating List, while Humpy has dropped 13.9 points to put her at risk of dropping out of the top 10. The more immediate question, however, is whether Lee can fight for first place. She has White against Muzychuk in round seven, while Tan is Black against Divya.
You can watch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Sinquefield Cup or 2026 Cairns Cup Events pages.
The Sinquefield Cup broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Maurice Ashley, Cristian Chirila, and Peter Svidler, while the Cairns Cup was covered by IMs Nazi Paikidze and Almira Skripchenko.

The 2026 Sinquefield Cup is the fifth and final leg of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players compete in a classical round-robin tournament with a $475,000 prize fund and points counting for qualification into the Grand Chess Tour Finals. It runs alongside the 2026 Cairns Cup, which is also a 10-player round-robin featuring some of the strongest women in the world, with a prize fund of $250,000.

news.title: Sindarov Wins On Demand With Black; Tan Bamboozles Divya To Extend Lead
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: With two rounds left, GM Wesley So continues to lead the 2026 Sinquefield Cup on 4.5/7 after making an almost instant draw with GM Anish Giri in round seven on Monday. He's trailed by GMs Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Fabiano
body: With two rounds left, GM Wesley So continues to lead the 2026 Sinquefield Cup on 4.5/7 after making an almost instant draw with GM Anish Giri in round seven on Monday. He's trailed by GMs Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Fabiano Caruana, and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, who are half a point behind. GM Javokhir Sindarov won the one decisive game, against GM Vincent Keymer, and both players join a group of four players on 3.5 points that includes GMs Sam Sevian and Levon Aronian.

GM Tan Zhongyi continues to lead the 2026 Cairns Cup on 5.5/7, though she was in huge trouble against GM Divya Deshmukh. She won from a much worse position to extend her lead to a full point over GM Bibisara Assaubayeva and IM Alice Lee. Assaubayeva won the only other decisive game of the day, against IM Stavroula Tsolakidou, while Lee didn't manage to convert a winning, pawn-up rook endgame against GM Anna Muzychuk.
Round eight is on Tuesday, August 18, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST.
So continues to coast in first place with a fourth consecutive draw. Sindarov is one of seven players within a point of the leader.
Tan continues to lead the Cairns Cup, despite a scare in round seven. Just two players are a point behind her, and she plays one of them, Assaubayeva, in round eight.
So kept the lead with a quick draw against Giri, finishing by move 32 with 12 more minutes than he started with.

For Sindarov, a win with the black pieces was necessary to stay in contention for the Grand Chess Tour Finals. He thought about the King's Indian Defense, but ultimately landed on the Benko Gambit, saying, "If I will lose, I will learn something, but maybe if I win I will get some chances." Keymer declined the pawn sacrifice and spent 13 minutes to decide on a double fianchetto setup.

Keymer played solidly, but kept control of the position, and eventually Sindarov erred with 20...Be4?. After having gained the advantage, Keymer decided to bail out to an opposite-color bishop endgame, but one where he'd be the one groveling for a draw. Though White could objectively hold, Keymer didn't manage to do it, making the final mistake with two minutes left against an hour and two minutes.
Surprisingly, it is the world championship challenger's first win in the event.

The other three games were all draws, with the most promise lying in GM Jorden van Foreest vs. Sevian. There, the American won a pawn and had great chances to deliver Van Foreest's fifth loss, but time trouble became a factor. He let go of the advantage with three minutes against almost 13, and Van Foreest avoided a second loss in a row. Had Sevian won this game, he (number 30 in the world) would have also jumped over Van Foreest (number 29) on the live rating list.

Aronian played 3.b3 against Vachier-Lagrave's Sicilian Defense, but the game was still a 99 accuracy draw. The last game to end was Caruana vs. Praggnanandhaa, with the American having an exchange for two pawns in the endgame. In this case, Praggnanandhaa had three connected passed pawns, but it still wasn't enough to change the evaluation.

So will have Black against Sevian in round eight, and then White against Sindarov in round nine. Another important clash in round eight will be Vachier-Lagrave vs. Praggnanandhaa, both players a half-point behind the leader.

There were nearly three decisive games, and at some point in round seven it seemed possible that Tan would lose and 16-year-old Lee, the lowest-rated player in the field, would overtake her. Lee won a clean pawn, but didn't manage to convert the resulting five vs. four endgame. It ended in a draw.

Divya, on the other hand, outplayed the tournament leader in a Vienna Game. In an advantageous position—with two extra pawns—the Indian grandmaster had to find a difficult move, 25.Ba7!!, to exchange queens and consolidate. Missing that, she allowed a pawn storm against her king, with queens still on the board.
It was the white king that was hunted, and even though Tan allowed an objective draw on move 31, Divya had just two minutes by that point. GM Rafael Leitao analyzes our Game of the Day below.

In the other decisive game, Assaubayeva vs. Tsolakidou, both players had a case of mutual blindness; 19.axb4 would have won a piece for Assaubayeva. About 10 moves later, however, the Kazakh grandmaster outplayed her opponent yet again, as they both dropped under 10 minutes, and when she won a pawn, it turned out Black had nothing to show for it. 30.Rxc4!! could have been a hyper-accurate way of putting away the game, but she won with an extra pawn in the heavy-piece endgame anyway, the human way.

GM Alexandra Kosteniuk vs. GM Humpy Koneru was an accurate truce between two players not having a good tournament, while GM Vaishali Rameshbabu vs. IM Carissa Yip was another virtually flawless draw in the Scotch Gambit.

In the penultimate round, Assaubayeva will have her only chance to take down the tournament leader herself, but she'll have the black pieces. Lee, on the other hand, will also have Black against Vaishali—with a matchup against her good friend Yip in the last round.
You can watch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Sinquefield Cup or 2026 Cairns Cup Events pages.
The Sinquefield Cup broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Maurice Ashley, Cristian Chirila, and Peter Svidler, while the Cairns Cup was covered by IMs Nazi Paikidze and Almira Skripchenko.

The 2026 Sinquefield Cup is the fifth and final leg of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players compete in a classical round-robin tournament with a $475,000 prize fund and points counting for qualification into the Grand Chess Tour Finals. It runs alongside the 2026 Cairns Cup, which is also a 10-player round-robin featuring some of the strongest women in the world, with a prize fund of $250,000.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: State Of Chess Returns September 1 With Liza Mandelup, Albert Cheng
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: We're excited to announce the next State of Chess, our live show where Chief Chess Officer IM Danny Rensch shares what Chess.com has been working on and what's coming next. It's also where you can ask us questions direct
body: We're excited to announce the next State of Chess, our live show where Chief Chess Officer IM Danny Rensch shares what Chess.com has been working on and what's coming next. It's also where you can ask us questions directly and get answers live on the broadcast. This is a big one, with two great guests and a long list of updates to get through, so make sure you don't miss it!
State of Chess starts on September 1 at 1:15 p.m. ET / 19:15 CEST, right after Titled Tuesday. Tune in to our Twitch and YouTube channels to catch the show live and get your questions in.

The show starts with Liza Mandelup, who joins Danny to talk about Grandmasters, our new limited series diving into the professional chess world. Liza will share what drew her to the project, what viewers can expect from the series, and what it was like documenting the pro circuit up close. This is also your chance to ask Liza your questions about the show, so make sure you join us live.

Albert Cheng is back on State of Chess, this time to talk about Gambit, our new non-gambling platform for poker, and Classic, an initiative to build and grow other games like Go, Backgammon, and Mahjong. Danny and Albert will cover what's new with both, and what sets them apart from other gaming websites

Next, Danny will run through everything happening at Chess.com right now—and there's a lot to cover. Between bot upgrades, advanced stats for our members, a new game database, and plenty more across the site, it's been a busy few months.
We're also discussing Titled Tuesday's new format, bigger prize fund, and elevated importance within the Esports World Cup cycle.

As always, we'll close out the show with a Q&A session with Danny. Whether you've got questions about chess, Chess.com, or anything in between, drop them in the comments below, and we'll try to get to them live.

news.title: Speedy Minh Le Wins 9 Straight To Take Titled Tuesday
news.author: nathanielgreen
news.excerpt: GM Tuan Minh Le won his first Titled Tuesday of the year on August 18, and the 12th of his career, after coming out ahead of GMs Parham Maghsoodloo and Arjun Erigaisi on tiebreaks with a score of 9.5/11. Le recovered fro
body: GM Tuan Minh Le won his first Titled Tuesday of the year on August 18, and the 12th of his career, after coming out ahead of GMs Parham Maghsoodloo and Arjun Erigaisi on tiebreaks with a score of 9.5/11. Le recovered from a first-round loss by ripping off nine consecutive wins thereafter, the first seven on the board and the last two by forcing his opponents out of time in equal positions.

The top three finishers at the recent Esports World Cup—GMs Magnus Carlsen, Denis Lazavik, and Hikaru Nakamura—all played and all suffered from an "Esports World Cup hangover," as Nakamura termed it on stream. All three had lost a game by the end of round three, and only Nakamura would end up in the top 20.

The last player with a perfect score was, in fact, GM Sergey Drygalov, who has won Titled Tuesday before, back on September 26, 2023. After six rounds, GM Christopher Yoo, GM Bharath Subramaniyam, and IM Yoseph Taher were also on 100 percent scores, but only Drygalov made it to 7/7. He did so with an impressive win over Bharath, pushing his edge on the board and the clock into victory as Yoo and Taher drifted into a draw.

Once again, however, a perfect score was not to be. Facing 16-year-old IM Aleksandr Usov in his next game, Drygalov was caught off guard by 21...Nxe5!! and resigned five moves later. Next week's ever-growing bounty, should someone hit 11/11, is worth $3,250.

Usov ended up the sole leader after Yoo and Taher lost to GMs Alexey Sarana and Sina Movahed, respectively. Meanwhile, Le scored his seventh straight win to join seven players on 7/8, creating an impressive-looking checkmate against Bharath.

Maghsoodloo, Arjun, and Nakamura were among those lurking farther back on 6.5/8 as the final break began. Play then resumed and Usov, like Drygalov, could not hold the lead, falling to Movahed. Le flagged GM Oleksandr Bortnyk for his eighth straight win, while IMs Marco Materia and Khuong Duy Dau won with more traditional methods against Sarana and Drygalov. As Movahed, Le, Materia, and Khuong moved to 8/9, Maghsoodloo and Arjun stayed half a point behind them, but Nakamura fell a bit more behind after only a draw with GM Nodirbek Yakubboev.

The 10th round saw, as the seventh had, just one of the four co-leaders take another W. And, as in the ninth round, Le's quickness decided his game; the computer evaluation and Materia's clock both read all zeroes, but Le's clock read 2.5 seconds, and he now held the sole lead by half a point. Maghsoodloo was among those just behind, after a game where reliance on the computer evaluation shows a sudden blunder from Yoo on move 45. In reality, Maghsoodloo's pieces from move 27 onward were ever so slightly better—more scope for his bishop, a better square for his knight, a more active king—and Yoo eventually cracked.

In the final round, despite some brief winning chances against Movahed that could have locked up sole first place, Le settled for a draw by agreement with the two of them on nearly equal time and positions. At the same time, Arjun had already long handled Khuong in a game that was basically over by move 22, although it ran for another 22.

Maghsoodloo won in the final round as well and, despite getting caught, Le's tiebreaks remained stronger than either Maghsoodloo or Arjun, who settled for the next two spots. Sarana and Nakamura rounded out the top five with nine points each, followed by Movahed and GM Martyn Kravtsiv, also on nine. Yoo, Taher, and Usov claimed the last spots in the top 10.
*Bounty grows by $250 per week without a perfect score, and resets once a perfect score has been achieved.
These winners are announced by Thursday each week. If you would like to nominate a game or a move (including your own) in this or future weeks, click here!
Titled Tuesday is Chess.com's weekly tournament for titled players. It begins at 11:00 a.m. Eastern Time/17:00 Central European/20:30 Indian Standard Time.

news.title: Praggnanandhaa Catches So In Lead; Tan Draw Away From Tournament Victory
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu has caught GM Wesley So in the lead of the 2026 Sinquefield Cup on 5/8, just before the final round. With the black pieces, Praggnanandhaa beat GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave in just 27 moves, whi
body: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu has caught GM Wesley So in the lead of the 2026 Sinquefield Cup on 5/8, just before the final round. With the black pieces, Praggnanandhaa beat GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave in just 27 moves, while So made a draw against GM Sam Sevian. GMs Vincent Keymer and Javokhir Sindarov are just a half-point behind after also winning against GMs Fabiano Caruana and Jorden van Foreest, respectively.

GM Tan Zhongyi, after beating GM Bibisara Assaubayeva in round eight, is a draw away from winning the 2026 Cairns Cup (her second title, after 2024). The only player who can catch her is IM Alice Lee, who won her game on Tuesday against GM Vaishali Rameshbabu. Lee will secure her first grandmaster norm if she makes a draw with IM Carissa Yip in round nine.
Round nine, which is the last, is on Wednesday, August 19, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST.
So has finally been caught, and eight players are still within one point of the lead. In case of a tie, there will be playoffs on Thursday.

The top four players in the GCT standings will qualify for the GCT Finals. Sindarov is just barely on the outside looking in, but he's won two games in a row and will be looking to make it three—against So in round nine.

After scoring her second consecutive victory against the highest seed, Tan will win the Cairns Cup outright if she draws against IM Stavroula Tsolakidou with the black pieces on Wednesday. The tournament is a two-horse race with Lee, who will have to weigh the prospects of winning the tournament or snagging a GM norm.
So coasted to a fifth consecutive draw, against Sevian. Since winning in rounds two and three, So has been impenetrable, though he has one more game to play.

So showed great opening preparation in a Queen's Gambit Declined, dropping under his original 90 minutes only on move 21—while Sevian was left with just over half an hour. The queens were soon exchanged and the game ended in a draw by threefold repetition on move 35.

The only other draw was the longest game of the day, GM Anish Giri vs. GM Levon Aronian. At 157 moves, it is also the longest game in Sinquefield Cup history. Giri attempted to win the rook and bishop vs. rook endgame, but Aronian demonstrated flawless technique, with over half an hour on his clock, to draw it.

On to the three decisive games, we start with Praggnanandhaa, who is now guaranteed to qualify for the GCT Finals. Unaware until his interview, Praggnanandhaa said, "I was guessing a draw should be good enough today, but this tournament is also a prestigious one, so I just wanted to have a fight, and I'm happy I managed to play well."

We saw a Ruy Lopez Arkhangelsk Variation, but one where Black never played ...b5. By playing 11...g5!?, Praggnanandhaa invited a piece sacrifice, and Vachier-Lagrave obliged by playing it. A few moves later, the Frenchman had to play 15.Qf3 to hold the balance, with Praggnanandhaa showing a perpetual check he'd calculated, but 15.cxd4? allowed the Indian GM a chance to play for more. He went on to win, quite quickly, with the extra piece.

Sindarov, who won his first game against Keymer in round seven, followed it up with another win against Van Foreest in round eight. It's a lousy result for the Dutchman, who's lost every game he's played with Black (five games).

Three days ago, Sindarov was third from last in the standings. Now, he even has a chance to win the tournament if he can somehow win with Black against an ultra-solid So in the final round. The Uzbek GM quipped, "When everyone's tired, I'm showing my level!" The game was exciting from the get-go, with the world championship challenger sacrificing a pawn on move six.

Van Foreest grabbed the pawn, and then parked his bishop on the e6-square. Sindarov explained, "I have some positional advantage here. His pieces are stuck and I have a lot of space." The turning point was when White sacrificed a second pawn with the imaginative 17.Qd3!?, prompting an immediate mistake on Black's next move. "I found all the moves," said the world championship challenger, proud of this game.

As fans, we'd love to see Sindarov go for the throat with the black pieces against So in the final round. But he quelled expectations: "I think Wesley will kill the game, but we'll see!... If I am in his position, I will do the same."

Keymer won the day's third decisive game, bouncing back from his loss in the previous round in an opposite-color bishop endgame against Sindarov. He said of that encounter, "I am a player who doesn't like to play for a draw from move one," but added that "during the game [against Sindarov], these thoughts creep in, that actually a draw is a good result, and that's how I made this Bxe5 move... Somehow I managed to lose that game, so that was tough to process, that going against my nature was what actually cost me that game." He decided he would not make the same psychological error in round eight against Caruana.

The opening was interesting in this game as well, with a surprise on move two (!) after 1.d4 d5 2.c3!?. We got an original opening, with the German's knight moving five times out of the first 10 moves to reach the d3-square.

He went on to outplay the world number-two, and with some poetic justice, he won an opposite-color bishop endgame, the same piece configuration he'd lost the day before. GM Rafael Leitao analyzes our Game of the Day below.

The main question in the Sinquefield Cup is whether So and Praggnanandhaa can hold onto the lead. Both of them have the white pieces, against Sindarov and Giri, and the priority is not only to win the Sinquefield Cup, but to qualify for the GCT Finals.
Tan's win against Assaubayeva could have clinched the tournament, were it not for Lee also winning her game. Yip won the third decisive game, against Tsolakidou.

With five wins and three draws, Tan has so far put up a 2746 performance in the Cairns Cup and is set to gain 23 rating points. As the commentators remarked more than once, in such form, she would not be out of place in the Sinquefield Cup.

The game against Assaubayeva, the top seed with a rating of 2538, was as convincing as it gets in the King's Indian Defense. The Kazakh's queenside play didn't pan out after 23...a3?, while White's attack with the h-pawn thrust did. A curious moment was at the end, when Tan may have blundered a pawn by allowing 45...Qxd5—she seemed shocked to see this move in the video feed. Fortunately, she recomposed herself and discovered that she was winning anyway.

Fresh off her victory at the 2026 Women's Speed Chess Championship the week prior, and now performing at a 2644 level in the Cairns Cup, Lee has shown that she is capable of playing at the grandmaster level. With four wins, one loss, and three draws, she still has a chance to win the tournament, and also to earn a grandmaster norm.

In an Italian Opening, Vaishali voluntarily doubled her e-pawns to open the f-file, and began a ferocious (and, at one point, advantageous) attack on the kingside. Lee defended, and ultimately showed that the long-term pawn structure counted more than the short-term attack. As Philidor said, pawns are the soul of chess, and Vaishali resigned only when she was four pawns down in the rook endgame.

In the third decisive game, Tsolakidou went for a temporary piece sacrifice with 27...Ng4?—when, in fact, the other temporary piece sacrifice 27...Bg4 would have equalized. Finding the key intermezzo, 29.f5!, Yip made sure that the piece sacrifice wasn't temporary after all, and she went on to win with the extra piece. In the conversion stage, the flashy 36.Rxf6! was a nice find to erase any doubts about the result in this game.
Like in the Sinquefield Cup, we saw just two draws, and both of them featured 98 accuracy by all players—GM Humpy Koneru vs. GM Divya Deshmukh and GM Anna Muzychuk vs. GM Alexandra Kosteniuk.

If Tan makes a draw in the final round, the tournament is hers. Meanwhile, it remains to be seen how hard Lee will press for the win against her compatriot, as a grandmaster norm is just around the corner—and how cooperative her compatriot, and also friend, will be.
You can watch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Sinquefield Cup or 2026 Cairns Cup Events pages.
The Sinquefield Cup broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Maurice Ashley, Cristian Chirila, and Peter Svidler, while the Cairns Cup was covered by IMs Nazi Paikidze and Almira Skripchenko.

The 2026 Sinquefield Cup is the fifth and final leg of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players compete in a classical round-robin tournament with a $475,000 prize fund and points counting for qualification into the Grand Chess Tour Finals. It runs alongside the 2026 Cairns Cup, which is also a 10-player round-robin featuring some of the strongest women in the world, with a prize fund of $250,000.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.
