news.title: Esports Nations Cup Postponed To November 2027
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: The inaugural Esports Nations Cup (ENC), which was set to feature a 128-player chess tournament in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on November 2-29, has been postponed by one year to November 2027, the Esports Foundation (EF) anno
body: The inaugural Esports Nations Cup (ENC), which was set to feature a 128-player chess tournament in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on November 2-29, has been postponed by one year to November 2027, the Esports Foundation (EF) announced on Tuesday.

The Foundation said the decision followed an ongoing assessment of the “wider regional situation” and consultation with key stakeholders. The organization said moving the competition to 2027 was the responsible decision given the scale of an event involving teams and stakeholders from more than 100 countries and territories.

"The decision to postpone the Esports Nations Cup was not taken lightly," said EF CEO Ralf Reichert. "We will continue investing in our National Team Partners, working with publishers and building the national ecosystems already taking shape around the competition. The work continues, and our ambition for ENC remains unchanged."
The ENC had been scheduled to run across four weeks in November, with chess among the titles played during the opening week.
The Esports Foundation is yet to comment on how the postponement will affect the players who have qualified for the finals, and whether they will retain their places in 2027.

GMs Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Liem Le, Matthias Bluebaum, Volodar Murzin, and Christopher Yoo are among the players who had secured their spots in the finals through the qualification process. The chess field was set to feature players from at least 82 countries and territories.

Chess was announced in February as one of 16 titles at the inaugural ENC, with a 128-player tournament designed to bring together players representing countries and territories rather than esports clubs. Chess.com joined the ENC as an official publishing partner in November 2025, alongside publishers including Electronic Arts, Krafton, Tencent, Ubisoft, MOONTON Games, and SNK. The competition was conceived as a nation-versus-nation counterpart to the club-focused Esports World Cup.

EF said all existing commitments made through the ENC Development Fund will remain in place despite the postponement, while its development programs and work with National Team Partners will continue.
The foundation said it will work with publishers and National Team Partners in the coming weeks to provide further details on the revised competition calendar and qualification pathways.

news.title: Champions Chess Tour 2026-2027: Adjusted Format, Same Road To The Esports World Cup
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: As GM Magnus Carlsen celebrates another Esports World Cup title, attention is already turning to the road to next year's event. The Champions Chess Tour (CCT) 2026-2027 cycle remains the main road to the next Esports Wor
body: As GM Magnus Carlsen celebrates another Esports World Cup title, attention is already turning to the road to next year's event. The Champions Chess Tour (CCT) 2026-2027 cycle remains the main road to the next Esports World Cup—with a tweaked format designed to simplify the tour and sharpen its competitiveness.

Running from September 1, 2026, to May 25, 2027, the CCT will comprise three of Chess.com's biggest events: Titled Tuesday, Speed Chess Championship, and Chess.com Open. With 12 Esports World Cup spots at stake, every week counts.

Players no longer earn a direct qualification spot by placing among the top three in the Speed Chess Championship or the Chess.com Open. Instead, qualification comes solely from the CCT Leaderboard, with the top 12 players making it to the Esports World Cup.
Placing at the top of these major events, however, remains critical. A win can earn players as many as 150 points, a considerable advantage in the race for a qualification spot.

Finishing among the top 10 in Titled Tuesday now earns players points that feed directly into the CCT Leaderboard. Points also accumulate throughout the year, rewarding players who perform consistently at a high level. The change replaces the Titled Tuesday Grand Prix format, which reset standings and capped each player's points within individual Splits.

Along with the recently increased prize fund, these changes make Titled Tuesday more important than ever. With 39 weeks in the 2026-2027 cycle, players can earn hundreds of points in Titled Tuesday alone.

Chess made its Esports World Cup debut in 2025, introducing competitive chess to a global esports audience for the first time, with Carlsen winning the inaugural title in Riyadh. The event returned for a second edition in 2026, building on that momentum with an expanded format and a growing spotlight within the wider esports calendar, as Carlsen successfully defended his title to become a back-to-back Chess at EWC champion. The Champions Chess Tour has anchored that path in both years, turning a full season of results into the sport's definitive qualification pathway to the esports world stage.
As the 2026-2027 season gets underway, more details on each of the tour's events are coming soon.

news.title: Titled Tuesday Broadcast Returns With GM Robert Hess As Main Host
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: Fans now have a reason to tune in to their favorite streaming platform every Tuesday. Titled Tuesday (TT) broadcasts are back, hosted by the one and only GM Robert Hess! Shows start weekly at 11 a.m. ET / 17:00 CEST / 8:
body: Fans now have a reason to tune in to their favorite streaming platform every Tuesday. Titled Tuesday (TT) broadcasts are back, hosted by the one and only GM Robert Hess! Shows start weekly at 11 a.m. ET / 17:00 CEST / 8:30 p.m. IST on our Twitch and YouTube channels.

Known for his enthusiasm and ability to explain complex positions to the audience, Hess is one of the most beloved commentators in the chess world. With events like FIDE World Championships, Candidates Tournaments, Speed Chess Championships, and others on his resume, Hess is ready to elevate TT's broadcast and deliver the show fans deserve.

"For over a decade, Titled Tuesday has been a playground for the world's best players and a proving ground for the next generation of top grandmasters. Titled players can log in from anywhere in the world and go head-to-head with the game's greats," said Hess. "I'm excited to get back on the mic to take fans through the emotional roller coaster that is elite blitz chess, and see who qualifies for the Speed Chess Championship and Esports World Cup."
I'm excited to get back on the mic to take fans through the emotional roller coaster that is elite blitz chess.— GM Robert Hess

"Titled Tuesday is the biggest weekly event in chess, and we know how much fans have missed watching it live," said Chess.com's Events Commissioner, Michael Brancato. "We're thrilled to bring it back, especially with a commentator as beloved as Robert Hess returning to host it."

The return of the broadcast is just one of the many recent additions to TT that make the tournament more important than ever! Here's a breakdown of everything you need to know about this new era of Titled Tuesday:

Since June 2, TT's weekly prize fund has increased to a whopping $10,000. With this bump, the event's yearly purse exceeds the half-million-dollar mark, giving players another opportunity to earn significant money from home.
The new prize structure awards top finishers with $7,500, including $2,500 for the winner. The remaining $2,500 goes to bonus prizes distributed among different categories.
TTs are now more important than ever for players looking to qualify for the Esports World Cup.

Last year, players competing in TT had a cap on how many Champions Chess Tour Leaderboard points they could accumulate during each Split of the Titled Tuesday Grand Prix. Now, the Split structure is gone, with players accumulating points throughout the year. With this new structure, players who consistently finish at the top of the TT standings can accumulate hundreds of CCT points—now the only way into the Esports World Cup through the Champions Chess Tour.
Are you excited to watch Titled Tuesday live with GM Robert Hess? Then tune in to our Twitch and YouTube channels every Tuesday to enjoy the show!

news.title: Wesley So Wins 3rd Sinquefield Cup; Tan Zhongyi Claims 2nd Cairns Cup
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Wesley So won his third title and $87,500 at the 2026 Sinquefield Cup on Wednesday. After all the classical games ended in draws, he and GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu contested the champion's title in rapid playoffs. T
body: GM Wesley So won his third title and $87,500 at the 2026 Sinquefield Cup on Wednesday. After all the classical games ended in draws, he and GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu contested the champion's title in rapid playoffs. The two rapid games ended in draws, and with a third draw in a nervy armageddon game, So claimed tournament victory with the black pieces.

GM Tan Zhongyi won her second title and $65,000 at the 2026 Cairns Cup, albeit with a loss in the final round against IM Stavroula Tsolakidou. Since runner-up IM Alice Lee only drew IM Carissa Yip, however, 6.5 points were still enough for Tan to win outright. That draw earned Lee her first grandmaster norm at the age of 16.
The Grand Chess Tour Finals kick off on Saturday, August 22, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. They will feature Praggnanandhaa, So, GM Fabiano Caruana, and GM Vincent Keymer.
So and Praggnanandhaa tied for first in the classical portion, but the American edged out his opponent in playoffs.
Caruana and Praggnanandhaa are the two players returning to the GCT Finals, having played in Sao Paulo last year. GM Javokhir Sindarov missed out by half a GCT point, just as So did in 2025.
Tan won the Cairns Cup for a second time with 6.5 points after nine rounds.

All five games ended in draws, and the most intriguing was the King's Gambit played by GM Jorden van Foreest against GM Vincent Keymer. It was a bold opening choice by the Dutch grandmaster, who was on 1.5/8. "Let's at least do something fun in the last game, I guess," he said after the game, explaining that his brother, GM Lucas van Foreest, suggested it the night before.

Keymer had never played against the King's Gambit over the board, and Van Foreest hoped to take advantage of the tournament situation. The German needed to avoid a loss. Keymer said, "In any other situation, I would be kind of happy to see this, because objectively it's not a great line, but today of course a win would have been nice, but not as nice as a loss would have been bad."

Keymer perhaps could have played more critically—the engines indicate an advantage for Black—but he was also never in danger. Eventually, White won his pawn back in an endgame, and the players repeated moves by move 39. "I'm really relieved," said Keymer on qualifying for the GCT Finals, which comes with a $50,000 bonus. "I made my life extremely difficult by losing to Javokhir [in round seven]."

The other games were all drawn, with the most important encounters being So vs. Sindarov and Praggnanandhaa vs. GM Anish Giri. Sindarov played the King's Indian Defense against So, but by move 11 decided to play the ...d5 pawn break and liquidate, rather than keep the game going with a slightly worse position. "Fortunately, I had the white pieces. I was able to trade, trade, trade," said the champion.
Fortunately, I had the white pieces. I was able to trade, trade, trade.

The other leader, Praggnanandhaa, vacuumed off the pieces with Giri in a Nimzo-Indian Defense and shook hands on move 37. With neither Praggnanandhaa nor So winning in the classical portion, we were guaranteed to see playoffs.

The quickest draw was GM Levon Aronian vs. GM Sam Sevian, which was over in 16 moves. Last but not least, Caruana made a quick draw with GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave in the Moscow Variation of the Sicilian Defense, and said, "The idea was not to lose another game. Maxime didn't have to win... I thought it was kind of a status quo game." Both players had lost in round eight and, evidently, just wanted to cross the finish line.

The playoffs between So and Praggnanandhaa featured two rapid games (10+5 time control), followed immediately by armageddon (five minutes for White, four for Black, with a two-second increment starting only on move 61).

Since winning in rounds two and three, So had coasted to the end of the tournament with draws in every single game. The salient question was: would his safety-first mentality backfire as the time control shortened? You can't argue with the facts: no.
So went undefeated in 12 games, winning two and drawing 10 with a performance of over 2800.

So's strategy was intentional, as he said, "I'm not proud of the early draws, but it's part of a bigger strategy, and it worked." The draws allowed him to conserve energy and also gave him time to prepare for the next games, he explained.

Game one, where So had the white pieces, went straight down a sharp line of the Queen's Gambit Declined, and Praggnanandhaa declared, "This is a well-known draw." If it was a memory test, the Indian grandmaster passed. To the unprofessional eye, however, the game looks bonkers.

The second rapid game was also a draw, in an Italian Opening. Praggnanandhaa played an ambitious—and dubious—pawn expansion with 16.g4, but So traded a pair of knights and offered a threefold repetition, which Praggnanandhaa accepted.

The players went straight to the armageddon game, with Praggnanandhaa winning the drawing of lots. He chose to play with the white pieces, with five minutes against four, and with So receiving draw odds. Given the time control, So said that he also would have picked White: "The time advantage is so big, and as you can see, he was winning in this game."
The time advantage is so big, and as you can see, he was winning in this game.

"I just picked White and tried to flag him... and he almost got flagged," said Praggnanandhaa. More than the time pressure, however, Pragg was winning on the board. But he explained that, without the increment, it was hard to tell where he needed to pause and think; he remarked that if he'd stopped for two or three seconds, he would have found one of the wins. There were several.

"You can't win all tournaments, not this year!" So told Praggnanandhaa right after the game. But the Indian GM, who can still win another $200,000 in the GCT Finals, took the loss in his stride. "It's always a little disappointing when you're so close and miss it, but I think overall it's great that I managed to make it to the Finals."
It's a third Sinquefield Cup for So, who won his first one exactly 10 years ago. He is also the only player to win it two years in a row.
You can see the prize breakdown below, which does not include another $125,000 distributed equally for each game win.

Regarding the tournament victory, it was a two-horse race between Tan and Lee. Nobody, not even Tan, could have known how critical her back-to-back wins in rounds seven and eight would be—they saved her from the playoffs.

Lee made her draw with Yip first, though she, too, was in big trouble. Had Yip played 17...Qc2, she might well have compromised her good friend's quest for a GM norm. Lee said, "The opening didn't go well for me, and I was on the defending side, but I'm glad that later I was able to hold." 22...Bc5 was the second big chance for Yip to play for the win, and once she missed that, Lee escaped into a slightly worse endgame.

Lee is likely the fifth-youngest girl to ever score a GM norm, after GMs Kateryna Lagno, Hou Yifan, Judit Polgar, and Humpy Koneru. She still needs the 2500 FIDE rating and two more norms for the grandmaster title. Her next two tournaments are the Olympiad and the U.S. Women's Championship, but Lee pointed out that she will not be able to earn norms at these events as she won't enough GM opponents. She said she'll have to earn the norms in open tournaments and round-robins.

Tan, who was still playing her game against Tsolakidou, could breathe a sigh of relief after that game ended, even though she was defending a worse position. Even with a loss, she would go on to win the tournament. In our Game of the Day, the Greek IM played the London System, but with an unorthodox plan of trading off her light-square bishop for a knight and, later, playing for dark-square domination. Curiously, her two wins in the tournament came against both Lee, in round four, and Tan.

The only other decisive game of the round was GM Alexandra Kosteniuk's win against GM Vaishali Rameshbabu. It's the first win for Kosteniuk, who started the event with four consecutive losses and then made all draws, while Vaishali—the world championship challenger—finished in last place with zero wins.
Tan is the only Chinese player to have won the Cairns Cup, and she now owns two trophies.
That's it for the Sinquefield Cup and Cairns Cup, but there's almost no time to rest. The GCT Finals start this Saturday!
You can rewatch the round's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated 2026 Sinquefield Cup or 2026 Cairns Cup Events pages.
The Sinquefield Cup broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Maurice Ashley, Cristian Chirila, and Peter Svidler, while the Cairns Cup was covered by IMs Nazi Paikidze and Almira Skripchenko.

The 2026 Sinquefield Cup we the fifth and final leg of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Ten players competed in a classical round-robin tournament with a $475,000 prize fund and points counting for qualification into the Grand Chess Tour Finals. It ran alongside the 2026 Cairns Cup, which was also a 10-player round-robin featuring some of the strongest women in the world, with a prize fund of $250,000.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Chess.com To Host Live FIDE Presidential Debate With Buettner, Rosenstein, Turlov
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: Chess.com will host the first debate of the 2026 FIDE presidential election on September 9, bringing together all three candidates—Jan Henric Buettner, Timur Turlov, and Wadim Rosenstein—to discuss their visions for the
body: Chess.com will host the first debate of the 2026 FIDE presidential election on September 9, bringing together all three candidates—Jan Henric Buettner, Timur Turlov, and Wadim Rosenstein—to discuss their visions for the future of international chess.

The live debate, moderated by GM Maurice Ashley, will give the chess community its first opportunity in this election campaign to hear all three presidential candidates. The debate will be streamed live on Chess.com, with all three candidates and Ashley joining remotely.

Questions will come from Ashley, who will also select some from the Chess.com community. You can submit your own questions in the comments below. The candidates will not receive the questions in advance, and the format has been designed to ensure equal speaking time and equal treatment throughout.
The candidates will begin with opening statements, before Ashley leads a moderated discussion across key topics.

The September 9 debate takes place just 17 days before FIDE's member federations are scheduled to elect the organization's next president at the General Assembly in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, on September 26.
Three candidates are running in the election: Buettner with IM Malcolm Pein, Rosenstein with Gordon Tang, and Turlov with five-time World Champion GM Viswanathan Anand.

Buettner and Rosenstein became the first two declared challengers on June 26, the opening day of FIDE's official electoral period. Two days later, Arkady Dvorkovich announced that he would seek a third term, with Turlov as his candidate for Deputy President. Dvorkovich had been FIDE President since defeating Georgios Makropoulos in 2018 and was overwhelmingly reelected in 2022, when he and Anand defeated the ticket of GMs Andrii Baryshpolets and Peter Heine Nielsen by 157 votes to 16.

A third term had only become possible after a controversial change to FIDE's rules in 2023. Dvorkovich had introduced a two-term presidential limit after first being elected, but delegates voted 108-27 at the 2023 General Assembly to remove that restriction from the FIDE Charter.

However, the election changed in July when Dvorkovich announced that he was suspending the exercise of his powers and duties as FIDE President after being placed under sanctions by the European Union. Dvorkovich called the sanctions "unlawful and unfair" and said he would challenge them. Anand, who had served as Deputy President since 2022, assumed the responsibilities of Interim President.
Turlov, who had been set to run as Dvorkovich's deputy, then launched his own presidential bid with Anand as his running mate.

Timur Turlov is a Moscow-born Kazakh billionaire who is worth an estimated $6.9 billion, according to Forbes. The 38-year-old is the founder and CEO of Freedom Holding and President of the Kazakhstan Chess Federation. His company has become FIDE's main sponsor in recent years, while Kazakhstan has hosted a growing number of major FIDE events.

Turlov entered the election in unusual circumstances. Initially chosen as Dvorkovich's candidate for Deputy President, he switched to the presidential race following Dvorkovich's suspension and announced Anand as his own candidate for deputy.

Jan Henric Buettner is a German entrepreneur who has emerged as a major figure in the chess world ever since organizing the 2024 Freestyle Chess G.O.A.T. Challenge at his luxury Weissenhaus resort on the Baltic coast.

The 61-year-old went on to become one of the driving forces behind Freestyle Chess, securing more than $27 million in investment for its Grand Slam Tour. His involvement also put him at the center of a high-profile dispute with FIDE over plans to award a Freestyle Chess world championship title, a conflict that was eventually resolved.

Buettner's campaign has said it will focus on strengthening national federations, governance and transparency, commercial partnerships, chess in schools, opportunities for women and developing chess nations, and digital innovation. His running mate Pein has been a prominent tournament organizer and an outspoken critic of FIDE's leadership.
Wadim Rosenstein, also from Germany, has become an increasingly prominent organizer and investor in chess through WR Chess. At 35 years old, he is the youngest of the three candidates.

Rosenstein has backed the WR Chess Masters and helped create what became FIDE's World Rapid & Blitz Team Championship. He is currently the German Chess Federation's FIDE Delegate. His presidential campaign has called for stronger leadership and governance at FIDE, improved digital infrastructure, more sponsorship and investment, and greater support for member federations.
The September 9 debate will give all three candidates the opportunity to make their case for leading FIDE before the federation's members vote 17 days later.
What questions do you have for Buettner, Rosenstein, and Turlov? Share them in the comments below.

Tarjei J. Svensen

news.title: Barcelona Legend Gerard Pique Doubles Down On Chess With American Gambits Investment
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: Former Barcelona and Spain star Gerard Pique has become a strategic shareholder in Global Chess League franchise FYERS American Gambits, adding to a chess portfolio that already includes an investment in Freestyle Chess.
body: Former Barcelona and Spain star Gerard Pique has become a strategic shareholder in Global Chess League franchise FYERS American Gambits, adding to a chess portfolio that already includes an investment in Freestyle Chess.

Pique is revealed as the latest member of the American Gambits' ownership group ahead of the fourth season of the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League, which takes place September 3-13 in Bengaluru, India.
He will join another sporting great, former Indian cricket star Ravichandran Ashwin, who became a co-owner when the American Gambits entered the Global Chess League in 2024.

Pique retired from professional soccer in 2022 after a fantastic career in which he made 615 official appearances for Barcelona and won 30 trophies with the club, including three Champions League titles. He was also part of the Spain team that won the 2010 World Cup.

"Chess has fascinated me for a long time because of its depth, its global appeal and the incredible mental strength it demands," the 39-year-old said in announcing the investment. "What attracts me to FYERS American Gambits is the ambition to take chess to a new level and its long-term vision for the sport," he added.
Chess has fascinated me for a long time because of its depth, its global appeal and the incredible mental strength it demands.—Gerard Pique

The American Gambits' six-player team is headed by none other than world championship challenger GM Javokhir Sindarov. He will be joined by GMs Nihal Sarin and Daniil Dubov, French youngster GM Marc'Andria Maurizzi, GM Bibisara Assaubayeva, and IM Sara Khadem. The team will be led by GM Srinath Narayanan.

Gerard Pique's investment in FYERS American Gambits is a landmark moment for our franchise and, we believe, for the evolution of chess as a global sport. Gerard understands what it takes to build a global sporting property, one that combines elite competition with compelling storytelling, passionate communities and a strong connection with fans. His belief in our vision is incredibly meaningful as we look to build a franchise that can represent the future of chess.

This is not Pique's first investment in chess. He is also an investor in Freestyle Chess, the venture founded by GM Magnus Carlsen and German entrepreneur Jan Henric Buettner. Pique's involvement was publicly known in 2025, and he made an appearance in the chess world at the Freestyle Chess Grand Slam Las Vegas that July.
Joining the official broadcast with GM David Howell, IM Tania Sachdev, as well as Buettner, he revealed he was attending his first top chess event.

Asked who his favorite player was, he said: "For me, Magnus. I think for everyone. He is a legend." And which position would Carlsen play on a soccer field? "I assume in the midfield because he will move the team all around!" the former defender said.
For me, Magnus. I think for everyone. He is a legend.—Gerard Pique on his favorite player.

Pique's interest in rethinking traditional sports predates his retirement. He founded sports and media company Kosmos in 2017 while still playing for Barcelona, and later created the Kings League, a seven-a-side soccer competition built around shorter games, unconventional rules, streamers and content creators, and a presentation designed for digital audiences.

The similarities with some of the recent experiments in chess are obvious. Both Freestyle Chess and the Global Chess League are in different ways attempts to market top-level chess as an entertainment product capable of attracting audiences beyond traditional chess fans.

Pique is also part of a growing group of sporting stars putting money behind chess. In March, Chess.com reported on Manchester City striker Erling Haaland's investment in the FIDE-approved Total Chess World Championship Tour, which is organized by the team behind Norway Chess.

A month later the Norwegians also revealed a $10 million funding round featuring Norwegian cross-country skiing superstar Johannes Hosflot Klaebo, former cycling world champion Thor Hushovd, and a group of prominent business investors.

Tarjei J. Svensen

news.title: Carlsen Wins 2026 Esports World Cup: 7 Conclusions
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Magnus Carlsen made it back-to-back victories as he claimed the $250,000 top prize in the 2026 Esports World Cup in Paris. We take a look back at an event that also featured brilliant performances by teenage stars GMs
body: GM Magnus Carlsen made it back-to-back victories as he claimed the $250,000 top prize in the 2026 Esports World Cup in Paris. We take a look back at an event that also featured brilliant performances by teenage stars GMs Denis Lazavik and Sina Movahed, some table slams and controversy, and content we had no right to expect from Carlsen and his speed chess arch-rival GM Hikaru Nakamura.

In 2025, Carlsen won all five matches he played in the first ever Chess Esports World Cup in Riyadh, but he did lose some games along the way—two against Nakamura in the Semifinals, and one against GM Alireza Firouzja in the Final. This time in Paris he again won all five matches, but didn't lose a single game, overcoming GMs Andrey Esipenko (1.5-0.5), Hans Niemann (1.5-0.5), Nihal Sarin (2.5-0.5), Firouzja (4-1), and Lazavik (3-1 and 3-1).

The dominance hadn't seemed a foregone conclusion when Carlsen survived a lost position in the second game against Esipenko and, clearly under the weather, commented: "I’m not in any shape to play chess, but I managed to survive the first match, so hopefully I can survive one more, and then we’ll see!"

My first match was a little bit shaky against Esipenko, and then against Niemann I felt I was more or less able to do exactly what I wanted to do, and then I kind of recovered a little bit, I didn’t feel as sick for the last two days. And I feel that I was able to play at a very, very good level in the last two matches, so I’m really happy with everything, especially the way things were. I feel like everything pretty much went like a 10/10!

Asked who or what could stop him, Carlsen commented, "I don’t know, I think in this format it’s not easy at the moment!" He pointed to Firouzja as having been the player who came closest, but despite some incredibly intense games, Carlsen won their Semifinal with two draws and then a three-game winning streak.
The second Esports World Cup title was yet another accomplishment to add to the world number-one's list.
19-year-old Lazavik had a rockier road to the Final, losing a match to Nakamura on the first day. He escaped a lost position only to lose a totally drawn one in a wild time scramble.

The Belarusian grandmaster shrugged that off, however, hitting back to knock out GM Ian Nepomniachtchi, then GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov, then get revenge on Nakamura, before finally falling to Carlsen with no real chances in the Final.
That failure was relative, since Lazavik had picked up a potentially life-changing $190,000.
*only the top-scoring member of a team counts for the overall standings

Lazavik's success, however, was hardly a shock. Carlsen commented on his reaching the final: "I think by this point anyone who underestimates him is in for a little bit of a surprise, so he’s earned his right to be here and it’s really no accident."
I think by this point anyone who underestimates him is in for a little bit of a surprise.
Lazavik reached the eight-player Finals of the 2023 Champions Chess Tour, and most notably this year played in the four-player Speed Chess Finals in Paris, which had a familiar lineup.
Back then Carlsen beat Lazavik in the Semifinals, while Lazavik edged out Nakamura in the match for third place, while this time those matches took place in reverse order, but with the same outcomes.

The only thing Lazavik may still need to work on is his key crushing. Instead of crushing Nepomniachtchi's key he saw an inviting gap and went for it—putting his defeated opponent's key in the winner's trophy!

The one controversy in the run-up to the event was that it clashed directly with the Sinquefield Cup in St. Louis. Seven of the world's top players published an open letter in February asking for the Esports World Cup and the Grand Chess Tour to work together to try and avoid the clash.

In the end, however, neither side was able to change the dates, with the majority of players deciding to honor a previous contract with the Grand Chess Tour. That meant GM Levon Aronian (a quarterfinalist in 2025), GMs Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Anish Giri, and Fabiano Caruana (all in the Last 16 in 2025), and GMs Wesley So, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, Vincent Keymer, and Javokhir Sindarov were among the players to miss out.

Firouzja, the runner-up in 2025, was the one who opted for the Esports World Cup instead. According to the Grand Chess Tour, he cited, "a scheduling conflict and his desire, as France's top-ranked player, to represent France in another competition."
The decision came with contractual penalties, but Firouzja did get to the final day in Paris, eventually taking the $100,000 prize for fourth place.
That wasn't what Firouzja was going for, of course, and he gave Carlsen a real fight in the Semifinals before his time management ultimately doomed him to defeat.
The third-place clash against Nakamura was much less significant, but the best-of-six match still had a $45,000 difference in prize money at stake.

When Nakamura sacrificed a rook to take the lead in game two it was already difficult for Firouzja, but everything fell apart for the 23-year-old in game three, when internet issues in the venue saw the game interrupted, before Nakamura took over and clinched a win that put him two points ahead with only two games to go. It was a mountain to climb, but far from outside the bounds of possibility for the Frenchman.

Firouzja left the stage, however, and a tense 20-minute wait followed, during which neither chess fans nor Nakamura knew what was happening. When the announcement came, it was that Firouzja wouldn't return—the fifth game was given as a forfeit win for Nakamura.

Some treated it as an issue with online chess and asked why the players weren't competing on chessboards in Paris, but—apart from it needing to be an esport!—some of the reasons have been brought up many times before. If the players were competing in 10+0 chess with wooden pieces we would be guaranteed chaotic finishes needing VAR-like interventions to decide who had toppled pieces first or failed to hit the clock before fixing the board.

Whether Firouzja was fined for his non-appearance (the regulations mention potential penalty points for players, each costing one percent of their winnings), it was a disappointing finish to the match. We want to see everything decided over the board.

While Lazavik put in a brilliant performance, it was another teenager who was perhaps the break-out star of the tournament. "Seen-a-move-ahead" is already an online legend, having won individual Titled Tuesdays, topped the Spring standings this year, and claimed the ChessKid Under 16 Youth Championship in a final where he defeated the junior number-one GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus. We've rarely seen Movahed in person, however, while in Paris the 16-year-old Iranian was both great fun on the board and eloquent off it.

Almost all his games and matches seemed to be wild. He hit back and forced armageddon before losing to Lazavik, traded wins before beating GM Alexey Sarana in armageddon, then came incredibly close to forcing a third armageddon, against Niemann. Movahed was totally winning, but in a chaotic time scramble he let the win slip away, and didn't hide his frustration.

Niemann had that effect on his opponents, with Nepomniachtchi giving the most dramatic reaction of the event when he seemed to mouse-slip, though in a position where he'd already blundered on the board, so that the intended move wouldn't have helped.

When Carlsen won 1,000 points in 2025, Team Liquid, represented by himself and Caruana, took the lead in the overall club championship. In the end, however, Team Falcons, who got 750 points for Firouzja's second-place finish, topped the table to earn $7 million to Liquid's $4 million.

Similar stakes are at play this year, with the winning team getting $7 million, and the runner-up $5 million, but things are very different. Team Liquid hasn't been competitive, with Carlsen's 1,000 points providing two-thirds of their 1,500 total, which leaves them in 11th place on the 2026 standings. The top, however, has been heavily influenced by chess.

When Lazavik finished runner-up for 750 points his AG.AL was top, but Team Falcons scored 500 points—which it would have scored regardless of who won the third-place match between its two players, Nakamura and Firouzja. That's been crucial, as Falcons currently leads by 300 points. Chess is very much part of the Esports World Cup battle.

If there was one big matchup we wanted to see but didn't, it was between Carlsen and Nakamura, who played a thrilling Semifinal in 2025. This year they could have met in the Final, but Lazavik intervened. We did, however, get more content involving the two than we could ever have expected.

The main highlight was a lie-detector episode featuring the two great rivals. Nakamura was asked if he considered Carlsen a friend, with the U.S. grandmaster responding (truthfully, says the tech): "Now I would say yes. The first 75 percent of my career, the answer would be 100 percent no!"

What's obvious is the huge mutual respect. Carlsen says "absolutely" when asked if Nakamura is his greatest rival in blitz, is flagged as lying when he says Caruana is a better player than Nakamura, and expands on Nakamura's greatest strengths: "Understanding of structures. I feel what sets you apart the most when I see you play people, especially when that’s not me, is finding the right structures and maneuvering. There’s no contest to people like Fabiano, for instance."

It's not that it's all mutual love. Both celebrate each other's losses, with Carlsen commenting: "Yeah, many times! It’s more of a stream hate watch kind of thing. That’s been many times, and my wife, when we first met, was a bit mad that I would watch your streams!"
My wife, when we first met, was a bit mad that I would watch your streams!
Carlsen says he isn't surprised but thinks others will be when Nakamura (seemingly) truthfully responds, "No," to the question, "Would you trade your streaming career for my chess career?"

The most remarkable answer, however, is perhaps to the question of whether Carlsen holds a grudge against Nakamura, to which the five-time classical world champion quickly responds: "The Norway blitz tournament back in 2009—that really hurt me, the pawn race!"
Carlsen was completely winning in the second game of the final of the BNbank Blitz 2009 and would have taken a 2-0 lead in a four-game match, but blundered and lost that game and then the match.
18-year-old Carlsen didn't hide his frustration when he realized he was lost.
Let's hope the Esports World Cup creates some grudges that still resonate 17 years later!

Colin McGourty
          
  

    
            
  
      
      
    
                        
                
                            
      
      
      
    
      


              
          Colin McGourty led news at Chess24 from its launch until it merged with Chess.com a decade later. An amateur player, he got into chess writing when he set up the website Chess in Translation after previously studying Slavic languages and literature in St. Andrews, Odesa, Oxford, and Krakow.

news.title: Kramnik Takes New In Chess To Court Over Naroditsky Article
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: GM Vladimir Kramnik has taken New In Chess magazine to court over an article that accused the former world champion of cyberbullying GM Daniel Naroditsky and examined the impact of his public comments on GM David Navara
body: GM Vladimir Kramnik has taken New In Chess magazine to court over an article that accused the former world champion of cyberbullying GM Daniel Naroditsky and examined the impact of his public comments on GM David Navara and others.

A hearing in the defamation case took place in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, on August 18, with Kramnik participating via video link. Following the hearing on Tuesday, the magazine said it was "profoundly pleased" with the defense, provided by Dutch law firm Kennedy Van der Laan. "In court we stood by the content of the article and our right to publish it."
A ruling in the case is expected on September 1, the magazine said.

The lawsuit concerns "A Very Public Feud," a six-page article by Leon Watson, a former Chess.com journalist, published in New In Chess 2025/8. The issue was released in December 2025, less than two months after Naroditsky died at the age of 29. His death was later ruled an accident by the medical examiner.
The article's introduction states: "Daniel Naroditsky was the victim of cyberbullying at the hands of Vladimir Kramnik."

It then recounts the increasingly bitter conflict between Kramnik and Naroditsky over the former world champion’s suspicions about cheating in online chess, along with Kramnik’s public allegations and insinuations involving Navara and other prominent players.

Watson’s article begins with an image from 2008 showing the then-13-year-old Naroditsky alongside Kramnik at the Tal Memorial in Moscow. Naroditsky, who had been too shy to approach the former world champion himself, later recalled that the picture "made me smile." The article contrasts that childhood admiration with the relationship between the two players 17 years later.

What cuts deep, what makes the pain so searing for so many, is that the final year of Naroditsky's life was dominated by a long, bruising dispute with Kramnik, the man he idolized. It was Kramnik who repeatedly insinuated that Naroditsky had used engine assistance online.

The New In Chess article also examined Kramnik's dispute with Navara, who had been named in connection with suspicious online results. Navara later said Kramnik's posts had left him sleeping poorly, that he had sought psychiatric help, and that at one stage he had considered taking his own life.

Watson went beyond Kramnik's public statements, also examining anonymous social-media accounts that attacked some of his critics and raising the possibility that Kramnik himself operated some of them.
Kramnik most likely used burner accounts on social media, such as the SleepyJoe account.

The article also included critical assessments of Kramnik from current and former friends and colleagues, including comments questioning his state of mind. However, it did not claim that Kramnik caused Naroditsky's death and explicitly cautioned against speculating about the circumstances, even while arguing that his accusations had weighed heavily on Naroditsky.
New In Chess first publicly announced the lawsuit on August 3, saying that defending the case was generating substantial legal costs. The magazine asked readers to support it by subscribing.

New In Chess said it would make no further comment before the September 1 ruling. New In Chess Group owner GM Jacob Aagaard also declined to comment when contacted by Chess.com, as did Watson, the author of the article.

Public statements about the lawsuit have so far not detailed precisely which passages Kramnik is asking the court to find defamatory, nor what specific remedies he is seeking. Chess.com reached out to Kramnik, who did not respond to the request for comment.

The New In Chess lawsuit is separate from FIDE's disciplinary case against Kramnik, but comes less than two months after the Ethics & Disciplinary Commission found him responsible for multiple violations of the FIDE Ethics Code and Disciplinary Code arising from his public statements about Naroditsky, Navara, and other players. Those included cyberbullying, psychological abuse, and false or unjustified public accusations.

The EDC imposed a two-year worldwide ban from FIDE competitions and official chess functions, with the final 12 months suspended. Kramnik was also ordered to perform 12 months of unpaid service for the benefit of the chess community.

Kramnik denied wrongdoing throughout the FIDE proceedings and has described the EDC ruling as unlawful. He said on X that he has since filed a formal appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

news.title: Minh Le Continues Blitz Run In 3 0 Thursday
news.author: coachjkane
news.excerpt: GM Tuan Minh Le followed up his Titled Tuesday victory by winning the first 3 0 Thursday tournament of the week on August 20. He's the fifth player to complete the Tuesday-Thursday double victory on the same week, joinin
body: GM Tuan Minh Le followed up his Titled Tuesday victory by winning the first 3 0 Thursday tournament of the week on August 20. He's the fifth player to complete the Tuesday-Thursday double victory on the same week, joining the company of GMs Fabiano Caruana, Denis Lazavik, Arjun Erigaisi, and Jan-Krzysztof Duda. Duda also had a successful day, winning the second tournament. GM Aravindh Chithambaram was first among equals in the third event, edging out three other players on tiebreaks to take the title.

Minh Le had a strong start to the first tournament, winning four games before giving up a draw to GM Maxim Matlakov in round five. He responded by winning a spectacular sixth-round game against GM Dmitrij Kollars, where he sacrificed both rooks for a mating attack.

news.title: Nakamura Comeback Seals Milestone 64th Victory
news.author: jackrodgers
news.excerpt: GM Hikaru Nakamura reached a tremendous milestone on Saturday after bringing up his 64th career Bullet Brawl victory, meaning he can now fill the squares of a chessboard with imaginary trophies for each win. Nakamura toi
body: GM Hikaru Nakamura reached a tremendous milestone on Saturday after bringing up his 64th career Bullet Brawl victory, meaning he can now fill the squares of a chessboard with imaginary trophies for each win. Nakamura toiled away in the two-hour arena and fought his way back from third to first place, finishing with 164 points and capturing the $400 first prize.
Seven points behind him in second place and winning $250 was GM Ediz Gurel, while GMs Nihal Sarin and Oleksandr Bortnyk earned the respective $150 and $100 third and fourth place prizes.
A duel for the $100 best women's prize between IM-elect Rose Atwell and WIM Melika Mohammadi was decided by a single point in favor of the American.
The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, August 29, at 12 p.m. ET / 18:00 CEST / 9:30 p.m. IST.

Heavyweights including Nakamura, Nihal, and Bortnyk made their return to the Bullet Brawl arena on Saturday following a brief hiatus due to their participation in the 2026 Esports World Cup. They were joined by prodigies in GMs Gurel, Andy Woodward, IM Faustino Oro, and 183 other titled players.

Nihal was the form player of the first quarter, courtesy of a nine-game winning streak, in which he finished three games in less than 25 moves. The piece de resistance of the streak was not one of his miniatures, however, but a 75-move grinding win over the 10-time winner Gurel.

When Nihal's streak was snapped by Hikaru, he responded resiliently with a second streak of seven wins. Still, a horde of bullet titans, led by the only player able to defeat him, closed the gap by playing a higher volume of games.

As the halfway mark drew near, GMs Nihal, Gurel, Nakamura, Sergei Zhigalko, Bortnyk, and Tuan Minh Le began to break away, with the former two trading spots at the top multiple times. Nakamura had several opportunities to make his move, but admitted on his Kick stream that "sloppy" play was holding him back.

Eighteen points was the difference between Nakamura and Nihal with 33 minutes to go and the chance for the former to win his 64th title seemed to be slipping away. Refusing to give up, Nakamura stayed within touch of the lead before going on a clutch, eight-game rampage that catapulted him into first.
His capitalization on Gurel's 48.Kg4?? was particularly crucial as the 17-year-old had surpassed Nihal and was threatening to run away with his 11th crown.
A draw with Gurel eventually saw Nakamura's streak come to an end but the damage on the leaderboard was significant—Nakamura held a lead of nine points with seven minutes left on the arena clock.

A subsequent loss to Nihal tightened things at the top end once again before a fateful clash between Nakamura and Gurel determined who would win the event. Their final confrontation was a rollercoaster that could have swung either way...
And so, Nakamura's dominance continues in the Bullet Brawl arena.
How to review games? The games from this week's Bullet Brawl can be found here.

Bullet Brawl is an exciting arena featuring Chess.com's top bullet specialists. It takes place weekly on Saturdays. The format is a two-hour arena with a 1+0 time control; the prize fund is $1,000. Like Titled Tuesday and Arena Kings, Bullet Brawl often features top GMs, including Hikaru Nakamura, Andrew Tang, Tuan Minh Le, and many more!

news.title: Fighting Draws As Grand Chess Tour Finals Begin In St. Louis
news.author: vsaravanan
news.excerpt: A high-voltage Gen Z clash between GMs Vincent Keymer and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, where both sides achieved a big advantage before it ended in a draw, was the highlight of an eventful first day of classical chess in t
body: A high-voltage Gen Z clash between GMs Vincent Keymer and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, where both sides achieved a big advantage before it ended in a draw, was the highlight of an eventful first day of classical chess in the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals in St. Louis. In the other semifinal, dubbed the Match of the Millennials, GM Fabiano Caruana survived anxious moments before holding a draw against GM Wesley So.
The Grand Chess Tour is currently in its 11th edition, with six different winners so far.
As the games got underway, the commentators revealed interesting predictions for the potential winner based on pre-tournament simulations.

The outcomes looked difficult to comprehend, as Keymer holds a high live rating as well as having shown a good performance in the Grand Chess Tour so far. It's likely the statistics heavily factored in Praggnanandhaa and So's performance in the recently concluded 2026 Sinquefield Cup.

Summing up the game afterward when he appeared for the post-game interview, So remarked, "My mistake was Fabi is really excellent in calculation, and I went for a forcing line."  But in fact, when the game started, the audience had nothing much to expect in terms of dynamism as the game followed the sedate Exchange Variation of the French Defense.

Long before the Berlin Defense of the Ruy Lopez appeared on the scene, the Petroff Defense and the Exchange French were the original dread of the king's pawn opening players for their drawish tendencies—just the e-file is open if the game persists with the same pawn structure.

Caruana's choice of adopting the French Defense was a repetition of his game against the same opponent from their earlier clash at The American Cup 2026. But when So preferred the Exchange Variation this time around, groans of "No!" went up from at least a couple of the commentators.
However, So made it pretty interesting quickly by playing 6.c4, creating an isolated pawn for himself, and changing the dynamic equation of the position.

Caruana made things difficult for himself with inconsistent decisions between moves 8 and 12, after which his king found life difficult in the center of the board. With 10...b5 and 11...Bb7, which came after 22 minutes of meditation, his position steadily went downhill.
Appearing for the post-game analysis, Caruana was quite self-critical of his own play at the beginning of the game.

Praggnanandhaa set the tone for the game with an early 4...Qb6, which has been his favorite ploy whenever he is Black and still willing to take risks to win the game. By adopting such unorthodox play early in the game, which might even be in violation of opening principles, he often aims to steer the game into original positions, hoping to catch his opponents out of preparation.
"With Pragg, Black, Green, (or) White, he plays for a win!" exclaimed So on Pragg's play when he turned up for the interview at the commentary room after his own game was over. He continued:

The new generation just plays a totally different kind of chess. I was watching this game, and I had absolutely no clue what was happening. And then Pragg seems very comfortable. He is like, 'I know what I am doing!' And I am like, what is this? Pragg just feels very much at home in these kinds of insane positions!
The new generation just plays a totally different kind of chess!

However, it was Keymer who dominated the early part of the game, showing uncompromising spirit by occupying space early in the center. By the 13th move, he had gained a slight advantage and seemed to be pressing, except for on the clock. He had fallen behind by more than half an hour, which prompted So to remark, "The problem is that Vincent, with three minutes on the clock, loses a hundred or two hundred rating points! When he gets into time trouble, he starts making big mistakes. That's a problem."
What resulted was a fascinating struggle between these two young stars, which made for a mesmerizing Game of the Day, which has been analyzed by GM Rafael Leitao below.
Both the clashes thus ended in draws, and the second set of classical games will be played tomorrow, with colors reversed, after which rapid and blitz sections follow.
You can watch the day's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club's YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated events page.
The broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Peter Svidler, and Maurice Ashley, and IMs Nazi Paikidze and Irine Sukandar.

The 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals is taking place from August 22 to 27 in St. Louis, USA. The $450,000 final event of the 2026 Tour sees GMs Fabiano Caruana, Wesley So, Vincent Keymer, and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu compete in a single-elimination knockout. Each match consists of eight games: two classical (6 points for a win, 3 for a draw, and 0 for a loss), two rapid (4/2/0), and four blitz (2/1/0). The winner claims the Grand Chess Tour title and the $200,000 top prize.

news.title: Narva Beats Zhu Twice To Dominate WR Women's Chess Tour Africa
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: Four-time Estonian Women's Champion IM Mai Narva won both the rapid and blitz segments of the WR Women's Chess Tour - Africa 2026 that took place in Maputo, Mozambique this weekend. She pulled off an upset to defeat wome
body: Four-time Estonian Women's Champion IM Mai Narva won both the rapid and blitz segments of the WR Women's Chess Tour - Africa 2026 that took place in Maputo, Mozambique this weekend. She pulled off an upset to defeat women's world number-four GM Zhu Jiner in both finals to take home $14,000, while both players qualify for the Grand Final in Stuttgart, Germany at the end of the year.
The next leg of the tour takes place in Saint-Tropez, France, starting Tuesday, August 25.

The WR Women's Chess Tour is a tournament series that spans four continents. There are four legs and then a Grand Final: Tokyo, Japan (in June), Punta Cana, the Dominican Republic (in July), Maputo, Mozambique (just finished), and Saint-Tropez, France (about to begin)—before the Grand Final in Germany (at the end of November).

Each leg lasts two days, with rapid on the first and blitz on the second. The day consists of an eight-player single-elimination knockout, with a rapid time control of 15+10 and a blitz time control of 3+2. Rapid matches are best-of-two and blitz matches are best-of-four, with armageddon tiebreaks if needed.
The winner of each event (rapid and blitz separately) earns $7,000 and a seat in the Grand Final later this year.

GMs Vaishali Rameshbabu and Kateryna Lagno were the winners of the event in Tokyo, IMs Carissa Yip and Leya Garifullina triumphed in Punta Cana, and with the addition of Narva and Zhu, we now know six of the eight players for the Grand Final.

Zhu and Narva outrated their rivals by at least 200 points, and in one case over 700 points, so that it looked destined they'd reach the finals, and that's just what happened. The remaining six players in the field managed to score just three draws against them across both rapid and blitz.

There were noteworthy results by African stars, including 19-year-old Angolan WFM Jemima Paulo overcoming four-time and reigning African Women's Champion WGM Shahenda Wafa from Egypt 2-0. Paulo fell 2-0 to Zhu in the semifinals, however, with Zhu previously having convincingly defeated 14-year-old Nigerian Women's Chess Champion WGM Deborah Quickpen.

For Narva it was a 2-0 victory over former African Women's Champion and Arab Women's Champion WIM Lina Nassr from Algeria, and then a 1.5-0.5 win over WGM Shrook Wafa—the elder sister of Shahenda and herself a five-time African Women's Champion.
The final was a great fight, with Zhu much better early on in both games. Nevertheless, Narva could have won the first game...
Narva took $7,000 and already booked her spot in the Finals, while Zhu had to settle for $4,000. Then they came back to the Radisson Blu Hotel in Maputo the next day to play blitz.

The number of games doubled with blitz, but the narrative remained the same. On the way to the final Zhu and Narva conceded two draws between them, but both from positions of strength when they only needed a draw to clinch a match. The final, meanwhile, was even more intense.

Narva continued the way she ended the rapid by clinching wins in the first two games. They both ended with stylish final moves. First, after breaking through in the center and launching an unstoppable attack on the black king, Narva got to sacrifice her queen.
Then in the second game Narva, playing Black, had overrun Zhu on the kingside before she was again able to finish things fast with a threatened fork.

Narva only needed a draw to clinch another victory, but what followed was the most extraordinary game of the match. It could have been over fast around move 32 as Zhu had mate-in-three, but both players were down to under five seconds and the game went on, and on. There were multiple twists, as wins were missed and Narva managed to reach what should have been a fortress, but only a final blunder on move 135 dropped a piece and lost the game.
Zhu carried that momentum through into the final regular blitz game, when she again won on demand to force armageddon.

The players bid how low they were willing to go to get the black pieces and only need a draw, with Zhu winning with a bid of three minutes and 36 seconds. It was a pyrrhic victory, however, since Zhu ultimately lost on time, even if by that point she was a piece down on the board as well.
The seeds of destruction were sown when she reacted badly to Narva's breakthrough in the center.
Narva had completed a fine double victory against the women's world number-four.

Zhu has also booked her spot in the Grand Final, however, and the question of who joins them will be decided this week. The event in France will be of a different caliber entirely, with eight players who could all challenge for the top-two places.
The games begin at 8 a.m. ET / 14:00 CEST / 5:30 p.m. IST on Tuesday, August 25 and can be watched here on Chess.com.

The WR Women's Chess Tour - Africa 2026, held in Maputo, Mozambique, on August 21-22, was the third leg of the inaugural tournament series. It consisted of two separate eight-player single-elimination knockouts, one rapid and one blitz, each with its own prize fund and Grand Final qualification spot. The rapid time control was 15+10 and the blitz was 3+2. The total prize fund was $40,000, with half allocated for the rapid and half for the blitz.
