news.title: Contrasting Wins For Pragg And Caruana
news.author: vsaravanan
news.excerpt: "People are very, very tired!" was the pronouncement of commentator GM Peter Svidler, as we witnessed a high number of errors on the second day of classical time control games at the Semifinals of the 2026 Grand Chess To
body: "People are very, very tired!" was the pronouncement of commentator GM Peter Svidler, as we witnessed a high number of errors on the second day of classical time control games at the Semifinals of the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals.

GM Vincent Keymer steadily outplayed GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu in a complex middlegame, only to commit a decisive blunder under his opponent's time pressure and lose the game in the classical time control. GM Fabiano Caruana was unable to convert his large advantage in the classical game and then won a one-sided bonus blitz tiebreak against GM Wesley So.
Praggnanandhaa now leads with a six-point margin, while Caruana has a two-point margin as the matches move on to quicker time controls.
Day three will move on to rapid and blitz games on Monday, August 24, at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST.

Curiously, the commentators once again repeated the predictions for the winner of the event, factoring in the results of day one of the Semifinals, and the simulation now increased the probability of So or Praggnanandhaa winning.

Since the format of the Semifinals warranted a bonus blitz match in case of another draw in either (or both) of the classical time-control games on the second day, it was eagerly awaited if there could indeed be such entertainment at the end of the day.

As the games entered their crucial middlegame phase, commentator GM Maurice Ashley came out with candid observations on the quality of the games: "Fatigue! ...They played the Saint Louis Rapid and Blitz—27 games of chess. Then they had to play the Sinquefield Cup—nine rounds of classical chess. And now they are playing the Finals. This is back to back to back. I know that they are superstars. But that much chess all within a span of three weeks—that's a lot!"
I know that they are superstars. But that much chess all within a span of three weeks—that's a lot!
Both the games actually opened energetically, as Caruana and Praggnanandhaa chose original and uncompromising opening choices with White, thus promising a good fight on both boards.
As the crucial second game loomed, the mutual score in classical time controls between these two iconic U.S. players was curious to see.
Caruana had just a marginal advantage of having scored a single victory more than So, with a staggering 41 games ending in draws.

The game started sedately as So employed the super-solid Berlin Defense of the Ruy Lopez, thus indicating his preference not to initiate the tactical play we saw in the first round. But Caruana showed his readiness for the opening and gambited a pawn on the sixth move, thus infusing dynamism early in the game.

And by the 14th move, he went even further, pushing his g-pawn two squares on the kingside, thus aiming to gain domination with risky play. And it was obviously going to be a spectator's delight, looking at the nature of the position.

Playing on both sides of the board in the middlegame is considered to be a measure of the strength of a player. Caruana showed his prowess in the second game, advancing his rook pawn on the queenside too, mainly to stifle the activity of Black's pawns and pieces.

But having built up such a large advantage in his favor, Caruana showed a rare case of tentativeness in his play. He failed to spot 27.Ra3! which would have given him a large advantage, instead preferring to play 27.Rac1?. Worse, he came down to having just over 13 minutes on the clock to play 13 moves and reach the time control at move 40.

That made commentator Ashley come out with candid observations on Caruana's play in the game: "I am not liking his body language at all! And the lack of confidence that has plagued him in the last couple of months."
In return, So replied with 27...d5? once again handing a huge advantage to Caruana. It was obvious that both the contestants weren't in their best form during this game.
But it didn't end there. Caruana went for 29.Kg2? with around six and a half minutes remaining on the clock, once again letting So off the hook.
Thus, there was an exciting announcement for spectators at the end of the game.
Now it was time to look at the other statistic between the players—their mutual score in blitz games.
But the tiebreak blitz game proved to be a one-sided affair with a fluent win for Caruana.
Between these two young stars too, the mutual score in classical time controls is almost level, with Pragg having scored just one win more than Keymer.

Perhaps stealing a sneak peek at the opening employed on the adjoining table, Praggnanandhaa decided to rule out the Berlin and employ the offbeat Bishop's Opening for the day. (Fun fact: it used to be called 'The Truth' back in the 19th century, allegedly because it still allows the f2-pawn to move forward by not developing the knight to f3 early. Of course, during that romantic era, it was default to push White's f-pawn forward in the opening against 1.e4 e5 openings liberally.)

And then Praggnanandhaa went even better by playing 4.a3, thus making sure that the light-squared bishop would not be exchanged off by the black knight. So, just as in the first game, we had a remarkably original position on the board by just the fourth move of the game.

This is when commentator Svidler came up with an absolute gem regarding the opening choices of Praggnanandhaa and Caruana for this crucial game. (Caruana had already unleashed a gambit in the opening against So's Berlin Defense on the other board at this point.)

"The difference in approach between the 20-year-olds and the 35-ish-year-olds here is quite pronounced! Fabi is playing a sacrificial line, but it is still a line inside an absolutely main stream opening... Pragg, on the other board, is just free-styling by move four, just to get a game!"
The difference in approach between the 20-year-olds and the 35-ish-year-olds here is quite pronounced!
An important detail during the middlegame was that Praggnanandhaa was lower on the clock than Keymer, as the former had consumed too much time in the phase planning the h2-h4 pawn break.

Just as a tense middlegame was developing, Keymer came up with a brilliant idea, which looked optically appealing. With 21...Nc4! he actually welcomed the white queen to come into his own fortress to attack the black king, not fearing the damage it would do to his own position. The concept, as well as the psychological risk, was a delight to watch as the game entered a tense middlegame phase.

A complex middlegame with both being short of time saw both the players lose their composure on the board and become visibly tense. Praggnanandhaa had just 39 seconds on his clock after move 32, while Keymer came down to as low as a minute and 15 seconds before replying.
This exciting game is our Game Of The Day, analyzed by GM Rafael Leitao below.

The Semifinals enter the final phase next, with the rapid and blitz games, where Pragg has a huge six-point advantage, while Caruana has a slender two-point lead. Another interesting day of quick time controls beckons.
You can watch the day's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club's YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated events page.
The broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Peter Svidler, and Maurice Ashley, and IM Nazi Paikidze.

The 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals is taking place from August 22-27 in St. Louis, USA. The $450,000 final event of the 2026 Tour sees GMs Fabiano Caruana, Wesley So, Vincent Keymer, and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu compete in a single-elimination knockout. Each match consists of eight games: two classical (6 points for a win, 3 for a draw, and 0 for a loss), two rapid (4/2/0), and four blitz (2/1/0). The winner claims the Grand Chess Tour title and the $200,000 top prize.

news.title: Daily Puzzles Just Got More Exciting
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: Your daily dose of puzzle practice just got a glow-up! The new Daily Puzzle now features five lives instead of just one shot at glory, a fresh way to brag about your puzzle prowess, and a puzzle that refreshes according
body: Your daily dose of puzzle practice just got a glow-up! The new Daily Puzzle now features five lives instead of just one shot at glory, a fresh way to brag about your puzzle prowess, and a puzzle that refreshes according to your local time.

Every day, more than a million members come to Chess.com to solve the exact same puzzle. Active for almost two decades, Daily Puzzle is not only a good way to stay sharp—it's also a fun tradition that our community looks forward to every day.
Here's everything you need to know about the new Daily Puzzle experience, and why now is a better time than ever to join in on the fun:

You now get five lives every day to complete your Daily Puzzle. If you miss a move, you'll lose one of your hearts—but the challenge keeps going, and your coach gives you a helpful tip! Now, you can enjoy your bragging rights when you finish with all five hearts intact, or just chill knowing you'll have another shot if you get it wrong. And even if you run out of hearts, your Daily Puzzle streak will still keep going!
If you're a hardcore solver who likes to find the answers on your own, you can still hide coach tips. Just click the settings icon and turn on "Hard Mode" to work through each one solo.

Are you particularly proud of a Daily Puzzle you've just solved? Maybe you got that Friday head-scratcher on your first try, and you feel like challenging your friends to do the same. You can now easily share your results as soon as the puzzle ends. Click the share button and get a results card with your heart count and a special nod for solving on Hard Mode.

Daily Puzzle used to refresh at the same time for everyone in the world. But now, it adjusts to your schedule and introduces a new puzzle at midnight in your local time. So whether you're in New York or Beijing, you'll have a brand-new challenge waiting for you when you wake up.
Have you tried the new Daily Puzzle yet? Solve it and share your results in the comments below!

news.title: Caruana, Praggnanandhaa Set Up Generational Clash In Final
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GMs Fabiano Caruana and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu are the two finalists in the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals. Praggnanandhaa won his match against GM Vincent Keymer with four games to spare, and then lost the last three b
body: GMs Fabiano Caruana and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu are the two finalists in the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals. Praggnanandhaa won his match against GM Vincent Keymer with four games to spare, and then lost the last three blitz games to end with a 19-9 score, while Caruana won the closer match against GM Wesley So 18-12.

The players start with a clean slate in the Final on Tuesday, August 25, at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. That will feature the first classical game of two matches: one for first place and the other for third place.

Keymer and So will play the match for third place, which still entails high stakes. The winner of that match guarantees their participation in next year's Grand Chess Tour, which comes with salary-like compensation for the players for an entire year.
With these results, we will see a battle of generations in the Final: Gen Z against the Millennial.
The format featured two rapid games, with the 25+10 time control, followed by four blitz games, with the 5+2 time control.

After having blown a winning position in the classical portion on Sunday, and losing it, Keymer was a shadow of himself in the rapid games. As GM Peter Svidler diagnosed, "Yesterday must have been such a shock to the system that he's clearly not recovered." The German grandmaster lost three games to start the day.
Yesterday must have been such a shock to the system that he's clearly not recovered.

The first rapid game was Praggnanandhaa's cleanest game up to that point, said IM Nazi Paikidze. Keymer was in a desperate situation with the black pieces, down six points, and his choice of opening was the Pirc Defense. Praggnanandhaa, content with a draw, traded queens on move five and played a two-result position with machine-like accuracy.

While Praggnanandhaa said the deciding game had already been played yesterday, he said that game one of the rapid blew the steam out of Keymer's sails. "If he had gotten better chances in the first game," Praggnanandhaa said, "maybe he would have been more energetic, but once you get such an endgame that is just one-sided, it just takes away all your energy." This masterclass in "two-result chess" is our Game Of The Day, analyzed by GM Rafael Leitao.

In the next game, Praggnanandhaa was already better with the black pieces by move seven. 7.Nc3? e5 allowed Black a dream position in the Rossolimo Sicilian, which quickly took on the character of a free King's Indian-style attack for Praggnanandhaa. White found his queen trapped on move 20.
All four blitz games were played anyway, though Praggnanandhaa won the match with four games to spare. In the first game, Praggnanandhaa went from a losing position to finding a forced mate in three.

Although it did not alter the match result, Keymer's hat trick to finish the match will give him the confidence he needs to put up a fight in the match for third place. As for Praggnanandhaa, he said he looks forward to the match with Caruana: "We've had some crazy matches in the past, so it's going to be interesting. We'll see, I mean it's going to be a close fight and who's going to show up at their best on a given day is going to take it."
We've had some crazy matches in the past, so it's going to be interesting.

Having won the bonus blitz game after two draws in classical, Caruana started the day with a two-point lead. He sat comfortably on the match advantage, making controlled draws in the two rapid games. "We could have seen a totally different match," said Caruana, if So had won a classical game.
The world number-two framed his win this way: "It's a close match, either of us could win, and it could very much come down to the form of the day, and that's what I think it came down to today."

The two draws in rapid were uneventful: first, Caruana was unable to find any dents in So's ultra-solid Berlin Defense, and then in the rook endgame So made a move that eliminated any winning chances and left the commentators speechless. The natural move is to recapture on d4 with the rook, so as to pressure the isolated pawn on the d-file.

After those two draws, Caruana extended his lead to four points when he won the first blitz game. 20...Nd7?? was one of those blunders you cannot come back from, even with the faster time control. So lost a pawn, and the position fell apart. As GM Maurice Ashley put it, "He just ran through Wesley in that one."
The second blitz game, Caruana just barely saved a lost position with a desperate breakthrough on the kingside, which fortunately for him, ended in a perpetual check.

So had to win with the black pieces and played the Modern Defense, but Caruana very cleanly made the most of the space advantage, winning a "dim knight" on the rim of the board, all while needing only a draw. Caruana clinched the match, and they made a fighting draw in the final game.
Caruana had the following to say about the upcoming match against the younger GM:

It is clear he's a player who takes a lot of risks, and he'll give you chances, and he'll also punish you if you don't take those chances. That's the kind of player that I play against... but I am very happy to be in the Final.

The worst-case scenario for the finalists at this point is losing the match and earning $125,000. But winning the match is another $75,000. Caruana, the defending champion, could be the first player to win the GCT two years in a row; for Praggnanandhaa, it would be his maiden title. With the drawing of lots, Praggnanandhaa and So will start with the black pieces.
Day four features two classical games, one in the Final and another in the match for third place.
You can watch the day's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club's YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated events page.
The broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Peter Svidler, and Maurice Ashley, and IM Nazi Paikidze.

The 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals take place from August 22-27 in St. Louis, Missouri. The $450,000 final event of the 2026 Tour sees GMs Fabiano Caruana, Wesley So, Vincent Keymer, and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu compete in a single-elimination knockout. Each match consists of eight games: two classical (6 points for a win, 3 for a draw, and 0 for a loss), two rapid (4/2/0), and four blitz (2/1/0). The winner claims the Grand Chess Tour title and the $200,000 top prize.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Ready Your Quacktics For The Chess.com Duck Chess Championship Starting On September 2
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: For most people, the rubber duck is a whimsical bath accessory. For chess players, though, it is an instrument of war—and we invite you to wield this powerful weapon in the upcoming Chess.com Duck Chess Championship. The
body: For most people, the rubber duck is a whimsical bath accessory. For chess players, though, it is an instrument of war—and we invite you to wield this powerful weapon in the upcoming Chess.com Duck Chess Championship. The event takes place from September 2 to 4 and features a $2,500 prize fund.

Duck Chess is one of Chess.com's most chaotic and beloved variants. Its rules are similar to regular chess, with one main addition—on their turn, players place a rubber duck on the board that serves as a barrier to other pieces. This barrier opens the possibility of new and surprising tactics (or quacktics, as they're known in Duck Chess) that can turn the tide of the game in a second. Below is a video of one of this variant's most famous enthusiasts, IM Eric Rosen.

The event kicks off with the qualifiers on September 2 and 3. Each of the eight qualifiers is a 75-minute arena with a 3+2 time control. Qualifiers are open to all Chess.com members. To participate, check out the qualifier schedule below and click Join in the qualifier you'd like to play.

During the qualifiers, players may be asked to join a fair play call to ensure everyone's safety (though no one is really 100% safe when it comes to Duck Chess). Players who join the call must be ready to set up two cameras from different angles in the room and share their screen. Failing to join the call or complete any security check will result in the player's disqualification from the tournament.
The winner of each qualifier then moves on to the Final, which takes place on September 4. The Final is a double-elimination knockout bracket with a 3+2 time control and best-of-four matches.

Last year, Duck Chess specialist IM Nhat Minh To defended the title with a perfect 12-0 run in the knockout portion of the tournament. Minh To defeated his Duck Chess rival Rosen twice on the way to the title—in the Winners Final and Grand Final—the latter a rematch of their 2024 Grand Final, which Minh To also won.
Are you ready to catch your opponents off guard with some impressive quacktics? Then join the qualifiers on September 2 and 3!

news.title: Carlsen, Caruana Lead 18 Confirmed Players For Total Chess Pilot In Budapest
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: World number-one GM Magnus Carlsen and GM Fabiano Caruana headline the first 18 confirmed players for the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot, November 10-21, in Budapest, which will test a new format combining fas
body: World number-one GM Magnus Carlsen and GM Fabiano Caruana headline the first 18 confirmed players for the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot, November 10-21, in Budapest, which will test a new format combining fast classical, rapid, and blitz chess.

Eight of the world’s top 10 and 14 of the top 30 appear in the initial lineup announced by the organizers on Tuesday. The 24-player event will take place at the five-star Anantara New York Palace Budapest Hotel. The remaining six participants are set to be announced in September.

The tournament in Budapest is a test for the FIDE-approved Total Chess World Championship Tour, a four-event annual circuit scheduled to launch in 2027 and crown the first combined champion in all three formats. The event was originally scheduled for October but has now been moved to November to avoid a clash with the U.S. Chess Championships.
"I look forward to playing the Total Chess World Championship in Budapest this year," Carlsen said. "It’s always interesting to try out new formats."
It’s always interesting to try out new formats.—Magnus Carlsen

Norway Chess/Total Chess CEO Kjell Madland is excited for the event: "The Budapest Pilot represents far more than another elite tournament. It is the first step towards creating a truly global championship ecosystem."
The field also includes GMs Vincent Keymer, Wesley So, Anish Giri, Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Arjun Erigaisi, and Alireza Firouzja, which means only two players from the August top 10 are missing.

Two of the world's leading women are also competing: GM Vaishali Rameshbabu, who won the 2026 FIDE Women’s Candidates Tournament, will be joined by the player who finished half a point behind her, three-time Women’s World Blitz Champion GM Bibisara Assaubayeva.

Vaishali’s brother, reigning Norway Chess Champion GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, said: "It's an exciting format which challenges players to show their best performance in all three classical, rapid, and blitz formats. Looking forward to being part of the first edition."

Some notable players are missing compared to the list of qualified players, but it's hardly a surprise to see Classical World Champion, GM Gukesh Dommaraju, and his challenger GM Javokhir Sindarov absent as they will begin their match in Geneva, Switzerland just four days after the conclusion in Budapest.

Also missing is GM Hikaru Nakamura, who is third on the August rating list. Nakamura earned the right to receive an invitation through rating, but criticized the new championship, describing its name as "clunky" and the concept as "total fluff" in a video on his YouTube channel.

The pilot begins with a nine-round 3+2 blitz Swiss, but its results will not determine who advances. Instead, the tournament will establish the tiebreak order for the group stage that follows. The 24 players will then be divided into four groups of six for five days of classical chess with a time control of 45 minutes plus a 30-second increment. Each group is a double round-robin, giving every player 10 games of fast classical chess.

Every player advances to a four-player knockout bracket, but the group standings determine which positions they can contest. The four group winners enter the top bracket and play for first through fourth place, the four runners-up compete for fifth through eighth, and so on down to the sixth-place finishers.

According to the published regulations, each knockout match is played over two days. On each day, the players contest four 3+2 blitz games, two 15+10 rapid games, and one 45+30 fast classical game. The disciplines are weighted heavily toward the longer games as a win in blitz is worth one point, a rapid win four, and a fast classical win eight, with half those totals awarded for draws. An armageddon game will decide any match that remains tied.

The first FIDE World Combined Champion will be crowned in 2027, when the minimum annual prize fund is $2.7 million, including at least $750,000 for each of the first three tournaments and $450,000 for the four-player final, plus performance bonuses. The prize fund for the Budapest pilot has not yet been announced.
The project was approved by FIDE in October 2025 and is developed, owned, and operated by Norway Chess. The agreement between the two organizations is set to run for at least 16 years.

Chess.com covered how the tour has attracted financial backing from global superstar Erling Haaland, who joined as an investor in Norway Chess earlier this year. The company completed a $10 million funding round involving several Norwegian sports and business figures.

Tarjei J. Svensen

news.title: Duda Takes 2026 Wins Lead In Titled Tuesday
news.author: nathanielgreen
news.excerpt: In the last Titled Tuesday before big changes coming shortly, GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda took home victory with a 9.5/10 start, while GM Arjun Erigaisi came in second place with a 9.5/10 finish after missing the first round.
body: In the last Titled Tuesday before big changes coming shortly, GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda took home victory with a 9.5/10 start, while GM Arjun Erigaisi came in second place with a 9.5/10 finish after missing the first round. Due to Arjun's missing round, tiebreaks favored Duda, giving him his fourth win of the year to break a tie with GMs Magnus Carlsen, Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, and Javokhir Sindarov for the most in 2026 so far.

The next Titled Tuesday tournament comes on September 1, and for the first time in months there will be a corresponding Titled Tuesday broadcast, hosted by GM Robert Hess. Qualification for the 2027 Esports World Cup will also be on the line once again.

Seven players began with a perfect 5/5, but only two got to 6/6: GMs Andrey Esipenko and Hans Niemann. In the sixth round, Esipenko defeated GM Steven Zierk, Niemann won over GM Oleksandr Bortnyk, while GMs Nikolas Theodorou and Alexander Grischuk drew against each other. Duda, who had only scored a draw in the third round, won against GM Dmitry Andreikin.

Those results set up the seventh-round battle between Esipenko and Niemann, which Esipenko won to move to 7/7. He was already up a piece in the final position when Niemann allowed his last 76 seconds to expire.

Duda, Theodorou, and GM Jingyao Tin were half a point behind Esipenko at this point. Tin, whose best Titled Tuesday finish in 25 efforts to date is eighth place, defeated Theodorou, seeking his second Titled Tuesday victory in 82 tries. Duda, meanwhile, ended Esipenko's run at the perfect score. The bounty for that achievement moves to $3,500 next week, or the equivalent of first and third place combined.

Fittingly, around this time, GM Hikaru Nakamura was explaining to viewers the difficulties of Titled Tuesday: "This is a frickin' tough tournament... It doesn't matter how good you are... Titled Tuesday is a brutal event."
Coming out of the ensuing break, Tin kept pace with Duda for much of the ninth round, but wasn't able to resist 39.Qxc6, a capture with check that nonetheless lost.

The win gave Duda the sole lead with 8.5/9, and only teenage IM Aleksandr Usov was on 8/9. Usov, who made noise last week and finished 10th, reached eight points for the third straight week with a win over Vachier-Lagrave. Usov ultimately scored nine points to finish in third, his best effort so far in Titled Tuesday in the 51 events he's played.

When Duda faced Usov in the 10th round, the result was looking like a lopsided Duda win. A brief Duda slipup in time pressure in the endgame—each player was below 20 seconds—wasn't enough to change the final outcome, putting Duda a full point ahead of the field with just one round remaining.

Only two players, Arjun and Theodorou, were within striking distance. Duda seemed like he might easily secure the draw that would clinch outright first place, and even had one moment to strike. But Arjun kept the game going long enough for Duda to make an error similar to the one Tin had played versus him two rounds earlier: capturing with check, but soon getting mated or losing material.
Theodorou only made a draw, and took fourth place. Arjun's tiebreaks thanks to missing round one were not good, and Duda secured victory despite the late loss.
In another notable result, teenage WIM Zarina Nurgaliyeva scored nine points to finish in seventh place.
*Bounty grows by $250 per week without a perfect score, and resets once a perfect score has been achieved.
These winners are announced by Thursday each week. If you would like to nominate a game or a move (including your own) in this or future weeks, click here!
Titled Tuesday is Chess.com's weekly tournament for titled players. It begins at 11:00 a.m. Eastern Time/17:00 Central European/20:30 Indian Standard Time.

news.title: Caruana Leads Praggnanandhaa In Final Match, Keymer-So Stays Even
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Fabiano Caruana won the first classical game of the title match against GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu in the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals, earning six points. The Indian grandmaster held his own in an unusual version o
body: GM Fabiano Caruana won the first classical game of the title match against GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu in the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals, earning six points. The Indian grandmaster held his own in an unusual version of the Italian Opening, but a one-move blunder cost a pawn and the game. In the match for third place between GMs Vincent Keymer and Wesley So, game one was an interesting fight but ended in a draw.
The second classical game, possibly with bonus blitz tiebreaks, takes place on Wednesday, August 26, at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST.
Caruana leads his match by six points, while So and Keymer are equal ahead of the second classical game.

The team of nearly all-grandmaster commentators talked at length about the curious opening in this first classical game. Beginners, when taught to develop their pieces, may think to play the following opening setup, but at some point on your path to the grandmaster title, someone tells you that you cannot play chess this way—placing Nc3 in front of the pawn, then calmly moving both rook pawns up one square. Supposedly, at some future date when you reach super-GM level, you may revert to a system that to a child looked logical, then later naive, and finally logical again.

Caruana got a middlegame position with bishop against knight, but no real advantage to speak of. In fact, by the time he played 26.Qb3, he said he was trying to stabilize. "I was mostly looking for something safe because I actually didn't like this position," said the American super-GM. Just three moves later, Praggnanandhaa—who had seen a way to essentially force a draw with an exchange sacrifice—played another move, 28...Rc8??, losing the game in one move.

Fatigue seems to play a tangible role as the players have been in St. Louis since the start of the month. GM Peter Svidler said, "It feels like we're making excuses for the best players in the world. You know, poor babies, they had to play chess for three weeks straight, but it does accumulate... things like this start slipping in."
It was nevertheless a fascinating game, and GM Rafael Leitao analyzes it below.

Caruana pointed out that he hadn't won a classical game in the GCT Finals in eight years, since it was introduced in 2018, though he has played just three times: in 2018, 2025, and 2026. He's up six points, but the match isn't over yet. With four points awarded to a single rapid game, Praggnanandhaa may not necessarily be in must-win territory yet.

But, for now, Caruana is focused on getting through the next classical game with the black pieces. He said, "If I survive that game, then it's a really good situation... the six-point lead is really nice. I wouldn't say that it's guaranteed anything but it's a really nice situation."

Keymer-So also featured a fight, even if the players halved the six points. Keymer repeated an idea he'd played in round eight of the Sinquefield Cup to beat Caruana, though he played c3 on move three instead of move two in this case. We got a London System where White parked his king on e2 and neither side castled the entire game—as GM Maurice Ashley said, it looked like a game of the (self-explanatory) variant "No Castling Chess." Another game where players showed just how far you can stretch opening principles.

Although the first new move of the game was on move nine, Keymer said that So's 13...Nf6 was the first move he hadn't seen before. There were mind-boggling complications, especially after the possible 20.g6!?, a pawn break that can be justified by sacrificing the exchange. The game went in a quieter direction, and ultimately the players made a draw in the rook endgame.
98 percent accuracy by both sides in a complex position didn't leave much hope for either side to win.

The day before, Keymer lost a tough match against Praggnanandhaa, but he said playing today was "easier because it's a new match." It also helped that he'd won the last three blitz games against Pragg, giving himself some confidence that he can still win games. He said, "The motivation [to win] is absolutely there. It's only, like, how much energy is left to actually fight? That's the biggest issue. We've been here for a month."

There are just two days left, and the eventual winners will have to find that energy within themselves to play at their best. Wednesday will feature one classical game (with bonus tiebreaks in the event of an even score), and we'll see rapid and blitz on Thursday.

Each match consists of eight games: two classical (6 points for a win, 3 for a draw, and 0 for a loss), two rapid (4/2/0), and four blitz (2/1/0). The winner claims the Grand Chess Tour title and the $200,000 top prize.

news.title: GothamChess Signs With BASILISK As Head Of Chess, Joins Giri & Keymer
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: IM Levy Rozman (GothamChess) is the latest addition to team BASILISK, the global esports organization. Rozman joins a team that already consists of super-GMs Anish Giri and Vincent Keymer, though his role will not be as
body: IM Levy Rozman (GothamChess) is the latest addition to team BASILISK, the global esports organization. Rozman joins a team that already consists of super-GMs Anish Giri and Vincent Keymer, though his role will not be as a player but as the Head of Chess—a position he compared to that of Chief Chess Officer Danny Rensch at Chess.com. This is the first time Rozman has signed with an esports organization, a milestone for both the YouTube star and the esports company.

BASILISK wrote, "The signing highlights BASILISK's long-term strategy to support chess and its wider ecosystem all-year-round, as well as its mission to generate fans of science through strategy-heavy titles." Adding Rozman, who has eight million subscribers on YouTube alone, to its roster, BASILISKwrites its total reach extends to "more than 20 million fans of the world's hardest games."

Christopher Bothur, CEO of BASILISK, said, "Levy has a rare ability to take something as complex and intimidating as chess and make it accessible and genuinely entertaining for hundreds of millions if not billions of people around the world." Rozman said in the press release, "I am dreaming big with what we will create together, the kind of content that has never been made before in chess... BASILISK is like a renaissance of nerds. We are making nerdy games and nerdy activities cool, and bringing them to the mainstream."
I am dreaming big with what we will create together, the kind of content that has never been made before in chess.
Rozman spoke to Chess.com and answered questions about what the future might hold for him, chess, and esports.

Unlike typical esports signings focused purely on competitive play, Rozman’s role centers on building the organization's chess presence, leading content initiatives, and driving creative projects that bridge chess and STEM. He explained:

I'm going to be Head of Chess... what that means is helping build the roster to obviously be competitive in esports, but also put out good content, whether it's short or long form, and combining chess and STEM for any project that we can think of.

How does Rozman's day-to-day schedule change with the new arrangement? He explained that his yearly schedule is cut into three, six, or 12-month deadlines, depending on various projects—like the release of his next two books that are coming soon.
He's planning on working BASILISK into his schedule in the following way:

I think this partnership will add, at a minimum, planning on a monthly basis various activations and collaborations that we can do both within chess with the team—because there's also Vincent Keymer and Anish Giri—and also what we can do beyond that. Some of the partners of BASILISK are, for example, the Planetary Society, which is not a standard partnership, but I would like to tap into things like that. Over the next few months, we're sort of going to map out where we can incorporate chess or where I can be activated in terms of learning a new skill.

The work with BASILISK doesn't sound like an overhaul of what he's already doing. "So, that's probably how it's all going to change, but it's not a change—it's like adding a vitamin or a supplement to a good diet and good sleep," he added.

BASILISK, in its mission statement, focuses on the connection between games and science, and Chess.com asked Rozman to talk about how chess fits into that vision. He cited other popular games like StarCraft and Magic: The Gathering, and chess is just another game that can satisfy the same role. Rozman didn't want to make any sweeping, grand statements (is chess a sport, art, or science?), but he did say, "For me, it's just people that like to think strategically, people that try, fail, try, fail, which is really what chess is about ultimately, and the same can be said in science."

He also compared his role within the space to science popularizers: "If Magnus Carlsen is chess' Albert Einstein, I'm chess' Bill Nye," referring to the American educator and television personality. "We serve sort of different roles."
If Magnus Carlsen is chess' Albert Einstein, I'm chess' Bill Nye.

As Rozman pointed out, there are very few esports teams that feature at least two top-10 players. Team Liquid has GMs Magnus Carlsen, Fabiano Caruana, and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, and Team Falcons boasts GMs Hikaru Nakamura and Alireza Firouzja. Rozman is among the best in the business as he joins Giri (number seven) and Keymer (number five).
Rozman clarified several times that his role is not coaching, but amplifying their success to a global audience. He said:

They play, they try to win trophies, and so on. I will not be playing. I thought it was cute that I was in Paris and some fans on the street thought I was playing in the Esports World Cup. I know what my role is: I will spread their games and their successes to the masses. I'm looking forward to working with them.
To conclude, Chess.com asked Rozman if there's anything about the deal that surprised him or may surprise his fans. He said that he appreciates the creative freedom that comes with the role.

I'm being trusted at the controls of the program... That's rare. Generally, whenever you do partnerships, people try to sort of get you to do the thing that they want to do, and in this case, it's very much the opposite... I'm very candid and very frank with anything from content to signings to initiatives we want to build. In a day and age where people are not always speaking their mind, not always transparent, and a little bit weird with this new development of social media and so on, I think that will go a long way.
Generally, whenever you do partnerships, people try to sort of get you to do the thing that they want to do, and in this case, it's very much the opposite.

Founded in 2020 and based in New York, BASILISK promotes itself as "science's esports team." The organization fields two top-10 chess grandmasters, StarCraft 2 world champions Serral and Reynor, and nine-time Evo champion Justin Wong. Its players have won three world championships and numerous premier tournaments wearing Science Victory on their jerseys. BASILISK supports scientific institutions and initiatives, including partnerships with The Planetary Society and Caltech's Institute for Quantum Information and Matter.

news.title: Caruana Survives To Lead Praggnanandhaa By 6; Keymer Leads So In 3rd-Place Match
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Fabiano Caruana continues to lead GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu 9-3 in the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals title match after making a draw in game two. Praggnanandhaa had huge winning chances in the opposite-color bishop
body: GM Fabiano Caruana continues to lead GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu 9-3 in the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals title match after making a draw in game two. Praggnanandhaa had huge winning chances in the opposite-color bishop endgame, but Caruana survived a torturous five and a half hours and 95 moves. With a six-point lead, Caruana is four games away from becoming the first person to win the GCT Finals two years in a row.

GM Vincent Keymer took an 8-6 lead against GM Wesley So in the match for third place. After a second draw in the classical portion, Keymer won the bonus blitz game after So made a blunder in the king-and-pawn endgame.
The final day of the event, featuring two rapid games and four blitz games, takes place on Thursday, August 27, at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST.
Praggnanandhaa will have to win a rapid game and a blitz game just to even the score on the final day. In the match for third place, So is only behind by the equivalent of one blitz game.

After losing the first classical game, on Tuesday, Praggnanandhaa wasn't exactly in a must-win situation, but a win would have greatly helped. With the white pieces, his big opening idea in the sharp Polerio Variation of the Italian was 11.Bf1!?, beckoning Caruana to push his e-pawn further. With best play, the computer even shows an advantage for the black pieces.
What did Praggnanandhaa have prepared? We won't know from this game, since Caruana castled instead.

Based on the players' time usage, it seems Praggnanandhaa mainly looked at 11...e4 and was out of book pretty quickly after Caruana deviated. But when the American sacrificed a second pawn with 14...e4?, the Indian grandmaster had a true chance of winning the game. At first, the advantage slipped through Pragg's hands, but in the late opposite-color bishop endgame with rooks on the board, more chances came up—starting on the notorious move 40.
The commentators are critical of Caruana's 40th move, and the engine indicates White has some advantage with the extra pawn!https://t.co/myH0jLTk8o pic.twitter.com/2lXtL1gXYC

Praggnanandhaa had more than one objective win, but the complications confounded even the commentary team of three grandmasters and one international master, despite engine access. Caruana slipped out this time, but it genuinely could have gone either way. GM Dejan Bojkov annotates the Game of the Day below.
The second classical encounter was a non-game, with So trading queens early and quickly exchanging pieces. At some point, Keymer had seven minutes more than he started with.
Keymer explained that his opponent probably expected the Berlin Defense and, when faced with the Marshall, bailed out.

With an even score, the players contested a bonus blitz game with the 5+2 time control, with the winner gaining two points. Keymer said, "Usually, he has a good record against me in shorter time controls, so I guess he didn't really want to play classical, but felt his chances were better in blitz and rapid. So it was even a better feeling to win that blitz game."

In another Ruy Lopez, this time without an early queen exchange, the players were evenly matched and traded down to an equal king-and-pawn endgame. Played under time pressure, So's 41.h4?? was the losing move that allowed Black to gain the opposition and win the game.

There are six games on Thursday, so a two-point lead isn't quite enough to sit on. But, as Keymer explained, the onus will be on So to fight his way back into the match. Keymer predicted, "It will be a big fight, that's for sure."
You can watch the day's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club's YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated events page.
The broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Peter Svidler, and Maurice Ashley, and IM Nazi Paikidze.

The 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals take place from August 22-27 in St. Louis, Missouri. The $450,000 final event of the 2026 Tour sees GMs Fabiano Caruana, Wesley So, Vincent Keymer, and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu compete in a single-elimination knockout. Each match consists of eight games: two classical (6 points for a win, 3 for a draw, and 0 for a loss), two rapid (4/2/0), and four blitz (2/1/0). The winner claims the Grand Chess Tour title and the $200,000 top prize.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Assaubayeva, Anna Muzychuk Grab Final Spots In WR Women's Chess Tour Final
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GMs Bibisara Assaubayeva and Anna Muzychuk have taken the final spots in the WR Women's Chess Tour 2026 Grand Final after winning the WR Women's Chess Tour Europe 2026 events in Saint-Tropez, France. Assaubayeva survived
body: GMs Bibisara Assaubayeva and Anna Muzychuk have taken the final spots in the WR Women's Chess Tour 2026 Grand Final after winning the WR Women's Chess Tour Europe 2026 events in Saint-Tropez, France. Assaubayeva survived two armageddon games before defeating GM Mariya Muzychuk 2-0 in the final of the rapid section, before Anna got revenge for her sister by defeating Assaubayeva 2.5-1.5 in the blitz final.
The Grand Final takes place in Stuttgart, Germany, on November 22-23.

The WR Women's Chess Tour is a tournament series spanning four continents, with four legs followed by a Grand Final. We've now seen events in Tokyo, Japan (June); Punta Cana, the Dominican Republic (July); Maputo, Mozambique (August); and lastly Saint-Tropez, France.

Each leg lasts two days, with rapid on the first and blitz on the second. The day consists of an eight-player single-elimination knockout, with a rapid time control of 15+10 and a blitz time control of 3+2. Rapid matches are best-of-two and blitz matches are best-of-four, with armageddon tiebreaks if needed.
The winner of each event (rapid and blitz) earns $7,000 and a spot in the Grand Final.

We've seen GMs Vaishali Rameshbabu and Kateryna Lagno win in Tokyo, IMs Carissa Yip and Leya Garifullina in Punta Cana, IM Mai Narva and GM Zhu Jiner in Maputo, and now with Assaubayeva and Anna Muzychuk we know the full lineup for the Grand Final in Stuttgart.
WR Women's Chess Tour 2026 Grand Final Players (Nov 22-23, Stuttgart, Germany)
Let's take a look at the event held in a vineyard in Saint-Tropez.

After the tournament in Africa where two players completely outclassed the field, the lineup for the European leg of the Tour had no weak links. That showed up in five of the six matches on the way to the rapid final going to armageddon.

Even the only quarterfinal match not to go to armageddon was balanced on a knife-edge. Mariya Muzychuk won the first game against IM Eline Roebers and held a draw in the second, but the Dutch IM briefly had a chance to win the first game on the spot. She spent eight seconds, but didn't find 35...Bf1!.

Roebers told IM Fiona Steil-Antoni: "I checked it shortly afterwards because I really felt at that moment that I had to be winning somehow, and then I don’t know, with the time pressure, and the pressure in general, I didn’t even consider ...Bf1, but I should have found that."
The most dramatic clash saw Anna Muzychuk knocked out by GM Koneru Humpy in an armageddon full of adventures and only finally decided by fractions of a second.
Before that, Muzychuk had missed a killer blow, though Humpy also missed some big chances to clinch the match, and for most of the game had a comfortable lead on the clock.

GM Nino Batsiashvili had come from behind to beat local hero IM Deimante Daulyte-Cornette in armageddon in the quarterfinals, and the Georgian GM gave Assaubayeva a very tough test in the semifinals. All three games were drawn, with the most interesting the first. Assaubayeva told Steil-Antoni, "I had a very tough game, I needed to defend the whole game, but in general in the end I even had a winning position!" It was a wild finish.
In the other semifinal, Humpy and Mariya Muzychuk traded wins before Muzychuk clinched victory in armageddon.

The final, however, was one-sided, and a lot came down to the opening of the first game. Assaubayeva commented: "It was my prep, and I already played it, but she didn’t know because it was, I think, a rapid game, and it’s very good normally for rapid because it’s very hard for Black to play. I had a big advantage in time and then converted the win."

Muzychuk had to hit back to force armageddon, but had little to work with except an advantage on the clock until her 38th move abruptly ended the game. It cost 30 seconds, using up all the time advantage, and blundered a fork.

As the three-time and reigning women's world blitz champion, Assaubayeva was asked how she was looking forward to the following day's blitz: "Yes, let’s see how I will play tomorrow! I have a little bit of jet lag after the Cairns Cup, but with this shape I’m happy how I played today."

Blitz saw far more clear-cut match wins, and while Assaubayeva again forged a path via armageddon, Anna Muzychuk won her quarterfinal and semifinal matches in the minimum number of games before clinching the title in the four regular blitz games.

The most notable quarterfinal pairing was a replay of the rapid final, with Assaubayeva once again taking on Mariya Muzychuk. This time it could have gone either way, including in the first game, which ended in a draw only after both sides had missed knockout blows.

Mariya scored a convincing win to take the lead in the second, missed some chances to clinch the match in game three, and then Assaubayeva struck back to force armageddon. Once again it was mayhem, with Mariya on the brink of victory before letting the win slip away—even if Assaubayeva didn't notice a chance to pick up a free piece!

Elsewhere in the quarterfinals, Anna Muzychuk cruised through 3-0 against Batsiashvili, Roebers beat Daulyte-Cornette by the same score, and GM Elisabeth Paehtz, getting back to chess full-time after giving birth to a daughter earlier this year, scored three wins and one loss against Humpy.

Anna again won in three games in the semifinal, this time against Roebers, though the Dutch IM had one big chance in the second game after a draw in the first. Anna's two-knights construction could have been exploited, and it would have meant a famous win with the King's Gambit!
Instead, Anna took the lead, and then the match was wrapped up a game later when Roebers was lost out of the opening on move 17.

Assaubayeva, meanwhile, once more needed armageddon, this time against Paehtz. The German women's number-one scored 1.5/2 in a wild first two games, and was pressing to win the match in the third. She had the better position and a huge lead on the clock, with Assaubayeva down to just four seconds against one minute when she played 32...Qh5. Disaster struck for Paehtz, however, as she played 33.Ne3??, overlooking the e2-rook was en prise.
The last regular blitz game was then a draw, before Assaubayeva won convincingly in armageddon.

The final was a chance for Anna to take revenge for her sister Mariya's losses to Assaubayeva both in the rapid final and in the blitz quarterfinals. The prospects didn't look good, however, when Assaubayeva won the first game, even if there was one notable moment—the Kazakh star missed mate-in-one and was forced to keep playing in a complex position.

Anna hit back convincingly in the next game, however, with the players then making a solid draw in game three. The fourth game would prove decisive, and f-pawns were a theme. Muzychuk opened with the Bird, 1.f4, while Assaubayeva provided another case of "never play ...f6!"
Muzychuk, who also recently played the Cairns Cup in St. Louis, was grateful for the opportunity to play another strong women's tournament. She commented:

In general, we really appreciate such occasions, because we girls like to complain! It’s a fact that compared to men’s tournaments we don’t have that much, actually we have very little, so every opportunity, especially when it’s well-organized, is really appreciated, so it really means a lot.
Both Anna Muzychuk and Assaubayeva are qualified for the WR Women's Chess Tour Grand Final in November.

The WR Women's Chess Tour - Europe 2026, held in Saint-Tropez, France, on August 25-26, was the fourth leg of the inaugural tournament series. It consisted of two separate eight-player single-elimination knockouts, one rapid and one blitz, each with its own prize fund and Grand Final qualification spot. The rapid time control was 15+10 and the blitz was 3+2. The total prize fund was $40,000, with half allocated for the rapid and half for the blitz.

Colin McGourty

news.title: Praggnanandhaa Wins 2026 Grand Chess Tour, Wesley So Clinches 3rd
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu came back from behind to win the final match against GM Fabiano Caruana and claim his maiden title in the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals, which comes with $200,000. The Indian grandmaster start
body: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu came back from behind to win the final match against GM Fabiano Caruana and claim his maiden title in the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals, which comes with $200,000. The Indian grandmaster started the day six points behind, but took the lead when he won both rapid games. From there, an even score in blitz left him two points ahead, with a final score of 15-13.

GM Wesley So also came back in the match for third place against GM Vincent Keymer. The pair traded wins in the rapid portion, but So won all four blitz games, clinching the title with a game to spare. The final score was 18-12.
The top three players qualify directly to the 2027 Grand Chess Tour. That's Praggnanandhaa, Caruana, and So.
Below, you can also see the total earnings across all events of the GCT. Praggnanandhaa takes home a whopping $404,354 from this series alone.

After the rapid portion, GM Maurice Ashley claimed this was the most exciting GCT Finals to date, and it's hard to argue with that. Just two out of the 12 games played on Thursday were draws; in the last three days, just 5/17 games were draws, which is a nearly 70% rate of decisive games in the Finals.
The players contested two rapid games, with the 25+10 time control, followed by four blitz games, with 5+2.

At 21, Praggnanandhaa is perhaps too old to be called the "comeback kid," but he's shown a knack for resurging at the end of elite events. At 2026 Norway Chess, he unforgettably won four classical games in a row to win the entire event. Those wins came against GM Alireza Firouzja, World Champions Magnus Carlsen and Gukesh Dommaraju, and GM Vincent Keymer.

He pulled another rabbit out of the hat on day six of the GCT Finals, which he started with a six-point deficit. He lost game one against Caruana on Tuesday, and he butchered a game he could have won on Wednesday, only making a draw. After two disappointments, what kind of Praggnanandhaa was going to walk into the Saint Louis Chess Club on Thursday?

"Honestly, I didn't think I had many chances today," said Praggnanandhaa, noting that six points is a lot to come back from. "It's not every day that you can get one win from Fabi, but to get two, it was important in the rapid."
It's not every day that you can get one win from Fabi, but to get two, it was important in the rapid.

His 5.Qd3 in the Ragozin Defense turned out to be an effective opening choice in the first rapid game. By move 12, he had fractured Caruana's pawn structure, and only dynamic factors kept the black position from falling apart. The computer claimed Black was only slightly worse, and equal at times, but the clock times told a different story. Caruana, down to his last three minutes, was clearly feeling the heat.
Praggnanandhaa went on to win this first game, which GM Dejan Bojkov annotates below. It set the tone for the rest of the day.

Even with the loss, Caruana still had a buffer. He was up two points in the match and had the white pieces in game two. Even a draw would have been an acceptable result, but he continued to slide. On the black side of a Rossolimo Sicilian, Praggnanandhaa equalized comfortably, gained a slight edge, and went on to blast open the center with 25...d5?!.

The move itself was objectively not great, but after 27.e5?, blitzed out, Caruana was close to dead lost. The best-case scenario would be a pawn-down endgame, and Praggnanandhaa didn't even give him that. Eventually, White even gave up a piece just to activate his rook, only to resign two moves later.

Then came four games of blitz, with Praggnanandhaa leading by two points. Game one was the first draw of the day in either match (!), but both sides could have won it. Caruana's blunder came first, as by putting the knight on e4, he blundered the a-pawn for no real compensation.

In the conversion stage, however, Praggnanandhaa was doing well until he wasn't. After 25.Bb5??, he overlooked a move that sent the evaluation from better for White to losing: 25...Nxf4!. If the knight is captured, White just gets checkmated by the battery of queen and bishop.
Finally, Caruana reached a winning exchange-up endgame, then blundered back the exchange, and the players finally repeated moves in an opposite-color bishop endgame. Talk about a thriller!

Caruana won game two to even the score. It was Pragg who cracked last in a mad time scramble, where the only move for Black was 43...Bf5, followed by a full rook sacrifice in the endgame. Instead, 43...Bg4? blundered the exchange, and this time Caruana brought the full point (two, technically) home.

Game three featured another time scramble, and Praggnanandhaa ended up on the better side. Moving his bishop off f6 allowed the decisive pawn break. Praggnanandhaa had 13 seconds, and he took 12 seconds to check and play the decisive blow.

Had Caruana won the last game on demand, he would have forced two more games with the peculiar time control of 8+3, followed by armageddon. He achieved an advantage in the Glek Variation, but one premature pawn break allowed Praggnanandhaa to equalize. Caruana quickly landed in a losing rook endgame, and the champion found a way to force a perpetual check. A draw was enough to win the match.

"It would have been nice to have it in the Candidates, but it's still nice to win tournaments like this," said Praggnanandhaa, who considers the GCT "second to the world championship, because of the tradition." He'd like to rest for a week or two, he said, but the Olympiad is coming in less than a month!
It would have been nice to have it in the Candidates, but it's still nice to win tournaments like this.
The match for third place was close until it wasn't, which was in the blitz portion.

After losing the bonus blitz game the previous day, So started with a two-point deficit. When he won the first rapid game, however, he took a two-point lead. The game was a very complicated Queen's Indian Defense, but the inaccurate 23...Ng6?! gave Black a difficult position, and in that difficult position, 25...Rh4? walked into a pawn-down endgame.

In the second game, however, Keymer showed that he would not go gentle into that good night. With two minor pieces, a rook, and a pawn, he finally converted the game after an epic 122 moves, though So found some incredible stalemate resources while playing on the increment—none of which Keymer allowed to transpire on the board.

Game three was a terrible blow for Keymer, as he had a winning position, squandered it when he missed the only winning move 28...Qxg3, and allowed So to not only escape but win a pawn. By move 34, So traded queens and then converted the pawn-up rook endgame.

So outplayed Keymer in a queen and knight endgame in the second blitz game, and then won the match in the third. It took just 25 moves for So to seal the game, and 15.Nxc6!? was the move that started the complications Keymer simply could not wade through.

Adding insult to injury, though it did not impact the match result, So again won the final game. With that, he's guaranteed himself a spot in next year's tour. He earns $75,000 and very likely a six-figure payout next year.
At the end of the broadcast, the Saint Louis Chess Club announced the dates for 2027.

In addition, GM Garry Kasparov will play a match against GM Veselin Topalov at the club on September 11-13. In October, we will see the U.S. and U.S. Women's Championships, followed by Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown.
That's it for our coverage for now, but it won't be long until we return to cover the Kasparov vs. Topalov match. See you then!
You can rewatch the day's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club's YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated events page.
The broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan, Peter Svidler, and Maurice Ashley, and IM Nazi Paikidze.

The 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals took place August 22-27 in St. Louis, Missouri. The $450,000 final event of the 2026 Tour saw GMs Fabiano Caruana, Wesley So, Vincent Keymer, and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu compete in a single-elimination knockout. Each match consisted of eight games: two classical (6 points for a win, 3 for a draw, and 0 for a loss), two rapid (4/2/0), and four blitz (2/1/0). The winner claimed the Grand Chess Tour title and the $200,000 top prize.

news.title: Xiong Nearly Perfect In 3 0 Thursday
news.author: coachjkane
news.excerpt: No one has ever scored a perfect 11/11 in 3 0 Thursday, but GM Jeffery Xiong became the closest player to that elusive mark in the second tournament on August 27. Xiong won his first 10 games and had a forced mate on the
body: No one has ever scored a perfect 11/11 in 3 0 Thursday, but GM Jeffery Xiong became the closest player to that elusive mark in the second tournament on August 27. Xiong won his first 10 games and had a forced mate on the board in the 11th, before one mistake allowed GM Jose Martinez to escape with a draw in the final game. Xiong still won the tournament by a sizeable 1.5-point margin. GM Pranesh M won the first tournament of the day, securing his third victory of August. IM Renato Terry won the final event of the day, his record 17th victory in a 3 0 Thursday tournament.

Pranesh started well in the first tournament of the day, winning his first six games. However, he lost a critical seventh-round game against GM Sina Movahed, which significantly dimmed his hopes for first. However, Pranesh kept playing well and reached 8.5/10 with this comeback victory against GM Denis Lazavik.

news.title: Kasparov, Topalov To Renew Rivalry In $144,000 Chess960 Match
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: The 13th World Champion GM Garry Kasparov will face GM Veselin Topalov, the opponent who defeated him in the final rated classical game of his career, in a $144,000 Chess960 match in St. Louis.
body: The 13th World Champion GM Garry Kasparov will face GM Veselin Topalov, the opponent who defeated him in the final rated classical game of his career, in a $144,000 Chess960 match in St. Louis.

The two former world champions will play 12 games over three days in Clutch Chess: The Legends, taking place September 11-13 at the Saint Louis Chess Club. The event was announced on the broadcast of the final day of the Grand Chess Tour Finals in St. Louis.

Kasparov, 63, and Topalov, 51, will play four games per day, with two rapid games followed by two blitz games. The match will be played as Chess960, also known as Fischer Random or, as Saint Louis calls it, Chess9LX. A new starting position will be drawn for each day.

The match comes almost exactly one year after Kasparov faced another former rival, GM Viswanathan Anand, in the inaugural edition of Clutch Chess: The Legends. Kasparov impressively won that match 13-11, clinching victory with two games to spare after winning four games to Anand's none. The Indian legend then won the final two blitz games, collecting $16,000 in bonus money and narrowing the final score.
"It’s my sacred duty to come here and entertain people," Kasparov joked afterward.
It’s my sacred duty to come here and entertain people.—Garry Kasparov on St. Louis

Topalov, meanwhile, considers himself more or less retired, having played only sporadically in recent years. However, he did make a classical appearance at the Clash of Generations III in Monaco in April against 14-year-old GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, a match the Turkish prodigy dominated by winning 5-1.
This time, Kasparov will seek revenge against a player who beat him in both their final classical encounter and their only previous Chess960 match.

Kasparov's last classical game took place in Linares, Spain, in 2005. He had already secured first place when he faced Topalov with black in the final round, but lost in just 30 moves after misplaying a pawn endgame.

The victory allowed Topalov to catch Kasparov on 8/12, although Kasparov still won the tournament on tiebreak, having scored more wins with the black pieces. Shortly afterward, Kasparov stunned the chess world by announcing his retirement.

Topalov went on to win the 2005 FIDE World Championship in San Luis, Argentina, later that year. He scored an incredible 6.5/7 in the first half before drawing all seven games in the second, finishing on 10/14 and winning by 1.5 points.

But their 2005 encounter wasn't their last competitive meeting. In 2018, Topalov defeated a rusty Kasparov 14.5-11.5 in Champions Showdown, a 20-game Chess960 match in St. Louis. It was Kasparov's first competitive experience in the variant, but since then he has regularly appeared in the U.S. chess capital to play, with mixed results.

His best result was at the 2021 Champions Showdown Chess9LX, where he finished fifth with 5/9, ahead of GMs Fabiano Caruana, Levon Aronian, Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, Hikaru Nakamura, and Peter Svidler. Kasparov was just one point behind the winner, GM Leinier Dominguez.
The following year, at the Champions Showdown: Chess 9LX 2022, it did not go as well, to put it mildly: Kasparov scored only 0.5/9, after spoiling several promising positions.

The Clutch Chess format is designed by GM Maurice Ashley and gives more importance to games as the match progresses. A win is worth one point on day one, two points on day two, and three points on the final day.

The prize money follows the same structure, where each win is worth a $1,000 bonus on day one, $2,000 on day two, and $3,000 on day three. The winner of the match receives $70,000, while the runner-up receives $50,000. An additional $24,000 is available in game-by-game bonuses.

Saint Louis Chess Club has also revealed another edition of the Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown during October 27-29. The four-player rapid event will feature GM Javokhir Sindarov, in what looks set to be his last test before he heads to Geneva, Switzerland, to challenge GM Gukesh Dommaraju for the world championship title.
Sindarov will face GMs Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, Fabiano Caruana, as well as Nakamura in a four-player rapid event, but additional details have not yet been announced.
