news.title: Nakamura Continues Unrivalled Bullet Brawl Dominance, Coasts To 65th Title
news.author: jackrodgers
news.excerpt: GM Hikaru Nakamura notched his 65th career Bullet Brawl title and 16th of 2026 on Saturday after finishing 23 points clear of the field, despite taking his "foot off the gas" at the end of the arena.
body: GM Hikaru Nakamura notched his 65th career Bullet Brawl title and 16th of 2026 on Saturday after finishing 23 points clear of the field, despite taking his "foot off the gas" at the end of the arena.
Nakamura scored 51/65 and posted a score of 170 points, marking one of the most comprehensive victories in recent history.

For his efforts, the American titan will receive $400, while GM Nihal Sarin, IM Renato Terry, and GM Amin Tabatabaei will receive $250, $150, and $100, respectively, for their 2nd-4th placed finishes. The best women's prize went to none other than FM Anastasia Avramidou.
The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, September 5, at 12 p.m. ET / 18:00 CEST / 9:30 p.m. IST.

Nakamura opened his campaign on Saturday with an authoritative 19-game streak packed with all the flair you'd expect from the best Bullet Brawler in history. GM Dmitry Andreikin was his closest pursuer thanks to an 11-game win streak, though the gap at the top was still 19 points at the 30-minute mark.

Although Nakamura suspected that he and Andreikin had benefitted from "soft pairings," a retrospective look at his opponents tells a different story. Ten of his 19 games were against GMs with nine Bullet Brawl titles between them.

During the streak, Nihal came close to toppling Nakamura on his second attempt with the incisive 32.Re6!!; however, he misfired on the follow-up and was immediately punished by Nakamura's defensive precision.

Later against Andreikin, Nakamura played the aggressor from the get-go, eventually crashing through and winning material with a series of crafty knight moves. His subsequent conversion was immaculate.
Like in the previous edition, Nakamura toiled through a relative slump around the halfway mark, though setbacks were interspersed with flashes of brilliance that kept his score ticking along.

Maghsoodloo looked like the most likely player to catch Nakamura when he accrued an eight-game winning streak, but he faded to eighth place in the second half. See if you can spot the tactic the Iranian found which put his game against IM Sergey Sklokin to bed quickly (several moves work but we're looking for a rook move).
Following a string of consecutive losses at the hands of GMs Tabatabaei, Maghsoodloo, and Oleksandr Bortnyk, Nakamura scored 21/23 and consolidated the top spot.
At one point, the margin between Nakamura and second place was 37 points, and the world number-two felt that if he hadn't relaxed at the end of the event, he may have won by 40 or more.

After his latest victory, one thing is clear... Nakamura's iron grip on Chess.com's speediest weekly arena has only tightened in 2026. Saturday's win reaffirms that when he is at his best, and often when he isn't, he has no nemeses in this format.
How to review games? The games from this week's Bullet Brawl can be found here.

Bullet Brawl is an exciting arena featuring Chess.com's top bullet specialists. It takes place weekly on Saturdays. The format is a two-hour arena with a 1+0 time control; the prize fund is $1,000. Like Titled Tuesday and Arena Kings, Bullet Brawl often features top GMs, including Hikaru Nakamura, Andrew Tang, Tuan Minh Le, and many more!

news.title: Get Coached By The Almighty Mittens And Other New Coaches On Chess.com
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: Hehehehehehehehe! Is it your dream coming true, or is it your worst nightmare? You can now get coached by the most formidable and cutest chess-playing entity in the world: Mittens! Along with the god-like chess-playing k
body: Hehehehehehehehe! Is it your dream coming true, or is it your worst nightmare? You can now get coached by the most formidable and cutest chess-playing entity in the world: Mittens! Along with the god-like chess-playing kitten, you can also get coached by Dr. Wolf, Sloane, Ruben, and Calvin.

You can choose any coach, old or new, by going to your coach settings page. You can also do it by clicking your coach's avatar whenever you see it—on Game Review, Puzzles, or even in Play after a game ends—to open the selection menu. Just select your coach and click the Choose Coach button.

Mittens, the destroyer of worlds, is the world's most famous chess-playing feline. The kitten that broke the internet is ready to guide you on a journey of chess enlightenment. The whiskered oracle has cracked the secrets of chess and can see the past, present, and future of every game. With ominous words and deep wisdom, Mittens is here to show us, mere mortals, how the game should be played.

Dr. Charles Wolf is a calm, thoughtful teacher who sees chess as both art and discipline. Dressed in his father's navy blue suit and maroon tie, he brings an old-school elegance to every lesson. He teaches with patience and warmth, helping you understand not just what move to play, but why it matters.
Dr. Wolf loves introducing players to the strategy, history, and the quiet poetry of the game. With him, chess is meaningful, structured, and deeply beautiful.

Sloane is a former women's world champion from Australia who believes confidence is built move by move. She coaches with precision, poise, and genuine belief in your potential. She celebrates your strong ideas, connects your play to famous games, and encourages you to trust your instincts. Her style is polished yet uplifting.
If you want to grow your skills while building real self-assurance at the board, Sloane is the coach who will raise your standard.

Ruben is a battle-tested street chess master who lives for the park tables and open-air competition. He teaches the way he plays—direct, fearless, and full of personality. You'll get sharp humor, honest feedback, and real respect when you earn it. Ruben believes improvement comes from bold ideas and heart.
If you want to sharpen your edge and learn to play with confidence and swagger, grab a seat at his table.

Calvin is a teen prodigy who loves teaching and streaming on the side. He is competitive, fast-paced, and always studying new ideas. He will call out your openings, laugh at chaotic positions, and treat every game like a chance to level up together.
With Calvin, learning feels current, energetic, and ambitious. If you want to improve quickly and keep things fun, he is ready to grind with you.
Who is your favorite coach on Chess.com? Let us know in the comments below!

news.title: Praggnanandhaa Indian No. 1 On September FIDE Rating List
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu is back in the top 10 and has overtaken GM Arjun Erigaisi as Indian number-one after winning the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. A marathon month in St. Louis had a big impact on the September FIDE ra
body: GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu is back in the top 10 and has overtaken GM Arjun Erigaisi as Indian number-one after winning the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. A marathon month in St. Louis had a big impact on the September FIDE rating list as victory in the 2026 Sinquefield Cup saw GM Wesley So return to the top five for the first time in four years. Victory in the 2026 Cairns Cup propelled GM Tan Zhongyi up to women's number-six, while 14-year-old Indian WCM Modipalli Deekshitha catapulted into the women's top 25 by gaining 297 points in one month.

At the very top, GM Magnus Carlsen continues his reign, while GM Hikaru Nakamura returns to the number-two spot after a three-month hiatus despite his focus, like Carlsen's, having been on the 2026 Esports World Cup. He owes the climb to GM Fabiano Caruana dropping a few points in the Sinquefield Cup.

news.title: SaVaToP1gG Wins Gambit Cup, Tops Field Of 1,454 Players
news.author: federico_marin
news.excerpt: SaVaToP1gG beat out a field of 1,454 players and was crowned champion on Monday in the first special edition of the Gambit Cup. The winner defeated Marzi in a heads-up final that lasted longer than expected. The favorite
body: SaVaToP1gG beat out a field of 1,454 players and was crowned champion on Monday in the first special edition of the Gambit Cup. The winner defeated Marzi in a heads-up final that lasted longer than expected. The favorite (his rating was 739 points, 200 points higher than his opponent's) also held a massive chip lead: a 68-to-1 ratio over his opponent. Marzi put up a fight, but ultimately succumbed with a pair of 9s against the straight that SaVaToP1gG hit on the final community card.

Earlier, QuebecPokerAddict was eliminated in third place. The tournament—which was free to enter and offered no cash prizes—began at 12 p.m. ET / 18:00 CEST / 9:30 p.m. IST and lasted just over two hours.

The Gambit Cup is a daily poker tournament hosted on Gambit.com, Chess.com's educational, gambling-free poker website. The site, which was soft-launched in May, now boasts more than 85,000 members—a number that is growing rapidly under the slogan: "All the Poker. None of the Gambling." This special edition was the first to be broadcast live, with commentary by WFM Alexandra Botez, an expert poker player and chess player, and IM Danny Rensch.

The idea behind Gambit is to give players the opportunity to get started and improve their Texas Hold'em skills from scratch, without having to risk any money to learn. The site offers free hand reviews by virtual coaches, daily tournaments, and constant practice against human opponents or 14 different bots. You can also unlock achievements and view your own game statistics, including a rating—similar to the one used in chess—that starts at 500 points.

Winning a tournament with nearly 1,500 players requires a mix of skill and luck. Poker is a game of incomplete information, where chance is an essential factor. In the long run, good players—those who make the best decisions—are the ones who win the most, but in a single tournament, especially one with such a fast-paced (turbo) format, something more is needed. Solvers (the equivalent of Stockfish and other programs) know the best theoretical move in every position, but making that move guarantees nothing in a single hand. You can play an entire tournament with their help and still get eliminated in the very first hands.
In any case, the official broadcast on Chess.com's Twitch and YouTube channels had a five-minute delay to prevent players from seeing their opponents' cards. Fair play was guaranteed.

Botez and Rensch, a teacher and a student, gave a two-hour lesson to enthusiasts attending a poker tournament for the first time. The experience was not so different from a chess tournament; in both cases, players must make critical and quick decisions, analyzing the available information before choosing an option. In the case of chess, the game is so rich that nothing needs to be at stake for the match to be interesting. It is often said that betting is essential in poker, but since there was no possibility of rebuying (something common in card tournaments), the fear of being eliminated was enough to ensure that the Gambit Cup didn't turn into a game of bingo.

Poker tournaments are very different from chess tournaments. There isn't a fixed number of games (or hands). All players start with the same number of chips, and they are eliminated as soon as they run out of them. The winner isn't the player with the most points, but the last player standing, who gets all the chips. Gambit Cup tables seat six players. In each hand, two of them (the big blind and the small blind) are forced to risk some chips. At each betting level, the size of the blinds increases, so it's not a good strategy to wait and play only the best hands. That's why it's necessary to bluff—to put pressure on your opponents even when you don't have a strong enough hand to win. GM Mikhail Tal would have made a great poker player.

Texas Hold'em is a card game using a standard 52-card deck. Each player receives two private hole cards, and betting occurs across four rounds: pre-flop, flop (three shared community cards), turn (one more), and river (one final card). Players act by folding, checking, calling, betting, or raising, with a rotating dealer button and forced small/big blind bets driving the action each hand. At showdown, each player builds the best possible five-card hand from their two hole cards and the five community cards, using standard poker hand rankings to determine the winner.

Of course, many mistakes were made at the Gambit Cup, as is typical in the best turbo tournaments. Alexandra Botez pointed out and explained many of them. Most players got involved in too many hands, and it was common to see them "call," which means matching the current bet to stay in the hand without raising it. Another common mistake was moving too quickly, without taking full advantage of the time available. However, in this game there are no absolute truths, and it's often possible to win with less orthodox playing styles.

A good example of this came in the next hand, when just 44 players remained. Kingoftheechobike was the clear chip leader and the bully at his table—a common (and advisable) tactic at that stage of the tournament. With 130 big blinds—nearly 100 more than the second-highest stack at his table—he was opening hands with any two cards.
Here, he defends his 8♣ 4♥ (offsuit) from the small blind. Qshio, in early position, limps with his A♥-2♠, and robertnicollaj1455 calls with 6♦-4♦.

The flop—the first three community cards—is A♠ K♣ 3♦. At this point, Qshio has an 88% chance of winning the hand, but he checks, and when the action reaches Kingoftheechobike, he bets to steal the pot. Qshio calls the bet, and robertnicollaj1455 folds. He would have won the hand, as we'll see, but in poker, you have to evaluate the quality of your moves regardless of the outcome.

The 5♠ on the turn (fourth community card) gives the chip leader a small chance—7% if the river brings a 2. King checks, and Qshio, who has just 11 big blinds left, makes a modest bet. King re-raises. Poker is a game of deception, and the deception seems to have worked. Qshio goes all-in with the rest of his chips. "Echo isn’t going to win this hand," Botez announces, but of course, one of the remaining deuces in the deck appears on the river (the fifth community card). “That’s crazy," exclaims Alexandra. "Unreal," adds Rensch. Kingoftheechobike extended his lead even further, and Qshio was eliminated.

At the rate the blinds were rising—set so that the tournament would last about two hours—the Gambit Cup unfolded at a frenetic pace. Fifteen minutes after it began, more than 300 players had been eliminated. By the 20-minute mark, 400 had been eliminated. By the 40-minute mark, there were a thousand casualties and barely 500 participants remained, with their average chip counts dwindling—which in turn forced them to take more risks. The battle was fierce.

For those used to playing on other online poker platforms, the experience felt strange. Getting started couldn't have been easier. Since there was no money at stake and no entry fee, all you had to do was click the "Register" button, and you'd find yourself seated at the table. For uninitiated spectators, the action surely moved too fast. Botez explained most situations very well, but a beginner might have had trouble keeping up in real time with what was happening in most hands—as if it were a bullet game.

One key difference from chess tournaments is that the overall standings were constantly shifting. It's even harder to dominate such a large tournament from start to finish than it is to win it. The leader's position is always provisional, no matter how big a lead he builds, even as players grow more conservative as the tournament goes on.

Rensch was pleased with the outcome. He was especially happy when he encountered a hand in which he recognized the concept of a gutshot. Like almost all the spectators, he learned from Alexandra Botez, and at the end he said he hoped to repeat the experience: "I can see doing this again," he said before saying goodbye.
You can watch the day's broadcast on Chess.com's YouTube or Twitch channels.
The broadcast was hosted by IM Danny Rensch and WFM Alexandra Botez.

The Gambit Cup is a daily poker tournament hosted on Gambit.com, Chess.com's educational, gambling-free poker website. On August 31, IM Danny Rensch and WFM Alexandra Botez hosted a special edition of the event, which is free to enter. Members compete for the coveted Queen Gambit crown—a unique flair that goes on the winner's profile picture for the day. Finishing at the top also nets players tournament points to help them climb the Player of the Month leaderboard for bragging rights.

news.title: Iranian GM Idani Switches To France: 'I Felt Forced Into It'
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: GM Pouya Idani, until now Iran’s third-highest-rated player, has officially transferred to France three years after moving to Brest with his wife. The 30-year-old joins GM Alireza Firouzja and WGM Mitra Hejazipour among
body: GM Pouya Idani, until now Iran’s third-highest-rated player, has officially transferred to France three years after moving to Brest with his wife. The 30-year-old joins GM Alireza Firouzja and WGM Mitra Hejazipour among the prominent Iranian-born players representing France. Iran’s top-two players, GMs Amin Tabatabaei and Parham Maghsoodloo, have also been based in France for a while, but continue to represent Iran.
[Editor's note September 2: This story was updated with comments from the French Chess Federation, correcting previous reporting about payment of the €3,500 transfer fee]

Idani's federation switch was confirmed by FIDE last week, and the 2615-rated grandmaster is now France's new number four, per FIDE's September list, behind GMs Firouzja, Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, and Etienne Bacrot.

Idani told Chess.com in an interview that his decision reflected the life he has built in France, but said broken promises and unpaid bonuses from the Iranian Chess Federation were a contributing factor in the move.

"I don’t think anybody, at the beginning, wants to change his federation," Idani said. "However, a lot of stuff happened in the past few years. There were promises by the federation that were not fulfilled, bonuses that were not given etc. So, in the end, I feel I was forced into it."
There were promises by the federation that were not fulfilled, bonuses that were not given, etc. So, in the end, I feel I was forced into it.—Pouya Idani

The 30-year-old reached a career-high of 2647, making him one of Iran's three highest-rated players in the last decade. In 2013, he won the World Under-18 Championship, and he achieved the grandmaster title the following year.
Together with Tabatabaei, Maghsoodloo, 20-year-old rising star GM Bardiya Daneshvar, and IM Amirreza Pour Agha Bala, Idani was part of the Iranian team that won the 2023 Asian Games.

His move to France came in part as a result of wanting to build a better future for himself and his family. Idani moved to Brest with his wife in April 2023 and their daughter was born shortly afterward.

"My wife applied for university and got accepted here in Brest, and it also felt better for my career to be in Europe," he said. "It is easier to get invitations to different leagues and easier to play in open tournaments."

He currently holds a French residence permit and plans to apply for citizenship when he becomes eligible. "I am planning to stay in France and I am happy to represent a country I am going to live in," he said. "If they need help in any way, I will do my best with that."
I am planning to stay in France and I am happy to represent a country I am going to live in.—Pouya Idani

In an email to Chess.com, The French Chess Federation (FFE) confirmed that Idani’s transfer has been registered by FIDE and that he now holds the FRA federation code. However, they clarified that they have not paid the €3,500 transfer fee, which means that his eligibility date is December 31, 2027.

Under FIDE regulations, when a player continues to represent his former federation after moving abroad, the residency period used to determine eligibility begins the day after his last such appearance. That explains why Idani’s eligibility period did not begin when he physically moved to France in April 2023.
The FFE also stressed that it had not actively recruited Idani or the other Iranian players who have settled in France.

“The fact that players of this calibre choose to settle in France reflects the attractiveness of our country,” the federation told Chess.com. “We can also see it as recognition of the current momentum of chess in France and of the work carried out by the Federation to support its development.”
"I am happy that they accepted me to represent them and helped me through the process. Everything happened without any problem."

The move was assisted by Reza Salami, an Iranian-born French politician and city councilor in Brest who has long been involved in the city’s chess scene. Idani explained the two first met when he played for Brest in the second division of the French League in 2019.

"Mr. Salami invited me, and ever since then we have been very good friends," Idani said. "However, since my wife got accepted in Brest, it was just a happy accident to come here! Immigration is tough, and it was nice to have a friend to help us."

Brest has become a key destination for Iranian chess players in France. Hejazipour settled there after competing for Iran without a headscarf at the 2019 World Rapid and Blitz Championship. This year, the port city in northwestern France also saw the arrival of Iran's two top grandmasters. Tabatabaei, now world number-15, and world number-31, Maghsoodloo, have been assisted by Salami in trying to settle in France.
"They were participating in a tournament in Europe and couldn't return home because of the conflict. So they contacted me," Salami told French newspaper Paris Match.

However, Tabatabaei was refused a residence permit and was asked to leave the country within one month. Salami said the decision would be challenged, and Tabatabaei remains in the country, according to Chess.com's sources. Maghsoodloo, who arrived in France with his wife, has an application still pending, according to Paris Match.

Neither player has publicly indicated that they intend to change federations, and Tabatabaei is listed on Iran's team at the Olympiad. Nevertheless, it represents a significant loss for an impressive generation of Iranian players who established the country as one of Asia’s strongest chess nations.

The FFE said it had no information about any residence permit applications submitted by Tabatabaei or Maghsoodloo, noting that immigration matters fall under the responsibility of the French authorities.

On the state of Iranian chess, Idani told Chess.com: "It is quite sad because I feel we are—or, better to say, were—one of the very strong and promising countries in the world. We even managed to win the Asian Games ahead of Uzbekistan and India. Hopefully things will get better in all aspects, but I am really unsure about it."
Idani has played less in recent years, but insists he still sees himself primarily as a competitor.
"My peak was around 2650 in 2022," he said. "Now I am less active compared to that time. I started doing more coaching and also collaborating with different websites for chess courses."

He is hopeful that transferring to France can give his career a boost. "I am still quite ambitious and consider myself more as a player, not a coach. If the circumstances and situation get better, I believe I can reach my peak again and go beyond that."

Idani is planning to play several open tournaments in the fall, but mentioned the Grand Swiss, World Rapid and Blitz Championships, and his first European Individual Championship under the French flag as his main targets.
"I do believe living in Europe will make things such as choosing tournaments and traveling easier," he said. "The facilities and opportunities here are also better compared to Iran."
Living in Europe will make things such as choosing tournaments and traveling easier.—Pouya Idani
"I am quite excited to play the European Championship because I feel it is a rare occasion for someone originally from Asia to play there. Let’s see what happens!"

Tarjei J. Svensen

news.title: Niemann Wins Thrilling Titled Tuesday In Broadcast Return
news.author: nathanielgreen
news.excerpt: GM Hans Niemann stole the show in September 1's Titled Tuesday at the latest possible moment. For most of the event, GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda not only threatened to win his second consecutive Titled Tuesday, but began 10/10
body: GM Hans Niemann stole the show in September 1's Titled Tuesday at the latest possible moment. For most of the event, GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda not only threatened to win his second consecutive Titled Tuesday, but began 10/10, looking to become the first perfect player of the year. Instead, Niemann won their 11th-round matchup and took the tournament on tiebreaks. GM Alexey Sarana also finished on 10/11, a score good enough to outright win this tournament more often than not in 2026, but had to settle for third place.

All three players are in good early shape for the 2027 Esports World Cup, with today's Titled Tuesday beginning the qualification cycle. This tournament also marked the return of a Titled Tuesday broadcast with GM Robert Hess.

In the first Titled Tuesday to crack 500 participants in over a year, since July 2025, 18 of them began with 4/4, with only Duda among that group making the eventual three-way tie for first. Niemann and Sarana were both on 3/4, Niemann having drawn his games in rounds two and four, and Sarana losing in round four. Both players were perfect the rest of the way.
Duda was one of three players to make 6/6, another being GM Sina Movahed, with Hess proclaiming 26...g5 "sick stuff."

Movahed's perfect score didn't last, with GM Andy Woodward winning their dramatic seventh-round encounter in "a match we may see for decades to come between two of the most talented teenagers in the world." (Hess)

Duda also won in round seven, of course, and about this time is when he started to emerge as the tournament's main storyline, after 41.f6 helped knock down Woodward and lock down an 8/8 start in what Hess called "an unbelievable demonstration of class."

Niemann and Sarana scored all four points possible each in rounds five through eight, but still had to jump not only Duda on 8/8 but GM Zhamsaran Tsydypov on 7.5/8 as well. Duda helped them by taking care of Tsydypov to reach 9/9 in "electric" fashion, posting five brilliant moves in the game of the day.
As Niemann and Sarana also continued to win, so did GMs Wesley So and Vincent Keymer, and the four of them remained in one-point range of Duda.

So was Duda's next challenge, but it wasn't much of one after 20...e5?, which Duda punished ruthlessly to move one step away from 11/11 and a $6,000 payday ($2,500 for first and $3,500 for the perfect score).

Duda could also lock in the outright victory with just a draw, which would get the first 10.5 score since June (which, coincidentally, was achieved by Sarana). But the task was tall, having Black against Niemann, who would of course be in no drawing mood.
In the meantime, Sarana had White against Woodward, and won easily on the board and on the clock to tie Duda at the top, complete with a clinching queen sacrifice.

The Niemann-Duda match was tense all the way through, and only in part due to the standings situation. The maximal central pawn tension on move 15 and Duda's 30...Nxf3—a piece sacrifice he played despite being down a minute on the clock—proved to anyone who still doubted that neither player was happy with a draw. As the game approached move 50 and both players' clocks fell below a minute, it was still anyone's game.

It was Duda who finally cracked, but Niemann needed the second crack to take control. After move 55, he was up two pieces and it was smooth sailing on the board. With 3.4 seconds left on his clock, Niemann clinched the tournament with checkmate.
After the three players on 10 points, there were six on nine points, with So and Keymer rounding out the top five.
*Bounty grows by $250 per week without a perfect score, and resets once a perfect score has been achieved.
These winners are announced by Thursday each week. If you would like to nominate a game or a move (including your own) in this or future weeks, click here!
Titled Tuesday is Chess.com's weekly tournament for titled players. It begins at 11:00 a.m. Eastern Time/17:00 Central European/20:30 Indian Standard Time.

Nathaniel Green

news.title: FIDE Election Heats Up As All 3 Presidential Tickets File Complaints
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: With less than a month until FIDE elects its next president, the campaign has entered an increasingly heated phase, with formal complaints from all three tickets, questions over Timur Turlov's eligibility, and allegation
body: With less than a month until FIDE elects its next president, the campaign has entered an increasingly heated phase, with formal complaints from all three tickets, questions over Timur Turlov's eligibility, and allegations that FIDE itself has failed to remain neutral.

FIDE has confirmed to Chess.com that its Electoral Commission has received complaints from each of the three presidential tickets: Jan Henric Buettner with IM Malcolm Pein; Wadim Rosenstein with Gordon Tang; and Turlov with five-time world champion GM Viswanathan Anand.

FIDE said the respondents in all three cases have submitted legal responses, while the Electoral Commission, chaired by Roberto Rivello, was expected to review the complaints and issue a report by the end of August. As of September 2, no report has been made public.

It should also be taken into account that, according to the rules, the Commission is reviewing other complaints related to electoral matters, for example, complaints concerning individuals eligible to be included in the delegates' lists.
A number of such complaints have also been filed, and this workload should be considered when assessing the Commission's work.
Here we will go through the latest developments ahead of the election:

In an August 6 cease-and-desist letter addressed to members of the FIDE Council, officers, and employees, Buettner alleged the "ongoing use of FIDE personnel, resources, and financial assets" to support Turlov's presidential campaign:

Over the course of this election campaign, my team has observed and received numerous credible reports suggesting that FIDE employees are actively participating in campaign activities benefiting one particular candidate.

Among those whose activities have raised particular concern are individually identifiable certain FIDE employees who appear to be accompanying, facilitating, or otherwise supporting Mr. Turlov during campaign-related activities in multiple jurisdictions, and/or who are making official FIDE phone calls to arrange for Mr. Turlov to meet delegates in certain places.

Our concern extends beyond the activities of individual employees. It also appears that FIDE funds may be used to finance salaries, international travel, accommodation and related expenses associated with these activities.
Buettner pointed specifically to events in Cape Town, Bucharest, and Addis Ababa, while saying similar arrangements were expected in Costa Rica, Aruba, Panama, and New York City.

He claimed his campaign could provide evidence including photographs, schedules, travel records, witness statements, and official announcements upon request, but did not publish that material with the letter.

#chess #FIDE_elections Yesterday, the FIDE Electoral Commission received from Presidential candidate @JanHBuettner an official Cease and Desist legal notice against Turlov's campaign. FIDE's own resources and staff seem to be used and exploited in these elections.You can read… pic.twitter.com/hkusWSH1cd

Article 9.8 of FIDE's Electoral Rules states that candidates who already hold FIDE positions should not use federation resources—including staff, materials, phones, facilities, or premises—for campaigning. It also states that "FIDE Offices should maintain neutrality at all times."

"The resulting effect is that one candidate enjoys repeated opportunities to engage delegates through events supported by FIDE personnel and infrastructure, while competing candidates are denied equivalent access," Buettner wrote.

The resulting effect is that one candidate enjoys repeated opportunities to engage delegates through events supported by FIDE personnel and infrastructure, while competing candidates are denied equivalent access.—Jan Henric Buettner

He demanded that FIDE instruct officers and employees not to assist presidential campaigns while acting in their official capacity, ensure that no federation money or resources are used for campaigning, and publicly confirm strict neutrality and equal treatment throughout the remainder of the election.
On August 18, his campaign said it had not received a substantive response to their cease-and-desist notice, adding:
We have deliberately tried to handle these matters through FIDE's institutions rather than through the media.
We believe in due process, and we believe the Electoral Commission must be given the opportunity to do its work independently. But due process also requires a process.

When serious questions concerning candidate eligibility, conflicts of interest, institutional neutrality and ballot integrity are formally submitted, candidates and federations are entitled to know that those questions are being examined and when a decision can be expected.
We are not asking FIDE to decide these matters in our favor. We are asking FIDE to decide them.

Turlov is facing separate challenges to his eligibility from both of his opponents. Buettner and Rosenstein have independently asked FIDE's Electoral Commission to examine issues surrounding Turlov's candidacy, although the challengers have different concerns.

On August 11, Buettner and Pein submitted a complaint concerning Turlov. Buettner initially did not reveal its substance, but disclosed more details in an interview with Conrad Schormann for his German chess website Perlen vom Bodensee on August 22.

He said the complaint centers on three connected issues: the participation of the all-Russian university team at the recent FIDE World University Team Championship, business involving subsidiaries of Turlov's Freedom Holding in connection with sanctions, and what Buettner alleges is a conflict of interest involving Freedom Holding, FIDE's main sponsor.

Buettner also cited a children's chess event in South Africa involving Turlov's International School Chess Federation (ISCF). He said the complaint contains attachments and supporting evidence and explicitly asks the Electoral Commission to decide whether Turlov should be permitted to remain in the presidential race.

Buettner has also made clear that he is prepared to take the dispute further, if necessary. "The Electoral Commission has to react now," he told Perlen vom Bodensee. "If it doesn't, we take the next step—to CAS," he said, referring to the Lausanne-based Court of Arbitration for Sport, which adjudicates international sports disputes.
Rosenstein also publicly challenged Turlov's eligibility on August 7, calling on FIDE's Electoral Commission and, where legally competent, the CAS to examine Turlov's eligibility and disclosures.
He said Turlov should be disqualified if the Commission concludes that applicable FIDE regulations or eligibility requirements have not been met.

Dear chess community,I am formally calling on the FIDE Electoral Commission and, where legally competent, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), to urgently examine Mr. Timur Turlov’s eligibility and disclosures in connection with the 2026 FIDE Presidential election and, if… pic.twitter.com/tHlUzxj7te
The first concerns Turlov's citizenship. Rosenstein cited publicly available documentation showing a Russian passport issued to Turlov in June 2018 with an expiration date of June 2028.

Turlov, who was born in Moscow, has said that he renounced his Russian citizenship and became a citizen of Kazakhstan. Rosenstein argued that Turlov should provide the Electoral Commission with official documentation establishing when and on what legal basis his Russian citizenship ceased.

Turlov's campaign provided Chess.com with a detailed response to Rosenstein's complaint, calling the allegations "entirely unfounded." The response addressed Rosenstein's complaint but did not respond to the separate allegations raised by Buettner.

On the citizenship issue, Turlov said he renounced his Russian citizenship on September 27, 2022, and is now solely a citizen of Kazakhstan. His response said official Russian documents confirm both the termination of his citizenship and the invalidation of his Russian passports.
Turlov also argued that Rosenstein's complaint relied on documents that pre-dated his renunciation and an "unauthenticated verification record" that was contradicted by official records.
His communications chief previously presented a document that states that Turlov was no longer a citizen by February 16, 2023.

Wadim, Bulat Latypov here, Chief Communications Officer at Freedom24.Your claim that Timur Turlov is a citizen of the Russian Federation is completely untrue.This is confirmed by an official certificate issued by the Russian Consulate General in Almaty.We also consider that… pic.twitter.com/ehf7PXVInr

Holding or having previously held Russian citizenship does not in itself make someone ineligible to stand for FIDE President. Candidates must disclose their citizenship as part of their application, and President and Deputy President candidates on the same ticket must not represent the same FIDE Member Federation.

Rosenstein also raised the issue of Turlov being sanctioned by Ukraine in October 2022, saying that the Electoral Commission should determine whether relevant sanctions information was properly disclosed and whether it could create legal, banking, commercial, or reputational risks for FIDE.

Turlov rejected the argument that the Ukrainian sanctions should have been disclosed on his FIDE application. His response argued that the sanctions apply within Ukraine, are unrelated to chess, and do not constitute either a criminal conviction or a sanction imposed for violating FIDE or national chess federation rules.
"Mr Turlov has never been sanctioned by FIDE or found guilty of a criminal offence," his response said.
Mr Turlov has never been sanctioned by FIDE or found guilty of a criminal offence.—Team Timur Turlov

FIDE's Electoral Rules require candidates to declare measures or sanctions arising from violations of FIDE regulations, regulations issued by a FIDE Member Federation, or conduct punished as a criminal offense.

Turlov's response also argued that the Ukrainian sanctions were based partly on alleged Russian citizenship, which he says he had already renounced when they were imposed. The response also shows that Rosenstein's complaint contained issues that were not included in his August 7 public statement.

Turlov's response revealed that Rosenstein's formal complaint cited a Wells Notice issued in March in connection with an investigation by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which was reported by Bloomberg in June.

A Wells Notice means SEC staff have reached a preliminary determination to recommend enforcement action. "It is merely part of a lengthy formal procedure and is addressed to the legal entity, not to Mr Turlov personally," the team said.

However, Freedom Holding's own SEC disclosure, as well as Bloomberg's reporting, states that both the company and Turlov received a Wells Notice on March 11, 2026, contradicting the campaign's assertion that the notice was addressed only to the legal entity. The filing says SEC staff had made a preliminary determination to recommend a civil enforcement action against the recipients.

The filing also stressed that a Wells Notice is neither a formal charge nor a final determination that the recipient has violated any law. Freedom Holding and Turlov have challenged the SEC staff's preliminary determination.

"No court or administrative authority has found that Mr Turlov committed any violation, and no sanction has been imposed on him in connection with the Wells Notice. Under the FIDE Electoral Rules, preliminary and disputed allegations of this kind do not have to be disclosed in a candidate application," his campaign argued.

Turlov's response also addressed Russian court proceedings cited in Rosenstein's formal complaint. Chess.com has not seen the original complaint, but according to Turlov, it stated that less than one percent of his assets remained frozen by a Russian court.

Turlov's team said the information was outdated and that the measures had already been lifted following a settlement in 2025. He characterized the freeze as a temporary measure in a commercial dispute rather than a sanction or finding of wrongdoing.
A report by Russian newspaper Kommersant confirms that the Nizhny Novgorod Arbitration Court approved a settlement and lifted the restrictions on Turlov's assets on September 26, 2025.

"This part of the complaint causes even greater astonishment. All court rulings and determinations are publicly available on the relevant website, and no effort is required to verify them. The use of such a minimal, indeed non-existent, ground in the complaint only proves the absence of any real violations on the part of the Turlov ticket," Turlov said.

His response also rejected the relevance of previous CAS and FIDE cases cited in Rosenstein's complaint, arguing that those involved people who had received formal sanctions or criminal penalties and were therefore not comparable to his situation.
Rosenstein's public August 7 statement also raised two issues that were not among the points addressed in Turlov's response provided to Chess.com.

He pointed to reports by Perlen vom Bodensee that Hamburger Sparkasse terminated its business banking relationship with ChessBase after Turlov's acquisition of the German chess company, asking whether similar compliance difficulties could potentially arise for FIDE.

Finally, Rosenstein challenged Turlov to document his public claim that he has invested approximately $75 million in chess by identifying the companies, organizations, tournaments, federations, and projects that received the money.
"This is not about personal attacks," Rosenstein said. "It is about the standards we expect from anyone seeking to lead the world chess federation."
In his interview with Schormann, Buettner also claimed that the going "price" for a vote in the current election is $40,000 in Europe and $5,000 in Africa.
Buettner did not identify who he alleges is offering such payments or provide evidence for the specific figures in the interview, and Chess.com has not independently verified his claims.
"Every four years, someone comes along and hands out money," he said, describing what he called a longstanding patronage system.
He linked the claims to his campaign's calls for stronger ballot secrecy, alleging that delegates have previously been asked to photograph their completed ballots to demonstrate how they voted.

FIDE's Electoral Rules prohibit candidates from offering an "undue advantage" to a member federation, including payments, benefits, property, services, loans, employment promises, or other items of more than nominal value. Candidates are also prohibited from offering or accepting remuneration or concealed benefits connected with a FIDE election.

"I say to the delegates: Take the 40,000, take the 5,000, take it. You can still vote for me," he said, arguing that a genuinely secret ballot would allow delegates to vote according to their own choice regardless of outside pressure.

The complaints are not all heading in Turlov's direction. On August 11, Turlov announced that he and Anand had submitted their own complaint against the Rosenstein-Tang ticket to the Electoral Commission.

📃Complaint regarding the Rosenstein–Tang TicketTogether with my FIDE Deputy President candidate Viswanathan Anand, I have submitted a complaint to the FIDE Electoral Commission regarding the Rosenstein–Tang presidential ticket.The complaint raises four issues:1.⁠… pic.twitter.com/0eymrohkDU
Turlov raised four issues: alleged invalid nominations, premature campaigning, what he called "groundless accusations," and allegedly defamatory statements from the Rosenstein campaign.
We are asking the FIDE Electoral Commission to examine these issues, establish the facts, and issue an official warning to the Rosenstein-Tang ticket.
And I want to be clear about one thing. This is not an attempt to remove an opponent from the election.

I believe the FIDE President should be chosen by the Member Federations. Candidates may strongly disagree, but the election should still be a battle of ideas, programs, and visions—not personal attacks or unfair advantages.
And I want to be clear about one thing. This is not an attempt to remove an opponent from the election.—Timur Turlov
In a comment to Chess.com, Rosenstein declined to comment on the complaint.
This leaves an unusual situation in which all three presidential tickets have formally complained about at least one rival, with legal responses now filed in all three cases.

FIDE's Electoral Commission must now consider the complaints, while the eligibility challenges against Turlov must be decided "in the shortest possible period." Under FIDE's rules, a final decision on any eligibility complaint must be communicated no later than 15 days before the election.
With the presidential vote scheduled for September 26, September 11 is the latest date for a final eligibility decision.
Before those decisions are due, Buettner, Rosenstein, and Turlov agreed to meet in Chess.com's live debate on the 2026 presidential election on September 9, moderated by GM Maurice Ashley.

news.title: The North American Corporate Chess League Returns For Season 14 Starting October 1
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: The North American Corporate Chess League (NACCL) is back on Chess.com for its 14th season. The event runs from October 1 to November 12, and registration is now open.
body: The North American Corporate Chess League (NACCL) is back on Chess.com for its 14th season. The event runs from October 1 to November 12, and registration is now open.

The NACCL is the world's largest corporate chess league, bringing together companies from across the United States, Canada, and Mexico. Any employee from participating companies can play online from home or the office, regardless of chess level. The league is a chance to bond with coworkers and enjoy the thrill of competitive chess—along with free weekly lessons on Mondays with GM Kayden Troff and IM Gauri Shankar.

This edition's regular season runs for six weeks before the top teams face off in a knockout to crown the champion. Here's what you need to know about the format, prizes, and other details before signing up:
To play in the event, companies must register as a team. The only requirements are that the company's headquarters is in North America and that it isn't a chess business.

To get started, head to the NACCL registration page and register the company. Once registration is complete, the organizers will send a sign-up link to share with employees so they can join the company's roster. Employees looking to join should reach out to their captain or check the current teams list to join.
Will your company be competing in this season of the NACCL? Let us know in the comments!

news.title: Kramnik Loses New In Chess Lawsuit Over Naroditsky Article, Vows To Appeal
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: GM Vladimir Kramnik has lost his lawsuit against Dutch chess magazine New In Chess over an article that accused the former world champion of cyberbullying GM Daniel Naroditsky. An Amsterdam court ruled that the article w
body: GM Vladimir Kramnik has lost his lawsuit against Dutch chess magazine New In Chess over an article that accused the former world champion of cyberbullying GM Daniel Naroditsky. An Amsterdam court ruled that the article was not unlawful, rejected all of Kramnik’s claims, and ordered him to pay €4,449 (~$5,150) in litigation costs.

A nine-page judgment, issued on Tuesday and reviewed by Chess.com, rejected Kramnik’s demands, which included removing the article, publishing a correction, prohibiting similar statements in the future, and making an immediate €30,000 payment in damages.

The court ruled that New In Chess, as the publisher of a journalistic publication covering a matter of public interest, was entitled to broad freedom of expression. It found that the description of Kramnik’s conduct as "cyberbullying" was sufficiently explained and substantiated.
New In Chess shared an email from its lawyer announcing the result.

Kramnik did not respond to Chess.com's request for comment. Shortly after the verdict, he said in a post on his X account that he had not received the judgment and alleged that New In Chess had received "privileged treatment" from the court.

He also claimed the magazine's lawyers were given more time to present their arguments during the August 18 hearing and that the judge interrupted him when he attempted to address what he described as "factual fabrications" by New In Chess.
In a follow-up on Wednesday, Kramnik said he had received the ruling and confirmed that he would appeal.
Kramnik did not specify the alleged flaws, but said he is convinced that the ruling will be overturned following his appeal.

New In Chess owner GM Jacob Aagaard, as well as Leon Watson, the author of the article, declined Chess.com's request for a comment on the ruling. However, Aagaard shared his thoughts in a post on X: "Importantly: the court did not grant him protection from insults, while he is busy insulting others."
The final judgment had not appeared in the Dutch judiciary’s public database at the time of writing, although New In Chess and Kramnik had both received copies.

The lawsuit concerned A Very Public Feud, a six-page article by former Chess.com journalist Leon Watson, published in New In Chess 2025/8 on December 15, 2025. Its introduction states, "Daniel Naroditsky was the victim of cyberbullying at the hands of Vladimir Kramnik."

The article examined the increasingly bitter dispute between Kramnik and Naroditsky over the former world champion’s suspicions of cheating in online chess. It also discussed the impact of Kramnik’s public allegations on Naroditsky, GM David Navara, and others, along with claims that anonymous social-media accounts attacking Kramnik’s critics may have been operated by Kramnik himself.

Naroditsky died unexpectedly on October 19, 2025, at the age of 29. His death was later ruled an accident. Although the article stressed that the circumstances surrounding his death should not be the subject of speculation, it argued that Kramnik’s accusations had weighed heavily on Naroditsky.

Kramnik first demanded that New In Chess remove the article in a letter dated April 13. He also sought a correction, information on the number of copies sold, damages, a signed undertaking to refrain from similar statements, and €6,000 in legal fees.
In an email the following day, New In Chess said there was "zero chance" of a settlement involving a payment as outlined by Kramnik.

New In Chess took the article offline temporarily on July 31, but the parties could not reach an agreement. A summons was issued on Kramnik's behalf on July 22, and a hearing took place in Amsterdam on August 18, with Kramnik participating by video link.
The court discussed Kramnik’s right to protect his honor and reputation against New In Chess’s right to comment critically on matters of public interest.
It described "cyberbullying" as a subjective concept and a value judgment, noting that value judgments cannot be proved in the same way as factual allegations.
The term cyberbullying is not used lightly in the article, but is explained and substantiated by the circumstances and statements presented.

The court also found the July 3 decision by FIDE's Ethics & Disciplinary Commission (EDC), which found Kramnik guilty of multiple violations, including cyberbullying, psychological abuse, and false or unjustified accusations, to be relevant.

The EDC concluded that Kramnik’s conduct toward Naroditsky and other players involved "unwanted, repeated and intentional, aggressive behavior." Although the FIDE decision was issued after the New In Chess article was published, the Amsterdam court cited it as additional support for the magazine's use of the term.
Under these circumstances, New in Chess did not act unlawfully by using the term.
The court also addressed Kramnik’s argument that the article created a suggestive connection between his conduct and Naroditsky’s death.
It found that the article discussed Naroditsky’s death alongside the cyberbullying preceding it but did not explicitly claim that one caused the other.

While the average reader may well get the impression that such a link exists, this is not in itself unlawful. The untimely death of chess grandmaster Naroditsky is a matter of the greatest conceivable public interest within the chess community. Furthermore, the fact that Naroditsky’s well-being had seriously deteriorated prior to his death, as a result of the "devastating impact" of accusations of cheating, is also of great public interest. By discussing these circumstances together, the article draws attention to an abuse within the chess community: cyberbullying. That abuse justifies an open public discussion, in which the fact that statements are perceived as shocking, offensive or disturbing is insufficient for a finding that they are unlawful.
The court also highlighted Kramnik's status and his prominent role in the public debate about cheating.

It is also relevant that Kramnik, as a public figure with a very wide reach within the chess community, himself actively participates in the public debate on subjects he regards as abuses, such as cheating through the use of electronic aids.

It is plausible that Kramnik, because of his status within the chess community and the active and provocative manner in which he participates in the public debate, has a significant impact within that community.
This means that Kramnik, in turn, must tolerate strong criticism and other statements concerning him, even where these do not benefit his honor and reputation.

The same reasoning applied to comments in the article questioning Kramnik’s mental well-being. The court referred to his public cheating accusations and insinuations of a criminal conspiracy, including his use of the term "chess mafia."
Criticism and comments concerning his mental health arising from that conduct were permissible within the context of a heated debate on a matter of public interest, the court ruled.

Kramnik denied operating anonymous "burner accounts" used to post comments online. The court did not find that Kramnik had used such accounts, but noted that the article presented the claims as something believed by "internet sleuths," rather than as an established fact. It also added that Kramnik had not made it plausible that the claim was incorrect.
Kramnik further alleged that several quotations in the article were inaccurate or fabricated.

The court said their accuracy could not be determined in summary proceedings, where there was no room for a more extensive factual investigation. As a result, it could not conclude that publishing them was unlawful.

New In Chess acknowledged that the words "Kramnik has blood on his hands," attributed to GM Nihal Sarin, were a paraphrase of Nihal’s actual statement, "He has kind of literally taken a life," said in an interview with The Indian Express.
To the extent that Kramnik objects to this paraphrase, this consideration in the present judgment sufficiently addresses his objection. There are no grounds for an injunction or a correction thereof.
New In Chess argued that Kramnik’s case was a Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation, commonly known as SLAPP, and sought reimbursement of its full legal costs.

The court acknowledged that the lawsuit sought to restrict New In Chess’s participation in public debate but found that Kramnik’s claims were neither manifestly unfounded nor an abuse of the legal process. He was therefore ordered to pay the standard litigation costs of €4,449 rather than New In Chess’s full legal bill, which the magazine said exceeded €25,000 (~$29,000).
In a response on X, New In Chess suggested readers help cover legal costs by subscribing, or buying one of Daniel Naroditsky's books.
The ruling was issued in summary proceedings. The ordinary appeal period in a Dutch kort geding is four weeks.
