news.title: State of Chess: 'Grandmasters,' Gambit & Classic Games, Titled Tuesday Updates & More
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: Chess.com’s Chief Chess Officer, IM Danny Rensch, hosted State of Chess on Tuesday to share all the latest updates for Chess.com. The show featured special guests Liza Mandelup, executive producer and director of the new
body: Chess.com’s Chief Chess Officer, IM Danny Rensch, hosted State of Chess on Tuesday to share all the latest updates for Chess.com. The show featured special guests Liza Mandelup, executive producer and director of the new film Grandmasters, and Albert Cheng, Chess.com's Chief Growth Officer.
First things first, Rensch congratulated GM Hans Niemann for winning Titled Tuesday just before the show, and shouted out GM Robert Hess for returning to the commentary booth this week.
For the last two years, Mandelup has been working on creating the newest chess movie, Grandmasters.

As a newcomer to the world of chess, Mandelup described her goal in the film: "I love the fact that I started this after chess has had this digital revolution; I mean, you guys blew up online. And that's very much my thing, bringing these online worlds to life." That was the entry point for her to tell the stories of our elite grandmasters, but she also wanted to bring in other newcomers to our world. "How can we get closer to how these players feel when they're playing chess, like the intensity of it? And also, how crazy the whole world was! I just felt really, genuinely, no one knew what was going on outside of the chess world."
I just felt really, genuinely, no one knew what was going on outside of the chess world.

What might the audience find to be the most surprising? "I truly was shocked at how famous everybody was," she said. "I think with that came egos that I wasn't prepared for because I didn't know how big everybody was. I think I quickly caught up to speed with all of that." Compared to celebrities you might recognize from basketball or tennis, she said the names of chess players aren't as recognizable—but once you're in the world, you realize how important they are. "This show will show other people how big these guys are and how much they've achieved," she said.

After showing a clip from the movie, Mandelup explained that she personally connected to Jan Henric Buettner's mission with Freestyle Chess, a major storyline. "That was a lot of the mission we were following in the show. How can we make chess sexy, how can we make this cool to the masses?" Mandelup realized that Buettner's goals with Freestyle Chess were the same as hers with the film, and she described this as a sort of when-life-imitates-art scenario.
How can we make chess sexy, how can we make this cool to the masses?
"I think you're going to be surprised with how funny it is and how much drama there is," she told future viewers of the movie. "I love the challenge of people thinking the chess world is boring."

GothamChess (IM Levy Rozman) joined the show to announce that the full movie will premiere on October 11 across the country. GothamChess and Danny will be present at the AMC Theater in Times Square in New York City.

Cheng returned to the State of Chess for the first time since March of last year. As the chief growth officer, he said, "What I do here is I work on growth. That's my main job, leading our product and marketing and data teams, or at least parts of them, to grow the wonderful game of chess." He shared that over a billion games are played every month on Chess.com.

He's launched the new product of Gambit.com, which is a free, educational website to learn poker. On Monday, Rensch and WFM Alexandra Botez hosted a special broadcast for the Gambit Cup, a daily tournament held on the website. Nearly 1,500 players joined the event.

Cheng quite literally took the foundations of Chess.com and built a similar product for poker. He explained, "What I did was I took our codebase and our design system and our bot characters and used that as the starting point to build out this game of poker." The website looks and feels a lot like Chess.com, intentionally.

He said that the business models of popular poker sites are dependent on beginners losing money. Rather than winning money, he added a rating system to poker as a way to incentivize beginners to learn in a safe environment. Over 75,000 players are already on the new website.
Chess.com is looking at expanding to other games in the future, but we are definitely not looking at checkers!

"If you have a game that you love, that you feel is classic enough, you want us to consider it, just toss it in the chat, and I'll give it a read! We ultimately want to... create a delightful experience, help grow them, essentially do the Chess.com thing. Let's do it," said Cheng.
Chess.com is proud to share several new products and features with our members.

Traditionally, the most fun part of the show! The community asks Danny questions and he answers them live, not with prepared answers, and with plenty of jokes. You can skip to that part of the broadcast and watch it here:
That's it for this State of Chess, and we look forward to circling back for the next one!
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: How To Watch Season 4 Of The Global Chess League
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: The main event of the fourth season of the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League, the world's largest chess league, starts on September 5. Soon, the very best players in the world will gather in Bengaluru, India, to play in
body: The main event of the fourth season of the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League, the world's largest chess league, starts on September 5. Soon, the very best players in the world will gather in Bengaluru, India, to play in one of this year's biggest chess spectacles.
Here's what you need to know about the Global Chess League to enjoy the event:

As always, fans are invited to join the action in person and experience the unique atmosphere of the Global Chess League firsthand. Join the roaring crowd of fans and watch your chess heroes up close as they fight for the title at the Lalit Ashok in Bengaluru, India.

You can still watch every move of the Global Chess League, even if you're not going to Bengaluru. This year, you can watch the live broadcast of the event on the Global Chess League YouTube channel, as well as on Chess24's YouTube and Twitch and Chess.com India's YouTube. IMs Tania Sachdev and Sagar Shah, along with GMs Sahaj Grover, Harshit Raja, and Irina Krush, will host the broadcast.

The Global Chess League is known for always attracting a stellar lineup of the world's best chess players. This season did not disappoint, with the return of chess legends like former World Champion GM Viswanathan Anand, world number-one GM Magnus Carlsen, current U.S. Women's champion IM Carissa Yip, and other stars.
Star power aside, the Global Chess League is the stage for many thrilling storylines that you can't miss. Here is some of the excitement that you can look forward to this season.

After missing last year, Carlsen returns to the Global Chess League as one of the highlights of the event. While every match involving the Norwegian is a treat on its own, day three of the event is especially promising. Carlsen's Alpine APL Pipers will go up against Anand's PBG Alaskan Knights, setting up a generational clash between two legends of the game.

The Triveni Continental Kings have been the most dominant team in the League's history. After winning the first two seasons, Triveni dominated the round-robin stage in 2025—but fell short after losing 2-0 to the Alpine Pipers in the final.

This year, they return with most of the same stars from last year, bringing GMs Alireza Firouzja, Wei Yi, Alexandra Kosteniuk, and Zhu Jiner to the battlefield. Now, the question is: can they turn continuity into a third title?

While the established heavyweights will bring exciting battles to the Icon and Superstar boards, you won't want to sleep on this year's Prodigies. Among the many players to watch, former World Rapid Champion Volodar Murzin and the youngest grandmaster in history, Abhimanyu Mishra, are making their debut in the League. Other Prodigy highlights include GM Leon Luke Mendonca, who won the title in 2025, and GM Bardiya Daneshvar, who led the category with 7.5/10 last year.
Who do you think will win this season of the Global Chess League? Let us know in the comments below!

news.title: Renowned Washington Square Park Player 'Chichi' Detained By ICE
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: Nigerian-born CM Chikwere Onyekwere (aka "Chichi"), the highest-rated hustler in New York's Washington Square Park, was detained by ICE (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement) on Tuesday, August 25, and is currently i
body: Nigerian-born CM Chikwere Onyekwere (aka "Chichi"), the highest-rated hustler in New York's Washington Square Park, was detained by ICE (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement) on Tuesday, August 25, and is currently in the Prairieland Detention Center in Alvarado, Texas. At the age of 20, he became the youngest player to win the Nigerian Championship.

Currently in the 99th percentile of US Chess-rated players, the 41-year-old is known as a consistent and visible presence in the park, which was frequented by the young GM Bobby Fischer and immortalized in the movie Searching for Bobby Fischer. Onyekwere recorded and posted videos of his chess battles on his Instagram page, under the handle @viciousattackingchess, as well as on his website. In addition to playing games for money, he also gave lessons.

He has a 2104 FIDE rating and a 2211 US Chess rating, and his most recent upset was a win against GM Vladimir Akopian in the 2023 North American Open in Las Vegas. Akopian won the 2026 U.S. Senior Championship just over a month ago. Onyekwere also told Chess.com he'd beaten French GM Marc'Andria Maurizzi in the park, though we could not verify that game.

Onyekwere's future, even in the short term, is unclear, as he seeks legal representation in Texas. His priority, he told Chess.com over the phone, is finding a good lawyer. He explained that he's lost his students and his apartment, and that he'll have to start from scratch when he gets out. "If everything works out, I would like to go out and play in tournaments," said the candidate master, who still harbors hopes of climbing to the grandmaster title.
If everything works out, I would like to go out and play in tournaments.—Chikwere "Chichi" Onyekwere

Onyekwere, a promising junior chess player, first came to the United States in the early 2000s. His older sister, Ms. Mary Onyekwere Fawaz, told Chess.com that he learned to play chess from his late father, High Chief Godwin Ukandu Onyekwere. The father sponsored his son's travels for chess, which included international trips to the 2001 World Youth Chess Championship in Spain and the 2002 World Chess Olympiad in Slovenia, where he represented his country as a 17-year-old.

By 2004, he had already won three under-14 national titles and the Junior Chess Championship of Nigeria, as reported by The Chess Drum. At the age of 20, he returned to Nigeria to win the national title at the Nigerian Breweries Chess Championship and was the youngest player in history to do so at the time.

Onyekwere studied civil engineering at the University of Port Harcourt in Nigeria for three years, without completing the four-year program, before relocating to the United States. He spent time in Minnesota and Texas before finally coming to New York in 2005. He believes he had the skill to become a grandmaster, but didn't have a coach. At some point, Onyekwere stopped playing chess out of frustration, made some Nigerian friends, and started a business.

In 2014, he and his sister Uchechi Onyekwere were charged in a $13 million medical fraud scheme. Healthfirst, a not-for-profit managed care organization affiliated with six large hospitals, was the victim of billing fraud. The siblings were registered owners and officers of a durable medical equipment company located in Brooklyn that submitted fake claims to Healthfirst for reimbursement for equipment, $4 million of which was paid. According to the FBI's report, the operation took place from approximately 2008 through at least the end of 2013.

"As alleged, the defendants used fictitious companies and fraudulent claims to steal very real health care dollars," said then-United States Attorney Loretta Lynch in 2014. "The Medicare and Medicaid systems serve our most vulnerable citizens, and those who seek to steal those tax dollars will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law." In 2015, Onyekwere, who was already in jail as a pretrial detainee, pleaded guilty.

Public information on CourtListener states that his sister's final judgment was on September 30, 2015: imprisonment for 21 months with three years of supervised release, as well as a restitution amount of $337,348.84. For Chikwere, however, CourtListener does not list a final judgment. He told Chess.com he spent about three years in jail, from 2014 to 2017.

Onyekwere said he had a green card, but in 2017, he was pressured to sign a document and be deported back to Nigeria. In 2020, he was arrested by immigration officers at the Mexico border and applied for asylum. After 10 months, he was released due to his pending asylum application.

Because he was deported earlier, he didn't qualify for asylum, but in 2024 he was granted a CAT Deferral (Deferral of Removal under the Convention Against Torture), a temporary form of protection that stops the U.S. government from deporting a person to a country where they would likely face torture. With this protection, he was able to work and live in the U.S.

Since 2021, Onyekwere had been a daily presence at Washington Square Park and worked as a chess coach. He reported to ICE annually in December 2024 and 2025. This year, he was told to come in August—earlier than the regular time in December. When he reported to 26 Federal Plaza on August 25, he was detained.

Onyekwere told Chess.com that he "never had any issues" in previous meetings. "I think it's the midterm [elections] coming up." A CAT deferral bars the government from removing Onyekwere to Nigeria, but under federal regulations, it does not limit ICE's authority to detain him. He said he was moved from New York to New Jersey, sent back to New York, and put on a plane at JFK Airport without knowing the destination. Next thing he knew, he was in Texas.

While his time in detention has been difficult, Onyekwere shared a piece of good news: he was able to play a blindfold game of chess—that is, a game against someone else without a chessboard. "I definitely need help to hire a good lawyer," he said. "I have not done anything wrong, but because of politics, it's just horrible." He has a 12-year-old son in New Jersey who lives with his mother. He acknowledged Mary Kennedy, Maddie Weber, Father Jonah Teller, Anthony Kozikowski, and Alan Stolyarov as a few community members who have supported him.

Asked what he'd like readers to know about himself, Onyekwere responded: "I want people to know that I'm a professional chess player. I am using the power of chess to stay calm and help others." Besides help with getting a lawyer, he said he'd love to have a chessboard and chess books while in detention—"something tactical."
I am using the power of chess to stay calm and help others.—Chikwere "Chichi" Onyekwere

Local players and content creators have spread awareness of Onyekwere's detention in the last week. Chessoptics made the following Instagram post on Monday, August 31, saying, "I would like to get the word out for anyone who can help."

Maddie Weber, a local university student and content creator (@maddieplayschess), told Chess.com Onyekwere is "a friendly face who represents the positive chess environment of the park—and it's Chichi! You're going to play a game for money, there's not going to be anything crazy about it. It's just going to be a Washington Square Park chess game."

Gabriella Bass, senior producer at Ackerley Creative, told Chess.com that they are editing and soon releasing a video about Onyekwere as part of their "Over the Board" series profiling chess players. She said, "A big thing was he had the potential for grandmaster status, but he's never really had the opportunities to be sponsored," pointing out how inaccessible the highest titles can be in chess if you don't have the resources to travel and play in tournaments. She clarified that this was based on their conversations and that she's not an authority on what it takes.

Tunde Onakoya, a renowned Nigerian chess player, coach, and founder of Chess In Slums Africa, met Onyekwere twice in New York City. In 2025, Onyekwere came to support Onakoya as he and NM Shawn Martinez broke the Guinness World Record for the longest chess marathon after playing continuously for 64 hours. Onakoya returned in 2026 and played a few games in Washington Square Park. Onyekwere also came to support Promoting Queens, which raises money to support girls' chess education in Africa.
You can watch them play a game below, where Onyekwere served what he calls his world-famous "Chichi Park Fried Rice" on the board, "EXTRA SPICY," a metaphor for a heated game of chess.

Onakoya told Chess.com: "He's a good person who loves chess who's trying to really find his way back. It's just quite unfortunate what has happened, and I hope that we can give him all of the support that he needs."

Ms. Fawaz, his older sister, said, "His entering the U.S. was a result of how bright he was. He had dreams, he had a future, he had focus." She went on: "Life has its stages. It's a pity he found himself in this situation. I think 2017, 2018, by the grace of God he... came out free, hoping that he's actually free as a young man... it's so heartbreaking; it's so painful to hear again that at this point in time such pain is happening again."
It's so heartbreaking; it's so painful to hear again that at this point in time such pain is happening again.

Peter Kozikowski created a GoFundMe page to support Onyekwere with legal fees. Chess.com is not involved with the collection or distribution of those funds. Peter's cousin, the "street philosopher and urban chess educator" Anthony Kozikowski (commonly known as "Cheese"), has led the search for a lawyer. He told Chess.com: "I realize he has an amazing heart; he extends kindness to all of the people receiving it, and the community that stands behind him is evidence of that claim."

Alan Stolyarov has helped the effort as well—cleaning out Onyekwere's apartment after he was detained, for instance. He said, "We're all fighting like heaven and hell to get him back. It's just the fact that no one else on this world would do something like this, but then we are; hopefully it inspires some more people."
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: 12-Year-Old Faustino Oro Confirmed As World's Youngest Grandmaster
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: GM Faustino Oro has officially been awarded the GM title by FIDE, making the 12-year-old Argentinian "Messi of Chess" the youngest current grandmaster. The confirmation comes shortly after he broke 3300 in blitz on Chess
body: GM Faustino Oro has officially been awarded the GM title by FIDE, making the 12-year-old Argentinian "Messi of Chess" the youngest current grandmaster. The confirmation comes shortly after he broke 3300 in blitz on Chess.com, giving an extra boost a week before he begins his next quest at the Legends & Prodigies II in Madrid, Spain.

Oro’s title was approved at the second FIDE Council meeting of 2026, held online on August 23, with the decision published five days later. His official FIDE profile has now been upgraded from international master to the shiny new grandmaster title.

The update completes the final step in a journey that began almost a year ago. Although Oro had already completed all requirements for the title at the Sardinia World Chess Festival on May 9, grandmaster titles are not formally awarded until they have been approved by the chess governing body.

Oro succeeds 15-year-old Turkish prodigy GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, who had been the world’s youngest current grandmaster since FIDE formally approved his title just over two years ago. Erdogmus completed the requirements for the title at 12 years, nine months, and 29 days.

Oro is the second-youngest player ever to qualify for the title, at the age of 12 years, six months, and 26 days, behind American GM Abhimanyu Mishra, who set the record at 12 years, four months, and 25 days in 2021. Oro surpassed former record-holder GM Sergey Karjakin, who became a grandmaster at 12 years and seven months in 2002.

The Argentinian scored 6/9 in the 158-player open in Sardinia, which featured 29 grandmasters. A penultimate-round victory over IM Bartlomiej Niedbala, followed by a final-round pairing against two-time world championship challenger GM Ian Nepomniachtchi, guaranteed Oro the required performance regardless of the result of his last game.
“Now I am a GM. I am really, really happy,” Oro said after securing his final norm in Sardinia.
Fausti, as he is nicknamed, analyzed the crucial game in a new video for Chess.com.

His first GM norm came at the inaugural Legends & Prodigies tournament in Madrid in September 2025, where he dominated the field with an undefeated 7.5/9. During the same event, he crossed 2500 to become the youngest player in history—and the first under the age of 12—to reach that rating.

The second norm followed three months later at the Szmetan-Giardelli Masters in Buenos Aires, where he scored 5.5/9. Oro then narrowly missed the chance to break Mishra’s age record at the Aeroflot Open in Moscow, losing a must-win final-round game, before completing the title in Sardinia two months later.
Oro's meteoric rise has continued online. Last week, he crossed 3300 in Chess.com's blitz rating for the first time, taking him to the top-10 highest-rated players on the platform.

The milestone improves on the personal best of 3295 he set in February, when he climbed to fifth place on the Chess.com blitz leaderboard. At the time, the 12-year-old had gained around 150 points in a month through a series of impressive Titled Tuesday performances.

At the age of 10, Oro became the youngest player to reach 3000 in Chess.com blitz, while his results against the world’s leading players have shown that the number is not merely symbolic. Last month, he defeated GM Magnus Carlsen in one of eight 3+0 blitz games between the pair. Carlsen won the informal match, with three draws, but it was Oro’s fourth online victory against his favorite player after his first win, a bullet game, as a 10-year-old in 2024.

His latest rating on FIDE's September list is 2537, placing him seventh in Argentina. He has been selected to represent his country for the first time at the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
Before that, Oro will make his first tournament appearance as a grandmaster when he returns to Madrid for Legends & Prodigies II, which takes place on September 7-12.
He returns as the defending champion and will face five experienced GMs: David Anton, Jose Martinez, Ivan Sokolov, Diego Flores, and Pepe Cuenca, competing in a double round-robin over 10 rounds.

One year ago, Oro arrived at the same venue as an international master chasing his first GM norm. He returns as the youngest grandmaster in the world, with 3300 broken online and his next over-the-board target already clear: 2600.

Oro was one of 77 players whose titles were approved at the FIDE Council meeting on August 23. The Council approved the Qualification Commission’s recommendations for 17 GM titles, four WGM titles, 49 IM titles, and seven WIM titles.
India accounted for 15 of the recipients, the most of any federation.

Tarjei J. Svensen

news.title: Praggnanandhaa On Fighting To Win, India's Olympiad Hopes, Gukesh-Sindarov & More
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: "I think, at the moment, I would say he's the number one player in the world," GM Viswanathan Anand recently told The Times of India about GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, who followed victory in Norway Chess 2026 by winnin
body: "I think, at the moment, I would say he's the number one player in the world," GM Viswanathan Anand recently told The Times of India about GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, who followed victory in Norway Chess 2026 by winning the 2026 Grand Chess Tour. Praggnanandhaa talked to CM Sahil Tickoo for Chess.com recently, covering the mindset that led to his recent victories, playing GM Magnus Carlsen, India's chances at the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad, the Gukesh-Sindarov FIDE World Championship match, and more.

I think it's about fighting till the end. For me, when I enjoy playing, I don't mind too much about what happened the previous day—I can come back and fight the next day. I think the mindset I have right now is to go for tournament victories, so that also helps. When you keep fighting and you’re pushing for the top spot, it can go your way. Sometimes it doesn't, but you're always pushing yourself, and you’ll get the maximum results when everything is in your favor.

Honestly, it was down to the last two blitz games—we were basically playing a two-game blitz match to decide the final. On any day, anything could have happened: some matches I’ll win, some matches Fabiano will win, it’s going to be a toss-up. I managed to win that, but overall, for me, I think the fight is what I like! I came back after being six down, and to be in that situation—it was more important for me that I was giving that fight. I didn't want to go down easy; I wanted to put up a fight.

I thought: can I win a two-game rapid match against Fabi? I thought I can. And can I win a blitz match against Fabi, and I thought, yeah, I can do that against anyone. So if I can do that, the six-point margin will be gone. It's still six points—but when you see it like this, it's manageable and it's possible.

I always enjoyed playing against Magnus—it was always exciting, I didn't feel the "Magnus effect." Yeah, sometimes when he puts on pressure, there will always be things that you might feel, but overall, for me, whenever I play him, I'm always excited. It brings a kind of excitement that makes me play my best, but also I enjoy those games—it's always fighting, and I'm always in some creative mode when I play Magnus. Maybe being the underdog also helps—you can just go and express yourself, and maybe that is also a thing. When I played him now, it was also after a long time that I played him in a classical game. You don’t get too many chances, so I was excited for it, and it went my way.

Carlsen played a simul against 20 kids on the eve of his 2013 world championship match in Chennai against Anand, later commenting, "I have never played a simul before when I cannot remember how many games I drew and lost!" It was 10 wins, six draws, and four losses, including to Praggnanandhaa's sister and now GM Vaishali Rameshbabu.

Yeah, it's a pity that I don't have the game. I lost the game… I lost the actual game, but I lost the game moves as well! I remember he played the Scotch Opening. At some point to me then I thought I was fine, and then he played some tactical move. I remember the move Rf3, because this is what is in my mind, but I don't remember the position or anything. This move was a complete surprise to me back then, and it was just too good. It's great to play such a strong player in a simul, and now it's nice to look at those moments in those clips.

I think watching is way more tense! When you're playing, you're just there, you're focused on the moment, you're completely concentrated, and of course all these thoughts about winning and everything are there, but maybe I'm used to it. Watching is the most stressful thing, especially when you're rooting for someone.

I can, I think, do multiple roles, but I think she has a great team of people to help her in the chess aspect. Obviously, I’ll do whatever I can, but I think I'll be more useful as a brother and someone who's always there by her side.

We have a great team, similar to last year. Nihal has come in instead of Pentala. Everyone else is the same. The captain is Srinath Narayanan, also seconds are the same, so it's just one change, and overall it's an extremely strong team. We're all good friends with each other, we're all in great spirits, so it's a fun team to hang around, and I'm excited for the Olympiad.

About the other teams—obviously Uzbekistan, the U.S., and China are there. Maybe Uzbekistan and the U.S. are at the absolute top. So it'll be interesting, but there are also all these teams which are capable of upsetting any team. It's not going to be an easy event, but we'll give our best—we have a good team and we have good spirits, so if we all give our best, I think we can do it again.

It matters, but I think you can give any board order and come up with a logic to make it make sense, because we're all so strong that anyone can play at any board. So it's not such a big difference, but it's interesting that everyone is talking about all these board orders and stuff—it's great to have such things, because it shows chess is growing. All the fans really care about all these little things, which was not the case five or six years back. So it's great to have that.

I honestly think it's 50/50. I don't think there's any one massive favorite. Obviously Gukesh's form hasn't been the best, but it's always one tournament, or even one game, to get that confidence and form back. Even for me—if you had seen me till Norway round six, I think everyone would be saying Pragg is not in great shape, and then four days later I won the tournament. So it's always a few games, or just one game, to get that confidence, and then we all know what Gukesh is capable of—he's really shown it at the top level.
It's always a few games, or just one game, to get that confidence, and then we all know what Gukesh is capable of!

And for Javokhir as well—the first few games in a World Championship match, everyone knows how much pressure it is, but no one has actually experienced it, so it will be a new experience for him, and that's also going to play a role. Overall, it's going to be a close match, and it's going to be quite interesting for me to watch, because I grew up with both of them—we're around the same age.

That's the first answer that came to my mind, Fischer or Kasparov, but Tal, because it would be interesting to face the sacrifices over the board, to see if I can react in a better way, if we’re stronger with calculation nowadays. It'd be interesting.
I think the world will be better if we run, honestly. I don't think dancing or singing skills… the world isn't ready to see that!

Praggnanandhaa will be next in action when he plays for India in the Olympiad starting September 16 in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. First, however, India is hosting the fourth edition of the Global Chess League, which kicks off tomorrow, September 5, in Bengaluru, with Carlsen and Anand among the players in action.

Colin McGourty

news.title: Collegiate Chess League Fall 2026 Registration
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: The Collegiate Chess League (CCL) is back for another thrilling season, and registrations for Fall 2026 are officially open! Once again, the CCL will boast a $25,000 prize fund and the exciting four-vs.-four team format
body: The Collegiate Chess League (CCL) is back for another thrilling season, and registrations for Fall 2026 are officially open! Once again, the CCL will boast a $25,000 prize fund and the exciting four-vs.-four team format that fans and players love.

The Collegiate Chess League is the premier online chess competition for college students. We invite all university students who love chess and would like to represent their school to compete. Register today:

Last season saw over 390 teams and 2,000 students from a record-breaking 228 colleges and universities across 25 countries! Will this season once again break participation records? This fall, teams will battle it out in the 5+2 time control. Fans and players can expect fast-paced battles, dramatic tactics, and all sorts of chess action.

Whether you're a casual player or a seasoned competitor, this is the perfect event for you to test your skills and have fun alongside your college mates. From hobbyists to professionals such as GMs Aryan Tari, Viktor Gazik, Gergely Kantor, Shawn Rodrigue-Lemieux, and others, the CCL is the perfect competition for all college students.

In the recently concluded Spring 2026 season, the University of Texas at Dallas (UTD) won its first-ever championship, becoming only the fifth school ever to win the CCL. Will UT Dallas be able to defend their championship—or will a new challenger come in and take the glory and the Division 1 $5,000 cash prize?
Team captains and coaches can register their teams until September 20 (originally September 18 but was extended two days). Check out all you need to know to register below.
Registrations have been extended to September 20 at 11:59 p.m. PT / 2:59 a.m. (+1) ET, so make sure you don't miss the deadline. To register, you must complete the following steps:
Optional: Check out our College Ambassador Program if you are a college club leader looking for free merch, memberships, and other opportunities to support your club.
Once your team captain has registered your team, follow the steps below:

Each team must have at least four players, with the option to add up to four additional team members as substitutes. Captains can register multiple teams, but no one on a lower team can be higher rated than a top four player from a higher team.

If you are unsure if your school has a team, you can find all the schools, teams, captains, and players from last season here and contact them through our Discord. If you are sure your school doesn't have a team and would like to connect with other players from your school to form one, contact us at CCL@Chess.com, and we'll connect you with other players from your school.
You can find the full regulations and prize information here.
The regular season runs from September 26 to November 7. The playoffs begin on November 14 and end on November 22.

Sign up to participate in the CCL and play alongside other great college players. If you can't compete in the event, you can still watch the live coverage on CCL's Twitch channel and follow all the action!

news.title: Terry Extends 3 0 Thursday Record
news.author: coachjkane
news.excerpt: IM Renato Terry extended his record for most 3 0 Thursday victories to 18 on September 3 after winning the final tournament of the day with a 9.5/11 score. Earlier, GMs Denis Lazavik and Parham Maghsoodloo took home the
body: IM Renato Terry extended his record for most 3 0 Thursday victories to 18 on September 3 after winning the final tournament of the day with a 9.5/11 score. Earlier, GMs Denis Lazavik and Parham Maghsoodloo took home the top prizes as well. NM Liudmyla Ivanytska had a big day, winning the women's prize in the first two tournaments. IM Rose Atwell claimed that prize in the third event, her fourth prize over the last three weeks.

Lazavik won his first seven games and then kept his lead to take clear first place in the first tournament. He dominated his fifth-round game with GM Karthik Venkataraman in a way that you'll rarely see between such highly-rated players.

White grabs the bishop pair and a better structure. The game isn't quite over, but White's in complete control.16. ...  Bxf3   17.   Bxf3    Nc5   18.   e5  ... The bishops soon win material on the queenside.18. ...  Rc8   19.   Bd6    Nd3   20.   Be2    Nxb2   21.   Bxb5+  ... Black's king gets stuck in the center and the b2-knight is trapped as well.21. ...  Kd8   22.   Rab1    a6   23.   Rxb2    axb5   24.   Rxb5   Black resigns. How often do you see a strong GM lose without moving two kingside pieces at all? 1-0     

Lazavik's task grew harder as he kept winning. In the seventh round, he survived a lost position for 70 moves to defeat GM Oleksandr Bortnyk by 0.4 seconds on the clock.
Lazavik finally lost in the eighth round against one of last week's winners, GM Jeffery Xiong. He won his next two games to take a half-point lead into his last-round game against GM Alexey Sarana.

The draw gave Lazavik first place with 9.5 points, ahead of a group of four players on nine points. Sarana had the best tiebreak score in that group, followed by GM Sergei Zhigalko, FM Artin Ashraf and GM Maxim Matlakov.

While Lazavik won his tournament with a strong start, Maghsoodloo took an opposite route to victory in the second event. After winning his first two games, Maghsoodloo ran into GM Anton Demchenko and got steamrolled by powerful play.

It didn't get any easier for Maghsoodloo in the next round, as he was checkmated on move 115 by GM Andrey Drygalov. It's hard to win an 11-round tournament by starting 2/4, but Maghsoodloo managed by winning his next seven games! The final three games were against GMs Jakub Kosakowski, Matlakov, and Nguyen Ngoc Truong Son, all with blitz ratings over 3100. His game against Kosakowski took 56 moves, but White could have resigned much earlier.

Maghsoodloo's winning streak brought him to nine points, which was enough for clear first place. He was followed by Sarana, with his second second-place finish of the day on 8.5 points. GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda took third, behind Sarana on tiebreaks.

The third 3 0 Thursday tournament of the day is Terry's specialty. Of his 18 tournament victories, 13 occurred in the final event of the day. He stayed true to form this week, winning the event by a full point. As usual, Terry stayed ahead on the clock most of the time. That speed helped him to recover from a lost position against GM Liem Le in the sixth round.
Terry didn't require luck in most of his other games. His tournament-clinching victory against FM Dincer Tasdogen was a messy, but one-sided affair.
That win secured first place for Terry on 9.5 points. Bortnyk took second with 8.5 points, half a point ahead of Maghsoodloo.

3 0 Thursday is a set of three weekly Swiss tournaments for verified titled players featuring their favorite time control. Each of the three tournaments is an 11-round Swiss with a 3+0 time control. The combined prize fund is $3,000 every week.
NM Jeremy Kane is the Instructional Content Manager for Chess.com, and the author of several courses in the Starting Out series, Queen’s Gambit Accepted, Trompowsky, and Tarrasch.

news.title: Khachatryan Upstages Nhat Minh Twice To Win Duck Chess Title
news.author: vsaravanan
news.excerpt: Duck Chess specialist Edward Khachatryan of Israel defeated defending champion IM Nhat Minh To in both the Winners Final and the Grand Final to triumph in the 2026 Duck Chess Championship and pocket the winner's purse of
body: Duck Chess specialist Edward Khachatryan of Israel defeated defending champion IM Nhat Minh To in both the Winners Final and the Grand Final to triumph in the 2026 Duck Chess Championship and pocket the winner's purse of $750. Nhat Minh gained $500.
Last year's runner-up IM Eric Rosen lost to Nhat Minh in the Winners Semifinals and then to Christiaan Smeets in the Losers Semifinals to finish fourth and gain $250. Smeets earned $350.
Other prize winners were Marco Monti and CM Hamlet Antonyan ($175 each) and CM Vahan Nalbandyan and Menil Ibrahimagic ($100 each). The streamer prize went to WGM Adriana Nikolova ($100).
This was the ninth of the 2026 Chess.com Community Chess Championships, with three more to go. The next one will be the Seirawan Chess Championship from September 30 till October 2.
The eight qualifiers were conducted September 2-3, with each being a 75-minute arena with a 3+2 time control.
Among the qualifiers were Nhat Minh and Rosen, the winner and the runner-up finishers in the previous two years of the championship.
The knockout was an eight-player double-elimination bracket featuring best-of-four matches. Each game featured a 3+2 time control.

Though Nhat Minh and Rosen were the favorites going into the knockout stage, Khachatryan is another leading exponent of the variant, as the leaderboards show. Nhat Minh upstaged Rosen in one of the Winners Semifinals with a score of 3-1, the unexpected king drop by Rosen in the third game being a highlight of the match.
Rosen had just played 39...Kg6-f6??, a move which isn't illegal in Duck Chess, allowing Nhat Minh to win the game by the brutal 40.Nxf6.

Thus, Khachatryan and Nhat Minh met in the Winners Final, where the score got tied 2-2 at the end of the regular games. In the tiebreak, being up by an exchange but low on time, Nhat Minh froze on the final move, thus losing the game and the tie to Khachatryan.
The Grand Final began with an efficient game by Khachatryan, who first trapped Nhat Minh's queen with a nice find: 26...Ne7-c6 and duck to a4!
...and then delivered a cute finish, blocking the white king equally efficiently.
With 28...Na5-b3 and duck to b1, the white king got captured on d2 on the next move.
This was the creativity of Duck Chess in full flow, trapping the queen and king effectively using the duck to one's advantage.
The match was effectively over when Khachatryan exploited a routine move by Nhat Minh in the second game to effect a quick and decisive king hunt.

Khachatryan exploited his opponent's oversight 21...Qxa3?? and duck to f1 here, by effecting a simple king capture 22.Qg7 and duck to h8, thus making sure that the black king is captured the next move. Though Nhat Minh won the next game, the match went in Khachatryan's favor when he won the fourth and final game.
You can rewatch the 2026 Chess.com Community Championships: Duck Chess on our community Twitch page or enjoy the show on YouTube.
The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Benjamin Bok and Pepe Cuenca.

The 2026 Duck Chess Championship was the ninth event of the Chess.com Community Championship series. Winners of eight qualifiers (each was a 75-minute arena with 3+2 time control) entered the Final on September 4, which was an eight-player double-elimination bracket. The time control was 3+2, and matches were best-of-four. The total prize fund was $2,500.

news.title: Xiong Captures His 5th Bullet Brawl Title
news.author: vsaravanan
news.excerpt: GM Jeffery Xiong emerged as the winner of a thrilling edition of Bullet Brawl on Saturday in an event that saw the lead change several times, with several players taking turns at the top of the standings.
body: GM Jeffery Xiong emerged as the winner of a thrilling edition of Bullet Brawl on Saturday in an event that saw the lead change several times, with several players taking turns at the top of the standings.

Xiong scored 49.5/68 to post 162 arena points, 18 more than GM Oleksandr Bortnyk, his main rival in the final stages of the race for the title. Xiong and Bortnyk will receive $400 and $250, respectively, for their efforts. The next two places went to GMs Matthias Bluebaum and Jose Martinez, who had also led the tournament at various points, earning $150 and $100, respectively.
The top women's prize of $100 went to IM Aleksandra Maltsevskaya with a score of 31/50 and 93 points.
Bullet Brawl will return on Saturday, September 12, at 12 p.m. ET / 18:00 CEST / 9:30 p.m. IST.
Bluebaum was the first to jump into the lead. The following game is typical of his impressive strategic style. The moves simply flow, guided by a strong positional sense on the board.
Bluebaum started with a six-game winning streak before he was stopped by CM Shakhrombek Karimov in an incredible attacking finish.

Martinez was the next tournament leader after winning two games against Bortnyk and Xiong from inferior positions by running his opponents out of time. Martinez has incredible mouse skills, as the following game testifies, where the players made 89 moves in a bullet game! He ran his opponent out of time to win.
That same quickness may also have been his downfall, at least as demonstrated in the following game from early in the tournament.
Bortnyk was another frontrunner whose natural positional style enables him to find fluent, intuitive moves in bullet chess.
Xiong's strengths are his resourcefulness and tactical sharpness, which enabled him to save many losing positions and win several games by spotting tactics quickly.

It was in the final stretch of the tournament that Xiong asserted his superiority, including a six-game winning streak. He also took his closest challengers head-on and beat them in individual encounters.
How to review games? The games from this week's Bullet Brawl can be found here.

Bullet Brawl is an exciting arena featuring Chess.com's top bullet specialists. It takes place weekly on Saturdays. The format is a two-hour arena with a 1+0 time control; the prize fund is $1,000. Like Titled Tuesday and Arena Kings, Bullet Brawl often features top GMs, including Hikaru Nakamura, Andrew Tang, Tuan Minh Le, and many more!

news.title: Sindarov's American Gambits Begin Global Chess League With Double Win
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Javokhir Sindarov beat GM Viswanathan Anand and made a draw against GM Alireza Firouzja as the FYERS American Gambits won both matches on day one of the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League. There were also wins for
body: GM Javokhir Sindarov beat GM Viswanathan Anand and made a draw against GM Alireza Firouzja as the FYERS American Gambits won both matches on day one of the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League. There were also wins for GM Magnus Carlsen's Alpine APL Pipers, who scraped a 10-8 win over GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave's CheQ Mumba Masters, while Ganges Grandmasters, led by GM Ian Nepomniachtchi, won by an even narrower 10-9 to be the second team of the day to defeat Firouzja's Triveni Continental Kings—the winner of the 2023 and 2024 editions of the event.
Day two starts on Sunday, September 6, at 6 a.m. ET / 12:00 CEST / 3:30 p.m. IST.

The six-team Global Chess League was conceived in India but first held in Dubai, UAE, in 2023, before moving to London, UK, in 2024. Then it switched to India, taking place in Mumbai last year. The 2026 edition is being held in the Lalit Ashok Hotel in Bengaluru and—despite the event ending just three days before the 46th Chess Olympiad begins in Samarkand, Uzbekistan—we have much of the world chess elite in action.

Each team is led by an "icon" player, with three icons from 2025 not playing in 2026—World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju and world numbers two and three GM Hikaru Nakamura and GM Fabiano Caruana. They're replaced, however, by World Championship Challenger Sindarov, Nepomniachtchi, and world number-one Carlsen, whose team won the whole event in 2025 when he wasn't playing for them.

It's notable that the teams change each year after bidding wars. GM Anish Giri mentioned he's the only surviving member of the title-defending Alpine APL Pipers, while it's the same story for GM Bibisara Assaubayeva, who was the only player to compete for FYERS American Gambits in 2025 as well. Two teams have four players returning, however, Triveni Continental Kings (Firouzja, GM Wei Yi, GM Zhu Jiner, and GM Alexandra Kosteniuk) and CheQ Mumba Masters (Vachier-Lagrave, GM Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, GM Harika Dronavalli, and GM Bardiya Daneshvar).

The format is almost unchanged, with each team fielding six players, including two women and one junior player. They play each other twice over the first eight days (nine in 2025) before the top two compete in the final on the last day. The scoring system gives four points for a win with Black and just three points for a win with White—making match draws unlikely. Each game is played with 20 minutes per player, with a two-second increment added after move 41.

Each team earns three points for a match win, one point for a draw, and zero for a loss. As four matches were held on the first day, two teams played twice—leaders FYERS American Gambits, and the unfortunate Triveni Continental Kings, who didn't get off the mark.
GM Daniil Dubov later commented on his team's tactics, "Be solid with White and try and crush with Black—today it worked well!"

However, the solidity wasn't entirely obvious in the first match of the day, which was much closer than it looks at a glance. Dubov missed a win against 15-year-old prodigy GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, while GM Nihal Sarin's game against GM Arjun Erigaisi was pure mayhem. Arjun calmly gave up both rooks for a position that, given his time advantage, was almost decisive.
Instead, however, Nihal took over and was winning—until dropping a full piece in one move!

Arjun was then winning and, if he'd won, PBG Alaskan Knights would be leading and GM Abhimanyu Mishra wouldn't need to fall on his sword on the bottom board while trying to win a drawn position against GM Marc'Andria Maurizzi. Instead, however, Arjun blundered last, and Nihal escaped.

That meant that the match was effectively decided by Sindarov's victory on the top board over Anand. It was a tense battle, but the former world champion couldn't find the narrow path to hold when things got tough.

Triveni Continental Kings won the first two editions of the Global Chess League and dominated the third before losing out in the final. They were powered by Firouzja, who in 2025 started with five wins in a row.

This time, however, the Iranian-French star started slowly, missing some chances to take down Nepomniachtchi, with Ganges Grandmasters taking the lead with a swashbuckling win for GM Levon Aronian, who needed just 29 moves to take down Wei.

Although Triveni hit back with two four-point wins with Black, for GCL debutants GMs Aravindh Chithambaram and Pranav Venkatesh, it wasn't enough, with Ganges winning on both women's boards. The wins were deserved, overall, but were decided on the finest of margins. IM Stavroula Tsolakidou's final position against Kosteniuk looks to be a draw, while Zhu had a one-move chance to beat IM Polina Shuvalova.
The next match featured the world number-one and recent winner of the Esports World Cup.
The dynamics of the Alpine APL Pipers are interesting. Giri is joined by GM Vidit Gujrathi, his great friend (!?)...
...and Carlsen. As they walked out onto the stage, Carlsen went a bit too far, while Giri kept an exaggerated distance.

Well, they started with a very narrow victory. Carlsen won a pawn against Vachier-Lagrave, but wasn't able to weave his normal endgame magic, while Giri stumbled and fell to GM Pranesh M, who was only playing as a late replacement for GM Vladimir Fedoseev. 32...h6?, played after over three minutes, was losing—though only to a precise response three moves later.

GM Divya Deshmukh almost pulled off an incredible escape a piece down, but GM Harika Dronavalli eventually delivered checkmate, while Vidit was the one player to give the Alpine Pipers a very convincing win.
That's our Game of the Day, which GM Dejan Bojkov has analyzed below.
...but it was a dramatic finish to IM Carissa Yip's game against GM Koneru Humpy that made all the difference.

After a sharp pawn race, Yip queened first, and when Humpy gave a saving check, all the U.S. star had to do was move her king. If Humpy had queened, then a queen sacrifice would force a draw, but instead Yip sacrificed her queen first and was lost.
That leaves two teams who had to play another match on the first day—Triveni, who had lost the first match, and American Gambits, which had won.

The momentum continued, with American Gambits powering to a second victory, which could have been even more convincing, since Sindarov and Assaubayeva both let chances slip. The most impressive finish came for Dubov, who punished one slip by Aravindh to play the day's most satisfying combination.
Dubov noted he'd finally lived to find himself the oldest player on a team but also remarked that it's a very impressive team. They may take some stopping!
The action continues Sunday, with another four matches, starting with a Carlsen-Nepomniachtchi clash as Alpine APL Pipers take on Ganges Grandmasters.
The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Irina Krush, Sahaj Grover, and Harshit Raja, IMs Tania Sachdev and Sagar Shah, and WGM Keti Tsatsalashvili.

The Tech Mahindra Global Chess League 2026 consists of a six-team double round-robin group stage and a final contested by the top two teams. In each match, all members of a team play with the same color, with four points for a win with Black and three for a win with White. All games have a 20-minute time control, with a two-second increment from move 41.

Colin McGourty

news.title: Carlsen Escapes Vs. Nepomniachtchi As Alpine Pipers Only Team Still Unbeaten
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Magnus Carlsen's Alpine APL Pipers has the only perfect record in the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League after scoring a dramatic win over GM Ian Nepomniachtchi's Ganges Grandmasters. Nepomniachtchi failed to beat
body: GM Magnus Carlsen's Alpine APL Pipers has the only perfect record in the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League after scoring a dramatic win over GM Ian Nepomniachtchi's Ganges Grandmasters. Nepomniachtchi failed to beat the world number-one with a two-pawn advantage, but his luck turned when GM Javokhir Sindarov lost to him on time as the FYERS American Gambits suffered a first loss.

Triveni Continental Kings, the dominant team of the first three editions of the event, remains on zero points from three matches, with CheQ Mumba Masters' GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave winning a crucial icon battle against GM Alireza Firouzja.
Day three starts on Monday, September 7, at 6 a.m. ET / 12:00 CEST / 3:30 p.m. IST.

FYERS American Gambits still tops the table, but has been caught by Ganges Grandmasters and Alpine APL Pipers—Carlsen's Pipers has played one fewer match, so will start day three with a chance to take the sole lead.
Carlsen arrived later than the rest of his team for a clash with Nepomniachtchi, whom he defeated in the 2021 World Championship Match.
The frenetic pace was kept up on the board when the world number-one went for an opening that probably requires a "don't try this at home" label.
It brought only suffering, as Nepomniachtchi calmly simplified to a position where he was completely dominant, with more time and more material.

It looked as though the game would decide the match, but things happened both at that board and elsewhere. Carlsen escaped, then slipped back into trouble, then finally survived when the outcome of the game was no longer critical. Nepomniachtchi blundered into a known draw.

That meant a "comfortable" match win for the Pipers, but it had really been anything but. IM Polina Shuvalova convincingly beat GM Divya Deshmukh, GM Levon Aronian made GM Anish Giri suffer before they drew, and GM Leinier Dominguez was somewhat better against GM Vidit Gujrathi before he hit the self-destruct button with 38.Nf6??.

Vidit's miracle let the team breathe easily, though GM Koneru Humpy was the hero. She won the player of the match award after dominating out of the opening against IM Stavroula Tsolakidou. 10.Bg5? is the moment Humpy knew she was clearly better.
So Alpine APL Pipers has a perfect score, but the team knows they'll need to play better to keep up such a record.
This was a match between two teams that had lost on the first day, and in the end it was GM Viswanathan Anand's PBG Alaskan Knights that got off the mark.

The one win for the Mumba Masters was perhaps a surprise, since it came for GM Shakhriyar Mamedyarov against the player he's mentoring into the world elite, 15-year-old GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus. They've often made quick draws in events during their collaboration, but this time, in a team event, they engaged in an all-out struggle. Erdogmus was winning at one point, but when his sacrificial attack fizzled out, Mamedyarov managed to consolidate and grab a four-point win. Erdogmus didn't hide his emotions.
That was the one black win, however, with some spectacular chess on the other boards as the Alaskan Knights racked up three wins. GM Arjun Erigaisi got to sacrifice his queen...
...but there was compensation for the move of the match from GM Nino Batsiashvili, who wrapped things up against IM Carissa Yip with the sumptuous 28.Ne7!!, ignoring the attack on her rook.
GM Abhimanyu Mishra wrapped up victory by squeezing out a win over GM Bardiya Daneshvar on the prodigy board.

The FYERS American Gambits team had looked very impressive in scoring two wins on the first day, and for much of this match they looked sure to pick up another win. Shuvalova again starred for the Ganges Grandmasters, picking up her third win in three games, but elsewhere four-point wins with the black pieces looked on the cards.

GM Nihal Sarin did wrap up victory, even if he gave Aronian chances to escape, but GM Daniil Dubov missed a tricky win over Dominguez, while Sindarov not only spoiled a winning position against Nepomniachtchi, but lost on time while pushing for a win in a game where a draw would have clinched match victory for his team.

The final match of the day was another painful loss for the Triveni Continental Kings, the team that dominated the group stage in 2025 with a similar lineup, and which won the first two editions of the Global Chess League. Firouzja had also been the dominant player, winning his first five games in 2025, but this year he'd made two draws before falling to a loss against his French rival Vachier-Lagrave.

Firouzja played his opponent's beloved Najdorf, but it didn't go well, with Vachier-Lagrave summing up as he received the player of the match award, "Today I calculated a little bit better!" That's our Game of the Day, which GM Dejan Bojkov has analyzed below.
The tone for the match was also set by a blunder, 16.Nxf7!, by GM Aravindh Chithambaram, which was punished by Mamedyarov.
The chances for Aravindh to survive such a position against an attacking legend such as Mamedyarov were small, but the Indian put up enough resistance to force a beautiful finish!

GM Alexandra Kosteniuk's win over the struggling Yip gave Triveni hope, but GM Harika Dronavalli's win over GM Zhu Jiner meant the match was over before GM Pranav Venkatesh added a consolation win on the bottom board.

Day three of the event will begin with a clash between the two teams that have played a match less—Anand's PBG Alaskan Knights and Carlsen's Alpine APL Pipers, with both teams then also playing again. We should get Carlsen-Sindarov in the third match of the day, before Anand-Firouzja will feature as Triveni seeks to get off the mark.
The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Irina Krush, Sahaj Grover, and Harshit Raja, IMs Tania Sachdev and Sagar Shah, and WGM Keti Tsatsalashvili.

The Tech Mahindra Global Chess League 2026 consists of a six-team double round-robin group stage and a final contested by the top two teams. In each match, all members of a team play with the same color, with four points for a win with Black and three for a win with White. All games have a 20-minute time control, with a two-second increment from move 41.

news.title: How To Watch The FIDE Presidential Debate On September 9
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: On September 9, Chess.com is hosting the first live FIDE presidential debate of this election. The three candidates—Jan Henric Buettner, Wadim Rosenstein, and Timur Turlov—will join to discuss their visions for the futur
body: On September 9, Chess.com is hosting the first live FIDE presidential debate of this election. The three candidates—Jan Henric Buettner, Wadim Rosenstein, and Timur Turlov—will join to discuss their visions for the future of chess.

You can watch the debate, moderated by GM Maurice Ashley, on Chess.com's Twitch and YouTube channels. The debate starts on September 9 at 10 a.m. ET / 16:00 CEST / 7:30 p.m. IST and is expected to last about 90 minutes.

FIDE holds presidential elections every four years. The FIDE president is not elected by popular vote but rather by FIDE's national member federations at the General Assembly. Each eligible federation receives one vote, regardless of its size, strength, or other factors. Voting is anonymous.

Candidates don't run for president alone—they must form a joint ticket with a candidate for deputy president. The presidential and deputy presidential candidates on a ticket cannot represent the same federation.
Three valid tickets are in the running for this election, scheduled for September 26 during the FIDE Congress in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. They are:

A ticket wins if it has at least 50% plus one of the votes cast, with abstentions not counting toward the majority calculation. Because three tickets are running, it's possible that no ticket achieves that vote count in the first round of voting. If so, the two tickets with the most votes go to another round of voting. If there's a tie at any relevant stage, the tied tickets go to another round of voting until one of them pulls ahead.

For the election to be valid, at least 50% of all eligible federations must be represented at the General Assembly. With a provisional count of 202 eligible federations (Russia and Rwanda are currently suspended), at least 101 must be present in Samarkand. FIDE will publish the definitive number of eligible federations on September 14.
You can learn more about each candidate running for FIDE president below. The information below comes primarily from each candidate's FIDE profile.

Buettner was born in 1964 in Hamburg, Germany. An entrepreneur and investor, he built his career in telecommunications, internet technology, venture capital, hospitality, and sports. Along with GM Magnus Carlsen, he co-founded the Freestyle Chess franchise.
His platform emphasizes commercial development, sponsorships, media revenue, financial sustainability, transparency, and directing more resources toward national federations.
His running mate is Malcolm Pein, a prominent English chess organizer, journalist, and founder of the London Chess Classic, as well as the Chess in Schools and Communities charity.

Rosenstein was born in 1990 in the Zhytomyr region of Ukraine, spent time in Russia, then moved to Germany in 2000, and currently holds German citizenship. An entrepreneur, he is the chairman of WR Group Holding. In chess, Rosenstein has founded WR Chess, through which he has organized or supported the WR Chess Masters, WR Chess Juniors, the WR Women's Chess Tour, and the FIDE World Team Rapid and Blitz Championship. He is also listed as the German Chess Federation's FIDE delegate.
His campaign centers on modernizing FIDE, strengthening its commercial operations, adopting more professional management, and improving responsiveness to member federations.
His running mate is Gordon Tang, the executive vice president of the Olympic Council of Asia and founder of the Asian Mind Sports Association.

Turlov was born in 1987 in Moscow, Russia, moved to Kazakhstan in 2011, and renounced his Russian citizenship in 2022. An entrepreneur and financier, he is the founder and CEO of Freedom Holding Corp. Turlov has served as president of the Kazakhstan Chess Federation since 2023 and president of the International School Chess Federation since 2025.

His campaign presents him as a technology—and business-oriented candidate, focused on digitalization, financial resilience, chess in education, and giving regions outside the traditional chess centers a larger role.
His running mate is five-time World Champion Viswanathan Anand, who became FIDE's deputy president in 2022 and is currently the interim president following Arkady Dvorkovitch's suspension.

news.title: Carlsen's Alpine Pipers Storms Back From Loss To Grab Sole Lead
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Magnus Carlsen flagged GM Viswanathan Anand in the opening match of day three of the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League, but it couldn't stop Alpine APL Pipers tasting its first defeat when GM Vidit Gujrathi also
body: GM Magnus Carlsen flagged GM Viswanathan Anand in the opening match of day three of the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League, but it couldn't stop Alpine APL Pipers tasting its first defeat when GM Vidit Gujrathi also lost on time. Vidit and the team would storm back later, however, to beat FYERS American Gambits 15-3 and take the sole lead on nine points out of a possible 12.
Four teams trail by three points, while Triveni Continental Kings finally got on the scoreboard with wins for GMs Wei Yi, Aravindh Chithambaram, and Alexandra Kosteniuk in the last match of the day.
Day four starts on Tuesday, September 8, at 6 a.m. ET / 12:00 CEST / 3:30 p.m. IST.
All teams have now played four matches, with Alpine APL Pipers the only team to win three. The top-two teams after each has played 10 matches will contest the final match for the title.

The headline clash here was, of course, a repeat of the 2013 and 2014 world championship matches, with Anand taking on Carlsen. The game was tense, with the current world number-one pressing hard with the black pieces but, by his own admission, losing control in time trouble:

I felt like I was outplaying him a little bit in the middlegame. I was really happy with the position from the opening and then later on, and then again I was a little bit shaky with little time and I think for a period there he was defending very, very well, not making it any worse, but then I just obviously resigned myself to a draw and then I randomly glanced at his clock and saw that it was out, which is how it goes sometimes.

Carlsen was briefly winning on the board, but in the end it was Anand who lost on time, somewhat against the run of play, since it had been the Norwegian who got down to seconds while his Indian rival still had time to think.
Carlsen's only win so far in Bengaluru wasn't enough for the team, however, since Vidit also flagged in an equal position, against 15-year-old prodigy GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus.

That enabled GM Nino Batsiashvili to be the hero, turning around a game where she admitted afterward, "After the opening I got no initiative, nothing, and she was playing so well at some point!" GM Koneru Humpy looked on course for a third win in three matches, but one false move, 25...Bb6?, allowed the game-transforming exchange sac 26.Rxc4!!.

The problem for Black is Ne5+, then the threat of Nd7+, forking the king and bishop, if Black takes the f6-pawn. Humpy correctly gave back the exchange instead, and objectively the position was equal, but it was suddenly much harder to play with the black pieces. Batsiashvili went on to win in style.
While that match could easily have gone differently, the next two matches were crushing wins.

The CheQ Mumba Masters team woke up and chose violence for this match. There were first wins of the event for GM Bardiya Daneshvar and IM Carissa Yip, with Yip recovering from losing her first three games. The players who made draws were all better with White, with GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave in particular looking likely to beat an elite grandmaster on the white side of the Sicilian for a second day in a row.

In the end, however, it was GM Pranesh M who did the Sicilian slaying, with his punishment of GM Levon Aronian's optimistic kingside pawn pushes close to perfection. Not bad for a player only taking part as a late replacement for GM Vladimir Fedoseev!
That crushing scoreline is hard to beat, but Alpine Pipers did, since Carlsen's team grabbed their three wins with the black pieces for an extra point each game.
Vidit, when asked about his team's "strategy" of picking Black, responded: "When it works, you can call it a strategy... We thought it would just be fun to play four Blacks in a row!"
The match featured some wild openings, with Carlsen opting for the "mouse-slip" novelty 3...f6?! against the world championship challenger.

He later explained it was indeed born of a mistake, but then got some polishing: "It was originally from my coach [GM Peter Heine Nielsen], it was a misclick, and then he started looking at it, and I kind of like the general idea of taking a random move in the opening and then, with computer analysis, you can make pretty much anything work. The main idea is that after 4...0-0 a6, it’s actually already not terrible."

Carlsen explained he was trying the opposite approach from what he'd done in the Esports World Cup, where he played only openings "I know very, very well." The world number-one confessed, "It’s been a little bit of a mixed bag so far," but it did ultimately lead to winning chances against GM Javokhir Sindarov. They came, however, when time was short, and Carlsen again failed to grind out a win.
Carlsen noted he got those chances because Sindarov needed a win for his team, and was full of praise for his opponent:

Sindarov is very good. He has a very, very good positional understanding and he certainly put a lot of pressure on me earlier in the game... He’s very, very well-rounded and doesn’t have any obvious weaknesses.
He's very, very well-rounded and doesn't have any obvious weaknesses.

In the end, however, that game didn't matter, since Carlsen's team had already wrapped up victory elsewhere. GM Volodar Murzin beat GM Marc'Andria Maurizzi on the prodigy board, Humpy struck back to defeat IM Sara Khadem, and Vidit also redeemed himself with a dramatic win over GM Daniil Dubov.

It was notable for Nihal-Giri on the adjacent board featuring the same line of the Scotch, and also for Vidit falling so far behind on the clock (around 19 minutes to three at one point) that his game looked to be the one where the Alpine Pipers was in most danger. Instead, however, it became the Game of the Day, which GM Dejan Bojkov has analyzed below.
"There were a lot of nerves today!" is how Vidit summed things up.

That win gave Alpine APL Pipers the clear lead, but midway through the day we had the curious situation of five teams leading on six points, while the remaining team, the Triveni Continental Kings, had zero. By the end of the day, however, GM Alireza Firouzja's team would be off the mark.

It wasn't easy. Firouzja has yet to win a game and was lost for a moment toward the end against Anand, while GM Zhu Jiner, who lost just one game in the 2025 edition, has now lost three in four rounds.

This time, however, wins for GM Alexandra Kosteniuk, GM Aravindh Chithambaram, and, above all, a dramatic win for GM Wei Yi against GM Arjun Erigaisi turned the tables. In the kind of wildly complex position that both players enjoy, Arjun picked up a poisoned pawn and never got another chance after 28.Rxd7!!.

Will that be the start of a recovery by Triveni Continental Kings? Well, they face another test as they complete the first half of the event on Tuesday, against leaders Alpine APL Pipers—which means, Carlsen vs. Firouzja!
The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Irina Krush, Sahaj Grover, and Harshit Raja, IMs Tania Sachdev and Sagar Shah, and WGM Keti Tsatsalashvili.

In each match, all members of a team play with the same color, with four points for a win with Black and three for a win with White. All games have a 20-minute time control, with a two-second increment from move 41.

news.title: Master Your Openings With Game Review's New Feature
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: Staying true to your opening repertoire just got easier with Game Review. Whenever you're reviewing a game, your coach will tell you when you've deviated from the lines taught in your Chess.com Courses. With this new Gam
body: Staying true to your opening repertoire just got easier with Game Review. Whenever you're reviewing a game, your coach will tell you when you've deviated from the lines taught in your Chess.com Courses. With this new Game Review feature, you can instantly recognize when you're leaving your repertoire—and get a refresher on what you should've played instead.

When playing a game, it's not uncommon to forget the exact moves you need to play in some lines of the opening—even when you've been studying that opening with Courses. Reviewing the game afterward doesn't always help, either, as it can be hard to remember when you strayed from your course's recommendation.

This is where Game Review's new feature comes in. Instead of relying solely on your memory to pinpoint where you deviated from your opening preparation, your coach will identify those moments for you.
You can then ask your coach to show you the line recommended by your course. Click See Best Moves to view it on the board, or hit Study to jump straight to that line in your course.

This new Game Review feature works with every opening course you own on Chess.com. Don't have any yet? You can start a free one to try out the feature. If you have more than one on the same opening, your coach will check for deviations from the last course you studied.
If you own a course but haven't finished it yet, your coach will still show you deviations. So don't worry if you haven't gone through all the lines—your coach has got your back!
Note that this feature does not work with courses you own exclusively on Chessable. However, you can import your courses from Chessable to Chess.com quickly and for free.

After logging in to your Chessable account, go to its dedicated page for exporting courses. There, you can follow the instructions to connect your Chessable and Chess.com accounts. Click the Add your courses to your Chess.com account button to import your courses.
This request can be made once every hour, so feel free to return to that page later if you buy a Chessable course after syncing.
Have you tried out the new Game Review feature yet? Let us know what you think in the comments below!

news.title: Le Last Leader In Back-And-Forth Titled Tuesday
news.author: nathanielgreen
news.excerpt: The lead wasn't necessarily the ideal place to be in Titled Tuesday on September 8, before GM Liem Le won his first of the year with a 9.5 score, ahead of GM Hikaru Nakamura and IM Tobias Koelle on tiebreaks. For the sec
body: The lead wasn't necessarily the ideal place to be in Titled Tuesday on September 8, before GM Liem Le won his first of the year with a 9.5 score, ahead of GM Hikaru Nakamura and IM Tobias Koelle on tiebreaks. For the second straight week, GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda was the last player with a perfect score, and Nakamura himself held the outright lead entering the final round, but the win went to Le, who recovered from a seventh-round loss and eighth-round draw to go 3/3 after the final break. GM Jeffery Xiong played spoiler, defeating Duda in round 10 and holding Nakamura to a draw in round 11 to finish in sixth place, behind GMs Hans Niemann and Dmitry Andreikin on tiebreaks but ahead of GM Shant Sargsyan.

After 17 players started 4/4, only one reached 7/7. Entering the seventh round, Duda, Nakamura, Le, and Niemann were on 6/6, Le having done so with a 106-move, often tactically tense win over GM Denis Lazavik.

But Le would lose to Duda in the seventh round, while Nakamura and Niemann made a tense draw. The result was a second straight week of Duda being the last perfect player, after he had begun 10/10 last time around. Unfortunately for Duda, he only scored 1.5 points in the last four rounds, finishing in eighth place.

In the eighth round, he made a draw by repetition with Nakamura, missing a clever win chance that GM Robert Hess demonstrated on the commentary board. With this, the perfect score bounty next week moves to an even $4,000, the same as first and second place combined.

With Duda making the draw, GM Parham Maghsoodloo moved into a share of first place, defeating Niemann. Duda would topple Maghsoodloo in the ninth round, putting himself back in the sole lead, but it was the last point he'd win on the day.
Xiong's win with Black over Duda in the 10th allowed Nakamura to move into the sole lead with his own win, also with Black, over Maghsoodloo.
With Nakamura on 9/10, Duda, Xiong, Le, Koelle, and GM David Paravyan were all on 8.5/10. For obvious reasons, Nakamura pushed for victory over Xiong, but could not find it.

Meanwhile, Le vs. Paravyan was a close game decided by a sudden mistake. The move 39...Qf3, by threatening 40...Rb1+ with mate to follow, would have saved Paravyan's c-pawn. Instead, after 39...Qd4??, the game swiftly finished.
The tournament still needed to conclude before the final tiebreaks, which were extremely close, could be decided. One of the last games to finish was Koelle's 111-move marathon victory against Duda.
With all games finished, Le's tiebreak just beat out Nakamura's score, as Koelle placed third.
*Bounty grows by $250 per week without a perfect score, and resets once a perfect score has been achieved.
These winners are announced by Thursday each week. If you would like to nominate a game or a move (including your own) in this or future weeks, click here!
Titled Tuesday is Chess.com's weekly tournament for titled players. It begins at 11:00 a.m. Eastern Time/17:00 Central European/20:30 Indian Standard Time.
