news.title: All Teams Still In Fight As Global Chess League Crosses Halfway
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Alireza Firouzja's Triveni Continental Kings continued their comeback by beating the leaders, GM Magnus Carlsen's Alpine APL Pipers, as the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League crossed the halfway mark with no teams
body: GM Alireza Firouzja's Triveni Continental Kings continued their comeback by beating the leaders, GM Magnus Carlsen's Alpine APL Pipers, as the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League crossed the halfway mark with no teams breaking clear of the pack.

It was a painful day for the PBG Alaskan Knights, with GM Viswanathan Anand losing to GMs Ian Nepomniachtchi and Javokhir Sindarov on top board, while GM Abhimanyu Mishra misplaced pieces in a winning position against GM Leon Luke Mendonca. The world's youngest ever grandmaster had two seconds removed from his clock, and couldn't queen a pawn in the single second remaining.
Day five starts on Wednesday, September 9, at 6 a.m. ET / 12:00 CEST / 3:30 p.m. IST.

We hit the halfway mark of the group stage with three teams on nine points, before FYERS American Gambits won the first match of the second half to join them. PBG Alaskan Knights is the other team to have played an extra match, so that effectively it's in last place despite having more game points than Triveni Continental Kings.

If you needed a sign that this might not be PBG Alaskan Knights' day it came early on, as five-time World Champion Anand went astray with 22...g6?? and had to resign after 23.Nc6!, winning a lot of material.
The match was wild, with decisive games on every board, but it was ultimately decided in the cruelest possible way—from the PBG Alaskan Knights' perspective.
On the prodigy board, a level position suddenly swung in Mishra's favor, and he even got a chance to deliver checkmate-in-four. The trick was not to queen a pawn.

When that was missed Leon got a chance to escape but missed it in turn, and was dead lost when Mishra tried to capture the rook with the pawn, making a queen at the same time. Mishra made the move with one second left on his clock, got two seconds added, but this is where Leon stopped the clock and appealed to the arbiter, since Mishra had put the queen on the wrong square (e1) and still left the rook half on the board.

If Mishra had been able to fix that mess before hitting the clock he might have gone on to win, but as it was, the arbiter removed the added two seconds, leaving a single second in which Mishra had to try and play his move.
It was something the great GM Vasyl Ivanchuk managed in a similar situation in Wijk aan Zee earlier this year...

Mishra had to juggle the pawn, rook, and queen again, which was an almost impossible test of manual dexterity (at this point it could be pointed out there are some advantages to playing on a computer as they do e.g. in the Esports World Cup!). He didn't manage in time, and in fact he still ended up with the queen on the wrong square.

It's hard to imagine a crueler way to lose a game with the fate of your team on the line (a win for Black would have given the Alaskan Knights victory), and it was no surprise that Mishra later went on to lose his second game of the day as well.
We got a moment of similar drama in the second match of the day, when GM Pranesh M, in a completely winning position, allowed GM Nihal Sarin to pounce with mate-in-one.

In this case, however, the individual drama made no difference to a convincing win for CheQ Mumba Masters, its third in a row after starting with two defeats. GM Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and IM Carissa Yip were the heroes.

Alpine APL Pipers had chosen a curious strategy for the tournament of picking the black pieces whenever they won the toss in a match. Their opponents were also happy to have White, so that the team has begun with five Blacks and will have White in every match in the second half. It was a strategy that was working, but it didn't on day four, as comeback kids Triveni Continental Kings won a second match in a row after losing their first three matches.

"Today it was like a final!" said their captain GM Loek van Wely, and if anything the team could have won by a bigger margin. Firouzja had moments when he was close to winning against Carlsen, GM Wei Yi missed a chance vs. GM Anish Giri, and GM Alexandra Kosteniuk was also winning in the endgame after earlier surviving a fierce attack by GM Koneru Humpy. The wins were convincing, with GM Pranav Venkatesh taking down GM Volodar Murzin, while GM Aravindh Chithambaram played 1.Nc3 on the way to beating star-performer GM Vidit Gujrathi.

Aravindh revealed he'd chosen the move after a discussion with Firouzja, who quipped: "I decided to choose the other knight, but maybe I should have kept the plan!" The opening was highly complicated and double-edged, but eventually Black's position collapsed.

Triveni Continental Kings is well within striking distance of a third final in three seasons, while Carlsen's team, which started the day with a three-point lead, had been caught by both the Ganges Grandmasters and CheQ Mumba Masters. The day would end with another team joining that pack.

Once again we got a match with no draws, and there was drama wherever you looked. For instance, 15-year-old GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus has had a tough event, suffering three losses, but he got to pull off one of the moves of the day to dispatch GM Daniil Dubov.

We also got a fantastic battle between GM Arjun Erigaisi and Nihal, whose swindling abilities and tactical awareness were visible in a wild rollercoaster of a game. Arjun won the opening battle, but walked into a tactical trick, looked set to lose without a fight, but then had brief winning chances in an endgame with a bishop for four pawns, before Nihal's pawns ultimately won the day.

You can argue that all boards were decisive, including the top-board clash between Anand and Sindarov. The five-time world champion could have been excused for playing for a draw after his earlier blunder, but Anand showed his fighting spirit as at one point he even declined a draw offer from Sindarov—the challenger to the crown confessed "I was so worried!" as after offering the draw he realized he needed to play for a win for his team.
In the end a great battle ended with Anand overlooking a trick and losing a second game of the day. GM Rafael Leitao analyzes our Game of the Day below.

PBG Alaskan Knights is three points off the lead having played a match more, but with four matches still to play the team still has its destiny in its own hands. That applies even more to all the other teams, with day five beginning with CheQ Mumba Masters vs. Alpine APL Pipers—there are no more coin tosses, since colors are reversed from the first round and we know we'll get Carlsen with White vs. GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave on top board.
The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Irina Krush, Sahaj Grover, and Harshit Raja, IMs Tania Sachdev and Sagar Shah, and WGM Keti Tsatsalashvili.

All games have a 20-minute time control, with a two-second increment from move 41.

news.title: Judit Polgar Hosts Simul Against Chess Community At 12th Global Chess Festival
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: Chess.com is once again partnering with legendary GM Judit Polgar to support her festival, the Judit Polgar Global Chess Festival. Judit will play a community simul on September 26 at 7:30 a.m. ET / 13:30 CEST / 5:00 p.m
body: Chess.com is once again partnering with legendary GM Judit Polgar to support her festival, the Judit Polgar Global Chess Festival. Judit will play a community simul on September 26 at 7:30 a.m. ET / 13:30 CEST / 5:00 p.m. IST. The event will take place at the Hungarian National Gallery and will be broadcast live on our Twitch and YouTube channels.

Judit is universally recognized as the strongest woman chess player of all time. Her story was recently the subject of the hit Netflix documentary Queen of Chess, which made it to the top 10 list of the most popular movies worldwide. Her ascent to the top of the game, along with the political and gender barriers she had to overcome, continues to inspire people everywhere—including those who don't play chess.

Since her retirement, Judit has dedicated herself to using chess to promote children's education. In 2015, she held the first Judit Polgar Global Chess Festival to share the beauty of chess and connect a wide range of chess-related activities. The festival is now in its 12th edition and kicks off on September 26 at 4 a.m. ET / 10:00 CEST / 1:30 p.m. IST. It will feature multiple activities, including a meet-and-greet with Judit, book signing, chess adventure courses, a "Master Relay" simul, and more. Check out the event's official website for the full list of activities.
Judit will play a simul against five players, each representing a different community in the chess world. Meet the five communities and their representatives:
IM Anna Rudolf will be on-site to host the simul's online broadcast. The star creator will provide expert commentary during the games and interview the participants.

Judit will play a clock simul with 110 minutes for each game and a 10-second increment per move. Her opponents will have 50 minutes to play their moves, plus a 10-second increment per move. Fans can watch every move of the games on our Events page.
Tune in to our Twitch and YouTube channels to watch the broadcast of the simul and be a part of this year's Global Chess Festival!

news.title: Sindarov Beats Firouzja To Give American Gambits Lead
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Javokhir Sindarov's second win in a row, this time over GM Alireza Firouzja, took FYERS American Gambits into the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League lead while Triveni Continental Kings slumped to the bottom after
body: GM Javokhir Sindarov's second win in a row, this time over GM Alireza Firouzja, took FYERS American Gambits into the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League lead while Triveni Continental Kings slumped to the bottom after a second loss of the day. The co-leaders, with a match in hand, are Alpine APL Pipers, for whom GM Magnus Carlsen beat GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, and Ganges Grandmasters, led by GM Ian Nepomniachtchi, which was the other team to defeat the Continental Kings.
Day six starts on Thursday, September 10, at 6 a.m. ET / 12:00 CEST / 3:30 p.m. IST.

With just three matches to play, Triveni Continental Kings, a finalist in each of the first three editions, has a mountain to climb after two losses on day five. FYERS American Gambits lead on game points, but Alpine APL Pipers and Ganges Grandmasters are better placed as they still have a match in hand.

After playing Black in their first five matches, Alpine APL Pipers switched to White, and scored a convincing win over CheQ Mumba Masters. GM Anish Giri, who had begun the tournament by losing to GM Pranesh M before making four draws, got revenge with a swashbuckling 27-move win after going for a g4-pawn-lunge on move six. Giri got to sacrifice a piece on g5—twice!

He really provoked me and this sort of attacking plan is something that Magnus played against me many years ago and he beat me there and in today’s game he provoked a weakness first, my opponent made the weakness himself, so it was basically the same thing but much easier. That’s why sometimes your painful experience can help you in future battles.
Sometimes your painful experience can help you in future battles.
Giri said of the prospect of only playing White before the final, "Every match is a big, big struggle, so I think it’s early to celebrate, but definitely looking good at this moment!"

Carlsen, who has defended some very shaky positions with the black pieces in Bengaluru, added to that impression with a convincing win over Vachier-Lagrave. He always had some pressure, everywhere but on the clock, and his French opponent's position suddenly collapsed in the space of a few moves.
GM Volodar Murzin also won on bottom board, so that GM Harika Dronavalli's victory over her countrywoman GM Divya Deshmukh was only a consolation win.

The second match of the day was by far the strangest. Midway through the action, Triveni Continental Kings looked on course to cruise to victory, with winning positions on board two and, at one point or another, on the bottom three boards. Incredibly, however, they would all turn around, with GM Pranav Venkatesh's 24.Rb7? (24.Qxa6+!) one example of all that went wrong.
GM Leon Luke Mendonca's 24...Qd7! was a very cold shower (25.Qxa6 Bxh2+! 26.Kxh2 Qxb7), ending an attack which had looked crushing when 21.Ba6! appeared on the board.
A similar scenario played out on the women's boards as IMs Polina Shuvalova and Stavroula Tsolakidou also turned around lost positions to win.
The icing on the cake for Ganges Grandmasters was GM Levon Aronian swindling GM Wei Yi, whose 36.Qc4? summed up the day for the Continental Kings.

On top board, Nepomniachtchi had taken some risks to play on because his team looked in trouble, but, as he saw the other results fall, no harm was done and he was able to make a draw against Firouzja.

PBG Alaskan Knights had lost both matches the day before and it seemed the team's misery might continue as GM Viswanathan Anand again suffered on top board. For long periods he played well against Vachier-Lagrave, who pushed a pawn to d6 and kept it there for five moves.
Anand even got the upper hand in the complications that followed, but ultimately found himself in a theoretically drawn but tough rook endgame two pawns down, which Vachier-Lagrave went on to win.

In the end, however, that didn't matter, and it was the Mumba Masters' turn to lose two matches in one day. The fate of the match turned on a moment of agony for GM Carissa Yip. She was completely winning, but was down to seconds against GM Nino Batsiashvili and didn't manage to make her final moves before the two-second increment kicked in after move 40.

GM Abhimanyu Mishra said he leveraged that result as he offered a draw by repetition to GM Bardiya Daneshvar. The Iranian grandmaster couldn't accept, given the team situation, and overpressed and lost.

The final match of the day was decided by a single game, though it has to be said that FYERS American Gambits could easily have scored more points. GMs Nihal Sarin, Daniil Dubov, and Marc'Andria Maurizzi were all better or winning, while there were only brief moments of danger for the team on the women's boards.

Sindarov watched it all unfold, tried not to rush, and commented afterward, "Alireza spent too much time to think and missed some tactical tricks." That's our Game of the Day, which GM Rafael Leitao analyzes below.
That was a second win in a row, after three losses in a row, after two wins in a row, for the unpredictable American Gambits, and put the team in first place on game points.

They've played one match more than Alpine APL Pipers and Ganges Grandmasters, so a huge amount will depend on how those teams perform on Thursday as they both play twice, starting with Carlsen vs. Nepomniachtchi in their head-to-head clash. One team could end the day close to qualifying for the final.
The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Irina Krush, Sahaj Grover, and Harshit Raja, IMs Tania Sachdev and Sagar Shah, and WGM Keti Tsatsalashvili.

news.title: Applications Open For $50,000 Naroditsky Fellowship
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: Applications are now open for the inaugural $50,000 Naroditsky Fellowship, which will support elite American junior players with training, travel, and tournament preparation in 2027. The deadline to apply is December 1.
body: Applications are now open for the inaugural $50,000 Naroditsky Fellowship, which will support elite American junior players with training, travel, and tournament preparation in 2027. The deadline to apply is December 1.

The Fellowship is one of two initiatives supported by the Naroditsky Memorial Fund, which has raised more than $1 million since the Charlotte Chess Center Foundation established it in partnership with the Naroditsky family.

The other initiative, the annual Naroditsky Memorial Rapid and Blitz, held its inaugural edition in Charlotte in July. Top grandmasters, chess creators, and fans gathered to honor GM Daniel Naroditsky, with GM Javokhir Sindarov winning both the rapid and blitz events and IM John Bartholomew taking the Creator Invitational with a perfect 9/9 score.
Both initiatives celebrate the legacy of Naroditsky and continue his commitment to chess excellence, education, and the next generation.

"Losing Danya was, and continues to be, heartbreaking for the entire chess community,” said FM Peter Giannatos, Executive Director of the Charlotte Chess Center and Charlotte Chess Center Foundation. "From the very beginning, our mission has been to meet that pain with purpose and honor his memory with positivity."
From the very beginning, our mission has been to meet the pain with purpose and honor his memory with positivity.—Peter Giannatos

Danya dedicated his life to elite excellence, commentary, and education. As a proud recipient of the prestigious Samford Fellowship, he understood firsthand the transformative impact that financial support can have on an ascending player. A fellowship was the natural choice to carry forward his legacy.
Alongside the annual Naroditsky Memorial tournament, this fellowship serves as a lasting force for good, ensuring Danya’s spirit lives on by empowering the next generation of American champions.

Naroditsky, who passed away at the age of 29 in October 2025, left an impact across virtually every part of the chess world. He was an elite player, one of the game’s most popular commentators, and an educator whose streams, videos, books, and lessons helped countless players understand chess more deeply.

The Fellowship was inspired in part by Naroditsky’s own experience as a recipient of the prestigious Samford Chess Fellowship in 2014. The new program will provide another generation of rising young players with financial support that can make a decisive difference during the early stages of a professional career.

The 2027 Fellowship is worth $50,000 and is open to players who are under 20 on the December 1 application deadline. Applicants must reside in the United States and represent the U.S. as their FIDE federation.

Applicants must submit a parent-guided grant overview and roadmap outlining their goals for the Fellowship year. The proposal should include planned international events, coaching objectives, and an overview of how the funding would be used.

Candidates must also submit either a two-to-three-minute video or a brief written statement answering one question: "How has playing chess changed your life, and what does this opportunity mean to your growth?"

Two recommendations are required from coaches, arbiters, or tournament organizers addressing the applicant’s work ethic, sportsmanship, and character. A parent or legal guardian must also co-sign the application.

Recipients will be expected to compete as invited players at the annual Naroditsky Memorial, attend its pre-event dinner, wear official Fellowship apparel during designated appearances, and engage with the U.S. chess community. They must also provide mid-year and annual updates on their progress and use of the funding.
The inaugural Fellows are expected to be announced in late fall or early winter, with the funding scheduled to be distributed in January 2027.
Eligible players and their families can review the complete criteria and register their interest on the official Naroditsky Fellowship page

news.title: Alpine APL Pipers, FYERS American Gambits, Ganges Grandmasters Share 3-Way Lead
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: The FYERS American Gambits, led by GM Javokhir Sindarov, dominated a critical match against the Ganges Grandmasters, led by GM Ian Nepomniachtchi, to join a three-way tie with the Grandmasters and GM Magnus Carlsen's Alp
body: The FYERS American Gambits, led by GM Javokhir Sindarov, dominated a critical match against the Ganges Grandmasters, led by GM Ian Nepomniachtchi, to join a three-way tie with the Grandmasters and GM Magnus Carlsen's Alpine APL Pipers on day six of the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League. Though they lost their second match, GM Levon Aronian of the Ganges Grandmasters was the player of the day as he swindled the Alpine APL Pipers' GM Anish Giri to score a potentially match-deciding four points.
Day seven starts on Friday, September 11, at 7:30 a.m. ET / 13:30 CEST / 5 p.m. IST.

The Triveni Continental Kings have reached the finals in all previous editions, but it won't happen this year as they've scored just six points with two matches left. The top three teams vie for the top two spots that will go to the finals.

The Ganges Grandmasters, with the black pieces, won their first match of the day with two decisive games against the Alpine APL Pipers. It's easy to imagine the match going the other way—Giri had a winning position against Aronian, and lost, while GM Volodar Murzin had a winning rook endgame against GM Leon Luke Mendonca, but only managed to draw.
Had those two games gone in the "correct" direction, IM Stavroula Tsolakidou's win for the Ganges Grandmasters would not have been enough.

The star players were Aronian and "the Greek Goddess" Stavroula (as she was introduced twice), who scored the only wins in the match. The Greek IM explained that the nickname came from an opening file her team's coach sent her.

Aronian's win was the most shocking turnaround of the day, as he had two minor pieces for a rook but was three pawns down. He's a player who often gets "lucky" in bad positions, which is the word he used to describe the win. He said:

Of course I got lucky, very lucky, but I will always believe and try to find the best moves... In a way, I think it was kind of deserved. Not losing the game was deserved, but winning, of course, was huge luck."

Giri managed to win two pawns by move 20, but Aronian never made it easy from there. Under time pressure, the Dutch number-one didn't manage to find a good solution to the American's counterplay on the queenside, and he ultimately sacrificed a piece out of desperation to stop the soon-to-be passed a-pawn.

Tsolakidou, who had lost against GM Humpy Koneru in their previous encounter, got her revenge in their second game. GM Irina Krush praised her 31...e3! as "classy," a pawn sacrifice to clear the diagonal for the bishop and promote the passed pawn.
It was a great start for the Ganges Grandmasters, but they had one more match to play at the end of the day, against the FYERS American Gambits.

The CheQ Mumba Masters extinguished any hopes the Triveni Continental Kings may have had of winning this year's GCL. There were four decisive games, and three of them were won by the Masters—scored by GMs Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, and Bardiya Daneshvar. It was another win for the team with the black pieces.
GM Alexandra Kosteniuk's one win against birthday girl IM Carissa Yip (who turned 23) was not enough to counteract the three black wins scored by the other team.
On the Icon board, GM Alireza Firouzja's winless streak extended to an eighth game, against his countryman, Vachier-Lagrave, who won on the black side of a Grunfeld Defense.

MVL's 14...f5? was objectively a mistake, and likely an in-form Firouzja would have put up a better fight, but the game justified this aggressive pawn thrust. Pretty soon, the white center collapsed, and a loss on the Icon board came quickly for the Triveni Continental Kings.

"It's good," said Vachier-Lagrave, "but the most important is always the team win." Mamedyarov, who repeated the sentiment that the team victory is paramount to any individual result, beat GM Aravindh Chithambaram a second time in the rook endgame when, in time trouble, Aravindh allowed a protected passed f-pawn.

The match was already over, in favor of the CheQ Mumba Masters, but Daneshvar won his game anyway, scoring a potentially critical four points for his team if tiebreaks are necessary. He said it was a comeback: "I also lost two games in a row, so it was important to be in better shape to win this game as well."
The CheQ Mumba Masters are three points behind the leading teams and are the closest trailers.

Bouncing back from their loss in the first match, the Alpine APL Pipers scored three wins, with Carlsen beating GM Viswanathan Anand a second time, Humpy defeating GM Nino Batsiashvili, and Murzin scoring against GM Abhimanyu Mishra. The one win for the PBG Alaskan Knights came from 15-year-old GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus against GM Vidit Gujrathi.

This year's GCL has been tough for India's most influential chess player, Anand, as he has now lost four games in a row. As GM Harshit Raja said in the commentary, "I wouldn't really say that it was Magnus Carlsen who won this game than Vishy Anand losing the game for himself."
I wouldn't really say that it was Magnus Carlsen who won this game than Vishy Anand losing the game for himself.
Just as the game got interesting, with Carlsen having a rook and two pawns for two minor pieces, Anand made a game-losing mistake.
Carlsen said, "Of course, he's had a tough tournament, so it was certainly a game that I was hoping to do some damage in."

Humpy lost to GM Nino Batsiashvili in their first encounter, so it was revenge in the second. She said after the game that her opponent missed 19.e3 and 20.Bf1, which won a pawn, though even after losing the pawn Black had good compensation. In the game, the Georgian grandmaster quickly collapsed.

Finally, Murzin scored the third win. Referring to his first game of the day, which was a draw, he said, "It should be 2/2 today... but I'm happy that I won the second game," one where his opponent went for a desperate piece sacrifice that did not work.

The FYERS American Gambits won the only match they played on Thursday, with four (!) wins, scored by Sindarov (against Nepomniachtchi), GM Daniil Dubov (against GM Leinier Dominguez), GM Bibisara Assaubayeva (against IM Polina Shuvalova), and Maurizzi (against GM Leon Luke Mendonca).
Commentator Krush pointed out that the top individual scorers in the GCL thus far, Shuvalova and GM Nihal Sarin, both lost in this match.

More than any other match, this was a whitewash, with only Aronian winning for the Ganges Grandmasters (against Nihal). Perhaps the most impressive win was Assaubayeva's against the on-fire Shuvalova, a player who came into the round on 6/7, the highest individual score in the event up to that point.
The star move of the game was her 29.Rb7!, an unusual line-blocking move. Having prevented the queen trade, White set up the unstoppable threat of Qxf7—and, oddly, there was nothing Black could do.
This was Assaubayeva's first win in the tournament. Even after this loss, Shuvalova's 6/8 is still the highest individual score.
On the Icon board, Nepomniachtchi collapsed against Sindarov after blundering a pawn, though the players inexplicably shared a laugh earlier in the game.

Dubov beat Dominguez with a thematic pawn break in the IQP position. 15.d5! was so powerful that the computer already suggested Black should give up the exchange, just to win a pawn and slow down the white initiative. Dominguez did play the exchange sacrifice, but it didn't alter the result of the game.
The match was already decided, but Maurizzi sealed it with an emotional finale as Mendonca slammed the clock and the table before resigning.
"What can I say? I'm happy to win like always!" said Sindarov after the match. "We have good chances to qualify for the finals now."

Below, you can see the pairings for Friday's matches. The latter two will be the most important in the fight for the top two spots. You especially won't want to miss match 26, which features the mouthwatering Carlsen vs. Sindarov on the Icon board.
The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Irina Krush, Sahaj Grover, and Harshit Raja, IMs Tania Sachdev and Sagar Shah, and WGM Keti Tsatsalashvili.

The Tech Mahindra Global Chess League 2026 consists of a six-team double round-robin group stage and a final contested by the top two teams. In each match, all members of a team play with the same color, with four points for a win with Black and three for a win with White. All games have a 20-minute time control, with a two-second increment from move 41.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Buettner, Turlov Clash Over Funding In FIDE Presidential Debate
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: FIDE presidential candidates Jan Henric Buettner and Timur Turlov clashed over how the world chess body should be funded—and whether it should continue relying on wealthy benefactors. The third candidate, Wadim Rosenstei
body: FIDE presidential candidates Jan Henric Buettner and Timur Turlov clashed over how the world chess body should be funded—and whether it should continue relying on wealthy benefactors. The third candidate, Wadim Rosenstein, disconnected shortly after his opening statement and did not return.

The Chess. com-hosted debate, moderated by GM Maurice Ashley on Wednesday, came just 17 days before FIDE’s presidential election in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. With Rosenstein absent, Buettner argued for a more commercial, self-sustaining organization, while Turlov defended his role as FIDE’s "financial backstop" and said immediate investment was needed to drive growth.
The two also differed on FIDE’s role in online chess, anti-cheating, and school programs, but found common ground in preserving traditional classical chess while expanding faster formats.
The candidates had not received the questions in advance. You can watch the full debate, which lasted nearly 90 minutes, below:

Rosenstein, who is running alongside businessman Gordon Tang, was the first candidate to deliver his opening statement. However, immediately after doing so, Rosenstein disconnected. Chess.com's team contacted him to rejoin, but the 35-year-old German did not respond or provide any explanation for his departure.

Before his departure, Rosenstein referred to the increasingly bitter campaign, which he said was being presented as a contest “between two candidates,” as well as recent decisions by FIDE’s Electoral Commission.
"Today, this election is presented as a contest between two candidates," he said. "I will not join personal disputes or turn the FIDE election into a political or financial show."
Today, this election is presented as a contest between two candidates.—Wadim Rosenstein
In his closing comment, Rosenstein said he would be accountable to all chess federations and that he would be available 24/7. "I will be there for all of you," he said before disconnecting.
With Rosenstein absent, Buettner and Turlov were left in the two-person debate.

Buettner, the co-founder of Freestyle Chess who is running with IM Malcolm Pein, said in his opening statement that FIDE must end what he called a decades-old system of dependence on wealthy presidents and their financial support.
“My mission is to make FIDE cooperate with everybody and depend on nobody, especially not on its president,” he said.

One of Buettner’s biggest pledges is to bring $50 million in new commercial revenue into chess over four years and distribute 20 percent of FIDE’s revenue, excluding prize funds, to national federations.
He said he raised $27.5 million for the Freestyle Chess tour, and that it was evidence that major commercial investment could be attracted to chess.
"We are not selecting a new king or somebody who takes responsibility and maybe finances stuff out of his own pocket if the sponsors are not coming," Buettner said.
We are not selecting a new king or somebody who takes responsibility and maybe finances stuff out of his own pocket if the sponsors are not coming.—Jan Henric Buettner
He characterized FIDE’s 2025 finances as “a disaster," claiming that its revenue from sponsorship, intellectual-property rights, and brands was zero.
Buettner also questioned a reported loss of approximately €500,000 from currency movements and said around €600,000 allocated to development had not been used.
Turlov rejected the criticism and described himself as FIDE’s “main financial backstop” over the last three years through his Nasdaq-listed company, Freedom Holding.

The Russian-born Kazakh billionaire said he also wanted to diversify FIDE’s income through intellectual-property rights, international sponsors, and partnerships with major technology companies. However, he argued that outside investment could not be guaranteed immediately and that FIDE needed firm financial commitments to plan its development work.
“Great governance is necessary, but not enough to make a federation successful,” Turlov said. “Sometimes someone needs to help push things forward. That’s why I’m offering a backstop.”

Turlov proposed increasing FIDE’s development fund to more than $6 million. He said it would support tournaments, arbiter and coach training, travel for players, federation staff, and marketing and communications programs.
Buettner responded by comparing Turlov’s proposal with the idea of a FIFA or Formula One president personally financing the organization.

"The election is mostly about whether we want to keep the same patronage system as before, or whether we want to have a new system where we make FIDE independent from the individual interests of single persons," he said.
Turlov agreed that long-term dependence on him would not be desirable but questioned whether Buettner’s alternative could immediately work in practice.

"That sounds great, but frankly, with my experience, I just don’t have a big understanding of how that might work in real life," he said. "I truly want to make FIDE sustainable and not dependent on me for a long period of time."
I truly want to make FIDE sustainable and not dependent on me for a long period of time.—Timur Turlov
Another disagreement came when Ashley asked what role FIDE should play in online chess and whether it should compete with commercial platforms.

Turlov described FIDE primarily as a regulator and nonprofit organization. He said it should be capable of organizing online tournaments and establishing standards for online and over-the-board chess, but should cooperate with existing platforms rather than compete directly against them.

"I truly believe that nonprofit organizations and regulators should not be directly engaged in business,” he said. “That never means that we don’t have to make money. We have to make money to be sustainable."

Buettner said he “definitely” disagreed. “FIDE has to be more commercial than before," he said, arguing that it needed to commercialize its leading events and players in the same way other sports use their stars as brand ambassadors.

Turlov maintained that FIDE could increase revenue without becoming a direct commercial operator. He said his administration would seek new sponsors while helping national federations attract support from governments and private companies.
The sharpest direct attack came during a discussion about chess in schools and opportunities for young players.

Buettner argued that developing federations generally suffered from a lack of opportunity rather than talent. He said predictable funding would allow them to organize local rated tournaments, train arbiters and coaches, create pathways for juniors, and reduce the need for expensive international travel.
He then questioned the International School Chess Federation’s recent event in Cape Town, South Africa. Turlov is the organization’s president.
Buettner, who primarily lives in South Africa and attended the event, claimed that 23 people had been flown in from Russia and Kazakhstan to organize the tournament that included 91 unrated players.
"The question really was whether it was for the kids or whether it was for other purposes," Buettner said.

He contrasted the event with the experience of the Panama Chess Federation, whose president, according to Buettner, had repeatedly completed lengthy applications before receiving just $100 from FIDE for a children’s tournament.
Buettner said the examples demonstrated why funding should be allocated according to transparent rules rather than at the discretion of FIDE’s leadership.

Turlov defended the International School Chess Federation’s work, pointing to events in Washington, Cape Town, Armenia, and Almaty, as well as its Smart Move Summit for officials and education ministers.
He said the events had both provided opportunities for children and encouraged governments to introduce chess in schools. “I’m sure that we do that in a very efficient way,” he said.
Turlov also cited Kazakhstan’s school chess program, saying it had been introduced in more than 1,500 schools, with another 1,000 to follow this year.
"It’s great to have 20 percent of some future money," he said in reference to Buettner’s revenue-sharing plan, "but sometimes we need real money today to move forward."
The candidates also shared their approaches to combating cheating in chess, whether online or over the board.

Turlov proposed introducing a biometric identification system using face recognition to ensure that each player could operate only one verified account, similar to identity checks used by banks in Kazakhstan.
He also called for investment in anti-cheating technology that could be made available to national federations, while acknowledging that no security system would ever be completely effective.
Buettner focused on due process, warning that powerful detection tools could create a second integrity problem if players did not know how decisions were reached or how to challenge them.
"Online detection tools are powerful, but no algorithm should become a secret court," he said.

He said players in official competitions should know in advance what evidence could be used, who would make decisions, and how they could respond or appeal. He also called for greater investment in prevention, venue security, education, technology, and trained arbiters.
The two seemed mostly aligned on faster time controls in chess.

Buettner said the classical world championship should remain "the pinnacle of the sport" and retain its traditional long time control. He nevertheless supported experimenting with rapid, blitz, fast classical, Chess960, and team formats elsewhere, in consultation with leading players.
Turlov agreed that FIDE should preserve traditional classical chess while recognizing that the sport was becoming faster.
"Everything is getting faster, whether we want that or not,” he said. “The introduction of fast classical, I think, is beneficial for chess players."
Both agreed that future changes should be made in consultation with the leading players.
In his closing statement, Turlov said his experience, resources, and record showed that he could execute his program.

He pledged to leave FIDE “more powerful, much more independent, much wealthier,” while preserving the achievements of the current administration and making the organization more digital, modern, open, and professional.

Buettner began his final statement with a reference to the absent third candidate. "Wadim dropped out of the race—maybe completely, I don’t know,” he said with a laugh. “It’s very interesting that he disappeared from this debate."

Buettner said he did not need a title, salary, business advantage, or political influence from FIDE. He promised that federations would receive equal treatment regardless of whether they supported him.
"After September 26, there should no longer be three campaigns—or maybe two campaigns right now," he joked. "There should be only one FIDE."

The race was drastically changed in July when Arkady Dvorkovich suspended the exercise of his powers as FIDE President after being sanctioned by the European Union. Anand took over the presidential duties on an interim basis, while Turlov—originally announced as Dvorkovich’s candidate for Deputy President—launched his own presidential bid with Anand as his running mate.

The election will take place at the FIDE General Assembly in Samarkand on September 26. Each member federation represented at the assembly receives one vote, with the winning President and Deputy President elected together for a four-year term ending in 2030.

Tarjei J. Svensen

news.title: Build A Rock-Solid Repertoire Against 1.e4 With GM Wesley So's New Course
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: You can now handle 1.e4 like a super-grandmaster. GM Wesley So has just released Elite 1.e4 e5 - Part 1, his new course built around his personal answer to White's most common opening move, 1.e4. With positional, dependa
body: You can now handle 1.e4 like a super-grandmaster. GM Wesley So has just released Elite 1.e4 e5 - Part 1, his new course built around his personal answer to White's most common opening move, 1.e4. With positional, dependable lines, So will teach you the repertoire he actually trusts in his own games.

You don't need to memorize forcing lines that go 20 moves deep to have a good game with Black against 1.e4. So's course will give you a reliable repertoire with solid structures and clear plans. From move one, So will show you how to shut down White's plans, build a position of strength, and then play for the win.
Do you want to see how a world-class player handles the aggressive 1.e4? Check out So's course below:

So has spent more than a decade among the world's elite. One of the world's most successful players, he has built a resume that includes several national championships, three Sinquefield Cup titles, the inaugural Fischer Random World Championship title, and many other accolades. In 2017, the American even reached the number-two ranking in the world with a peak rating of 2822, making him the fifth-highest-rated player of all time.

Beyond his trophies, So has built a reputation as one of the toughest players in the world to beat. Much of his success comes from disciplined opening preparation and deep positional understanding—two concepts that So brings to this course.

Throughout the course, he covers nearly everything White can try after 1.e4 e5 besides the Ruy Lopez. You will learn how to play lines including the Center Game, the King's Gambit, and the Vienna Game, along with other sidelines, so you're never caught off guard.

The main focus of the course, however, is the Italian Game, one of the most popular openings in chess. With several chapters dedicated to this opening, So will break down all of White's main continuations—whether they go for the aggressive 4.Ng5, the quiet 4.d3, or even the tricky 4.d4.
Staying true to his philosophy on how to play against 1.e4, So's approach remains consistent: fewer forced lines to memorize and more emphasis on the ideas behind each line.
Are you ready to add So's battle-tested 1.e4 e5 lines to your own repertoire? Then check out his Elite 1.e4 e5 - Part 1 course!

news.title: Tiebreaks Decide 3 0 Thursday: Lazavik, Duda, Taher Triumph
news.author: coachjkane
news.excerpt: It was a day of tiebreaks in 3 0 Thursday on September 10. In the first tournament, GM Denis Lazavik surpassed three other players on tiebreaks to take the title for the second straight week. In the second event, GM Jan-
body: It was a day of tiebreaks in 3 0 Thursday on September 10. In the first tournament, GM Denis Lazavik surpassed three other players on tiebreaks to take the title for the second straight week. In the second event, GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda surpassed two others thanks to a better tiebreak score. In the final tournament, IM Yoseph Theolifus Taher only had to beat one player on tiebreaks to take first. The leading score in every event was nine points, indicating a competitive set of tournaments, where no one dominated throughout the day.
For the second week in a row, Lazavik started the first 3 0 Thursday tournament by winning his first seven games. His fourth-round win against GM Bogdan-Daniel Deac demonstrated his good form.

After seven rounds, Lazavik slowed down, scoring two points in his remaining four games. That proved to be barely enough, as he surpassed GM Dmitry Andreikin by just half a point on tiebreaks. The top two finishers played each other in the ninth round, resulting in a very precise draw.

GMs Sina Movahed and Elham Amar also finished on nine points to take third and fourth respectively. WIM Margarita Potapova won the women's prize with 6.5 points, just ahead of IM Meri Arabidze on tiebreaks.

Duda recently won his first 10 games in Titled Tuesday, but a last-round loss dropped him to second place. His luck worked better this week, as he came from behind to take first place on tiebreaks in 3 0 Thursday. After nine rounds, Duda trailed GMs Alexey Sarana and Jeffery Xiong. However, he gained ground in the 10th round when those players drew against each other. Meanwhile, Duda won a complicated game against GM Sergei Zhigalko. White had one surprising tactical opportunity to win the game, but after that one missed chance, Duda took over.
In the final round, GM Fabiano Caruana knocked Sarana out of contention while Duda won a nice game against GM Martyn Kravtsiv.

Those results left Duda, Xiong, and Caruana all on nine points, which was the order they finished on tiebreaks. Sarana, who led going into the final round had to settle for fourth place. Potapova improved on her earlier result, taking the women's prize with 7.5/11, defeating four GMs with blitz ratings over 3000 along the way.

In the third event of the day, Taher took the title, leaving Caruana just short on tiebreaks for the second straight tournament. Taher defeated past 3 0 Thursday winners, GMs Parham Maghsoodloo, Xiong, and Tuan Minh Le along the way. His game against Xiong was short and decisive.
Taher's final round matchup with Minh Le was much more difficult. He was in trouble throughout, but he secured equality and then took advantage of a hanging queen to secure the full point.

That win brought Taher to nine points, surpassing Caruana on tiebreaks. GM Oleksandr Bortnyk took third place, a half point behind the leaders. IM Rose Atwell won the women's prize with seven points, her fifth such prize in the last month.

3 0 Thursday is a set of three weekly Swiss tournaments for verified titled players featuring their favorite time control. Each of the three tournaments is an 11-round Swiss with a 3+0 time control. The combined prize fund is $3,000 every week.
NM Jeremy Kane is the Instructional Content Manager for Chess.com, and the author of several courses in the Starting Out series, Queen’s Gambit Accepted, Trompowsky, and Tarrasch.

news.title: Carlsen Gives Trophy To Vidit As Alpine APL Pipers Lead With Ganges Grandmasters
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Magnus Carlsen's Alpine APL Pipers and GM Ian Nepomniachtchi's Ganges Grandmasters lead the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League after day seven, with just one more match left in the round-robin stage. The Alpine AP
body: GM Magnus Carlsen's Alpine APL Pipers and GM Ian Nepomniachtchi's Ganges Grandmasters lead the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League after day seven, with just one more match left in the round-robin stage. The Alpine APL Pipers won by a thin, two-point margin against the FYERS American Gambits, who started the day in the shared lead. The Ganges Grandmasters, on the other hand, dominated the CheQ Mumba Masters, winning five games and drawing just one.
Day eight starts on Saturday, September 12, at 7:30 a.m. ET / 13:30 CEST / 5 p.m. IST.
The Ganges Grandmasters and Alpine APL Pipers look like the teams most likely to finish in the top two spots and reach the finals. They do, however, need to lock in for one last match on Saturday.

The first match didn't have much impact on the finals, but it was a confidence boost for the Triveni Continental Kings. They are nevertheless tied with the PBG Alaskan Knights in last place, even after this win.

Five of the six games were decisive, with the Triveni Continental Kings winning three games and the PBG Alaskan Knights winning two. The scorers on the winning team were GMs Alexandra Kosteniuk, Zhu Jiner, and Pranav Venkatesh.

GM Alireza Firouzja, who drew GM Viswanathan Anand on the Icon board, said, "I think we have a very good team, it's just a few things that went wrong from the beginning... I'm happy that we won this match at least."

The first win, by Kosteniuk, came suddenly as the innocent move 36...Bf4, intending to trade a pair of minor pieces, lost the game on the spot. Kosteniuk spent one of her two remaining minutes to work out the refutation, and the key was her pawn majority on the queenside.

The former women's world champion admitted she was lost out of the opening, but, "at the end I managed to find a trick and to promote a pawn, which decided the game." Despite the tournament situation, she said, "We take every match as a new match, and we try to do our best."
We take every match as a new match, and we try to do our best.
PBG Alaskan Knights' GM Kateryna Lagno blundered a piece against Zhu, and it was Pranav who scored the final four points.
He said his preparation worked well and that he won what he called a "clean game." Things started to go wrong for GM Abhimanyu Mishra after his opponent created a queenside pawn majority.
The next match featured a direct encounter between two leaders of the tournament.

Carlsen and GM Vidit Gujrathi scored the two wins necessary for the Alpine APL Pipers to win the match, even with GM Divya Deshmukh's loss against GM Bibisara Assaubayeva. The margin really was a single classical win.

On top of the wins, GM Anish Giri's draw against GM Nihal Sarin was also critical for his team's success. The Dutch number-one said that, usually, getting into a mutual time scramble with Nihal is a death sentence. "I was happy that it didn't follow the expected script and I held it," he said, but he also pointed to Vidit's win as the most important win of the day.
Carlsen was the first to win, in the much-anticipated matchup with GM Javokhir Sindarov—a generational clash between a five-time world champion and the next world championship challenger.

Carlsen said: "Much like the team, he put up a good fight, but I was able to kind of wiggle myself out of it and find some good moves to win." After allowing his pawns to be doubled on the e-file in the Ruy Lopez, opening the f-file, Carlsen won with a convincing kingside attack.
That's our Game of the Day, which GM Dejan Bojkov analyzes below.
Carlsen received the Player of the Match award, but he gave it to Vidit, the player who truly deserved it, in his opinion.

Vidit was the last player to win, and indeed it was a must-win game. GM Daniil Dubov had two pawns for a piece and objective drawing chances, but the position was too difficult to hold given the time control. Still, the 51...f3! resource, to trade off all of White's pawns, is an instructive tactic for readers. Vidit went on to convert the advantage routinely.

Vidit said after the game: "There are no expectations when you are at home, but when you have to play the next day you start expecting from yourself... You don't want to let your team down, so you start putting in the work."
You don't want to let your team down, so you start putting in the work.

The Ganges Grandmasters nearly won on every board in this match, and the only draw was IM Polina Shuvalova vs. GM Harika Dronavalli. With this match loss, the CheQ Mumba Masters aren't going to finish in the top two, but they can still play in the match for third place.

On the Icon board, Nepomniachtchi outplayed GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave in the Four Knights Sicilian, while GM Levon Aronian beat GM Pranesh M after finding the following tactic to win a pawn. "I think today's win fortifies my hopes," said Aronian. "I am so proud of everybody. After yesterday's last match, we were in a dangerous situation; I think today we proved that we have serious intentions for this league."

GM Leinier Dominguez won an endgame with bishop vs. knight (plus one pair of rooks) against GM Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, but the move of the day undoubtedly went to IM Stavroula Tsolakidou. She played many good moves against IM Carissa Yip, but the  stunner 26.Be6!! was certainly the prettiest.
Like Carlsen, Tsolakidou did not accept her trophy and, instead, presented it to her team captain, GM Adhiban "the Beast" Baskaran.
Although it was far from necessary to win the match, GM Leon Luke Mendonca won the final game against GM Bardiya Daneshvar.

It was a near-sweep by the Ganges Grandmasters. The Icon, Nepomniachtchi, said, "Yesterday we had a very mixed experience, from beating arguably the main rival to losing to another one. I'm just speechless. It was far ahead of any expectations."

After Saturday's three matches, we will know which teams will fight in the first-place match and third-place match. The first two matches on Saturday, of course, will be the most important for the top two spots.
The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Irina Krush, Sahaj Grover, and Harshit Raja, IMs Tania Sachdev and Sagar Shah, and WGM Keti Tsatsalashvili.

All games have a 20-minute time control, with a two-second increment from move 41.

news.title: Topalov Leads Kasparov 2.5-1.5 After Eventful Day
news.author: vsaravanan
news.excerpt: Thirteenth World Champion GM Garry Kasparov found it tough to keep the clock and his nerves in control, as GM Veselin Topalov exploited his opportunities to gain a 2.5-1.5 lead at the end of the first day of the 2026 Clu
body: Thirteenth World Champion GM Garry Kasparov found it tough to keep the clock and his nerves in control, as GM Veselin Topalov exploited his opportunities to gain a 2.5-1.5 lead at the end of the first day of the 2026 Clutch Chess: The Legends, the $144,000 Chess960 match. Though Kasparov held better positions at some points in most of the games, his nemesis was time management and Topalov's resilience.

In the traditional event being held at the Saint Louis Chess Club, the two former world champions provided great entertainment on the first day, playing two rapid games and two blitz games. The match will continue for two more days, with the second day's action continuing on Saturday, September 12, at 12.00 p.m. CDT / 19.00 CEST / 10.30 p.m. IST.

The protagonists have a curious history of encounters in classical chess. While one of the best victories of Kasparov's career was against Topalov in their 1999 Hoogovens Wijk aan Zee encounter, Topalov defeated Kasparov in the last professional game of the latter's career in Linares 2005.
In the Chess960 format, Topalov had defeated Kasparov with a score of 14.5-11.5 in their previous 960 Champions Showdown match at St. Louis in 2018.
Position number 742 of Chess960 was the pick for the day, which can lead to a near-equal starting position in regular classical chess, except for the placement of the queens and kings.

Just as in classical chess, it is possible to develop both knights to their ideal squares (c3 and f3 for White and c6 and f6 for Black) while the bishops and rooks are already in their regular starting positions. In this position, the queens are misplaced at g1 and g8.

With White, Topalov preferred unorthodox squares for all his pieces in the beginning—knights to d3 and e3, while his bishops looked relatively smothered. Kasparov played all natural moves possible from the setup—knights on c6 and f6, and both bishops ready to be fianchettoed.

But what made the game exciting from the beginning was Topalov's early 5.g4 and 7.g5. His desire to play actively, looking for dynamic attacking chances from the beginning, was commendable and provided ample entertainment.

With 13.h4, Topalov gave up his f4-pawn but missed a tactic to gain it back, blundering it away with 14.Rg1?, thus ending up a pawn down. It looked like the day had started very well for Kasparov, but he consumed copious amounts of time, eventually getting into pressure and trailing his opponent by more than five minutes on the clock. This ultimately proved to be his undoing, as he blundered away his crucial passed pawn on the f-file when he had less than two minutes on his clock.
Kasparov was obviously dejected with the result and was seen muttering to himself as he resigned and walked out of the tournament hall.

This looked like a comparatively quiet encounter until Kasparov decided to sacrifice a pawn for activity while just nearing the endgame. But he seemed to get into trouble in an endgame with rooks and bishops of opposite colors, especially when having less than a minute on his clock. However, Topalov missed his chance and allowed the game to end in a draw.

This game was a heartbreak for Kasparov. He played impressively in the opening phase and got an early edge with the decision 4...Bxe3! that saddled White with doubled pawns in the middle of the board. But he misplayed his position in the middlegame and had to resign after impulsively touching the d7-pawn on the 22nd move. This exciting game is our Game of the Day, which has been analyzed by GM Dejan Bojkov.

Kasparov looked distraught as he sat waiting at the board for the game to begin. It was definitely difficult for the former world champion, as he had lost two games in the match by this point in spite of having the upper hand. However, he recovered to win the fourth game.
You can rewatch the day's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated events page.
The broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan and Maurice Ashley and James "Dash" Patterson.

The Saint Louis Chess Club continues with the traditional Clutch Chess Legends from September 11 to 13, featuring former world champions Garry Kasparov and Veselin Topalov. The format is Chess960 (Fischer Random) over six 25+10 rapid and six 5+3 blitz games for $144,000, with escalating points and bonus prize money—a win worth one point on day one (and a $1,000 bonus), two points on day two ($2,000), and three points on day three ($3,000), and drawn games getting their prize money rolled over until the last two games.

news.title: Carlsen To Play Nepomniachtchi In Final After Both Leaders Lose Last Match
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: GM Magnus Carlsen's Alpine APL Pipers will play GM Ian Nepomniachtchi's Ganges Grandmasters in this year's title match at the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League. In a rare outcome for a chess tournament, both leaders
body: GM Magnus Carlsen's Alpine APL Pipers will play GM Ian Nepomniachtchi's Ganges Grandmasters in this year's title match at the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League. In a rare outcome for a chess tournament, both leaders lost on the final day but still qualified for the two top spots of the round-robin stage.
GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave's CheQ Mumba Masters defeated GM Javokhir Sindarov's FYERS American Gambits, but they'll play again on Sunday in the match for third place.
The tournament concludes on Sunday, September 13, starting at 6:00 a.m. ET / 12:00 CEST / 3:30 p.m. IST.

Even with losses, the earlier achievements of the Ganges Grandmasters and Alpine APL Pipers carried them through to the finals. Curiously, the three bottom teams won Saturday's matches, and only the CheQ Mumba Masters finished in the top four.

GM Irina Krush compared the final day of the round-robin stage to the last round of the 2013 Candidates, where both leaders lost. In an amazing turn of events, Carlsen won that Candidates Tournament and went on to claim his world championship title later that year.

With two black wins, the Triveni Continental Kings won the first match of the day. On the Icon board, GM Alireza Firouzja delivered Carlsen's first individual loss, and GM Aravindh Chithambaram scored the other win against GM Vidit Gujrathi. GM Volodar Murzin scored the only win for the Alpine APL Pipers against GM Pranav Venkatesh.

The standout result was, of course, Firouzja's win against the world number-one. It was a double-edged Grunfeld Defense where the Norwegian grandmaster made concessions with his pawn structure, as well as king safety, in order to generate a flank attack with h4-h5. Firouzja's counterattack in the center was faster, and Carlsen collapsed after losing a pawn on move 28.

Aravindh scored the other critical win against his countryman Vidit. Aravindh said that after White's 22.Ng4, he navigated the complications well, even if he didn't find the best moves. Much later, the tricky 26.Nf4!? was the game-winner as Aravindh sacrificed a piece for a direct assault on the king.

It's a strong finish for the Triveni Continental Kings, even if they won't make it onto the podium this year. GM Alexandra Kosteniuk, who drew GM Humpy Koneru, said: "If everything goes well, if you keep on winning, then it's easy, but real champions, I think, are determined by the way you proceed in very hard situations, and I'm very proud of the team that we managed to end the qualification stage with a win."
Real champions, I think, are determined by the way you proceed in very hard situations.

The other leader, the Ganges Grandmasters, also lost their match. The winners for the PBG Alaskan Knights were GM Abhimanyu Mishra (against GM Leon Luke Mendonca) and GM Yagiz Erdogmus (against GM Leinier Dominguez)—and IM Stavroula Tsolakidou inflicted their only loss (against GM Nino Batsiashvili).
Mishra said after the match: "I believe whatever happened in the last 10 seconds in the match is karma for what happened the first match! It was really nice to see justice being served."

It was a dominant win for White in the French Defense, and Mishra highlighted one piece: the knight on d6. He said that the piece reminded him of GM Garry Kasparov's "octopus knight" on d3 against GM Anatoly Karpov, likely alluding to game 16 of their 1985 World Championship match. The kids know their classics!
The other win was dramatic, as Dominguez lost on time after sending his pieces flying in the time scramble without increment.
Erdogmus explained, "I thought I should beat him because I have much more practice than him, and I also like playing fast chess. It was good content for the watchers, yeah!"
The team's Icon, GM Viswanathan Anand, said of the youngsters: "Both their wins, it looked really chaotic at one point, but somehow they always pull it off!"
Even with the loss, the Ganges Grandmasters finished tied for first, and the PBG Alaskan Knights tied last with the Triveni Continental Kings.

With four decisive games out of six, the CheQ Mumba Masters won the match to finish fourth overall. GM Pranesh M, IM Carissa Yip, and GM Bardiya Daneshvar scored three wins, while they dropped just one loss on the Icon board.

Vachier-Lagrave, the CheQ Mumba Masters Icon, was happy to see the rest of his team pick up three wins as he himself lost an admittedly great game against Sindarov. He said, "My team delivered, and Javokhir delivered; he played an amazing game, so credit to him, but the most important thing is we won it."

In a Catalan Opening (yes, MVL playing the white pieces!), Sindarov equalized with the liberating pawn break 11...c5, finding a temporary pawn sacrifice to push the move through. Several turns later, with the queenside majority, he found another pawn sacrifice, and this one was decisive; the c-pawn decided the game.
Yip defeated IM Sara Khadem, even though Black could have objectively held the pawn-down ending.

Daneshvar, on the other hand, won thanks to a blunder by GM Marc'Andria Maurizzi. 24...Bxe4?? lost a whole piece, since White had the in-between move 25.Nxd6. That was, in fact, the last move of the game.

Pranesh won the last game, against GM Nihal Sarin. Though he was better on the board, time was the most important factor, as without an increment, Nihal could not make his moves in time. Pranesh happily pointed out that he had a winning position in their previous encounter but lost on time, so this one was payback!
On the final day, we will see two matches. Each of those will be a best-of-two, starting with the match for third place. You won't want to miss them!
The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Irina Krush, Sahaj Grover, and Harshit Raja, IMs Tania Sachdev and Sagar Shah, and WGM Keti Tsatsalashvili.

news.title: Topalov Builds Solid Lead Over Kasparov
news.author: vsaravanan
news.excerpt: GM Veselin Topalov won both blitz games to take a five-point lead over GM Garry Kasparov at the end of the second day of the 2026 Clutch Chess: The Legends Chess960 match. Topalov leads the match with a score of 8.5-3.5.
body: GM Veselin Topalov won both blitz games to take a five-point lead over GM Garry Kasparov at the end of the second day of the 2026 Clutch Chess: The Legends Chess960 match. Topalov leads the match with a score of 8.5-3.5.

Kasparov failed to convert a huge advantage in the fifth game and suffered defeats in the final two blitz games. He now faces an uphill challenge on the final day to mount a comeback. With the escalating-point scoring system in the four remaining games, 12 more points are at stake. Kasparov needs to score at least two more wins on the final day to turn the match around.
The match concludes on the third and final day on Sunday, September 13, at 12.00 p.m. CDT / 19.00 CEST / 10.30 p.m. IST.
Position number 668 of Chess960 was the pick for the day, which is an awkward setup except perhaps for the bishops and the rooks.

At first glance, it is clear that a king cannot castle on either side of the board without disturbing at least one pawn in front of it after castling. The queens are languishing on the edge of the board, a place where they would otherwise never be moved in a classical game. The knights also have difficulty reaching their usual developing squares.

The position is relatively kinder to the bishops, which can influence the center of the board more easily. Rooks are, of course, fine, as one of them is already in the center, and the other sits on its traditional square in the corner.
Kasparov seemed to play actively from the beginning of the game; 8.a6! was his seventh pawn move in the first eight moves, which created a permanent light-square weakness in Black's position.
By move 18, Kasparov had a clear advantage. However, he had just about two minutes left on the clock to Topalov's eight by the 19th move, which proved to be his undoing.
With just a minute on the clock, Kasparov could not find 25.Qa3!, which would have given him the much-needed final breakthrough in the game.

After the game liquidated into an endgame, in spite of having a rook and knight against the traditionally stronger rook and bishop, Kasparov continued to press for a win. However, he lost his way in mutual time pressure. Although Topalov gained a considerable advantage, he misplayed the endgame to allow Kasparov to escape with a draw.

Familiarity with the position from the two rapid games helped both players, and they moved their pieces confidently from the beginning. With 12...Nca4!, Topalov took over the initiative, moving his knights boldly toward the white king.

In response, Kasparov decided on a radical exchange sacrifice, adventurously moving his rook toward the queenside. However, Topalov found the fantastic piece sacrifice 14...Nxc3! which effectively sealed the game in his favor.
This excellent win by Topalov is our Game of the Day, analyzed by GM Dejan Bojkov (analysis to be added soon.)
The final game of the day went disastrously wrong for Kasparov. By the fourth move, he was already shaking his head as he seemed to be unhappy with his position.
8.e4? allowed Kasparov a chance to sacrifice a piece with  8...Bxc3!? but he missed it. After the game, he was seen discussing the missed sacrifice with his friend Michael Khodarkovsky.
You can rewatch the day's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated events page.
The broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan and Maurice Ashley, WGM Thalia Cervantes Landeiro, and James "Dash" Patterson.

The format is Chess960 (Fischer Random) over six 25+10 rapid and six 5+3 blitz games for $144,000, with escalating points and bonus prize money—a win worth one point on day one (and a $1,000 bonus), two points on day two ($2,000), and three points on day three ($3,000), and drawn games getting their prize money rolled over until the last two games.

news.title: 🏆 Nepomniachtchi Beats Carlsen, Tsolakidou Clinches For Ganges Grandmasters
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: The Ganges Grandmasters won their maiden title at the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League after defeating the defending champions Alpine APL Pipers in an exhilarating final match. GM Ian Nepomniachtchi turned around a
body: The Ganges Grandmasters won their maiden title at the 2026 Tech Mahindra Global Chess League after defeating the defending champions Alpine APL Pipers in an exhilarating final match. GM Ian Nepomniachtchi turned around a losing position with a bishop sacrifice against GM Magnus Carlsen on the Icon board, while IM Stavroula Tsolakidou delivered the match point against GM Humpy Koneru to win the match with a game to spare.
Losing just one game out of 12, GM Javokhir Sindarov's FYERS American Gambits won the third-place match against GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave's CheQ Mumba Masters by three points.
The Ganges Grandmasters won by two points, while the FYERS American Gambits won by a margin of three.
The Ganges Grandmasters won the lion's share of the $1 million prize fund.

The two teams played a set of two matches each, one match with the white pieces and another with the black pieces. The last day featured the regular scoring system, with a win worth one point (regardless of color), a draw a half-point, and a loss zero. The time control was unchanged: 20 minutes for the entire game plus a two-second increment starting on move 41.

In both matches, GMs Nihal Sarin and GM Marc'Andria Maurizzi scored the wins. Across all 12 games, GM Harika Dronavalli was the only player to score a point for the CheQ Mumba Masters, against GM Bibisara Assaubayeva.

Both Nihal and Maurizzi lost their last games on Saturday but came back looking to redeem themselves. Maurizzi, after a perfect 2/2 on Sunday, said, "I played a very bad game, so today I wanted to do my best for the team, and I was a bit lucky."

Game one was a Trompowsky Opening gone wrong very early for Maurizzi's opponent, GM Bardiya Daneshvar. By move 14, White's position was so bad that he sacrificed the exchange. Black is better without taking it, but Black is also better if he does take the rook. Maurizzi grabbed on a1, put his central pawns on the dark squares to blunt White's bishop, and converted the material advantage.

Several minutes later, Nihal won the time scramble against GM Pranesh M. On move 28, Pranesh found a nice pawn sacrifice to improve the position of his knight, but his 36.Nxd6? was an instantly losing move that dropped a full piece. White could have alternatively gone into a dead-lost, pawn-down ending, but it would have made no difference.
The FYERS American Gambits sealed the match with another two wins from the same players, not dropping a single loss in the second encounter.
In contrast to the previous games, Nihal won first and clinched the match with a game to spare. Maurizzi won as well, though the match was already decided in favor of the American Gambits.

Nihal's nicely calculated 22.Nxf5! should have been a decisive desperado (it only works because White has 24.Qc4+ two moves later), as it allowed White to reach a pawn-up endgame, but Pranesh fought his way back into the game. Even if he could have objectively held, Pranesh's weak king position was untenable given the time control.

The match was already decided, but Maurizzi ended it in style by using his king as an attacking piece. 50.Kh5! is the culmination of a king walk up the board—perhaps not as impressive as GM Nigel Short's immortal example in 1991 but still reminiscent of it—and the black king is hopelessly exposed.

The win was a comeback from their loss on Saturday, and Nihal said, "We were definitely unlucky, but also it was not a complete accident. It happens with the pressure, and they completely deserve it." In the end, the FYERS American Gambits had the last word.
There were two decisive games in the first match, with GM Levon Aronian scoring the win for the Ganges Grandmasters, but GM Volodar Murzin also winning to tie the score.

Aronian started with the London System, and the game exploded as both players left their rooks hanging on the a-file by move 23. Going into this variation, Aronian had to foresee a tactical line that ended with 28.Rc1—otherwise, White would be lost. Although the position was still even, GM Anish Giri had just one minute against nine and collapsed when White activated his king in the center.

With all the other games ending in draws, the one game left was GM Leon Luke Mendonca vs. GM Volodar Murzin. The Ganges Grandmasters looked likely to make that draw, but under pressure and under the eyes of all the teammates, Mendonca collapsed and dropped two pawns. Murzin saved the day for the Alpine APL Pipers, at least in this first match.

With draws on all other boards, Nepomniachtchi and Tsolakidou brought in the victory for the Ganges Grandmasters. Aronian credited the team coach, GM Adhiban Baskaran, with giving the following advice, highlighting that drawing the first match may have even been better than winning it:

Adhiban said the correct thing. Basically, repeating a thought of Machiavelli, which is very correct. When you are attacking, you don't want to corner your opponent that he has nowhere to go. You have to attack in a way that they are not sure if they should attack or stay solid. And because they made a draw, they were not sure how to fight. Had we won, maybe it wouldn't be so easy.
And because they made a draw, they were not sure how to fight. Had we won, maybe it wouldn't be so easy.

Without a doubt, the Game of the Day is Nepomniachtchi's sparkling win against his 2024 world blitz co-champion Carlsen. He explained that he was "unlucky" as he got tricked by the move order in the opening, and by move 19 Carlsen already planted a rook on d6. It's a beautiful exchange sacrifice, even if it gives no objective advantage.

Five moves later, Carlsen did muster a winning advantage. But his 28.Qxb5? opened the floodgates for counterplay, and Nepomniachtchi found the move of the day, a bishop sacrifice, to turn the tables. He said: "I got insanely lucky, it was my only idea, ...Bxf2, it reminded me of some kid's tournament when you badly hope that the guy will blunder something... and it worked out!"
It reminded me of some kid's tournament when you badly hope that the guy will blunder something... and it worked out!

The entire match hinged on the following board, Humpy vs. Tsolakidou. Twice, the Greek IM had a chance to win on the spot with ...Ne3+, but when she missed it, Humpy's king ran to the queenside. In the time scramble, the Indian actually had a winning position with a pawn up in the heavy-piece endgame, but her unfortunate 44.Kb2?? was the only losing king move. A win for Humpy would have saved the match, but Tsolakidou went on to clinch it after all.

"It's special winning against the defending champions; now we gotta win it ourselves next year!" said Tsolakidou, who also received a bicycle as the prize for best player of the tournament. She doesn't know how to ride a bike, she said, but now she has a reason to learn!
It's special winning against the defending champions; now we gotta win it ourselves next year!

Upon receiving the award, she gave credit to Adhiban, saying that his help in the openings was instrumental to her strong performance in the second half of the event. Tsolakidou said the critical moment of the tournament for her was in game six, where she broke a losing streak with a win over GM Alexandra Kosteniuk, which she followed up with another win over Humpy in game seven. That is when she started believing in herself.
Although she did not score a win on the final day, and instead made two draws, IM Polina Shuvalova deserves to be mentioned as the player with the highest individual score, 7/10.
That's a wrap for the fourth season of the GCL, and the dates for next year's edition are already on the calendar. We look forward to resuming the action on September 3-27, 2027!
