news.title: Blitz Skills Help Topalov Win Match With Big Bonus
news.author: vsaravanan
news.excerpt: GM Veselin Topalov staved off a counterthrust from GM Garry Kasparov by winning both blitz games to win the 2026 Clutch Chess: The Legends Chess960 match at the end of the third and final day. In the final analysis, Topa
body: GM Veselin Topalov staved off a counterthrust from GM Garry Kasparov by winning both blitz games to win the 2026 Clutch Chess: The Legends Chess960 match at the end of the third and final day. In the final analysis, Topalov scored 11-1 in blitz game points alone to prevail with a final score of 16-8.

In addition to the winner's purse of $70,000, he also picked up a substantial bonus on the final day, for a final gain of $90,000. Kasparov picked up the runner-up tab of $50,000 along with $4,000 in accumulated bonuses, for a final kitty of $54,000.

Kasparov put up his bid for a comeback in the match by winning the first rapid game of the day, thus cutting Topalov's lead to 8.5-6.5. After a draw in the next game, the first blitz encounter in game 11 was the decisive game of the day, which went Topalov's way in the final minute of play, allowing him to reach 13 points and win the match with one game still to play.
Position number 089 of Chess960 was the pick for the day, which put most of the pieces in unusual squares, especially the queens.

After the queens, one of the knights had an especially awkward starting square in the corner of the board. Finally, the bishops, being right in the middle of the board, couldn't come out easily to exert pressure on the center.

Things heated up quite early with 5.0-0, when Topalov offered an exchange sacrifice, one of his favorite dynamic devices that he has employed throughout his career. Kasparov took about nine minutes to respond. Though he ultimately prevailed in the game, this moment was significant, showing that Kasparov had difficulties in pacing himself throughout the match; thus, time management was his biggest issue.
Topalov held an advantage for most of the middlegame until he allowed Kasparov to create dangerous counterplay with 24...f4!
After an eventful opening and early middlegame, the crucial turnaround came with Topalov's 24...Rxc5, which gave White a dangerous initiative.
The match moved into top gear at this point with just two more games of blitz left and a two-point lead for Topalov, and all the carried-over bonus prize money from the draws was up for grabs.

14...Na8? was the turning point of the game, as it sent the black knight to the corner of the board, and it wouldn't come back into the game soon. With 17.e4, Topalov seemed to be playing smoothly as he opened up the position for his pieces to get active. But Kasparov fought to equalize the game once again. The critical moment came much later when both players were down to their final minutes on the clock.
This decisive game is our Game of the Day, analyzed by GM Dejan Bojkov.

The final game of the day showed Topalov's smooth handling of the blitz format. He kept control of the game throughout and steadily increased his advantage over Kasparov. After the game Kasparov admitted that he wasn't really fully "interested" in it, and he did not put up the best defense as he succumbed to Topalov's pressure.

Overall, pragmatic handling of the clock seemed to be the main reason for Topalov's win in the match, as he opined in the chat with commentators after his win: "I try to be practical. I am not very good in time scrambles. Garry tries to find the best moves. It is just not practical."
You can rewatch the day's broadcast on the Saint Louis Chess Club YouTube or Twitch channels. The games can also be reviewed from our dedicated events page.
The broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan and Maurice Ashley, WGM Thalia Cervantes Landeiro, and James "Dash" Patterson.

The Saint Louis Chess Club conducted the traditional Clutch Chess Legends from September 11 to 13, featuring former world champions Garry Kasparov and Veselin Topalov. The format was Chess960 (Fischer Random) over six 25+10 rapid and six 5+3 blitz games for $144,000, with escalating points and bonus prize money—a win worth one point on day one (and a $1,000 bonus), two points on day two ($2,000), and three points on day three ($3,000), and drawn games getting their prize money rolled over until the last two games.

news.title: Chess To Be Played At The South Pole In Antarctica’s 1st-Ever FIDE-Rated Tournament
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: No, it’s not an April Fool's. More than six years after Chess.com joked that the pandemic-interrupted FIDE Candidates Tournament 2020 would resume in Antarctica, rated chess really is heading to the world’s coldest conti
body: No, it’s not an April Fool's. More than six years after Chess.com joked that the pandemic-interrupted FIDE Candidates Tournament 2020 would resume in Antarctica, rated chess really is heading to the world’s coldest continent.

The world’s first FIDE-rated chess tournament in Antarctica is set to take place during the upcoming Antarctic summer in a 12-day window in January 2027, with six players representing all six inhabited continents traveling to the ice—and eventually the Geographic South Pole.

The Polar Chess Expedition will feature a rapid tournament played across multiple locations, the organizers told Chess.com. The opening rounds will take place on the Antarctic ice before the event culminates at 90° South, in an attempt to become the southernmost chess tournament ever played.

The six-player field features one player from each inhabited continent, headed by former world championship challenger GM Nigel Short. The 61-year-old Englishman, who currently serves as FIDE’s Director for Chess Development.
"I've won tournaments on six continents. Antarctica is the one still missing," he said.

Aung, who is also one of the six players, became the driving force behind the expedition. He worked with national chess federations across all six continents to assemble the field and turn Short’s idea into a FIDE-rated tournament.
"Nigel had the idea; my job was to make it real. Now it is, and we’re taking it to the end of the earth," he commented.

The tournament has been privately funded by sponsors who have chosen to remain anonymous. Organizers described them as chess enthusiasts interested in promoting the game rather than receiving public recognition for their financial support.

This must be one of the few chess tournaments in history where the exact timetable depends on the weather conditions. The organizers said they are still finalizing the playing locations with the expedition’s logistics company.

Reaching the playing venues will be quite an adventure in itself. The players will fly from Cape Town, South Africa, directly into Antarctica's interior—a journey of just over five-and-a-half hours covering approximately 4,220 kilometers (2,622 miles) across the Southern Ocean.

They will then continue to the Geographic South Pole aboard a Basler BT-67, a small turboprop aircraft designed for remote polar operations. That leg of the journey is expected to take approximately seven-and-a-half hours.

If successful, the organizers will seek recognition as the southernmost chess tournament ever played. They also hope to establish a record as the first competitive chess event to bring players representing all six inhabited continents to the Geographic South Pole.

For the participants, reaching the board may prove more challenging than anything that happens on it. FM Shaun Press, the Oceania representative, noted that the elements could be the toughest opponent of all.
"Chess has taken me to some strange places over the years. This might be the first one where the biggest opponent isn’t across the board; it’s the weather," he said.
Chess has taken me to some strange places over the years. This might be the first one where the biggest opponent isn’t across the board; it’s the weather.—Shaun Press
Every round is set to be broadcast live, while the exact time control, tournament format, and broadcast details have not yet been announced.

news.title: Bullet King Nakamura Takes 66th Bullet Brawl Title
news.author: coachjkane
news.excerpt: GM Hikaru Nakamura emerged as the winner of Bullet Brawl for a record 66th time on Saturday, September 12. It was a dominant performance, with Nakamura's 184 points leaving him 42 points clear of IM Yoseph Theolifus Tahe
body: GM Hikaru Nakamura emerged as the winner of Bullet Brawl for a record 66th time on Saturday, September 12. It was a dominant performance, with Nakamura's 184 points leaving him 42 points clear of IM Yoseph Theolifus Taher in second place. With Nakamura's impressive score, the fight for second was more exciting than the race for first. Behind Taher, five players—GM Sina Movahed, GM Andrew Tang, GM Oleksandr Bortnyk, GM Maarten Solleveld, and IM Reza Mahdavi—all finished within 10 points of second place. WIM Melika Mohammadi took the top women's prize with 91 points.
Bullet Brawl will return on Saturday, September 19, at 12 p.m. ET / 18:00 CEST / 9:30 p.m. IST.

Nakamura had a strong start to the tournament, winning 14 out of his first 15 games. He nearly did even better. His only loss in that span was his fifth game against GM Maarten Solleveld, when he blundered mate in one in an otherwise winning position.
Nakamura responded by winning his next 10 games, including a rematch with Solleveld.
Bortnyk finally ended Nakamura's winning streak with a draw, but Nakamura picked up again with an impressive tactical win against IM Renato Terry in the next game.
Nakamura is a universal player, just as capable of winning a long endgame as a tactical fight. He demonstrated that skill against last week's Bullet Brawl winner, GM Jeffery Xiong.

While Nakamura won the tournament, Taher's 41/54 score was enough to beat the rest of the field. He began the tournament by winning his first 11 games and later won 14 in a row, the longest streak of any player in the event.

Movahed took third place with a score of 48/68. He finished just a point behind Taher, ending with 141 points total. The following game, a crushing win against Terry, demonstrates Movahed's strong play.
How to review games? The games from this week's Bullet Brawl can be found here.

Bullet Brawl is an exciting arena featuring Chess.com's top bullet specialists. It takes place weekly on Saturdays. The format is a two-hour arena with a 1+0 time control; the prize fund is $1,000. Like Titled Tuesday and Arena Kings, Bullet Brawl often features top GMs, including Hikaru Nakamura, Andrew Tang, Tuan Minh Le, and many more!
NM Jeremy Kane is the Instructional Content Manager for Chess.com, and the author of several courses in the Starting Out series, Queen’s Gambit Accepted, Trompowsky, and Tarrasch.

news.title: FIDE Bans Minor For 2 Years After Phone Found Hidden In Shoe
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: The FIDE Ethics & Disciplinary Commission has handed a two-year ban to a minor after he was caught with a mobile phone hidden inside his shoe during a tournament in Slovenia. The phone had the game position open on Chess
body: The FIDE Ethics & Disciplinary Commission has handed a two-year ban to a minor after he was caught with a mobile phone hidden inside his shoe during a tournament in Slovenia. The phone had the game position open on Chess.com.

The five-page decision by the FIDE Ethics & Disciplinary Commission (EDC) is dated April 9 this year, but was published last week. It concerns an incident at the 165-player Ljubljana Chess Festival in Slovenia, held from April 28 to May 4, 2025, that had not previously been made public.
FIDE named the player in its ruling, but Chess.com has chosen not to identify him because he was a minor at the time of the incident.
According to a report by the chief arbiter of the tournament, the phone was discovered during a post-game inspection following the fifth round. The EDC concluded:
The EDC Chamber further finds that [the player] attempted to cheat, as his game position was open on Chess.com.

The chamber ruled that the incident went beyond merely bringing a prohibited electronic device into the playing venue and amounted to attempted cheating under Article 11.7(e) of FIDE’s Ethics and Disciplinary Code.
The case was referred to FIDE’s Fair Play Commission (FPL), which opened an investigation and made several attempts to contact the player and his mother. Neither responded, according to the decision.

After the case reached the EDC, the player was again given an opportunity to answer the allegations, with the notice sent to his mother due to his being a minor. No response was received by the deadline.

When deciding the sanction, the chamber noted several mitigating factors. It was the player's first offense; he had a clean disciplinary record; he was a minor at the time; he had limited experience, no official FIDE title, and a relatively low rating.
The Respondent’s failure to co-operate during the investigation and adjudication process has been taken into account as an aggravating factor.

The player was found guilty of breaching Article 11.7(e) and given a two-year worldwide ban, effective from April 9. The ruling could be appealed to the EDC Appeal Chamber within 21 days of being received by the player. The public decision does not state when it was communicated to the family, and no appeal has been published on the EDC website.

The incident resembles a case involving a Dutch teenager, who received a three-year ban—with one year suspended—after a phone was discovered inside his sock at the HZ University Chess Tournament in Vlissingen in 2024.

In that case, the player initially refused to undergo a scan and later declined to unlock the phone. The EDC found him guilty of cheating and failing to cooperate, despite an earlier Dutch Chess Federation ruling that there was insufficient evidence to prove he had intended to use the device.

news.title: Georgios Makropoulos, Former FIDE Deputy President, Dies At 72
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: IM Georgios Makropoulos, a seven-time Greek chess champion who became one of the most powerful figures in international chess for decades, has passed away at the age of 72.
body: IM Georgios Makropoulos, a seven-time Greek chess champion who became one of the most powerful figures in international chess for decades, has passed away at the age of 72.
The Greek Chess Federation and the International Chess Federation (FIDE) announced his death on Tuesday, September 15.

Born in Thessaloniki in 1953, Makropoulos won the Greek Championship seven times between 1971 and 1985 and received the IM title in 1979. He represented Greece at three Chess Olympiads, twice playing on the first board.

Makropoulos led the Greek Chess Federation from 1982 until 2021 and helped bring the 1984 and 1988 Chess Olympiads to Thessaloniki. He entered FIDE's senior leadership in 1986, later serving as general secretary from 1990 to 1996, deputy president from 1996 to 2015, and acting FIDE president from 2015-2018, when Kirsan Ilyumzhinov stepped down from an active role after being sanctioned. After losing the 2018 presidential election to Arkady Dvorkovich, he returned to FIDE's leadership as an elected vice president in 2022.

At the time of his death, Makropoulos was serving on the FIDE Council. He was one of 18 approved candidates seeking election for four elected vice-president positions at this month's General Assembly in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
“Makropulos was a person, whose absence is immediately noticeable,” FIDE CEO GM Emil Sutovsky wrote on X. “And I find it difficult to grasp he is no more.”

news.title: Sina Movahed Again In Titled Tuesday
news.author: nathanielgreen
news.excerpt: GM Sina Movahed claimed his third Titled Tuesday of the year and fourth of his career on September 15, coming out ahead of GM Vincent Keymer on tiebreaks after both scored 9.5/11. One move of extra tactical foresight in
body: GM Sina Movahed claimed his third Titled Tuesday of the year and fourth of his career on September 15, coming out ahead of GM Vincent Keymer on tiebreaks after both scored 9.5/11. One move of extra tactical foresight in round 10 helped move Movahed ahead of the pack.
In case you missed it, this week's broadcast with GM Robert Hess:

In the first four rounds, several players achieved 4/4 starts, but neither Movahed nor Keymer was among them. Both were stymied in the third round, Movahed making a draw and Keymer dropping his game. GM Zhamsaran Tsydypov was one of the players on 4/4, and he would also go four for his next four. He finished in third place, however, and the perfect score bounty remains intact and moves to $4,250 next week.
By the end of six rounds, only Tsydypov and last week's victor, GM Liem Le, were still perfect. Tsydypov had done so with a sixth-round win over GM Oleksandr Bortnyk.

Le got Tsydypov into some big trouble in the seventh round, but it was Tsydypov who retained the last 100 percent score after Le, pushing toward a win, lost control of the mating track and flagged. By the end of the round, only GM Haik Martirosyan was half a point away from Tsydypov. Movahed made only a draw, making him one of the players a full point behind.

Martirosyan misplayed the opening in his eighth-round encounter with Tsydypov and went on to lose, creating a full-point gap between the lead and second place. Movahed also won in the eighth round, but Keymer made only a draw (against GM Ian Nepomniachtchi, to be fair), putting him 1.5 points out of the lead.

GM Andy Woodward, coming off a dirty flag, got White against Tsydypov in the ninth round and seemed to be cruising, but suddenly allowed a threefold repetition. Tsydypov still held sole first, but now three players moved back within a half-point: Movahed, GM Maxim Matlakov, and IM Tobias Koelle after finding a shot against Le.

With two rounds left, Tsydypov vs. Movahed and Koelle vs. Matlakov were the next key games. Movahed was able to take the sole lead by delivering a loss to Tsydypov, while the other game was drawn. Just moments after Hess demonstrated a key tactic on the broadcast, it nearly happened on the board!

At the same time, Keymer defeated GM Alireza Firouzja to join the tie for second at 8.5/10, with GM Vladislav Artemiev also winning, against Woodward. And so the final round came down to the games Movahed–Artemiev, Matlakov–Tsydypov, and Keymer–Koelle. As Matlakov was winning an exchange and Keymer took a winning edge against Koelle, Movahed had to bail into a draw with a bad time situation despite a pawn-up ending. While Matlakov could not convert his advantage, Keymer did, and moved into a tie for first with Movahed.

It wasn't enough for Keymer to completely overtake first place. Neither Movahed nor he had very good tiebreaks—of the five players half a point below them in the standings, four would have had better—but Movahed's outdid Keymer's in the ones that mattered. After Tsydypov among players on nine points came Artemiev, Nepomniachtchi, Matlakov, and GM Pranav Venkatesh.
*Bounty grows by $250 per week without a perfect score, and resets once a perfect score has been achieved.
These winners are announced by Thursday each week. If you would like to nominate a game or a move (including your own) in this or future weeks, click here!

news.title: Carlsen Calls Sindarov 'Significant Favorite,' Gives Verdict On Gukesh
news.author: tarjeijs
news.excerpt: GM Magnus Carlsen expects GM Javokhir Sindarov to defeat World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju, calling the challenger a "pretty significant favorite" and warning that the match could "get a little bit ugly" if Gukesh falls be
body: GM Magnus Carlsen expects GM Javokhir Sindarov to defeat World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju, calling the challenger a "pretty significant favorite" and warning that the match could "get a little bit ugly" if Gukesh falls behind early.

The world number-one gave a 35-minute interview to Indian podcaster Prakhar Gupta during the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League last week, speaking candidly about Gukesh's talent, India's young stars, his own future in chess, and the rivals who challenged him throughout his career.

The 35-year-old also said he is "more and more certain" that he will never return to the classical World Championship, and he hinted that he may step away from chess as a full-time career within the next few years.
Carlsen was unequivocal when asked to predict the winner of the upcoming FIDE World Championship 2026, which takes place in Geneva, Switzerland from November 24 to December 12.

"I would say at the moment Sindarov is probably a pretty significant favorite," he said, later adding: "I think Sindarov will win because he’s somewhat better-rounded and he is more objective in his evaluations."
I would say at the moment Sindarov is probably a pretty significant favorite.—Magnus Carlsen

Carlsen did caution that the match could remain close even if Sindarov enters as a clear favorite. With just 14 games and a wide drawing margin in classical chess, he noted that even a one-sided matchup could be decided by only one or two points.
Carlsen’s assessment of Gukesh’s weaknesses was among the bluntest sections of the interview.

"I don’t think it’s a secret to most people that his evaluations are way too optimistic," he said. "That kind of makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now that his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much."

Carlsen suggested that Gukesh’s talent can become a problem when he attempts to reproduce the level he reached in 2024, when he won the FIDE Candidates, scored a fantastic performance at the 45th FIDE Chess Olympiad, and then topped that by becoming the youngest-ever undisputed world chess champion.

Since then, Gukesh has struggled. In Norway Chess in June 2026, he finished clear last with five losses and only one win. He lost 15 rating points at the event and is now rated 2703—91 points below his October 2024 peak of 2794—and ranked 32nd in the world.

"He was able to show the whole array of his talent in 2024, and it must be really frustrating that he’s not able to" now, Carlsen said. "When you’re not able to, you kind of try desperately to do it still, and it doesn’t work."
He was able to show the whole array of his talent in 2024, and it must be really frustrating that he’s not able to.—Magnus Carlsen on Gukesh
He added that Gukesh does not have an obvious "safety net" when his aggressive approach fails.
"He doesn’t find it easy to just switch gears," Carlsen said, referring to the ability to settle for solid positions and draws.
During the final rapid-fire segment of the interview, Carlsen rejected the suggestion that Gukesh is currently the world’s best player.

"He’s a very good player. He had a fantastic 2024, one of the best years that anybody’s ever had," he said. "But to argue that he’s anywhere close to being the best player in the world now is not realistic."

Asked to rank five leading players from the younger generation based on their current strength, Carlsen placed GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu first, followed by Sindarov, GM Alireza Firouzja, GM Arjun Erigaisi, and Gukesh.
Despite his criticism of Gukesh, Carlsen was highly positive about Indian chess. "India certainly has the most talented pool of players in the world, especially on the younger side," he said.

India began its bid to retain the gold medal it won in Budapest in 2024 when the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad commenced Wednesday in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, defeating Thailand 3-1. Alongside host Uzbekistan and the United States, the powerhouse Indian squad is among the leading contenders for the open title.

Carlsen described many of the Indian players as concrete and calculation-oriented, although he noted that their individual styles vary. He also said he generally enjoys facing them because of their aggressive approach.
Carlsen identified Praggnanandhaa—who was interviewed by Chess.com after winning Norway Chess—as the player producing the best results, while stressing that the hierarchy has changed repeatedly.
"Their peaks are already very, very high, on par with practically everyone," he said. "But none of them are consistent enough yet to set themselves very much apart from the others."

The world number-one thinks Praggnanandhaa has a real chance of reaching a World Championship match: "I like his fighting spirit a lot," he said. "He has a really good feeling for the game. He calculates well."
Carlsen, who declined to defend his classical world championship title again after defeating GM Ian Nepomniachtchi in Dubai in 2021, once again ruled out returning to the cycle.

"The further away that I get from having played my last World Championship, I just am more and more certain that I’m never coming back," he said. "I never liked it particularly, and now I’m able to do other things that I like more."
The further away that I get from having played my last World Championship, I just am more and more certain that I’m never coming back.—Magnus Carlsen
Asked whether any player could motivate him to return, he said: "At the moment, it has nothing to do with the players. I just have no interest in it."
He also declined to propose changes to the format, despite having previously advocated for a championship incorporating faster time controls.

"I’m not a part of the classical World Championship. I’m not going to be there. I’ve kind of been there, done that," he said. "I think the classical World Championship has a right to exist the way that it is, and I let others both play and have opinions on the matter."
He also said organizers should not plan the long-term future of chess around his preferences. "I don’t have any ambitions in chess at this point," he said. "I just like playing."
However, he stopped short of announcing an imminent retirement. "I kind of want to do this a few more years, and then we’ll see. That’s kind of what I’m thinking."
I kind of want to do this a few more years, and then we’ll see.—Magnus Carlsen

Asked what he meant by "we’ll see," Carlsen said: "I don’t see myself leaving completely anytime soon, and I’ll probably want to play occasionally. But as kind of a full-time thing, then no, I don’t see that for super long."

Carlsen also discussed his rivalry with GM Hikaru Nakamura, saying he has enjoyed competing against the American in blitz and bullet for around 20 years. His assessment of their rivalry in classical chess was considerably more dismissive.

"In terms of classical chess, it’s not really been that much of a competition," he said, referring to his 14-1 advantage in decisive classical games. "I think he certainly had some ambitions back in the day that kind of made it at least a rivalry in his mind, but for me it hasn’t been."
Asked whether there was an especially tricky opponent he did not enjoy facing, Carlsen rejected the premise.
"I kind of enjoy playing the trickier opponents—the ones that play with a little bit of a different style than I do and challenge me to get out of my comfort zone," he said.

Carlsen named several players who had presented that kind of challenge throughout his career. "I would say Alireza still does that. When I was very young, Vishy [Anand] for sure. Hikaru to some extent, Fabi [Caruana], Levon Aronian very much so," he said. "There are certainly many of those opponents. [Alexander] Morozevich back in the day is another one, [Vladimir] Kramnik to some degree."

"There have been tons and tons of very interesting opponents and people who can outplay me on a good day and really challenge me to realize that there are some things that others can do better than me at times," Carlsen added.

There have been tons and tons of very interesting opponents and people who can outplay me on a good day and really challenge me to realize that there are some things that others can do better than me at times.—Magnus Carlsen
When asked to rank four of his leading contemporaries by classical strength, Carlsen put GM Fabiano Caruana first, followed by Nepomniachtchi, Nakamura, and GM Sergey Karjakin.

Asked whether he had ever experienced a moment when he recognized himself as the greatest player of all time, Carlsen rejected the premise. "I don’t look at myself that way," he said. "I’m rarely very happy with my games."

The interview also touched on artificial intelligence, Carlsen’s approach to evaluating positions, football, and his life away from chess. Asked what excites him now, his answer was considerably less complicated than many of his chess evaluations.
"I like being with my family," Carlsen said, before describing his young son as "the greatest human being in the history of the world."
