news.title: Thai IM Upsets Indian Number-2 As Favorites Prevail
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: The favorites won in round one of the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026, but there were a number of shocking individual upsets. Thai IM Prin Laohawirapap's win against Indian super-GM Arjun Erigaisi is the Game of the Day, while
body: The favorites won in round one of the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026, but there were a number of shocking individual upsets. Thai IM Prin Laohawirapap's win against Indian super-GM Arjun Erigaisi is the Game of the Day, while Iraqi CM Ali Ehsan Aryan's draw against American super-GM Levon Aronian was the only other upset against a 2700-rated grandmaster.

The favorites dominated even more clearly on day one of the 2026 FIDE Women's Chess Olympiad, with 4-0 clean sweeps for nine of the top-10 teams—only Germany was made to sweat by Malta, seeded 104th, before taking a 3-1 win. 11-year-old FM Bodhana Sivanandan and 63-year-old GM Pia Cramling were among the notable players leading their teams, England and Sweden, to 4-0 wins.
Full results (*Uzbekistan, as the host team, is fixed on board one)

As GM Judit Polgar said on the broadcast, the early intrigue at the start of each Olympiad is who will show up as well as who will not. A notable absence is French number-one GM Alireza Firouzja, who declined to represent the nation. Since obtaining full citizenship in 2021, Firouzja has not played in the Olympiad in three editions: 2022, 2024, and 2026.

Other notable absentees are world numbers one and two, Norwegian GM Magnus Carlsen and American GM Hikaru Nakamura. Compounding Carlsen's absence for Norway are GMs Aryan Tari and Jon Ludvig Hammer, also missing. Nakamura, as well as GM Leinier Dominguez, were replaced by the younger GMs Hans Niemann and Awonder Liang. The U.S. is top seed by rating, followed by India, Uzbekistan, and China, in that order.

Also absent are Iranian GM Parham Maghsoodloo, Indian GM Pentala Harikrishna, and Vietnamese number-one GM Liem Le. For three editions since 2022, FIDE has officially suspended the Russian national team following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, while Belarus was able to return this year.

1,028 players participated in the open tournament in 205 teams. As teams flooded the Silk Road International Exhibition Center in Samarkand, some voiced complaints on social media about the lack of a hotel room. India's coach GM Srinath Narayanan was the loudest of those voices.

FIDE published a response acknowledging the complaints. They wrote that, "Although accommodation matters fall within the remit of the local Organizing Committee," and are not within FIDE's authority, the international chess federation "has found additional financial resources and officially confirms that all teams which had to secure their own rooms will be reimbursed for the cost of accommodation of the appropriate standard, for a period of up to three days."

India is the defending champion, but the most striking part of their lineup is that World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju is on board four. In round one, he played on board three as GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu sat out, and all other boards moved up one.
In contrast, former World Champion Ding Liren is playing on China's board one even if GM Wei Yi is higher-rated than him.

There are 11 rounds played over two weeks, with four boards per team (and one reserve). A match win earns two points, a draw one, and a loss zero. In addition to valuable team prizes, there are also individual awards for best performances on respective boards. Let's dive into the games.

Round one always begins with the biggest mismatch in the tournament, and favorites are expected to win across the board. The point of interest in the early rounds is the upset, and we saw a number of them in round one. For teams, rather than individuals, the biggest upset was Botswana (133rd seed) drawing Brazil (31st seed) 2-2, with IM Providence Oatlhotse defeating GM Alexandr Fier on board one and Mogotsi Arnold Mothudi (rated 1914) beating IM Roberto Molina (2390) on board four.
While the favorite teams prevailed in the other matches, there were a number of exceptions. The standouts were the following:

We'll start with the Thai headliner, who was born in 2006. In fairness, Arjun did have a winning position, and perhaps GM David Howell's suggestion of 40.Rg3 in the commentary was a simpler way of getting the job done. Arjun kept the queens on, following GM Judit Polgar's suggested line with 40.Qh7, but the game remained complicated.

Rather than taking the exchange on e4, Arjun opted for 47.Nf3?, a move that not only threw away the entire advantage but also gave Black easy play. It was Arjun who had to find only moves to survive, and he didn't.
The game didn't last another 10 moves, and GM Rafael Leitao goes over the action in the Game of the Day below.

Iraq's Aryan may not have beaten Aronian, but he convincingly held the American in a pawn-down rook endgame. He told Chess.com's FM Mike Klein that he was happy to have won the unofficial competition with his team members!

Homayoun's 500+ point upset against Uzbekistan 2's board four is amplified more so by their age difference: the untitled Afghan player is 54, against a 16-year-old grandmaster. Like Arjun, the latter was winning but allowed counterplay. In this case, 26...Qf5?? was a one-move blunder that lost the rook in the corner.
Note that, as the hosting nation, Uzbekistan fields three teams in the tournament: Uzbekistan*, 2, and 3.
Malta's Portelli overpowered Hungary's Gledura on board two after blowing open the black king, still in the center, with a central pawn thrust.
Austria's GM Blohberger on board one suffered an upset against 42-year-old Wahab, rated 2066, when he got his knight trapped in enemy territory.
Spain's GM Alexei Shirov came within range of suffering an upset in the match against Libya, but managed to draw FM Yousef Alhassadi in the pawn-down endgame.

Shirov is one of the most experienced players, with this being his 14th time playing in an Olympiad. On the other end of the spectrum is the (newly-minted) youngest grandmaster in the world, Faustino Oro, who at the age of 12 is already Argentina's board one. His team swept Kenya 4-0.

One match was decided without a single move being played. Pakistan forfeited on all four boards against Israel. In both individual and team tournaments, players—especially from Iran—have refused to begin a game with Israelis.
The action continues on Thursday with Uzbekistan playing Peru, the U.S. against Mongolia, and Indonesia against India on the top-three boards.

The first round of the Women's Olympiad featured almost total dominance for the higher-rated teams, with just eight of the 93 matches seeing the favorite drop even half a point. Malta came closest to pulling off a sensation, holding Germany to two draws, one of which could easily have been a win.
Full results (*Uzbekistan, as the host team, is fixed on board one)

news.title: Gukesh Drops Under 2700 As India Beats Indonesia
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: With the striking exception of El Salvador (94th seed) upsetting Cuba (44th seed), the favorite teams won their matches in round two of the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026. It wasn't smooth sailing, as Uzbekistan, the United St
body: With the striking exception of El Salvador (94th seed) upsetting Cuba (44th seed), the favorite teams won their matches in round two of the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026. It wasn't smooth sailing, as Uzbekistan, the United States, India, the Netherlands, and Hungary found themselves to be in very real danger against Peru, Mongolia, Indonesia, North Macedonia, and Colombia, respectively—even if they went on to win their matches. World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju, after a draw with IM Satria Duta Cahaya, has dropped under 2700 on the live rating list.

While most favorites continued to cruise in round two of the 2026 FIDE Women's Chess Olympiad, we got the first major team upset, with second seed Georgia held to a 2-2 draw by 48th seed Montenegro. GM Bela Khotenashvili's loss to 300-point-lower-rated WFM Alena Skvortsova looked like an isolated incident until IM Lela Javakhishvili lost a winning position against WIM Aleksandra Milovic. Further down the field, the Czech Republic (36) was held to a draw by the UAE (83), while Slovakia (37) and Norway (46) lost to Tajikistan (84) and Kenya (93), respectively.

On paper, the favorites simply advanced, but Mongolia, Indonesia, North Macedonia, and Colombia on the top-10 boards lost by a single point in matches that were expected to be more lopsided. In a few cases, the underdog had a legitimate shot at winning, as we will see.

Although Uzbekistan won convincingly 3.5-0.5 over Peru, early on it looked like Peruvian board three IM Steven Rojas might score the first win against GM Shamsiddin Vokhidov. 19...dxc4 would have reached a decisive, opposite-color bishop middlegame—but after 19...Qd7?, played in the game, it took Vokhidov just four moves to right the ship and win the game.

On board two, World Championship Challenger GM Javokhir Sindarov played a brilliancy against IM Diego Quillas, with the penultimate move certainly being one for the puzzle books. The Uzbek star sacrificed his queen for a king move, but one that completed the checkmating net around the white king. GM Rafael Leitao goes over all the action in the Game of the Day below.
With that win, Uzbekistan had already cleared the hurdle of round two, but GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov delivered a win against GM Jorge Cori for good measure.

In contrast, India advanced with a single win and three draws against Indonesia—and they could have lost on that board! Three pawns down, GM Nihal Sarin was indeed losing against IM Arif Abdul Hafiz, nearly 300 points lower-rated, but the moves were extremely difficult for Black to find. Nihal won with a counterattack, dropping the exchange sacrifice 28.Rxc6! like a hammer, a crushing blow to expose the enemy king for the rest of the game.

Indonesia held draws on all other boards, nearly overcoming the chasm in average rating: 2428 against 2720. With a draw on board three, the world champion fell under 2700 on the live rating list for the first time since he crossed it in 2022—though, for the team result, a draw was completely fine.

Gukesh's opponent spoke to Chess.com's FM Mike Klein before the game and said, "Hopefully I'll have a good game against him!" He'd played GM Magnus Carlsen online, but it was his first over-the-board game against a world champion. "I just tried to keep my position stable. I thought there were many moments where he could have pushed for more, but surprisingly he didn't," he told FIDE.
I thought there were many moments where he could have pushed for more.
The United States was another favorite in early trouble as Mongolia's board four IM Khuyagtsogt Itgelt struck first blood against American GM Awonder Liang.
Perhaps it was overambition, but Liang's 30...f6?, which opened up his second rank, was a single and decisive mistake. White took over the a-file and won with shocking ease.
GMs Fabiano Caruana and Levon Aronian delivered two wins, with GM Hans Niemann drawing, to nevertheless win the match.

Like Sindarov, GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, and Caruana, France's GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave is another board-one player who sat out the first round but came in refreshed. Against Bosnia and Herzegovina's IM Sanjin Culum, his 14.Nc3! was a lovely move that left his pawn on f2 hanging, and he followed it up by ignoring a discovered check with 15.Na4!. He won by giving back material for an attack in the center of the board.

North Macedonia was another underdog that put up a great fight, against the Netherlands. Their IM Nikola Nikolovski upset the struggling GM Casper Schoppen on board four, who in the previous round drew a player rated 1896. There must be an error with the transmission of moves, as it appears the Dutch GM rejected a mate in five moves (with checks on every move) to inexplicably allow a winning counterattack.
GM Anish Giri scored the match point for the Netherlands, outplaying IM Emil Risteski in the rook endgame on board one after the latter played the wrong king move.

Like India, Hungary only squeezed past Colombia with a single win and three draws. GM Benjamin Gledura redeemed his loss in the previous round by squeezing water from stone against IM Esteban Valderrama in the rook endgame. GM Gleb Dudin, on board four, critically saved a lost position against GM Cristhian Camilo Rios.

As far as individual upsets go, Estonian IM Ilja Sirosh's approximately 250-point upset against legendary Ukrainian GM Vasyl Ivanchuk stands out the most. Ivanchuk found a brilliant piece sacrifice to outplay his opponent earlier in the game, but he must have been shocked to see the brilliant counterblow 21...Nd4!! appear on the board, turning the tables.

Other important upsets were scored by El Salvador's FMs Carlos Morales and Santiago Jose Guevara Ruiz, who beat their grandmaster opposition. The all-FM team, with an average rating of 2165, defeated Cuba's 2467.

In another huge upset, Trinidad and Tobago's FM Ryan Harper (2085) delivered GM Alexandr Fier's (2537) second loss, even if Brazil won 2.5-1.5. The Brazilian grandmaster played an unsound exchange sacrifice, and Harper made no mistakes in converting the advantage.
The pairings will only get more intense as the top seeds begin to clash.
The favorites won the top 35 matches, with Georgia, Women's Olympiad winners in 2008 and medalists in 2010, 2018, and 2022, the only exception.

Round two of the Women's Chess Olympiad saw more stars join the fray, with the highest-rated player, China's GM Zhu Jiner, almost the only top player yet to feature. There were winning individual and team starts for the likes of GM Divya Deshmukh (India), GM Anna Ushenina (Ukraine), GM Marie Sebag (France), GM Elisabeth Paehtz (Germany), GM Alexandra Kosteniuk (Switzerland), IM Nurgyul Salimova (Bulgaria), IM Stavroula Tsolakidou (Greece), and IM Carissa Yip, with Yip playing on top board as the USA defeated a strong Belgium team 4-0.
Yip was much better after WIM Hanne Goosens played 11.Ng3? and from the moment Black got in 14...c5! the outcome looked in little doubt.
GM Irina Krush, playing her 13th Olympiad, didn't pretend to be thrilled to be playing on third board behind both Yip and IM Alice Lee, but she had no complaints.

GM Bibisara Assaubayeva, the second-highest-rated player in the event, had a frustrating 59-move draw against young WFM Milana Babic, but Kazakhstan wasn't in danger as they overcame Bosnia and Herzegovina 3-1.
Another player whose campaign began in round two was WFM Anna Cramling, who was thrilled to be able to play with her mother and chess legend GM Pia Cramling.

It looked like it would be a perfect start on the board as well, as Anna raced into a winning position against Paraguayan WFM Renata Mayeregger. Things got tougher, however, as Anna missed countless wins in a crazy position before finally losing—though Sweden still claimed a 2.5-1.5 victory.

One player who went from strength to strength, meanwhile, was 11-year-old FM Bodhana Sivanandan, who has moved from reserve board to top board for England over the course of two years. She vowed, "I want to stay at board one for the next few team events as well," which feels like an ambition in little doubt.

Sivanandan, the most promising women's European chess prodigy, picked up a second win by defeating 14-year-old WFM Deborah Quickpen, the most promising African prodigy. Sivanandan explained why she didn't go for a flashy win near the end: "In the game I saw the better-looking move, I couldn’t see a clear win, but with the move I played I could see exactly how to win, so I thought, why not just do the simpler option?"
The logic was flawless, as was the move—the strongest in the position!

There were some shocks for strong teams, including Turkmenistan's Mahri Agamyradova defeating 385-point-higher-rated WGM Alicja Sliwicka, but in the end Poland dug out a 3-1 win. The one top seed to fail to gain two match points was Georgia, featuring a hugely experienced line-up still rated as second favorites to claim the title.

The spark for underdogs Montenegro was provided by Skvortsova, who sacrificed a pawn to infiltrate with her queen. It probably shouldn't have worked, but Khotenashvili lost her way in the complications.

That was an unfortunate loss for one of Georgia's star players, but they'd won on top and bottom boards, and Javakhishvili was winning a game she only needed to draw to give Georgia a match win. Strange things can happen in such situations, however, and Milovic, outrated by 356 points, managed to pull off an unlikely win.
That dropped point complicates Georgia's potential path to medals, but there are still nine rounds to go.
Elsewhere we had to drop as far as the 36th match to find favorites Czech Republic held by the UAE, with WGM Joanna Worek's 23.b4? walking into a fork from teenage star WGM Alserkal Essa.

One table lower and we had the first team loss by a favorite, with the Czech Republic's neighbors Slovakia falling 2.5-1.5 to Tajikistan. There were three draws and one decisive game that could have featured a brilliant queen sac for WFM Viktoria Nadzamova but instead saw a win for 253-point-lower-rated Rukhshona Saidova.

There were more upsets lower down the standings, and we can expect the battle to get fiercer by the round. The pairings for round three include tougher opposition for the top teams, with GM Koneru Humpy vs. Tsolakidou one possibility as India takes on Greece.
The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Robert Hess, David Howell, and Arturs Neiksans.

The 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad is a massive team event for national federations that takes place every two years. In 2026 it's being held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, with 11 rounds that run September 16-27. In Open and Women's sections teams of five players compete in a Swiss system, with each match played over four boards. There are two match points for a win and one for a draw, with board points taken into account only if teams are tied. Players have 90 minutes per game, plus 30 minutes from move 40, with a 30-second increment per move.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Tickets Now On Sale For 'Grandmasters' As Film Hits U.S. Theaters On October 11 & 14
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: Chess is hitting the big screen. Grandmasters, the new chess film following the dramatic tides and incredible characters of top-level chess, is showing in 90+ AMC theaters across the United States on October 11 and 14. F
body: Chess is hitting the big screen. Grandmasters, the new chess film following the dramatic tides and incredible characters of top-level chess, is showing in 90+ AMC theaters across the United States on October 11 and 14. For the first time, you can witness the intrigue and competing ambitions behind the tensest matches and political maneuvering of the chess world.

Grandmasters is a three-episode limited series directed by Liza Mandelup (Jawline) and produced by Boardwalk Pictures, the studio behind hit titles like Welcome to Wrexham, Cheer, and Chef's Table. The show follows what happens when Jan Henric Buettner, an eccentric German entrepreneur, recruits GM Magnus Carlsen to launch a new league. Their goal: to shake up the chess world, challenge FIDE, and make chess cool for the masses. Along the way, viewers are invited into the lives of the game's stars, including Carlsen, GM Wesley So, and GM Hans Niemann, and to follow the paradigm-shifting power plays made by chess executives like Buettner, Arkady Dvorkovitch, and IM Danny Rensch.

"I'm constantly drawn to people who have built their lives around a single pursuit," said Mandelup in a statement for Deadline. "I wanted to get beyond the idea of a chess genius and make something funny, intimate, and deeply human about the people behind the game."
I wanted to get beyond the idea of a chess genius and make something funny, intimate, and deeply human about the people behind the game.— Liza Mandelup
The series had a successful world premiere at the Tribeca Festival in June, when the screening attracted a large crowd that packed the SVA Theater in Manhattan.

Now, the theatrical version will be released as a supercut that combines all three episodes into one film. The film is releasing across 90+ AMC theaters nationwide. You can check the theater nearest you and get your tickets below:

Chess.com will be organizing premiere events around the country. Fans in New York can join a special Times Square event on October 11 at 6 p.m. ET featuring the world's biggest chess creator, IM Levy Rozman. The star behind YouTube channel GothamChess will be at AMC Empire 25, the largest AMC theater in the city, for a live Q&A session. Levy, who's featured in the documentary, will take questions from the audience before the screening.
You know the game. You don't know the story. Grab your ticket, bring your friends, and enjoy the screening of Grandmasters, in theaters for two days only: October 11 and 14.

news.title: Find Local Chess Clubs Near You With Chess.com's New Feature
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: Playing chess online is great, but meeting new people and playing chess in real life is, too! Now, you can easily find physical chess clubs near you right here on our Local Clubs page. Club owners can also get their club
body: Playing chess online is great, but meeting new people and playing chess in real life is, too! Now, you can easily find physical chess clubs near you right here on our Local Clubs page. Club owners can also get their club verified and listed as an over-the-board club so members can find it easily. On top of it all, club members and owners can enjoy an improved overall experience on Chess.com.
Here's everything you need to know about the new Local Clubs feature:
Finding a chess club near you is now easier than ever. Go to our Local Clubs page, and you'll immediately see the clubs nearest your current location.

If you're planning a trip and want to make sure to include chess in your travel plans, don't worry! You can use the search bar to find clubs anywhere in the world. If you're going to Paris this year, you can plan ahead to see the city's most iconic sites—not the Eiffel Tower or the Louvre, but rather the many chess clubs the City of Light has to offer.

We've also redesigned our entire Clubs experience on Chess.com. Your Clubs Home page now displays a section for your clubs and another to help you discover new ones. It also includes a shortcut to your federation's club and clubs near you.
Club profile pages also have a new look, with a focus on chat and events. Upcoming events also appear as featured to facilitate and encourage participation.
Finally, we're also improving how we recommend clubs for you to join. Club recommendations now reflect your activity, location, friends, and more.

If you run a chess club with a physical location, you can get your club verified so it shows up on our map. Mark your club as a Local Club when you create or edit it to get started. Note that verification is done manually, and you'll need to provide information to confirm your club has a physical location.
Have you found a new chess club near you? Let us know in the comments below!

news.title: Dominant Starts For Ashraf, Sarana, Xiong, Bring 3 0 Thursday Wins
news.author: coachjkane
news.excerpt: No one has ever scored a perfect 11-0 in 3 0 Thursday, but FM Artin Ashraf and GM Jeffery Xiong both came close on Thursday, September 17. Ashraf started by winning 10 consecutive games in the first event. His final-roun
body: No one has ever scored a perfect 11-0 in 3 0 Thursday, but FM Artin Ashraf and GM Jeffery Xiong both came close on Thursday, September 17. Ashraf started by winning 10 consecutive games in the first event. His final-round loss cost him perfection, but first place was a good consolation prize. In the second event, GM Alexey Sarana drew in the fourth round, but his 9.5/10 start was enough to secure the top spot in the second tournament despite a last-round stumble. In the third tournament, Xiong won his first nine games, securing first place, despite only half a point in his final two games.

In online chess circles, ten consecutive wins against an opponent is called an adoption. Ashraf adopted the field to start the day, defeating Super GMs Parham Maghsoodloo, Sarana, Hikaru Nakamura and Fabiano Caruana (who is concurrently playing at the Olympiad as well) along the way!
In addition to those victories against top players, Ashraf's win against the most frequent 3 0 Thursday winner, IM Renato Terry, was a dominant performance.

With first place secure entering the last round, Ashraf tried a Sicilian Dragon, aiming for a perfect score. However, his opponent, IM Sergey Sklokin, played well and hunted down Ashraf's king to secure the win.

Despite the loss, Ashraf earned top prize with 10 points. There was a four-way tie for second place with nine points. Terry had the best tiebreak score, followed by Sarana, Nakamura and Sklokin. WIM Margarita Potapova secured the top women's prize with seven points, her third prize in the last two weeks.

In the second event of the day, Sarana won his first three games before a tough game against GM Jose Martinez. Martinez had good chances to win on the clock in a bad position before allowing a skewer while Sarana had just 1.3 seconds on his clock.
Sarana won the white rook, but then sacrificed his queen for White's final pawn, securing a draw with just half a second remaining.
Sarana responded by winning his next six games. In the eighth round he built a strong attacking position and eventually won material against GM Oleksandr Bortnyk.
Sarana then reached 9.5 points with a 10th-round win against Xiong.

Like Ashraf before him, Sarana lost a meaningless last round game. He still took first with 9.5/11, ahead of GM Haik Martirosyan's nine points and GM Eric Hansen's 8.5 points. WFM Veronika Shubenkova took the top women's prize with six points.

Surprisingly, the toughest test for Xiong on his way to a 9-0 start came in the second round. His opponent, IM Eric Rosen, blundered a rook in the opening, but came back and equalized in a wild position. Fortunately for Xiong, Rosen took too many risks in trying to win on time, and Xiong was able to win the game.
After that scare, Xiong just kept winning, defeating opponents rated over 3000 in each of his next seven games. His victory against GM Luka Budisavljevic demonstrated his good form.

Xiong finally slowed down in the tenth round, blundering a piece against GM Christopher Yoo. That result kept the fight for first open heading into the final round. Xiong calmly secured the better end of a draw against IM Bryan Lin to reach 9.5 points. Yoo finished second with nine points, and Budisavljevic finished third with eight points. GM Tan Zhongyi secured the top women's prize with seven points.

3 0 Thursday is a set of three weekly Swiss tournaments for verified titled players featuring their favorite time control. Each of the three tournaments is an 11-round Swiss with a 3+0 time control. The combined prize fund is $3,000 every week.
NM Jeremy Kane is the Instructional Content Manager for Chess.com, and the author of several courses in the Starting Out series, Queen’s Gambit Accepted, Trompowsky, and Tarrasch.

news.title: Giri Saves Netherlands; Argentina, Iran Upset Ukraine, France In Women's
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: The seed favorites generally won in round three of the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026, with two notable exceptions on the top 50 boards. The 79th seed Kyrgyzstan beat the 31st seed Brazil 2.5-1.5, while 50th seed Singapore ups
body: The seed favorites generally won in round three of the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026, with two notable exceptions on the top 50 boards. The 79th seed Kyrgyzstan beat the 31st seed Brazil 2.5-1.5, while 50th seed Singapore upset 21st seed Norway with the same score. Australia nearly tied the Netherlands, but in our Game of the Day, GM Anish Giri squeezed water from stone in an endgame against GM Bobby Cheng to push his team through.

GM Koneru Humpy got revenge over IM Stavroula Tsolakidou for losing a crucial game a week ago in the Global Chess League final as India beat Greece 3.5-0.5 in round three of the 2026 FIDE Women's Chess Olympiad. Favorites Kazakhstan, China, and USA were among the teams to march on with wins, but sixth seed Ukraine crashed to a 3-1 loss to 38th seed Argentina, while eighth seed France was also taken down by 30th seed Iran.
The matches ended with expected results in the top 10 matches, but not without individual casualties.

There were a few very real but transient scares on the top five boards. Uzbekistan had no worries, with Olympiad debutant GM Mukhiddin Madaminov scoring the first win on board four after winning the exchange and converting it. The final sequence against Austria's IM Konstantin Peyrer was nice:

They made draws on boards one and three, with GM Javokhir Sindarov getting the chance to land a checkmate against GM Felix Blohberger on board two. One could say it was the team's birthday present for the now 22-year-old GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov, playing on board one!

The U.S. was in trouble early on, with Denmark's GM Bjorn Moller Ochsner outplaying GM Awonder Liang on board four and, impressively, GM Jonas Buhl Bjerre gaining a large advantage against GM Fabiano Caruana on board one.

Even with a terrible knight on a8, however, Caruana slipped out with a draw. The same could not be said for Liang, who escaped into a complicated endgame but lost his way again (a second loss in a row). On boards two and three, GMs Wesley So and Hans Niemann won the match for the U.S., with So earning a quick and beautiful win on a queen sacrifice after a blunder by GM Jesper Thybo.
So, in a joint interview with IM Carissa Yip, told Chess.com's FM Mike Klein that gold matters more than anything else, even two silver medals.

If India seemed shaky in previous rounds, they subdued that narrative in round three. World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju's dip under 2700 on the live rating list didn't last 24 hours, as his win against Italian GM Sabino Brunello on board four brought him back over to a live rating of 2702. He called 14.Ng5 "a bit too creative," and indeed it led to a slight advantage for Black. White's 20.Nc2? was the decisive mistake, and Gukesh found a strong pawn sacrifice for a decisive initiative.

"I wouldn't really consider yesterday a disappointment because it was just a very good game by both sides, I think... sometimes you can't do anything," said Gukesh about drawing against an international master on the previous day. He also said that the first round was unfortunate for GM Arjun Erigaisi and that organizational issues were partly to blame—Team India waited six hours for a hotel room.

But, since then, things have gotten better, he said. Gukesh also revealed that it was his idea to play on boards three and four, rather than board one, and that his team agreed. "This is the order that gives us the best chance of winning the tournament," he said, pointing out that the nation's victory is more important than any individual.

Speaking of world champions turning a new page, GM Ding Liren scored his second win in three rounds against Bulgaria's GM Arkadij Naiditsch, with the team winning the match 3.5-0.5. Ding said his opponent missed the move 25.Nce2, and two moves later he coordinated his pieces wonderfully for a long tactical sequence that won.

Ding talked to Chess.com after the game and pointed out that it's his first foreign tournament since the world championship in 2024. In the last two years, he has played in China, but he said he's also spent time playing sports and watching movies.

Germany defeated Uzbekistan's second team (as the host country, they have multiple squads here), 2.5-1.5, with GM Vincent Keymer winning on board one and draws on the rest, but the closest match on the top 10 boards was the Netherlands (sixth seed) vs. Australia (32nd). Australian IM Rishi Sardana defeated GM Loek van Wely on board three, but GM Jorden van Foreest hit back with a win against GM Temur Kuybokarov on board two. With a draw on board four, we had an even score of 1.5-1.5, and an equal endgame with opposite-color bishops on board one.
The Dutch number-one pulled some endgame magic to win that game on demand and bring victory to the Netherlands. That's our Game of the Day with annotations to come by GM Rafael Leitao.
Continuing down the list, Azerbaijan beat Switzerland 3-1, but Hungary was in early trouble against Slovenia when GM Richard Rapport blundered and resigned against GM Anton Demchenko on board one.

It was Rapport's first game in the event, and he was only slightly worse before he played an instantly losing king move. Demchenko needed less than two minutes to double- and triple-check 23...Qh4, which won on the spot against his nearly 150-point higher-rated opponent.
You can check out FIDE's nine-minute video recap for more detail as well.
France beat Kazakhstan 3.5-0.5, while Armenia won against Sweden by a narrow 2.5-1.5.

Moving on to team upsets, we must immediately jump to Kyrgyzstan, a team with no grandmasters, defeating Brazil, a team with three. With draws on the top three boards, it was the untitled player Timur Daudov (2063) who pulled the individual upset of the day against IM Diego Di Berardino on board four. Di Berardino had a few chances to save the pawn-down knight endgame, and his last mistake was not capturing the pawn on move 54.

The other big upset was Singapore vs. Norway, with three draws and one win on board one. There, GM Jingyao Tin overwhelmed GM Johan-Sebastian Christiansen in the rook endgame (yes, Norway does not have GM Magnus Carlsen this year).

Notable draws included Lithuania holding England 2-2, with GM Paulius Pultinevicius's win over GM Gawain Maroroa Jones on board three cancelling out GM Luke McShane's win over GM Tomas Laurusas. Moldova held Croatia and Belgium held Iran as well.
You can see several more match scores in the screenshot below.

The pairings continue to get harder as the winning teams face each other in round four. Uzbekistan vs. Turkiye is an exciting clash of two young teams. We should expect a great fight from Turkiye, led by the 15-year-old, 2716-rated GM Yagiz Erdogmus on board one and 17-year-old GM Ediz Gurel (2636) on board two.
The top 11 boards feature teams with a perfect 3/3 match wins, with Singapore floating down to play England, on two wins with one draw.
We got the first upset wins on the top tables, as Ukraine and France both suffered defeat.

Twenty teams still have a perfect 6/6 match points in the Women's section, including most of the favorites. Defending champion and top seed India was one team to power on, with a 3.5-0.5 victory over Greece. That carried more significance on the top board, where Humpy faced Tsolakidou less than a week after losing a winning position and seeing her team, led by GM Magnus Carlsen, lose the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League. Tsolakidou was gifted a motorcycle as the MVP.

In Samarkand, the narrative remained the same as Humpy again built up an overwhelming position, but this time, even if her conversion wasn't perfect, she never lost the advantage and went on to lead her team to victory.

Only GM Divya Deshmukh was held to a draw by FM Anastasia Avramidou, and it was a pattern elsewhere that the perfection we saw in the first two rounds was rare—of the teams in the top-10 matches, only Poland managed a 4-0 win, against Latvia.
GM Bibisara Assaubayeva was held to a draw for a second day in a row, but third seed Kazakhstan beat Slovenia 3.5-0.5.

Meanwhile, the debut of GM Zhu Jiner, China's top player and the highest-rated player in the event, was shaky. Turkiye's IM Ekaterina Atalik had a big positional advantage early on, but it required precision. Instead, she played too actively, and collapsed in time trouble.
A match China could easily have lost ended in a 3-1 win, since 16-year-old IM Lu Miaoyi was able to make a repetition in a position WIM Gulenay Aydin was winning...
...and WIM Tianqi Yan rescued a draw against WFM Ceren Tirpan.

Another match that briefly looked too close to call was on the top table—fixed for 13th seed Uzbekistan—where Indonesian WIM Diajeng Theresa Singgih found an incredible escape from a piece down against WGM Afruza Khamdamova.
Her teammates rallied, however, and Uzbekistan won 3-1 on home soil.

The U.S. team continues to look convincing, and raced out of the blocks in round three when Yip exploited an early blunder by her Cuban opponent, WGM Maritza Arribas. Wins followed for IMs Tatev Abrahamyan and Alice Lee, with the match decided when IM Rose Atwell rescued a draw against WIM Ineymig Hernandez.
Yip was confident that, even if this isn't their year, their turn will be soon.
Not all the favorites made it through round three unscathed, however, with two big upsets on the top tables.

Sixth seed Ukraine rested their rising star WFM Anastasiia Hnatyshyn on top board, but still outrated their Argentine opponents on all four boards. The spark for the remarkable upset came in the battle of two teenagers on bottom board, with WFM Ernestina Adam suddenly taking over with the black pieces against Tetyana Skarbarchuk, who resigned on move 18 in a position that was falling apart.

WIM Anapaola Borda won remarkably smoothly with White on board three, so that Ukraine's top-two boards were in a must-win position. That ended with IM Nataliya Buksa overpressing and losing to WIM Majo Campos, while the score became crushing when former Women's World Champion GM Anna Ushenina spoiled a winning position against WGM Candela Guecamburu and could only claim a consolation draw.

Iran, seeded 30th, won 3-1, but the score could even have been 4-0, since Iran had winning positions on the bottom-two boards. The standout moment was when GM Marie Sebag, down to under a minute, went for a kingside attack against young WIM Melika Mohammadi. It was flawed, yet playable, but on move 40 Sebag guessed wrongly with six seconds to spare.
It was essential to play 40.Rxd7!, while after 40.Nxf7? Nxg4 there was nothing better to do than resign.
Those were the standout results, while a little further down the standings, 12th seed Netherlands was held to a 2-2 draw by 34th seed Austria.

One match result that would normally raise few eyebrows was Monaco defeating Lebanon 3.5-0.5, but the bottom board featured an incredible 71-year age gap between nine-year-old Jessica Kobeissey and 80-year-old WIM Julia Lebel-Arias. It was a real battle that could have gone either way, as the evaluation graph illustrates.
In round four we'll already see top-20 sides clashing with each other.

news.title: U.S. Wins 3.5-0.5 In Both Sections As Favorites Allow No Upsets
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: Round four of the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026 saw no major upsets on the top-11 boards, which consisted of the 21 teams with perfect scores. The most dominant score was the U.S.'s 3.5-0.5 against Ukraine, with GM Levon Aron
body: Round four of the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026 saw no major upsets on the top-11 boards, which consisted of the 21 teams with perfect scores. The most dominant score was the U.S.'s 3.5-0.5 against Ukraine, with GM Levon Aronian winning the Game of the Day from a losing position against 18-year-old European Champion GM Roman Dehtiarov. The two draws on the top-10 boards were between Azerbaijan vs. the Czech Republic and France vs. Romania.

Just as in the open tournament, the United States scored 3.5-0.5 against Spain in the 2026 FIDE Women's Chess Olympiad on Saturday, as did China against Hungary, Bulgaria against Romania, and Serbia against Iran. IM Alice Lee, on 4/4, looks to be an early contender for an individual medal.
In the open tournament, there are just eight teams with perfect scores and 10 teams in the women's. Round five is on Sunday, September 20, starting at 6:15 a.m. ET / 12:15 CEST / 3:45 p.m. IST.
"I would have expected there would be a bigger surprise," said GM Arturs Neiksans about both sections at the end of the broadcast. The favorites won, with just two draws on the top boards.

Uzbekistan wrapped up the match against Turkiye in the first three hours, one of the early finishers in round four. An opening mistake on board three was the cause, with GM Nodirbek Yakubboev beating GM Vahap Sanal. Black's 9...Nxd4? is a fancy tactic that traded pieces and didn't lose material, but the problem was that White isolated the d-pawn and captured it quickly.

With draws on all other boards, Uzbekistan secured the match 2.5-1.5. The young matchups of GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov vs. GM Yagiz Erdogmus and GM Javokhir Sindarov vs. GM Ediz Gurel on the top two boards were exciting, but the Uzbek super-GMs are likely happy (at the expense of fans) that there wasn't much drama there. The only player older than 20 in those pairings, the 22-year-old Abdusattorov is already quite the veteran!

In the match between the U.S. and Ukraine, GM Wesley So (with Black) scored the first win against GM Anton Korobov on board two after, similarly, isolating a pawn and then winning it. But things weren't so clear, as it looked like the 18-year-old European champion was on his way to crushing GM Levon Aronian on board four.

Aronian said he evaluated his position as "dead lost," and he saw the correct 24.Bd3 for his opponent as a simple but crushing move. Yet the trend turned in the other direction after the Ukrainian went another way: with a knight sacrifice. Aronian was forced to sacrifice his queen in return for an absolutely chaotic position and went on to outplay his opponent—yet another example of the Armenian-American landing a knockout with his back against the wall.

"I didn't see many chances, but I thought to myself, I'm going to get mated... I could just suffer, but I thought at least I'll die standing up!" Aronian told Chess.com's FM Mike Klein. GM Rafael Leitao analyzes the Game of the Day below.
I could just suffer, but I thought at least I'll die standing up!

Although it wasn't necessary to win the match, GM Fabiano Caruana also defeated GM Vasyl Ivanchuk (who substituted GM Igor Kovalenko, on 2.5/3) on board one, and the United States won the match 3.5-0.5, with the one draw in GM Hans Niemann vs. GM Ihor Samunenkov.

After losing two games in a row, America's debutant GM Awonder Liang sat out of round four, but Aronian said he's sure the 23-year-old will bounce back. Aronian said that the pressure seems to have affected Liang's play, but also, "He's a tremendously strong player. He just needs to get his positions. He'll get it, I'm sure."

GM Arjun Erigaisi scored the first point for India against Spain with one of his trademark attacks. 26.0-0!! is the move that stood out most, leaving his knight hanging to finish development. GM Maksim Chigaev managed to avoid checkmate by trading into a pawn-down endgame, but that was the only good news. The endgame was lost.

Draws on the remaining boards would have been enough, but Gukesh scored his third win in the event against GM Alexei Shirov on board four after his opening advantage led to winning the exchange. The game was still very complicated, but World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju converted the advantage and India won 3-1.
Since briefly dropping under 2700 in round two, Gukesh has won twice to reverse the trend in the positive direction.

With 13.5/16, China has scored the most points of any team in the Olympiad so far, and this may count toward tiebreaks later. Their board two, GM Wei Yi, won a sparkling game against Serbia's GM Aleksandar Indjic with White in the Petroff Defense.

A methodical buildup, with White gaining space on the kingside, culminated in the stunning sacrifice 32.Nxf7!! that led to a windmill motif, one we don't often see played out at the elite level. Indjic had little choice in the matter from there, shuffling his queen between a8 and b8 as White swung a wrecking ball at the black center and king.
China's board four GM Xiangrui Kong scored another win against GM Bojan Maksimovic to win the match 3-1, with draws on the other two boards.

Germany vs. Poland was a close encounter, but GM Alexander Donchenko pulled through for Germany, with the black pieces on board four, to win the only game of the match against GM Jakub Kosakowski. Hungary vs. Israel was a similar story, with GM Benjamin Gledura scoring the match point for a second time, against GM Avital Boruchovsky.
Looking at the next 20 boards down, we can see that England recovered from an upset draw in the previous round to beat Singapore, the team that upset Norway in round three.

Lithuania has continued to impress, after making that draw against the higher-rated English team in round three. In round four, they overcame the nearly 100-points higher-rated Croatia 3-1, with two wins scored by GM Paulius Pultinevicius (against GM Ante Brkic) and IM Pijus Stremavicius (against GM Sasa Martinovic). Both players are on a perfect 3/3 score.

On board 54, Sri Lanka defeated the approximately 150-point higher-rated Chile as well, with one win by CM S Sivathanujan (2180) against IM Mauricio Marrujo (2422) on board two, with three draws in the other games.
In round five, the first four matches feature teams with perfect scores. The eight teams may be cut to four!
There were no major surprises in the top 10 matches, with China, the U.S., Romania, and Serbia putting up the most dramatic scores.

The United States, which has yet to win team gold at the Olympiad, defeated Spain 3.5-0.5. Across four matches and 16 games, they have made just two draws to attain an unmatched 15/16 points. Is this their year?

Board four IM Tatev Abrahamyan scored the first point thanks to an opening snafu from WGM Monica Calzetta, who dropped a pawn after allowing 10.Bxc5!. If the bishop is taken, 11.axb4 wins the rook in the corner.

And then IM Carissa Yip won a rook endgame against IM Marta Garcia on board one, while IM Alice Lee defeated IM Sabrina Vega with a deadly pair of connected passed pawns in the center. Lee is the only player with a perfect 4/4 on her team and is a strong contender to win an individual medal if she carries on with this quality of play.

India looked great against Mongolia with wins on board three (WCM Khishigbaatar Bayasgalan vs. GM Divya Deshmukh 0-1) and board four (IM Savitha Shri vs. IM Batkhuyag Munguntuul) coming in first. Savitha, who's on a perfect 4/4 in her first Olympiad, found a forcing way to win her fourth game in a row.

With draws on the top two boards, India triumphed 3-1. As Divya told FIDE, top seed India hopes to repeat what they did in Budapest in 2024: win gold. "It will be the first for India. It was our first last time that we won, and it will be the first if we defend it!" she said.

Kazakhstan defeated Armenia 3-1 with wins by GM Bibisara Assaubayeva on board one and WIM Elnaz Kaliakhmet on board four, while China put up another monstrous score of 3.5-0.5 with wins by GM Zhu Jiner on board one, IM Song Yuxin on board two, and IM Lu Miaoyi on board three. Song found a simple yet effective sacrifice to put away her game, calculating that her pawn (a) cannot be stopped and (b) outruns Black's pawn by one tempo.

Lower down, we can see that second seed Georgia was held to a draw by 34th seed Austria, and so they are now a full match win behind the leading teams. Sixty-second seed Singapore held 24th seed Greece to a draw, as did 67th seed Costa Rica against 29th seed Sweden.
In round five, the top five boards feature the teams with perfect scores. You won't want to miss the coming rounds, as the top teams are finally clashing.
The live broadcast was hosted by GMs David Howell and Arturs Neiksans and IM Tania Sachdev.

The 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad is a massive team event for national federations that takes place every two years. In 2026 it's being held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, with 11 rounds that run September 16-27. In Open and Women's sections, teams of five players compete in a Swiss system, with each match played over four boards. There are two match points for a win and one for a draw, with board points taken into account only if teams are tied. Players have 90 minutes per game, plus 30 minutes from move 40, with a 30-second increment per move.
NM Anthony Levin caught the chess bug at the "late" age of 18 and never turned back. He earned his national master title in 2021, actually the night before his first day of work at Chess.com.

Anthony, who also earned his Master's in teaching English in 2018, taught English and chess in New York schools for five years and strives to make chess content accessible and enjoyable for people of all ages. At Chess.com, he writes news articles and manages social media for chess24.

news.title: Top Seeds Tumble As Germany Beats U.S. While Poland Defeats Indian Women
news.author: colin_mcgourty
news.excerpt: GM Frederik Svane's win over GM Hans Niemann saw Germany defeat the top-seeded U.S. 2.5-1.5 in round five of the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026. Germany is joined in the lead on 10/10 match points by Uzbekistan, who crushed Hu
body: GM Frederik Svane's win over GM Hans Niemann saw Germany defeat the top-seeded U.S. 2.5-1.5 in round five of the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026. Germany is joined in the lead on 10/10 match points by Uzbekistan, who crushed Hungary 4-0, and India, who defeated the Netherlands 3-1 after GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu won a rollercoaster game against GM Anish Giri, while World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju pounced on a blunder by GM Erwin l'Ami. China was held to four draws by Armenia.

The top seed also lost in round five of the 2026 FIDE Women's Chess Olympiad, as defending champion India fell to Poland for a third Olympiad in a row. IM Aleksandra Maltsevskaya grabbed the only win of the match, against GM Vaishali Rameshbabu. Poland was joined on a perfect score by China, Kazakhstan, and Azerbaijan, while the U.S. team scraped a 2-2 draw after IM Alice Lee rescued the team with a win after WGM Afruza Khamdamova defeated IM Carissa Yip on top board.
Round six, the last before the rest day, is on Monday, September 21, starting at 6:15 a.m. ET / 12:15 CEST / 3:45 p.m. IST.
We got the first big upset win of the event with Germany defeating the top-seeded U.S. team.
Only Uzbekistan, India, and Germany are still on a perfect 10 points, with five teams a point behind.

Eight teams came into round five of the Open section of the Olympiad on a perfect score, but just three maintained that record, with the biggest sensation the loss of the top-seeded U.S. team, which fielded what on paper was its strongest lineup.
The early action came in Donchenko-Aronian, with the German star going for some very sharp and sacrificial theory.
GM Levon Aronian couldn't grab a piece and hold onto it without getting checkmated down the h-file, but the early action fizzled out into a 26-move draw by repetition.
We saw an even quicker draw on the top board, where GMs Vincent Keymer and Fabiano Caruana achieved perfect symmetry on move 20 and also drew by repetition shortly afterward.

That increased the pressure on the other boards, but for Svane against Niemann things were going like a dream. Svane told FM Mike Klein afterward that he'd played the same first 15 moves against GM Michael Adams in a 2022 game in the German League.

Nevertheless, Svane said "it was kind of tough to do anything," before Niemann blundered a pawn. From there, it was one-way traffic, with Svane not only finding the winning move 27.Nc5!! but banging it out on the board almost instantly.
There was no way back for Niemann, as Svane wrapped up a fine win, which is our Game of the Day. GM Rafael Leitao has analyzed it below.
That wasn't quite the end, as GM Wesley So could save the match with a win over GM Matthias Bluebaum. The game was wild, with the German number-two going for a remarkable queen sacrifice.
In the end, however, German team captain GM Jan Gustafsson didn't even have to pretend to read his book, since the ending was headed to a clear fortress.

That was the one defeat for a top team, but others were held to a draw. 23rd seed Romania held seventh seed Azerbaijan 2-2 after GM Daniel Bogdan-Deac beat GM Shakhriyar Mamedyarov on top board, while 10th seed Armenia made four draws against fourth seed China. That match witnessed a near miss for GM Ding Liren, who spotted a nice sting in the tail after GM Haik Martirosyan gave up his queen, but in the end there was another unbreakable fortress.
Two teams joined Germany in the lead, with the most emphatic performance coming from the host nation, Uzbekistan.

The Uzbek players need to deal with added attention, as we saw with the ceremonial first move. It was to be made by Arkady Dvorkovich, who recently stepped down from performing his duties as FIDE President after being sanctioned by the European Union. Curiouser still, the move was delayed as both GMs Richard Rapport and Peter Leko showed up five minutes late for their games with GMs Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Javokhir Sindarov.
If that was awkward, there was nothing awkward about the way Uzbekistan played the match. The team received a huge boost when Rapport dropped a key pawn with 17.g4?.

Abdusattorov's win never seriously looked in doubt, and the team win looked certain when GM Benjamin Gledura's aggressive opening also backfired against GM Nodirbek Yakubboev. It just emphasized the power of the Uzbek squad, as the "other Nodirbek" is now a 2700-live-rated player as well.

Leko and GM Gleb Dudin were left with the unenviable task of needing to win with the black pieces against Sindarov and GM Shamsiddin Vokhidov, respectively. Though their positions were decent for a long time, that never looked likely, and instead both got ground into dust as Uzbekistan made it 4-0 to head the standings.

Uzbekistan's biggest rivals again look to be India, and the Indian team found a way to win, even if it was somewhat shakier. Giri had won all four of his previous games, while Praggnanandhaa had been held to draws, and initially it seemed like the Dutch number-one's momentum might continue when he found a sacrifice on h3 and the correct follow-up.
Praggnanandhaa looked on the ropes, but noted, "In some critical moments in time trouble, I managed to outplay him."

Praggnanandhaa also revealed he was offered a draw by Giri, explaining: "I had to make a call if I should take a draw or go for it. I felt Gukesh was pushing, but it was not really clear to me. It could also be that White can manage a fortress, so I felt keeping the game going can make sense, and it worked out today."
Gukesh moved to 4.5/5 after L'Ami blundered with 23.f4?, running into 23...c3! and the black bishop coming to c4.

We've got the most anticipated clash of the whole Olympiad in round six, as 2022 champion and host Uzbekistan takes on 2024 champion India in the one meeting of teams on a perfect score. Germany is given China as a reward for beating the U.S. team.

news.title: Play For Your Favorite Esports Team In The Chess Club Showdown, Starting September 30
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: You can now help your favorite esports organization fight for the top spot in our new monthly event, the Chess Club Showdown. Play alongside your chess heroes, outscore other clubs, and bring home the title. With a $15,0
body: You can now help your favorite esports organization fight for the top spot in our new monthly event, the Chess Club Showdown. Play alongside your chess heroes, outscore other clubs, and bring home the title. With a $15,000 monthly prize fund up for grabs, the event is open to everyone in the chess community who joins an esports club on Chess.com.

The event's first edition kicks off on September 30 at 11 a.m. ET / 17:00 CEST / 8:30 p.m. IST and will feature a special $25,000 prize fund. Join any participating team's official Chess.com club to compete, or tune in to our Twitch and YouTube channels to watch the event's broadcast.

In this first edition, members can expect to play side by side with Team Liquid's GM Magnus Carlsen. After bringing two Esports World Cup titles to his team, Carlsen is now striving to lead Team Liquid to the Chess Club Showdown's inaugural title.
Another familiar face expected to join is IM Levy Rozman. The world's biggest creator recently joined BASILISK and will be competing for his team for the first time since signing.

"Esports fans bring real passion to the games they love, and we wanted to give them a new way to bring that same energy to chess," said Michael Brancato, Chess.com's Events Commissioner. "Chess Club Showdown builds that community on Chess.com and lets any member step up and play for their favorite team, alongside the players they look up to."
The Chess Club Showdown will take place on the last Wednesday of each month. Each event will consist of a multi-club arena followed by a club match finale.

In the multi-club arena portion, players sign up to represent any participating club. Players compete in a two-hour, score-paired arena with a 5+0 time control; each club's top 50 scorers contribute to the club's score. When the arena ends, the two clubs with the highest scores advance to the next stage.

Players can then sign up to represent either of the top two clubs in the club match, with the 50 higher-rated players having priority. Players on each club get paired to play a two-game match with a 5+0 time control. The club with the most points wins the club match and that month's showdown.

Every month, $6,500 in prizes goes directly to the players competing in the event. The remaining $8,500 is distributed among the participating clubs. Community members can earn one of the five $100 prizes by submitting their favorite game on social media, tagging Chess.com and the club they played for, and briefly explaining what makes it their favorite game.

For its inaugural event, an extra $10,000 will be on offer for the club match, bringing the total purse to $25,000. The winning club will take home $10,000, while the runner-up will receive $5,000. Check out the prize distribution below, or read the event's official rulebook for more information.

The event is open to any club registered with the Esports World Cup. To support a team, you must first join its official Chess.com club. You'll then see a button to join the next Chess Club Showdown event. Check out the list of participating clubs (at the time of writing) below, or check the full list on the event's official page:
Are you ready to play for your club in the inaugural Chess Club Showdown? Then sign up with your club and hop into the arena on September 30!

news.title: Play Chess Against NFL Star Mack Hollins
news.author: chesscom
news.excerpt: Think you can take down an NFL receiver at chess? Now’s your chance. BlitzChamps V Champion Mack Hollins is now a bot on Chess.com! Head to the Play Bots page and test your skills against the Super Bowl champ.
body: Think you can take down an NFL receiver at chess? Now’s your chance. BlitzChamps V Champion Mack Hollins is now a bot on Chess.com! Head to the Play Bots page and test your skills against the Super Bowl champ.
Mack’s bot is rated 1400 and plays a wild game worthy of his nickname, Tarzan. You’re going to need fast hands (and feet) to keep up with the Patriots wide receiver.
You might remember Mack from his BlitzChamps V run, where he won every match and defeated Justin Herbert in the final to claim the BlitzChamps crown and $30,000 charity prize.

Mack is one of the BlitzChamps veterans. After making the semifinals in his debut in BlitzChamps III, before losing to eventual champion Justin Reid in a sudden-death tiebreak, Mack returned for BlitzChamps IV, where he lost two matches against Herbert (thanks in part to a faulty internet connection). Mack would exact his revenge on both Reid and Herbert while becoming the champion of BlitzChamps V.

Outside of BlitzChamps, Mack’s love for chess has been well known for years. Earlier this year, he brought a board with him to challenge reporters during the media days leading up to Super Bowl LX. In 2024, he visited the FIDE World Rapid and Blitz Championship in Toronto to make the ceremonial first move in a match between GM Ian Nepomniatchtchi and GM Hikaru Nakamura. During last year’s lead up to Halloween weekend, Mack famously donned a bishop costume before the game.

news.title: Nakamura Makes It Back-To-Back Bullet Brawls
news.author: coachjkane
news.excerpt: GM Hikaru Nakamura added to his Bullet Brawl dominance on September 19, winning the tournament once again. It was Nakamura's second straight week in first place, his 18th win of the year, and his 67th total to date. To p
body: GM Hikaru Nakamura added to his Bullet Brawl dominance on September 19, winning the tournament once again. It was Nakamura's second straight week in first place, his 18th win of the year, and his 67th total to date. To put that in perspective, no other players have won more than 32 Bullet Brawls or more than four events this year.
Bullet Brawl will return on Saturday, September 26, at 12 p.m. ET / 18:00 CEST / 9:30 p.m. IST.

Nakamura led the event from start-to-finish. He began with a 13-game winning streak, tied for the longest streak of any player throughout the entire tournament. In his 10th game, he took down the eventual third-place finisher, GM Tuan Minh Le. It only took one tactical mistake and Black's position crumbled.

GM Salem Saleh finally stopped Nakamura, checkmating him in an endgame. However, Nakamura immediately started another streak, winning his next nine games, including this sharp battle against IM Renato Terry.

Nakamura finished strong, ending with nine consecutive wins before a final draw against Minh Le. This brought him to 56.5/66 on the day and 188 points. That final winning streak included a nice attacking game against Saleh.

Behind Nakamura's clear first was a tough battle for second place. In the end, GM Emin Ohanyan scored 45.5/60 to surpass Minh Le by just a point, 150-149. Ohanyan's strong result included a win over GM Magnus Carlsen. Carlsen played only part of the event, scoring a strong 17/21, but not partaking in the fight for the top spots.
How to review games? The games from this week's Bullet Brawl can be found here.

Bullet Brawl is an exciting arena featuring Chess.com's top bullet specialists. It takes place weekly on Saturdays. The format is a two-hour arena with a 1+0 time control; the prize fund is $1,000. Like Titled Tuesday and Arena Kings, Bullet Brawl often features top GMs, including Hikaru Nakamura, Magnus Carlsen, Tuan Minh Le, and many more!
NM Jeremy Kane is the Instructional Content Manager for Chess.com, and the author of several courses in the Starting Out series, Queen’s Gambit Accepted, Trompowsky, and Tarrasch.

news.title: Nihal Blunders Queen As Uzbekistan Takes Sole Lead; Indian Women Hit Back To Beat U.S.
news.author: anthonylevin
news.excerpt: With a shock win on board three against India, Uzbekistan has taken sole lead of the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026 after six rounds. GM Nihal Sarin was better on board and clock against GM Nodirbek Yakubboev, but he blundered
body: With a shock win on board three against India, Uzbekistan has taken sole lead of the 46th Chess Olympiad 2026 after six rounds. GM Nihal Sarin was better on board and clock against GM Nodirbek Yakubboev, but he blundered his queen in the consequential game with half an hour on his clock. Germany, the only other team on a perfect score, lost to China 3-1 after GM Ding Liren beat GM Vincent Keymer on board one and GM Xu Xiangyu beat GM Alexander Donchenko on board four. China is just one point behind Uzbekistan, as is Armenia, who overcame Iran 2.5-1.5.

China and Kazakhstan are the only teams on a perfect 12/12 after round six of the 2026 FIDE Women's Chess Olympiad, giving them a two-point lead over an 11-team chasing pack. China overwhelmed round-five heroes Poland 3.5-0.5, while IM Alua Nurman's single win gave Kazakhstan a 2.5-1.5 victory over Azerbaijan. India scored a crucial 3-1 bounce-back victory over the U.S., with IMs Savitha Shri and Vantika Agrawal grabbing the wins. Second seed Georgia is also right back in contention after defeating hosts Uzbekistan 3.5-0.5 to join India and co. on 10 points.
After a rest day, round seven is on Wednesday, September 23, starting at 6:15 a.m. ET / 12:15 CEST / 3:45 p.m. IST.

Uzbekistan, China, Armenia, and the United States won on the top five boards. Readers will notice the Netherlands 4-0 sweep against Israel, but the match was won by forfeit (more on this at the end of this section).
That leaves the Netherlands as one of 11 teams on 10 points, with China and Armenia on 11, and Uzbekistan as the only team on 12.

The winners of the 2022 and 2024 Chess Olympiads, Uzbekistan and India, were finally paired as two of the three teams on a perfect 10/10 match points. Each of their encounters is among the most memorable clashes, if not the most memorable, in recent Olympiad history.

Boards one, two, and four all ended in heavy-piece endgame draws. GMs Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Gukesh Dommaraju were a pawn up in rook endgames against GMs Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Shamsiddin Vokhidov, but with no advantage. GM Javokhir Sindarov vs. GM Arjun Erigaisi ended in another endgame with all the heavy pieces.

Board three was the decider, and it was the last board in play when the pre-move-40 time scramble approached. Dropping under 10 minutes by move 31, Yakubboev was up against a speed-chess specialist. Nihal had 38 minutes, so only one of them would be playing blitz. Or so it seemed. Yakubboev told Chess.com:

It was at some moment very, very emotional. It was a tough match, my opponent surprised me with the opening choice, but then he tried to push on my time and I got time trouble, but in time trouble he hurried and missed on 37...Nf5??, this beautiful tactic. Otherwise, I was worse and almost lost the game, but I am happy he missed that.
I was worse and almost lost the game, but I am happy he missed that.

The beautiful and winning move 38.Ne6!! is likely the move of the tournament so far, forcing Black to give up his queen. GM Rafael Leitao takes a look at this great turnaround, which is our Game of the Day.
GM Peter Svidler also made a recap for FIDE, if you prefer a nine-minute video on the game.

Germany, the third leader, was toppled by China this round, after losing on boards one and four, with draws on two and three. Xu, on board four, outplayed Donchenko with two bishops against two knights; Ding, against Keymer on board one, traded into a winning opposite-color bishop endgame (with rooks). The finishing 40.f5!, a pawn sacrifice followed by another with 41.h5!, was the hammer blow.

Armenia, after defeating Iran 2.5-1.5, is on the same score as China with five match wins and one draw. The team has finished in the top-10 in all Olympiads they have played since the year 2000 (they boycotted the 2016 Olympiad in Azerbaijan).

We saw draws on the top three boards, but board four GM Gabriel Sargissian scored the match-winning point against IM Reza Mahdavi. White's pieces flooded into the seventh and eighth ranks, but more in an attempt to save each other rather than coordinate an attack. Black pushed a passed pawn down the central d-file, and White could not untangle in time.

England held an incredibly close match against France, with GM Michael Adams scoring a needed win against GM Etienne Bacrot on board two to offset GM Gawain Maroroa Jones' loss on board three against GM Marc'Andria Maurizzi.

Another clutch victory was scored by GM Hans Niemann for the United States against Norway's GM Frode Urkedal, which won the match 2.5-1.5—a fantastic redemption for the American player who lost the decisive game against Germany in round five. It was an incredibly tense encounter that saw both sides trading game-changing errors in a complicated endgame. After bouncing from a draw to a win and back several times, Niemann landed a lethal blow on move 68 after a one-move blunder.

Yet another extremely close encounter was that between Turkiye and Switzerland. GM Emre Can won on board four against FM Colin Federer (no relation to the tennis player Roger Federer), but Turkiye's board one GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus was suffering against Swiss GM Sebastian Bogner. Had Bogner won that game, Switzerland would have drawn the match 2-2, but two pawns down and with under a minute, the 15-year-old Turkish prodigy turned the game around.

The Netherlands' victory over Israel by forfeit to land on 10/12 points has sparked debate on social media. Israel proposed playing their round-six match with the Netherlands at night after Yom Kippur ended, or on the rest day, but the Netherlands were within their right to decline and be awarded two match points. As GM Peter Heine Nielsen wrote on X, the scheduling conflict will have an impact on medal contenders, especially as the 4-0 score helps the Netherlands' tiebreaks.

The Israeli Chess Federation posted a letter from FIDE that confirmed that the schedule of the Israeli team's matches "will be adjusted" to accommodate Yom Kippur. Gil Borochovsky, CEO of the Israel Chess Association, said, "FIDE did nothing to reduce the damage it caused. They could have at least tried to prevent a 4:0 score, which would greatly hurt us in the rankings later on. We will consider our steps - this will not pass in silence."

Uzbekistan's next match against China in round seven will have great implications for who medals this year. China won their last encounter in Budapest 2024, but right now the Uzbek team looks unstoppable. Can they keep it up?

There were no upsets on the top tables in the Women's Olympiad—unless you count the higher-seeded Netherlands and Serbia being held to draws—but there were hugely important results for the battle for medals.
China and Kazakhstan have broken two points clear of the pack, but, as the only teams on a perfect score, will face each other in round seven.

sections.heading: Openings
paragraphs: Alekhine's Defense is a hypermodern response to 1.e4. Black lets White establish a presence in the center with the goal of proving it overextended. Although 1...Nf6 is only Black's eighth-most popular response to 1.e4, it scores as well as some much more common moves like the #3 French (1...e6) and #5 Pirc (1...d6).

sections.heading: Starting Position
paragraphs: The Alekhine Defense is 1.e4 Nf6. Games almost always continue 2.e5 Nd5 followed mostly by 3.d4 d6. Black's third move is the first little poke at White's center.

sections.heading: Variations
paragraphs: White has two main fourth moves in Alekhine's Defense: 4.Nf3, the Modern Variation, and 4.c4 Nb6, which turns into the Exchange Variation after 5.exd6 or the Four Pawns Attack after 5.f4.
White and Black have the same main goals in each variation: White is trying to hold ground in the center and Black is trying to take it down.

sections.heading: Modern Variation
paragraphs: The Modern Variation is White's most popular choice, focusing on development to support the center with pieces. It is called the Modern in comparison to the more classical approach of continuing to place pawns in the center.
Black's main responses are the Main Line 4...Bg4, the Alburt Variation 4...g6, and the Larsen Variation 4...dxe5.

All three moves fight for e5: the Main Line pins one of White's defenders of the square; the Alburt Variation will hit e5 after the ...Bg7 fianchetto; and the Larsen Variation simply captures White's occupant of the square.

sections.heading: Exchange Variation
paragraphs: After 4.c4 Nb6 5.exd6, Black can and does recapture all three ways, but almost always with one of the pawns. (Although 5...) Black can either keep pawn structure symmetry with 5...exd6, or go for imbalance [and a central pawn majority] with 5...cxd6. Both moves are about equally popular, with a slight edge to the c-pawn recapture.

sections.heading: Four Pawns Attack
paragraphs: The Four Pawns Attack is White's most confrontational response to Alekhine's Defense. Although it establishes a gigantic center, White gives Black much better statistical chances than in the Exchange Variation. The main continuation for Black is 5...dxe5, but 5...Bf5 and 5...g6 can also be played.
The Four Pawns is also the most important line in Alekhine theory: If it were crushing for White, the entire opening would be dubious, but as things are Black has enough counterplay.

sections.heading: Other Variations
paragraphs: Instead of 2.e5, a beginner may be tempted to protect the e-pawn with 2.d3. This is called the Maroczy Variation but it is extremely passive and scores poorly after 2...e5 by Black.
Black on move two can also play the rather amusing 2...Ng8 instead of 2...Nd5. This is called the Brooklyn Variation, but it is a bit too provocative to be recommended.
3.c4 on move three is the Two Pawns Attack. It usually transposes with White playing 4.d4 next, as 4.c5 Nd5 performs well for Black, with the d5-knight now untouchable by White's pawns.
3.Nc3 was Friedrich Samisch's move. White can recapture either way after 3...Nxc3 but the variation is not very testing of Black's idea behind the opening.

sections.heading: How to Play Against the Alekhine
paragraphs: The Modern Variation is White's most successful in addition to most popular. Black's responses to it all score about the same, with a slight edge to the Alburt Variation.
Against the Exchange Variation, 5...exd6 results in many more draws (31%) because it maintains a symmetrical pawn structure. 5...cxd6 is better if Black needs a decisive result.
Although the most common response to the Four Pawns is to capture on e5, Black scores better with 5...Bf5 (Trifunovic Variation) or 5...g6 (Fianchetto Variation).

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Alexander Alekhine first played Alekhine's Defense at Budapest in 1921, scoring a win and a draw, and continued playing it during the 1920s. Alekhine did not create the opening, and games from the 19th century that begin with 1.e4 Nf6 can be found, but his use popularized it.

The opening first appeared in a world championship in 1935, but it was Max Euwe playing it against Alekhine! They drew the game. The only other player to ever use the opening in the classical world championship was GM Bobby Fischer in 1972, who scored a famous win over GM Boris Spassky in Game 13.
GM Lev Alburt is one of the few grandmasters in history to use the Alekhine as a main weapon against 1.e4. The opening is also a favorite of Chess.com's NM Sam Copeland.

sections.heading: Famous Games
paragraphs: Fischer effectively wrapped up his world title in this marathon of a game, the 13th of the match, drawing the next seven contests before clinching the match in game 21.
For a win with White against the Alekhine, few games are as stunning as GM Nigel Short's king walk against GM Jan Timman in 1991.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Alekhine's Defense isn't the most common way for Black to meet 1.e4, but it is effective in the right hands, and logical in its goal of creating targets in the opposing side's center. Study it more in our Chess.com Opening Explorer.
